events.title: Embracing the Experience Economy
events.summary: As CSTS Enterprises pivots from a 78-year history of traditional corporate travel into luxury experiences, global events and tech-enabled service, Group CEO and executive director Abel Zhao is betting that the future of travel and experience economy will be defined less by where people go and more by what they can do once they get there. When Abel Zhao thinks about the future of travel and live experience, he begins with a memory. As a high school student during the 1998 FIFA World Cup, Zhao was too young to enter the stadium. Instead, he stood outside with friends, listening to the roar of the crowd and absorbing the energy of thousands of people gathered from around the world. “We could only stand outside and hear the cheering, but that was already exciting enough,” he recalls. Decades later, that experience has become part of the strategic thinking behind one of Hong Kong’s most ambitious travel transformations. Following its acquisition of Connexus, one of Hong Kong’s leading travel agencies, CSTS Enterprises has repositioned itself at the intersection of travel, sports, entertainment, technology and major live events. Its ambition is to become “the world’s leading experience innovator” – connecting people, brands and cultures through travel and shared experiences. For Zhao, Group CEO and executive director of CSTS Enterprises, the transformation was prompted partly by necessity. Covid-19 severely disrupted the travel industry, and more than half of Hong Kong’s travel agencies disappeared, he says. “We needed to find a way to grow,” Zhao says. CSTS’ transformation began with a shift in how travellers define luxury. Premium flights, five-star hotels and expensive restaurants are no longer enough. Customers increasingly seek access, rarity, meaning and memorable experiences. “Traditionally, when people thought about travel, they thought about booking flights and hotels,” Zhao says. “But now it’s completely redefined.” Through Connexus, CSTS already had a strong B2B foundation, serving multinational corporate clients. That business provided trusted relationships, operational expertise and travel infrastructure. The next step was to apply those strengths to the experience economy, particularly global sports, entertainment and exclusive live events. Events such as the FIFA World Cup, UEFA Euro Championship and Formula 1 require much more than tickets. They involve logistics, hospitality, local knowledge, contingency planning and personalised service. CSTS therefore aims to become an “experience company” rather than simply a travel intermediary. For event customers, the experience begins “once they step onto a plane” and continues until they return home safely. Behind the scenes, multi-location teams coordinate suppliers, solve problems in real time and manage every stage of the journey. “Precision and personalisation,” Zhao says, are central to the model. The company also challenges the idea that luxury is defined solely by spending. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, CSTS served ultra-high-spending clients, including one family whose expenditure exceeded US$2 million. At the same time, college students saved money, flew economy and stayed in modest hotels to attend an iconic event in New York. “Premium or experience tourism does not just mean you spend more money,” Zhao says. “It is something that can be created with special content and something that has a significant impact on yourself.” CSTS’s role is to curate moments that customers cannot easily arrange themselves, from access to football legends and exclusive hospitality to entertainment and culturally significant cross-border experiences. Partnerships with major sports and entertainment organisations are central to the strategy. They provide access, expertise and a significant barrier to entry. “Working with some of the largest brands or IPs already creates a very high market entry barrier,” Zhao says. Technology is the other pillar of CSTS’s future. Zhao sees the technology evolution is necessary for improving corporate travel, analysing customer behaviour and making daily service more efficient. The company plans to apply those capabilities gradually to its newer, more bespoke experience businesses. The aim, he says, is to use technology to “significantly increase efficiency and create value for our customers”. However, Zhao does not believe technology will replace the human element of travel. On the contrary, as people spend more time online, they may place greater value on concerts, sporting events, cultural gatherings and other shared experiences. “The one thing technology cannot impact is the experience,” he says. “The more technology is adopted, the more people want to go out there and find a reason to sit in the crowd watching a football game with everyone else.” CSTS is building an international operating structure with core teams in New York, Hong Kong and Shanghai.

events.title: ‘They are here to sweep the market’: Minor Food chief sees more Chinese chains opening in S’pore
events.summary: Minor Food Group chief executive Dellen Soh believes there is still money to be made in F&B, but survival will increasingly depend on the ability to rework the business model. Chinese restaurant chains are entering Singapore faster, using efficient kitchens, low prices and strong concepts. Dellen Soh said they are here to “sweep the market”. Local F&B firms must adapt with tighter menus, faster service and better cost control. Soh said weak hawker stalls and older brands may disappear if they cannot compete. Minor Food is refreshing brands, testing food retail and watching the 2027 RTS Link. It is also considering a Singapore listing to support future growth. SINGAPORE – As the Singapore economy expands, more Chinese restaurant chains are likely to enter the Republic, bringing efficient kitchens, competitive prices and “beautiful” concepts that could leave older local favourites struggling to keep up, said Minor Food Group chief executive Dellen Soh. These operators are not just testing whether Singaporeans like their food. They are also bringing business models honed in China’s fiercely competitive food and beverage (F&B) market, with targets to expand across South-east Asia. “They are here to sweep the market,” Soh, a Singaporean, told The Straits Times in an interview. The influx of Chinese chains, from hotpot and grilled fish to coffee and tea, is reshaping Singapore’s dining scene and raising the stakes for local operators whose menus, staffing and prices have not kept pace. While Soh believes there is still money to be made in the business, survival will increasingly depend on the ability to rework the business model, with some local favourites inevitably disappearing from the scene. Minor Food is a subsidiary of Thailand-listed Minor International, whose businesses span hotels, restaurants and lifestyle retail. Soh, who also heads Minor Food Singapore – operator of about 120 restaurants across 24 brand s, including Sanook Kitchen, Poulet and Mamma Mia – predicts that some longstanding hawker stalls and local brands will eventually disappear. This comes as owners retire and successors prove difficult to find, while heavier operating models struggle to compete with efficient global chains. For many foreign chains, however, Singapore is a demanding but valuable testing ground, filled with busy malls and well-travelled consumers who dine out regularly and have a deep appetite for global cuisines. If these chains can operate profitably here with their focused menus, lean staffing, fast preparation and competitive prices while satisfying discerning diners, they will be better placed to expand into other regional markets, Soh said. “If you can make it in Singapore, you can make it anywhere else in South-east Asia.” Good food and service, fast preparation and a cost structure that makes commercial sense may seem basic, but they are essential requirements for F&B brands to survive in Singapore, Soh said. Menu engineering helps bring these together. A carefully chosen range of dishes can make a kitchen easier to run, reduce the number of cooks needed and help restaurants serve consistently good meals at competitive prices. Soh pointed to shrinking dim sum menus at some restaurants as an example. “Maintaining a team of skilled chefs to hand-make each basket of dim sum is costly.” Minor Food has applied that thinking to Xin Wang Hong Kong Cafe, which is part of its Singapore portfolio. While the brand offered about 300 dishes when it opened 22 years ago, its menu has since been reduced to just 80 to 90 items. Streamlining the menu also speeds up service, cutting wait time and boosting table turnover during peak hours, Soh added. Keeping costs down must go hand in hand with giving diners a reason to visit, said the F&B veteran, adding that he would accept a higher food-cost ratio if lower menu prices helped fill the restaurant. An impressive margin on each dish means little if the tables are empty, especially when around 80% of people in Singapore eat out, he said. “The key is to offer good food at prices that encourage diners to return regularly.” Rising rents are a common complaint among Singapore’s F&B operators. But Soh said businesses should know their commitments when signing a lease and develop operating models capable of covering the rent. “It’s only when you cannot do well, then the rental becomes expensive,” he said. Soh expects rents to keep rising, pointing to pressure on real estate investment trusts and listed mall operators to grow their returns. Rather than count on concessions, he urged business operators to put themselves in the landlord’s shoes. “Overseas chains bring fresh concepts, attract crowds and can afford rents that some established businesses cannot. events.title: These are the tech and product leaders who survived the Paramount-WBD merger — and the ones who are out
events.summary: Skydance's co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz. NYSE Skydance is cutting tech and product leaders after closing its merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Four WBD technology executives are out, per a memo from Skydance chief product officer Dane Glasgow. Its new team will mostly feature Paramount execs who worked on its recent tech transformation. Consolidation is underway at David Ellison's Skydance just a few weeks after the company closed its $110 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Skydance's chief product officer, Dane Glasgow, laid out the product and tech leadership structure of the combined entity in a memo viewed by Business Insider. Four top WBD executives are leaving, according to the memo. They include: Avi Saxena , Warner Bros. Discovery's chief technology officer Tyler Whitworth , chief product officer for WBD's streaming business Dave Duvall , WBD's chief information officer Trish Collins Weedon , WBD's chief information security officer (CISO) Duvall, Saxena, and Whitworth will stay on in an "advisory capacity as we undergo this transition," Glasgow wrote. The company is mostly keeping Paramount executives in charge of its combined tech and product organization. These leaders include: Lakshman Nathan , Paramount's chief information officer Carlo Joseph, its chief information security officer Jim Harrison, its executive vice president of infrastructure, broadcast, and distribution Nick Lee , Paramount's executive vice president of media systems A few WBD executives are staying on in Skydance's post-merger leadership, per Glasgow's memo. They include  Brinton Miller,  formerly WBD's media technology and operations lead, who will serve as Skydance's executive vice president of production and studio technology, and  James Crossland , formerly head of global content operations at WBD, who will serve as its EVP of global content operations. Skydance has spent the past year revamping its tech and product team, often recruiting talent from tech companies. Glasgow joined Paramount from Meta, while Lee joined from Microsoft's AI division . Other team leaders in its post-merger structure include head of design  Suzanne Pellican , formerly a Google exec;  Hugh Williams , a former Google, eBay, and Microsoft exec; and Barak Turovsky , who came to Paramount after serving as chief AI officer at General Motors and VP of AI at Cisco. Bringing technical expertise to Paramount has been a priority for Ellison, who wants to turn the century-old media brand into a modern, tech-forward business like Netflix. The company revamped its data and insights strategy in January, and merged some engineering teams in March to bolster its streaming tech. "We are building a product and tech organization that can compete with anybody coming out of Silicon Valley," Ellison told CNBC earlier this month. In his memo, Glasgow expressed gratitude for the work of both Paramount and WBD staffers, writing that he was "encouraged by the early collaboration, the bold new ideas you're bringing forward, and your openness to exploring new ways of working with your colleagues." He also acknowledged the structural changes could be disruptive. "I know a change of this scale brings questions, especially as we get to know new teams and colleagues," Glasgow wrote. "Your leaders will share more about their organizations in the coming weeks and we'll bring our teams together soon to keep building with and learning from each other." events.title: Disney’s multiplatform Super Bowl plan frustrates ABC affiliates
events.summary: The Super Bowl used to be exclusive to broadcast networks. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006. Airing the Super Bowl on many platforms cuts into the viewership and associated advertising revenue for broadcast stations. Get the CNBC Sport newsletter directly to your inbox The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox. Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house from feuding among executives . Sometimes they come in court, from battling the Federal Communications Commission . And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates. ABC station owners are irritated with Disney's recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private. Disney has the broadcast rights to this season's Super Bowl. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006. Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recent media rights deal with the NFL in 2021 . The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna. Fox said last year that Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that's $680 million. Most advertising campaigns are national, but some brands buy big markets only. That allows smaller markets to sell advertising locally. An average primetime audience is around eight million viewers. So, if the Super Bowl gets 15 times the audience, advertising rates increase in lockstep. Super Bowl LX, held in February, had 125.6 million viewers. About 3% of a typical local affiliate station's annual advertising revenue comes from the Super Bowl when the game is on its air, according to a person familiar with the matter. The number can be much higher for the owned-and-operated big market stations, which typically take in about $10 million in advertising revenue from the Super Bowl, according to a source familiar with the matter. Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming. There's a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and charge them retrans fees. This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee. For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past. Given the game is an ESPN production with ESPN's primary "Monday Night Football" announcing crew — Joe Buck and Troy Aikman — it's reasonable to assume the cable network will get a fair amount of viewership for the game. Disney is also putting the game on Disney+ — a streaming service that's never been about sports. Airing the Super Bowl on a streaming service isn't new. NBCUniversal's Peacock, Fox's Tubi and Skydance's Paramount+ have streamed the game in the past. But those services allow for geofenced dynamic advertising insertion (DAI), allowing local affiliates to sell commercials to a streaming audience. Disney+, which doesn't typically air live ABC sports programming, doesn't have DAI. Disney is also airing so-called "alt-casts " of the game on ESPN2 (Eli and Peyton Manning will do their typical "ManningCast"), ESPNU ("Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show"), and NFL Network ("Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats"). Disney is even airing a "Star Wars"- themed alt-cast on Disney Channel and Disney XD. The "Star Wars" alternative broadcast will also be on Disney+. The commercials that run nationally will be the same on all platforms, according to a Disney spokesperson. The "Star Wars" alt-cast will be ad-free. Disney wants to synergize its platforms to maximize viewership — and collect the ad revenue.

events.title: I run an interior design company to the stars. Here are 5 affordable tips for making your home look more expensive.
events.summary: Julian Buckner started his own interior design and staging company in 2018. Venjhamin Reyes Julian Buckner founded Vesta Home, a luxury interior design company in 2018. He's worked with celebrities and high-end clients staging their homes and selling custom furniture. He gives his advice on how to make your home feel more luxurious without breaking the bank. For luxury and elegance, homeowners often have to shell out for professional help finding the latest trends and big-ticket items. But what if you want your home to look expensive , but you can't break the bank? According to the CEO of a luxury interior design company, there are still ways to communicate luxury via your own personal taste. "Anyone with money can walk into a B&B Italia and spend $1 million on furniture and have it look like a B&B Italia showroom," said Julian Buckner, who founded the Los Angeles-based staging, interior design, and furniture sales company Vesta Home in 2018. "Taste is knowing when to put in the ultra-modern leather casino sofa and then marry it with some vintage nightstand that you found at the design mart in Texas." Buckner, who has worked with clients like LeBron James, Travis Scott, and Jonah Hill, said the average home he stages is worth about $6 million. But his advice applies regardless of price point. Below, he shares his tips for how people can make their homes feel more luxurious without the hefty price tag. Bring a personal touch to your decorating. aire images/Getty Images Bringing something unique and unexpected into a room as decoration shows a level of thought that conveys luxury unlike anything else, Buckner said. "Those small knickknacks or found items may be the single biggest thing to add personality to a space," he said. "I've seen those antique old wooden shoe horns, antique toys, plaster or marble busts, anything you just wanted to tie into the broader aesthetic." Just make sure not to get carried away. "I see people go to HomeGoods and just buy a bunch of random knickknacks and put them on every shelf, and I think that cheapens it," Buckner said. "It's like informal men's dress wear," he added. "There are a couple of areas you can express personality, and it's maybe in your socks and your choice of a wristwatch. I think that same thing is true in luxury design, where it's in those found items, those antiques, and ultimately the accessories; that's a really unique opportunity to express yourself." Make furniture unique by having fun with different fabrics. You can change the style of furniture simply by reupholstering it. Jayne Howard There are other subtle ways to show off your personality, too. Buckner said a great way to add a unique fixture to your home is to reupholster furniture. "I think that the average consumer does not appreciate, does not understand, or does not even know that reupholstering is an option," he said. "You can take a relatively inexpensive sofa and for not a ton of money, reupholster it in a really unique fabric that ties into the rest of the home, and that can absolutely make a space." Try not to have everything match. Tohid Hashemkhani/Getty Images While having a theme to a room is fine, Buckner said having things too "matchy-matchy" is no longer in style. "You can see that with the emergence and the popularity of a company like a Restoration Hardware, this more monotone type of furniture and people buying full rooms together and having everything matchy-matchy," Buckner said. "We're seeing a shift away from that and a real focus on curation — on things not matching." Sometimes, things clashing can actually make a room more interesting. "I think when things don't match, when there's a little bit of dissonance in the design, that's an area — when it's done tastefully, not tons of different fabrics and colors and textures everywhere — to make you stop and think, 'Oh, that's interesting,'" he said. "We're starting to see a lot more of that." Window treatments are the most important and easiest fixes for your home. Bulgac/Getty Images Buckner's No. 1 fix for adding style to your home is adjusting your window treatments. "Window treatments, I think, are often massively overlooked, and it's a very inexpensive way to make a space feel very high-end," he said. "Whether the curtains are too heavy, they're poorly positioned, or the rods look cheap, there's such an opportunity there in fabric and layering on the window treatment side that I think can add a ton to a room." Trendy isn't always better. Jayne Howard It's hard not to be inspired when you see a celebrity's home with a special lamp or a  certain style of couch  (Buckner said  Bouclé has had its moment ), but it's often better to stay away from popular trends. While Buckner's high-end clients change their homes around every three to five years, trying to keep up with trends isn't cost-effective for the average consumer. It's more important to find pieces that you like first. "I would stay away from trends and focus on timeless design and products that you actually love. Spend the time on putting that together, whether it's something you found in a unique place, or has a story behind it, or something that resonates," Buckner said. "When it's thoughtfully done, it really conveys the highest level of taste." Read the original article on Business Insider

OpenAI is closing in on a funding round that could value the artificial intelligence giant at more than $1 trillion ahead of a potential initial public offering . The San Francisco-based AI company is raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, according to people familiar with the deal, who asked not to be named because the details were confidential. That valuation does not include new capital raised. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are leading the round alongside Coatue, according to the people. The financing is being positioned as an "opportunistic" bridge ahead of a potential IPO. OpenAI kickstarted discussions for a new funding round after investors approached the company with proposals in September, as CNBC previously reported. OpenAI told investors on Thursday that it is aiming to secure signatures by the end of next week, but the final size of the round is still being determined, the people said. Alongside the new investment, OpenAI is negotiating a commercial deal that would secure more computing capacity from the UAE, according to one person. OpenAI told investors in February that it's targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, but it has not disclosed exactly when it plans to debut. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told employees in August that the AI lab "will be a public company in 2027." The following month, CEO Sam Altman said that "right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public." Anthropic, OpenAI's chief rival, is also gearing up for what is widely expected to be a massive IPO. The company confidentially filed its prospectus with regulators in June and is actively engaging in meetings with prospective investors, as CNBC previously reported. events.title: S&P 500, Nasdaq end sharply lower as revived AI doubts ignite tech selloff
events.summary: Traders at work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City. US stocks fell sharply as renewed doubts about AI spending hit tech shares, with the Nasdaq suffering its biggest drop since June. Meta and Tesla both fell after earnings, while chip stocks slumped and the Philadelphia semiconductor index lost about a quarter from its June peak. Oil prices rose after new Houthi strikes, adding inflation fears, while strong labour data kept the Federal Reserve under pressure to raise rates again. NEW YORK - US stocks tumbled on Oct 22 and the Nasdaq posted its steepest daily drop since June as a batch of high-profile earnings reports ignited fresh fears about the AI spending race. The S&P 500 ended deep in negative territory. The tech-laden Nasdaq, dragged down by microchips, fell the most in the wake of a spate of high-profile AI-related earnings results. Meta Platforms’ results beat analyst expectations, but its stock tumbled after the Facebook parent posted its first cash outflow in more than a decade due to its AI-related expenditures and announced plans to issue non-voting shares in a two-for-one split to raise capital to spend on the nascent technology. Tesla shares fell even though the electric car maker unexpectedly posted positive free cash flow in the quarter and cut its 2026 capital spending plans. The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index, which has driven much of the current bull market’s gains, plunged. With the Oct 22 decline, the SOX has lost about one-fourth its value since its record closing high reached on June 22, yet it remains sharply higher for the year, well outperforming the S&P 500‘s year-to-date gain. “It’s a wonderful day on Wall Street,” said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest, in Elmhurst, Illinois. “The only part of the market that is really suffering here is technology, which has been the golden child of the markets up until about June.” “Investors are starting to realise that there are some holes in the AI story,” Nolte added. “And that’s having an impact on the indices because they’re so heavily weighted towards technology.” On the geopolitical stage, Iran-backed Houthis launched new strikes against Saudi targets, sending crude prices to a five-month high. Investors worried that ongoing Middle East strife could keep inflation hot and force the US Federal Reserve to keep raising interest rates. Data from the Labour Department showed initial claims for unemployment benefits kept drifting along near multi-decade lows. Signs of labour market stability will allow the Fed to focus on fighting inflation. Financial markets are currently pricing in the probability that the central bank will raise its policy rate by another 25 basis points before year-end. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 92.40 points, or 1.19%, to end at 7,664.77 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 690.28 points, or 2.58%, to 26,008.86. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 17.51 points, or 0.03%, to 52,873.60. Third-quarter earnings season is well under way, with 111 of the companies in the S&P 500 having reported. Of those, 83% have beaten analyst expectations, according to the most recent LSEG data. Procter & Gamble warned that rising cost pressures would take an increasing bite out of profit, but beat analyst estimates, sending the stock sharply higher and supporting consumer staples. Blackstone advanced after the company said widening credit spreads on AI-related debt could present an opportunity to lock in higher returns. Lockheed Martin climbed after the aerospace/defence firm raised its annual sales and profit forecast. Spotify jumped after the Swedish music streaming firm forecast fourth-quarter profit above Wall Street estimates, betting on its AI-powered features to drive user growth. Union Pacific rose following the company’s quarterly earnings beat, which was helped by core pricing gains, although the railroad flagged a hit from rising fuel prices. Chipmakers Western Digital, Intel, ADM , Sandisk, and Marvell all posted steep percentage losses amid the broader semiconductor selloff. REUTERS

events.title: Trump defends Ramaswamy ad with Acton's estranged mom after bipartisan criticism
events.summary: President Donald Trump defended a controversial campaign ad by Vivek Ramaswamy featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race. Trump's defense of the Republican nominee's ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it. In the ad, Acton's mother, Donna Arthur, says Acton has "lied her entire life." "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do," Acton said. "My mother is not well." President Donald Trump on Thursday defended a controversial ad by the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton , his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race, calling Acton a liar. Trump's defense of the ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it, which focused on the fact that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur , was charged with raping her when she was a child and was married to Acton's mother, Donna Arthur. In the ad, Donna Arthur says Acton has "lied her entire life." "Don't vote for people who lie," Arthur says in the ad . "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse." Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004. Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse." "The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor." Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him. "The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday. Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing." "I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said. Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim. Trump must sit for deposition in BBC lawsuit by Dec. 11, judge orders Virginia state Sen. Lucas, a Trump critic, charged in marijuana racketeering case California's Proposition 40: What voters need to know about billionaire wealth tax battle Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate. But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America." "The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts." Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets. Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad. Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do." "My mother is not well," Acton said. Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested. "Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants." Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down. "The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line.

events.title: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
events.summary: eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business. V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers. Don't let the door hit you on the butt “However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.” Read full article Comments

events.title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
events.summary: CoreWeave's stock is down 36% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening. The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds. CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors. With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space. "Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis." CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $31 billion, with its stock down 36% this month after plunging 10% on Thursday. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%. The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 179% in the past year and 39% in October. It last stood at 1,145 basis points, or 11.45%. The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 33% this month, while IREN's stock is down 38%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions. U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month. A representative from Nscale declined to comment. CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft . That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing. Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing. "Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options. "Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant." CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet. One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027. "Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter." Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary? Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement. While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

events.title: SpaceX $40 billion debt deal gets pricey as AI fears spread
events.summary: SpaceX’s $40 billion debt raise is being finalized at sharply higher interest rates than when the rocket company last tapped bondholders, a sign of growing jitters in the AI world. The lowest-rated portion is expected to carry interest rates of about 8.3%, according to people familiar with the deal, which is being led by Apollo and Goldman Sachs. A safer piece of debt, which is backed by some of SpaceX’s chips, is likely to price next week around 7.75%, the people said. That is more than 1 percentage point more than where SpaceX’s current bonds trade, reflecting an AI-loan market that has pulled back sharply over the past few weeks. President Donald Trump purchased $5 million in SpaceX bonds in August. Goldman and Apollo declined to comment. Pricing could change by the time the debt is finalized, which is expected sometime next week. Existing bonds at SpaceX, which is currently considering merging with Tesla, have weakened in recent days as strong earnings were overshadowed by massive spending plans and concerns about the company’s debt load, plus broader AI fears fueled by CoreWeave’s debt selloff. Default insurance on the company also widened, signaling some misgivings on the company’s plans.

events.title: Kevin O'Leary's data center company pushes back on the 'bragawatt' label
events.summary: Kevin O'Leary. Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images O'Leary Digital's CEO says a Wall Street firm's analysis misses work happening before construction. Paul Palandjian, the CEO, said the company's two campuses will generate their own electricity. He outlined land deals, permitting, and early funding, saying delivery should be judged in phases. Kevin O'Leary 's data center company has a message for analysts who doubt its enormous AI ambitions: You're not seeing the whole picture. Paul Palandjian , CEO of O'Leary Digital , pushed back on a Bernstein Research assessment that put the firm near the bottom of the data center industry's credibility rankings. In an emailed response to Business Insider, he detailed land agreements, water applications and licensing, engineering work, and funding that he said the analysis overlooks. "Scrutiny during this cycle is fair," Palandjian wrote. He added, "A score built from announced-capacity data ranks every pre-construction project low on construction progress by definition, and it cannot see confidential work." His response gets at a central question in the AI building boom: How much weight should investors give the work that happens before data center construction begins? Paul Palandjian, CEO of O'Leary Digital. Paul Palandjian/O'Leary Digital Bernstein examined thousands of data center projects using data from the tracking firm Aterio, assessing factors such as construction progress, electricity availability, and industry experience. Its analysis concluded that only about 35% of announced data center capacity in the US will get built. O'Leary Digital received a credibility score of 0.35 out of 5. Bernstein estimated that 489 megawatts of its announced 15-gigawatt pipeline would materialize, roughly 3%. The analysts grouped it with ambitious newcomers described as "bragawatts." Palandjian said the 15-gigawatt figure represents the full build-out of two campuses in Utah and Alberta over several years. "We would rather be judged on milestones than on a model," he wrote. Data center power without the queue Palandjian's clearest distinction concerns electricity, one of the biggest obstacles facing data center developers. "We are not in an interconnection queue," he wrote, referring to the waiting lists for connections to the electricity grid. Instead, both campuses are designed to generate all their electricity on-site, he said, with direct access to natural gas pipelines and supplies. That's what the industry calls " behind the meter ": producing power at the facility rather than relying on an electricity utility to supply it from the grid. Data center land, water, and early money In Utah, Palandjian said the Military Installation Development Authority had approved and executed a 30-year development agreement naming O'Leary Digital as master developer of the project area. About 11,000 acres are under binding agreements, he said. Master planning, ground studies, and laser-based land surveying have finished at both sites, and the company filed an engineered Utah water application in late September, he added. In Alberta, about 13,000 acres are under a binding agreement, and a water license for 6 million cubic meters a year has been granted, Palandjian said. He also said that both sites are away from densely populated residential communities. On money, Palandjian said his firm has capital for both pre-development and advancing the project toward key milestones. He did not specify a funding amount or say the entire build-out was financed. He said that the engineering, power, and construction firms working with the company, and the global banks advising it, provide evidence of its ability to deliver. "With that team, every critical part of the project is being worked through, gaps are identified early, and we are closing them to raise our probability of success," he wrote. Palandjian said that while O'Leary Digital is young, its team has decades of experience in real estate, power, and infrastructure. Bernstein's skepticism does not mean every newcomer will fail. "It's not that all of these guys are sort of terrible and not going to deliver, but we just have lower confidence because we don't know them," analyst Madison Rezaei said. With Palandjian's update, now we know a bit more. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 10-year Treasury yield tumbles below 5% to lowest level in nearly a month
events.summary: Treasury yields fell sharply on Thursday, with investors turning to safe havens amid a steep sell-off in stocks driven by concerns around the artificial intelligence trade and surging oil prices. The benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury yield — used to price mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, the first time below 5% since Sept. 23. The yield saw its biggest one-day decline since March 10, 2023. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note , which closely tracks short-term Federal Reserve rate policy, tumbled more than 16 basis points to 4.659%. The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — most sensitive to geopolitical developments — was more than 14 basis points lower at 5.296%. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another. "It is a flight to safety," said Mitch Goldberg, president of ClientFirst Strategy. "People are all of a sudden terrified of the amount of bond issuance by AI-related companies. They see the rates going up and people want to hold on to something that they think will be there at maturity." Others on Wall Street also sought to explain the turnaround in bond prices. "For the first time in a while, Treasurys are enjoying haven status," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds. "You have weakness in tech, an escalation of risk in the Middle East and higher oil. On a relative basis Treasurys start to look like the safe place to hide again in the short term." The reversal in bonds this week emerged as questions persisted about the billions being spent to build artificial intelligence networks. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that while demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ," capital was scarce. Neoclouds are a specialized cloud computing providers that focus on high-performance tech infrastructure designed specifically for artificial intelligence. This week's rebound in Treasury prices marks a turnaround from earlier this month, when 10- and 30-year yields reached their highest levels in more than two decades amid investor concern over inflation and high energy prices. Above 5%, however, attitudes began to shift and yields suddenly starting looking like an attractive entry point, compensating even for the risk of inflation above 3%. Tensions in the Middle East added to risk-off behavior Thursday. Oil prices moved sharply higher, with West Texas Intermediate futures closing up 2.39% at $99.47 per barrel. Brent crude futures, the global price benchmark, jumped 4%, rising to $113.17 a barrel. Higher energy prices followed a New York Times report, citing unnamed U.S. officials, that the U.S. and Israel are considering resuming strikes on Iran in a "short but intensive" operation following the Nov. 3 midterm elections. "You always look for one risk point, and there isn't really just one at the moment, which makes it a little bit more challenging," said Gregory Faranello, head of U.S. macro strategy at South Street Securities. "But if I had to take one of those and say what's most important right now, it has to be what's going on geopolitically." "The consumer is clearly getting pinched here in the U.S., so it becomes tricky for central bankers" setting monetary policy going forward, he said. If energy prices "stay elevated, it could force the Fed's hand to do even more, which certainly wouldn't be wouldn't be a good thing for the bond market." — CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed reporting.

events.title: Venture capitalists are questioning the neolab math
events.summary: Menlo Ventures' Matt Murphy speaking to Ben Bergman at Tech Insider: Growth Mode. JY Studio A version of this story originally appeared in Business Insider's weekly VC Insider newsletter. Sign up for BI's VC Insider newsletter here. Ben here. Up until recently, it was a great time to be the founder of a neolab, the lavishly funded, research-first AI startups founded by top talent who defected from the likes of OpenAI or Google DeepMind. We reported last month that Jeff Dean, Google's former chief scientist, is seeking a valuation as high as $50 billion for his new AI science startup. OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever's Safe Superintelligence is worth $32 billion. Another OpenAI alum, Mira Murati, is raising a round for Thinking Machines Lab at a valuation of around $40 billion. But lately, in conversations with multiple VCs around Silicon Valley, there is a growing divide about whether neolabs can make the economics work with their multibillion-dollar price tags and formidable competition from frontier labs. One VC at a top firm, who asked that I not use his name, told me neolabs are the most hotly debated type of investment right now. "Some would say you shouldn't invest in any, and others would say this is basically all you should be investing in because software's dead, and you either have to own models or hardware, and even if you enter at a billion, the company could be worth a trillion," he said. Business Insider; Randy Yeip When I recently asked Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy at Business Insider's Growth Mode conference which sector he thought was most overhyped, he immediately cited neolabs, which was noteworthy, given that Menlo invested in some of them . Murphy pointed to an example from his time as an early board advisor at Google, which he said did so well because it "was like a match thrown into a bonfire." "The opposite thing you want to do is start a match with a bonfire," Murphy told me. "That's the risk of what's going on now with companies raising such large rounds." Another Menlo partner, Deedy Das, posted last month about the "difficult game" of making neolab math work. Das seemed a bit taken aback by the reaction to his post and later texted me: "Like all startups, many will fail, some will work." Picking which ones will work is why VCs get paid the big bucks. Neolabs are a power-law bet taken to an extreme, Radical Ventures' Aaron Rosenberg told me. Investors know most will likely burn enormous sums on compute and talent without ever becoming profitable. But the rare winner could become a foundational AI company worth hundreds of billions or more. "We're confident that the best neolabs will attract ongoing support," Rosenberg said. "Talent continues to transition out of the incumbents and academia into founder roles, and we see no signs of that slowing." Like Radical, New Enterprise Associates wrote a bullish view in June . One of the authors, Andrew Schoen, told me his views have not changed. "There are neolabs I know of that are finalizing billion-plus-dollar rounds of equity financing, and those processes are moving very smoothly and quickly," he said. The Buzz Menlo Ventures' partners Shawn Carolan, Matt Murphy, and Venky Ganesan. Will Mackie Productions Katie here. Many of tech's biggest names gathered at the Ritz-Carlton in San Francisco on Saturday, at a black-tie event in the name of Menlo Ventures' 50th anniversary. Hollywood titan turned venture capitalist Jeffrey Katzenberg of Dreamworks fame asked the audience to join a prayer "for the blockbuster IPO of Anthropic," a joking reference to Menlo's early investment in the company. I also spotted Morgan Stanley's storied technology banker Michael Grimes, who is undoubtedly holding his own AI IPO prayers. Other attendees included an array of public company and startup CEOs, including those from Snowflake, Zscaler, Legora, and OpenRouter. As Menlo partner Venky Ganesan quipped, there was more AUM (assets under management) in the room than in many countries, given the attendees' net worth and the investment capital they manage. Menlo isn't the first venture firm to host a splashy anniversary party; Index Ventures recently went big for its 30th anniversary . A person at a rival venture shop expressed disappointment that their firm doesn't host such celebrations. Menlo's night ended with concerts from two super confidential Grammy Award winners trying to rake in those AI bucks! Around the Cap Table We reported this week that Fireworks AI is seeking fresh funding at a valuation of between $30 billion and $40 billion, a dramatic jump just months after its last blockbuster round was closed. "You Can See Everything" has everyone talking . Ben thought it was absolute genius, if a bit long. It will make this year's Oscars race exciting. See it in theaters before the experience is lessened by spoilers. Our colleague Rya Jetha explored the excitement and pitfalls of investing in robotics startups. Like neolabs, robotics companies are commanding big valuations with little to show for it, yet. Foursquare's $0 acquisition ended with no payout for employees or investors, according to founder Dennis Crowley . Post of The Week There are only 130 US tech companies, public or private, valued at $10B or more (decacorns). That’s roughly 20 to 30 new companies per decade, for the last five decades. This year alone, with a quarter to go, there have been 42 decacorns minted privately. Either this is the most… — Rory O'Driscoll (@rodriscoll) October 21, 2026 The VC Insider team Ben Bergman, chief correspondent, in Los Angeles. Katie Roof, editor at large, in San Francisco. events.title: Meta stock sinks nearly 7% as AI spend pushes free cash flow negative
events.summary: Meta stock sank almost 7% Thursday as free cash flow turned negative and the company raised the floor of its expected capex spend. Prices for the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs. Meta also revealed it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock. Meta shares slumped nearly 7% on Thursday as the social media giant showed negative free cash flow in its third-quarter earnings and raised the floor of its full-year capital expenditures. The spread on the social media giant's five-year credit default swaps reached all-time highs on Thursday, a signal of growing credit concerns from investors as the company leans deeper into its artificial intelligence spending plans. Meta said it expects its full-year capex to range from $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from a previous $130 billion. Free cash flow came in at a negative $2.12 billion during the quarter. The company revealed Wednesday that it would create a new class of nonvoting Class C common stock during its earnings release, meant to maintain its "founder-led structure" and "provide Meta the ability to finance its growth." Meta also said CEO Mark Zuckerberg could leave the state if the "California Wealth Tax" were to pass, as he "could become liable for a significant, multi-billion-dollar tax payment based on his ownership of stock in the Company," according to the SEC filing. Zuckerberg was convinced to stay in California with the company's new stock plan, the filing noted. Revenue for the social media giant jumped 26% in the third quarter from a year ago, coming in at $64.60 billion versus the $63.37 billion analysts expected. Earnings per share were reported at $3.83, though it wasn't clear if it was directly comparable with the $5.75 per share Wall Street was looking for. — CNBC's Jonathan Vanian and Seema Mody contributed to this report. events.title: Arc browser sunsets December 22 as The Browser Company doubles down on Dia
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The Browser Company is sunsetting its design-forward Arc browser on December 22, 2026, and directing users to Dia, its AI-first browser. The company announced the decision on Thursday, citing the rising cost of keeping a browser secure in the age of AI. “Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI,” the company wrote. “Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.” The wind-down is staged into three parts. As of Thursday, new Arc accounts can no longer be created. On November 23, Arc Search on iOS and Android will lose its AI features, including “Browse for Me.” Users will no longer be able to sign in or sync tabs, though the app will continue functioning as a basic local browser. On December 22, Arc will stop working entirely on Mac and Windows. Accounts will be deactivated, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days. Arc Search will also be removed from the Google Play Store. While The Browser Company claims Dia now surpasses Arc in speed, stability, and security benchmarks, user reactions on social media were largely disappointed , with many reviving requests for the company to make Arc open source. But CEO Josh Miller previously pointed out that Arc is built on the Arc Development Kit (ADK) — a proprietary internal SDK that is also the core engine powering Dia. Open-sourcing Arc would mean giving away Dia’s intellectual property. “While we’d love to open-source Arc someday, we can’t do that meaningfully without also open-sourcing ADK,” Miller previously noted. “And ADK is still core to our company’s value.” For users making the switch, Dia will carry over equivalents of several core Arc features. Users can still swipe between different work and personal environments using Dia’s “Profiles” (formerly Arc’s Spaces). Arc’s signature vertical tabs will remain as an optional sidebar layout, while Folders have been rebranded as “Pinned Tab Groups.” Passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history will seamlessly transfer to Dia. Arc features will remain free in Dia, with AI optional. The shutdown officially closes a chapter that began in 2025, when the startup stopped active feature development on Arc. The Browser Company — which was acquired by Atlassian for $610 million in 2025 — conceded at the time that while early adopters loved the browser’s novel interface, the “ novelty tax ” and complexity limited mainstream adoption. Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned. events.title: UK to relax post-2008 rules that hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing
events.summary: Regulators say removing ‘unnecessary burdens’ will save businesses about £2bn over 10 years The UK is watering down rules introduced in the aftermath of the financial crisis that were designed to hold City bosses accountable for wrongdoing. The plans, put forward by the financial industry’s two top regulators, the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), include a reduction in reporting for “lower-level misconduct” and would also free 140,000 managers from extra checks. The proposals were announced as regulators hosted a dinner for City executives at the Mansion House in central London. They are meant to“significantly” reduce the number of roles that will be required to undergo enhanced checks and would require only the most senior executives – such as chief executives and chief financial officers – to be forced to prove they are “fit and proper” each year, and before taking new jobs. This will free about 140,000 staff from having to illustrate they are operating with “integrity” and following regulators’ conduct rules. It would be a watering down of measures that came into force in the mid-2010s , in response to widespread public anger over the 2008 banking crash. The senior managers regime was meant to address the fact that few bank bosses were held to account for actions that contributed to the ensuing financial crisis. While the regime originally covered banks, it was later expanded to cover all financial services companies including asset managers and hedge funds. It is the latest set of City rules to have been scaled back since the government gave regulators a new objective: ensuring UK firms are competitive on the world stage. Those efforts have already helped lift the cap on banker bonuses , which were previously limited to two times a banker’s salary. The new changes will also lead to the loosening of rules around how often firms report bad behaviour by lower level staff. It means they will no longer have to report first warnings or “lower-level misconduct of limited relevance” to regulator’s targets, such as if staff are showing up late or dropping calls. Instead, they only want to hear about “serious misconduct” and cases where staff are given final warnings or fired. Any initial cases of misconduct will still have to be flagged for top brass, including chief executive and chief financial officers. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The regulators said removing these “unnecessary burdens” would save businesses about £2bn over 10 years while cutting the Bank of England’s and FCA’s costs by £11.5m and £229m each year, respectively. The Bank of England and FCA said that this would not mean bosses would get away with bad behaviour. They said in a joint statement that the “high standards of individual accountability and conduct will remain unchanged, including the regulators’ commitment to ensuring that individuals are accountable for misconduct that affects society as well as their employers”.

events.title: Trump lacks options to lower gas prices without ending war
events.summary: President Donald Trump has just one way left to bring down gas prices: ending the Iran war. Already, his administration has expanded access to red-dyed diesel; unlocked Russian diesel; waived the Jones Act; and tapped the US strategic reserve in an effort to lower costs. Yet oil prices hit a five-month high today, even as Trump touted that Middle East exports were surpassing pre-war levels . “There isn’t a marginal thing he can do,” particularly after scaling back investments in clean energy, Heather Boushey, who served on former President Joe Biden’s Council of Economic Advisers, said. Trump’s attempts are “not going to move the needle sufficiently” because they don’t “solve a fundamental problem.” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers blamed high gas prices on “preexisting issues” like “Democrat politics that shuttered US refineries” and “the destruction of refineries in the Russia-Ukraine war.” She added that Trump is “taking tangible steps to increase our refining capacity here in the United States.” — Eleanor Mueller

Please enter a search term. The number of financial services roles required to face enhanced checks from regulators will fall significantly under proposals that will support growth. The changes are expected to save firms around £2 billion over a 10-year period. The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) have today announced parallel consultations on proposals to significantly streamline the Senior Managers and Certification regime (SM&CR). The SM&CR was introduced 10 years ago to instil a culture of accountability among senior decision-makers in regulated firms. Under the proposals, unnecessary burdens will be removed while high standards of individual accountability and conduct will remain unchanged, including the regulators’ commitment to ensuring that individuals are accountable for misconduct that affects society as well as their employers. The changes will allow firms to focus more resources to ensure good customer and market outcomes, recruit and appoint talent, and prioritise innovation and investment, all supporting UK growth and competitiveness. The key changes to the regime include: Regulator pre-approval will be removed for a range of regulatory functions, including Chief Actuaries and Chairs of Risk and Audit Committees. Firms will instead notify regulators of these appointments directly, gaining speed and flexibility while remaining responsible for ensuring candidates are fit and proper. Removing the Certification Regime and associated administrative requirements for around 139,000 individuals below senior manager level to be subject to annual certification checks and appear on the Financial Services Register. Raising the conduct rule breach reporting threshold for most staff below senior manager level and streamlining Conduct Rule training requirements. This enables firms to better target more serious misconduct. Certain Senior Manager roles, such as CEOs, CFOs and Chairs, will continue to require regulator pre-approval, including fit and proper tests, before appointment. Regulators will also be able to require pre-approval for otherwise notified roles in high-risk cases. Firms will remain responsible for ensuring their employees remain competent, suitable and meet appropriate standards of conduct, and those no longer requiring pre-approval will continue to be held to the same level of accountability as before. Katharine Braddick, Deputy Governor for Prudential Regulation and Chief Executive Officer of the PRA, said: “The Senior Managers Regime is an essential part of the UK’s regulatory framework. These proposals keep checks in place for the most important roles, meaning individuals are accountable for their actions, but reduce the administrative burden where it isn’t needed, giving firms more time to invest in growth-focused activities and greater flexibility in onboarding senior talent.” Sarah Pritchard, Deputy CEO, said: “SM&CR has delivered significant improvements in accountability and governance across financial services. We remain committed to ensuring individual accountability and good standards of behaviour across financial services. But we can achieve the same impact with a more streamlined regime, supporting our aim to be a smarter regulator.” Some of the proposed reforms require legislative change. By consulting now, the FCA and PRA will be ready to implement reforms quickly once legislation is passed.

events.title: The secret to fast startup growth isn’t early sales, top names in tech say
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The AI era has changed how fast startups can grow. Startups can grow so fast that they hit high annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers, only to crash and burn a few months later. At this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt , Lovable go-to-market lead Luke Arno, Ben Broca of the AI platform Polsia, and Theory Ventures’ Tomasz Tunguz gave founders some tips on how to set their companies up for success in those first 90 days. Broca, whose company Polsia uses AI agents to build and run businesses with almost no human staff (Broca says he is its only employee), said that product-market fit is one of the hardest things to find right now, especially in an era when so many products can easily be copied by competitors. In response, Arno said that durable go-to-market strategies are those that can be reliably repeated. “The most critical thing for founders or earlier-stage companies to do is develop learning density or pattern recognition for where your customers are,” Arno said. “Don’t rush to build out a top-down go-to-market motion if you’re not there yet.” That’s why, in those first 90 days after launching a commercial product that’s ready to sell, founders should not mistake early, fast revenue for a sign that the startup is ready to scale, Arno said. Once a startup finds use cases that work, it will only be ready to build out a sales team and go for growth after it can attract new customers by repeating what has worked. If every sale requires new tactics, the startup hasn’t truly hit product-market fit. “If I bring on 10 new customers in 10 different ways to solve 10 different problems, sure, I brought revenue in, but I don’t have a way to go scale a go-to-market,” Arno said. “If I bring three customers in with a similar motion to solve a similar problem, now I have high confidence that I can go scale.” Lovable, the AI app-building startup, set a lot of those early benchmarks with how fast it grew, and now founders everywhere are feeling the pressure to do the same. Lovable is valued at more than $13 billion by its investors, says its ARR has passed $600 million, and has raised more than $700 million in funding to date. “The expectations for overall execution speed are absolutely tremendous,” Tunguz said. But Tunguz said growth like Lovable’s is still the exception, though founders should still move fast. The pressure they feel is real, he said, because far more money flows through the startup ecosystem at every stage than when he began investing in 2008. Today, a seed deal brought in by one of his partners could just as easily be a $5 million raise, a $50 million raise, or a $500 million raise. The winners all focus on one thing: understanding their customers well enough to know what will keep them around even after any hype subsides. “Community building is very important and being close to customers is very important,” Broca said. He said founders can send emails and throw events, and he personally likes to talk to a lot of his customers: “The general rule is always to be talking to customers.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: The Social Society Helping Women Join the AI Boom
events.summary: I’m not even going to try to pretend I don’t have a bit of a girl-crush on Shoshana Berger. She’s a former WIRED editor turned editorial leader for companies like Notion and Ideo. She’s super smart and chic. And she’s the cofounder, with Nina Willdorf, of the Aged Intelligence Society , a buzzy events startup that hosts invite-only dinner parties where women “solve midlife problems using frontier tools .” Berger and Willdorf having a refreshingly practical take on AI. “This is the most formative technology of our generation, and it’s here,” Willdorf says. “If you choose to sit it out, you are doing yourself a disservice.” That thesis resonates. Their events have been oversubscribed since day one. The second dinner party they hosted was covered by The New York Times . Hundreds of women reached out asking to attend future events. Their Substack, where they share tools and tips, quickly got over 1,000 subscribers, including a New Yorker writer and a small-town mayor. Women outside the Bay Area are now hosting their own Aged Intelligence meetups. They also practice what they preach, especially as they juggle kids entering college, their own aging parents, and their increasingly in-demand business. “The midlife cognitive and emotional labor is so heavy and so intense that we need an assistant,” Berger says. “Actually, we need the National Guard, but AI will help in the interim.” This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. Zoë Schiffer: How did the Aged Intelligence Society start? Shoshana Berger: Nina and I are both recovering magazine editors. We ended up at a friend's birthday party, and we were both obsessing over Claude, our new French lover. All the other women had glazed eyes while we were talking; they just weren’t part of the conversation. At some point I said, “Nina, I think this might be a business, because all these women need to be doing what we're doing.” Nina Willdorf: We were super nervous before the first event … Berger: We needed to take beta blockers and ashwagandha because we were like, wait, we're inviting all of these baller women, these really smart, incredibly accomplished women, and we’re not AI experts. But we have been doing what we usually did as reporters, which is test the tools in a way many women did not seem to be doing. There's a million reasons for women to bow out of the conversation, and we were like, “no, no, no, you cannot bow out of this conversation if you are going to be relevant in the work world. You need to be fluent.” Willdorf: We are not like pom-pom advocates for everything about this, but we feel committed to this idea that being involved is really important. How do you set up expectations around the event for attendees? Berger: There are rules of engagement for every party. One is we have an ideological parking lot. So if you want to talk about how AI is going to ruin everything, this is not the best space to do that. There are lots of ways in which we are also terrified about AI and find it can be quite menacing, especially for creatives like us, but that's not what we're here to do. We're here to gain fluency, test things out, and reduce our administrative load. Willdorf: And eat some really good cheese and drink some wine. Berger: We have everyone bring a laptop and a midlife problem. We call it a midlife quandary. We spend 15 minutes doing what we call library time. We all bring our laptops out, and you work on your problem. And Nina and I kind of walk around the room sherpa-ing people through the experience: “You might want to try this tool, try this LLM instead. Your prompt is feeling a little weak. You're not getting the answer that you like. Let's work on that and iterate.” Willdorf: Sometimes people are like, “You know what? I don't really want AI to write for me.” And we're like, “Oh no, no, we don't either. Let us show you a couple other things you can think about.” You’ve had a wait list for these parties since you started. How do you decide who gets to attend? Willdorf: We have really found that the optimal number is between like eight and 12. When it gets bigger than that, it's a little bit chaotic. Our best events have been ones where there is a magical mix, and you have somebody that works in nonprofit next to somebody who works in design next to somebody who is home with the kids next to a CEO next to someone who works in philanthropy. Most people, in my experience, cannot immediately identify a software-shaped problem in their life. How do you help people see an issue that AI could actually help with? Berger: So much of what we're trying to do is show the pragmatic ways in which it's helping with midlife overload. We're often labeled the sandwich generation. We hate that term because it just sounds like we're the tasteless tomato in between two slabs of bread. But the real part of that is that we are dealing with parents who increasingly need help and kids who maybe are launching, maybe not.
