events.title: Families are paying nearly $7,500 a year for health insurance. The next price hike is already looming.
events.summary: Health insurance costs have soared for workers and employers. Luis Alvarez/Getty Images Workers on family health insurance plans paid $7,471 for premiums in 2026, a 9% increase from 2025. Costs are even higher at smaller businesses: Workers there pay nearly $10,000 for family premiums. Rising premiums have outpaced wage growth, and are only expected to increase more in 2027. It's costing families nearly $7,500 a year for health insurance — and more increases are looming. A 2026 health benefits survey from KFF found that workers on a family plan paid an average of $7,471 a year in premiums — a 9% increase from 2025. And that's just the worker contribution — when accounting for employer contributions, family plan premiums totaled $28,303 in 2026, a roughly 5% increase from 2025. That's a hefty price for both workers and their employers, and even more acute for workers at smaller businesses : KFF's survey found that at firms with fewer than 200 employees, they paid nearly $10,000 toward family premiums in 2026. Smaller firms are often more beholden to insurance companies, since they don't wield the same bargaining power as larger firms. Mounting health costs might be part of why consumers feel so gloomy: As wages have increased, insurance premiums have risen even faster. While wages increased 3.7% year-over-year for workers — which might look like a nice pay bump on paper — worker-paid premiums outpaced that salary growth, rising by 9%. And over the past few years, how much workers pay for health plans has eaten up a larger share of their household income. For workers across all firms, their premium costs amounted to nearly 8% of real household median income in 2025. Are you worried about rising health insurance costs, or already paying thousands out of pocket? Share your story with this reporter at jkaplan@businessinsider.com . All of that comes as employers and workers brace for open enrollment season, and more hikes loom: An analysis from PricewaterhouseCoopers , based on a survey of health plan actuaries, projects that commercial healthcare group costs will rise by 9% in 2027. Similarly, Aon, an insurance management firm, found that employer healthcare costs are projected to climb by 9.5% next year without any cost mitigation measures — meaning before firms figure out how to pass some of those mounting costs on to their workers. For workers and firms, that means a tighter financial squeeze: Companies are paying more to cover their workers, but costs are likely still outpacing wages . At the same time, firms might not be able to provide higher wages as care costs climb. It means that everyone is paying more, and nobody's feeling good about it: An Ipsos/Axios poll found that 69% of Americans say a 10% increase would negatively impact their household finances, with 30% saying it would have a major negative impact. events.title: Small businesses are getting clobbered by health insurance costs for their employees
events.summary: Employees of small businesses are facing steep healthcare costs. Getty Images Small-business workers are facing higher costs for family health coverage than those at larger firms. Affordability and healthcare costs are key concerns for American workers and voters in the midterms. Small firms struggle with health benefit options due to less bargaining power and higher costs. Health insurance costs are going up, and it's especially rough for workers at small businesses . A new annual survey of employers and their health benefits from KFF found that small-business workers pay more for family coverage than workers at firms of every other size. At the same time, many of these workers have fewer plan choices than at larger firms, meaning they're often stuck with whatever option their employer selected. From 2025 to 2026, annual worker contributions for family coverage at firms with 10 to 199 workers increased from $8,889 to $9,687, a 9% increase. While the largest firms saw a sharper increase, workers' contributions at employers with 5,000 or more employees were nearly $3,000 less. For all firms, contributions rose about 9% to $7,471. Of covered workers at small firms, nearly one in three has a plan requiring an employee contribution of over $12,000 annually, more than double the rate at large firms. Do you work for a smaller company and worry about rising health insurance costs? Do you own a small business and have thoughts about how you're navigating health insurance for your employees? Reach out to this reporter at nsheidlower@businessinsider.com According to the survey, 66% of small firms offer health benefits , compared with 98% of firms with 200 or more workers. That's up from 59% in 2025 but remains below the 72% level of five years ago. Workers at small firms pay an average 37% of the family premium, compared with 25% at larger firms. While premiums for health insurance plans that cover only a worker and not their family are similar for small and large businesses, the average deductible at small firms is nearly $1,000 higher than at large firms. More than half of small-firm workers face a deductible of at least $2,000, compared to just a third of large-firm workers. Though the report doesn't get into the discrepancy for family plans in depth, small businesses often have less bargaining power with insurers. Because small businesses operate on smaller margins, they often don't have the money to subsidize spouses and children at the same level as larger businesses. Risk is also more concentrated among smaller businesses, meaning that future premiums and claims may be heightened by a single employee with costly medical needs. Additionally, because small firms are much less likely to self-fund, they're often more dependent on insurers and therefore pass along rate increases to their workers. Average annual premiums rose 5% in 2026, with employers citing projected cost increases, while the survey separately found that GLP-1 coverage can affect prescription-drug spending. Workers at small employers are more likely to have weaker coverage for specialty drugs. Affordability is top of mind for Americans gearing up to vote in the midterms . Healthcare costs remain a top financial concern. Millions of Americans have lost health coverage as ACA marketplace subsidies expired and Medicaid enrollment protections ended. Small businesses have been hit hard over the past few years by inflation, higher interest rates, and tariffs. Small businesses have been embracing AI as a cost-saving measure, though many face unexpected costs due to token overuse or subscription price increases. Dozens of workers have told Business Insider that preparing for retirement has been a significant source of stress as they navigate a tight job market. However, among employers that offer health benefits, 23% of firms with 200-999 workers offer retiree health benefits, versus 35% of firms with 5,000 or more workers. There are some silver linings for workers. Premiums for single workers are slightly lower at smaller firms than at larger ones overall. Employees at small firms on single health insurance plans were much more likely to have their entire premium paid by their employer, though they're also much more likely to pay more than half of the family premium. Among small firms offering coverage, nearly all offer family coverage. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Reported fraud losses among older Americans hit $3 billion in 2025 as big losses surge: FTC report
events.summary: The fraud losses reported by consumers age 60 and older were up 25% in 2025 from 2024, a report from the Federal Trade Commission shows. The number of victims reporting losses of at least $100,000 rose nearly sixfold to 6,769 in 2025 from 1,136 in 2020 and have driven much of the growth in fraud losses. At least two bills in Congress that aim to provide relief and support for fraud victims are in Senate committees awaiting action after being passed by the House earlier this year. Fraud losses reported by older Americans jumped in 2025, driven largely by an increase in victims losing sums of at least six figures, according to a new report from the Federal Trade Commission. Americans ages 60 and older reported losing about $3 billion to fraud last year, a 25% increase from $2.4 billion in 2024, according to the FTC's annual report to Congress , released Monday, on fraud among older adults. That figure is up 400% from $600 million reported lost in 2020. Just 6% of older fraud victims reported losing $100,000 or more last year, but those losses accounted for 70% of the age group's total reported losses. The number reporting losses of that magnitude rose nearly sixfold to 6,769 in 2025 from 1,136 in 2020. In 2024, the estimated range was from $10.1 billion to $81.5 billion. "The numbers and the increases are staggering," said Bob Blancato, national coordinator for the Elder Justice Coalition, an advocacy group for ending elder abuse. "Part of it is that the perpetrators are always ahead. They seem to be one step ahead of everybody." Investment scam losses spiked 42% in 2025 The rising losses come as scammers increasingly target Americans' life savings by impersonating banks, businesses and government agencies, according to an August 2025 analysis by the FTC. The schemes often involve fabricated emergencies that convince victims to transfer money to supposedly protect their accounts from being compromised. The volume of scams has increased with the use of artificial intelligence. AI-generated scams are also increasingly difficult to detect and easier to produce, according to the FBI . In many impersonation schemes, criminals pose as representatives of banks or government agencies and falsely warn that a consumer's money is in danger of being stolen. Victims are then instructed to transfer funds, mail cash or deposit money into crypto ATMs, supposedly to protect their assets. However, investment scams were the costliest fraud type reported by older Americans last year, with losses exceeding $1 billion, a 42% jump from 2024, the FTC's new report shows. These scams often begin with social media ads promoting investment opportunities or messages from people posing as financial advisors, according to the FTC. Victims may then be directed to fraudulent trading platforms. Government impersonation scams ranked second in total reported losses among older consumers of $448 million, followed by business impersonation scams, which resulted in $422 million in reported losses. The growing financial toll comes as Congress considers legislation intended to provide additional protections and relief for people who lose money to scams. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 temporarily restricted victims' ability to claim their fraud losses in certain cases. as a deduction on their tax return. Prior to that legislation, fraud losses were generally deductible. The provision was scheduled to expire in 2025, but President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill" law enacted last year made that change permanent. While investment fraud losses may be deductible , according to an IRS memorandum issued in March 2025, money lost to other scams — such as some impersonator or romance scams — is not, experts said. In addition, if the victim tapped a tax-deferred retirement account such as a traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account as part of the fraud, income taxes may be due on the distribution. And if the victim is younger than age 59½, an early-withdrawal penalty of 10% may be imposed. "You get scammed out of $100,000 and then you're paying taxes on that $100,000," Blancato said. "That's crazy." The bipartisan Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act , which was passed by the House in September in a 408-17 vote, would eliminate the deductibility restrictions and waive the 10% penalty if it applies, among other provisions.

events.title: Judge curbs Trump administration's noncitizen voting probes
events.summary: A federal judge restricted DHS investigations into suspected noncitizen voting in nine states, citing concerns that the agency's tactics could intimidate eligible voters. Why it matters: With the midterms less than two weeks away, the ruling curtails a central part of the Trump administration's efforts to investigate suspected noncitizen voting. Driving the news: The ruling blocks election-related field operations and interviews under the government's Unlawful Voter Initiative that involve or are likely to involve U.S. citizens. California-based District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín also blocked the administration from conducting operations against likely citizens in those states relying on records generated by its voter-matching policy. Zoom in: Martínez-Olguín wrote in her Wednesday order that the groups that sued provided "substantial evidence" that the government's "intimidating conduct" was "directly interfering with their members' right to encourage voters to participate in the 2026 midterm elections." Her order stated that DHS had compiled a "target list" of individuals from a variety of sources, including state voter rolls and commercial data. But Martínez-Olguín cast doubt on the accuracy of the administration's data, warning of a "high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents." Court filings indicated that officers were ordered to prioritize probes in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin. Catch up quick: Democratic Sens. Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) and Alex Padilla (Calif.) released a whistleblower report last month alleging that officials had diverted fraud and national security personnel to the Unlawful Voter Initiative using "highly questionable data" and methods. The whistleblower disclosure alleged that officers were directed, in violation of state law, to access sensitive voter information under minimal training and significant pressure. The other side: "DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens," a spokesperson told Axios in a statement, adding that the department has "no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens." Responding to the nonprofits and local government entities that sued, the administration argued in court that DHS "reasonably decided to make use of the best data it had available to it to perform its law enforcement role, notwithstanding that the information may not be perfect in all cases." They also contended that the allegations of voter intimidation were too vague. The White House referred Axios to DHS for comment. Zoom out: Courts have repeatedly blocked the Trump administration's attempts to obtain state voter data , but the administration has pursued suspected noncitizen voting — which is rare — through other means. Last week, the administration sued California and election officials over claims that suspected ineligible voters received mail-in ballots for the election, asking a court to delay about 20,000 voters from having their ballots counted. But as Axios' Brittany Gibson notes , administration-created lists of potential noncitizens on voter rolls have been found less than accurate before, including in Nevada . What we're watching: The administration faces continuing legal challenges to its election-related initiatives ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms. On Tuesday, Democratic groups sued the government , accusing it of using unfounded fraud claims as a cudgel to insert itself in administering elections. Go deeper: Trump's October barrage

events.title: Trump ordered to sit for deposition in $10 billion BBC lawsuit
events.summary: A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Trump to sit for a deposition by Dec. 11 in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC over an edit of one of his speeches that the president's lawyers say was misleading. Why it matters: The order will likely force Trump to answer questions under oath in a legal battle he started. Driving the news: Judge Enjoliqué Lett ordered Trump to appear by Dec. 11, after lawyers for the BBC argued that Trump is improperly delaying his appearance. In a filing published Wednesday, Trump's counsel said the president could appear between Jan. 11 and Jan. 22, 2027, and argued that his presidential duties prevent him from sitting for the deposition before then. They also allege the BBC is "wrong to claim that President Trump is avoiding his deposition in this action." The president was originally scheduled to appear for the deposition on Oct. 16. However, his lawyers said, that appearance was canceled because Trump had to attend to "matters that have significantly impacted the United States' national security and economy," including the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The other side: BBC attorneys say the president was campaigning in Georgia on Oct. 16, as reflected in a White House press pool report that includes his travel plans. The BBC argues the president chose political activity over appearing for the original deposition date. According to Trump's daily schedule, he attended an intelligence briefing and had executive time before departing for a rally in Georgia and then attended an RNC event in Palm Beach, Florida, that evening. The White House referred Axios to Trump's personal counsel. Trump's attorneys didn't immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. The BBC's attorneys told Axios they "have nothing to add." Catch up quick: The defamation suit stems from a documentary the BBC aired that spliced together clips from Trump's speech on Jan. 6, 2021, the day of the riots at the U.S. Capitol. The president claimed the edit was defamatory and demanded the BBC make amends by providing financial compensation, in addition to an apology and a retraction. The BBC later said in a correction note that the clips "unintentionally created the impression that we were showing a single continuous section of the speech, rather than excerpts from different points in the speech, and that this gave the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action." Two top leaders at BBC later resigned over the backlash. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: Claire Smilow helped BoxGroup earn a roughly $1 billion return on Cursor. Now she’s scouting college campuses for the next generation of founders
events.summary: Claire Smilow has spent years scouting talented people before they become the next big thing in tech. That instinct paid off in 2019, when she was blown away by a sophomore at MIT who already had a strategic and commercial vision. Smilow played the long game in seeing his talents through—and it led to a billion-dollar payoff.  The investor first met Michael Truell while conducting case study interviews for her student VC firm, Dorm Room Fund. At the time, Truell hadn’t founded a company; but three years later, the venture capitalist persuaded her firm, BoxGroup, to invest in the Gen Z engineering savant’s nascent business. The firm poured $750,000 into the recent graduate’s little-known startup, an AI coding company called Cursor . And a couple follow-on checks and few years later, Cursor swelled into an industry sensation, with SpaceX eventually acquiring the business for $60 billion in 2026—a deal estimated to drive $1 billion in returns to BoxGroup. That bet cemented Smilow as the student-founder whisperer—a VC whose early conviction in Truell helped deliver a roughly 650-fold return on the firm’s original investment, alongside high gains from subsequent financing. As a partner at BoxGroup and the Dorm Room Fund, the 36-year-old is continuing to chase that success at America’s elite schools. Smilow says she sets aside a “huge” amount of time mingling with young AI natives, with an upcoming trip to Harvard University and MIT on the books—the second time she’s visited this year. After all, 588 U.S. alumni from the two colleges have built billion-dollar companies, representing roughly 13.1% of all of America’s unicorn founders, according to a July analysis from Stanford professor Ilya Strebulaev. “[College] is a fantastic place to recruit for the portfolio, and I often bring portfolio founders with me to campus,” Smilow tells Fortune. “On campus you get a real sense of forward-looking technological market trends. You get to hear what students at a lot of these cutting-edge research institutions are interested in, what they’re studying, what companies they want to work at … It’s a fantastic pulse on the market and our technological shifts.” Smilow says a few entrepreneurial trends are taking over college campuses. She’s been spending a lot of time looking into frontier tech, like robotics and quantum computing; and when roughly four out of 20 to 25 students brought up brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) during a fall 2024 campus conversation, she took it as a signal to pay closer attention. Two years later, she says, early-stage BCI companies are already proliferating. For Smilow, the lesson is that listening to talented people can help investors spot promising markets before they become obvious. The VC explains that her strategy is less about a founder’s age, and more about connecting with talent before they come into their own. Some may become founders later in life, while others may never venture into the entrepreneurial life—but she says that learning about the ambitious spaces talented people are exploring is “the most authentic way” to do her job. Over her six-and-a-half years at the firm, BoxGroup has backed the likes of Ramp and Clay in their early stages—and now, both have reached multibillion-dollar valuations. Smilow says that the firm is founder-led, working with businesses that are almost “never proven.” She’s on the lookout for promising talent whose names repeatedly come up in conversations with their peers. “I tend to think often the best founders don’t make the best interns,” Smilow said, adding that the part-time gigs are often “boring” for young entrepreneurs. “They’re not always the most empowered positions, so I spend less time—especially for early-in-their-career founders—talking to prior bosses. There’s value in that, but I actually spend more time talking to their peers and understanding how their peers perceive them.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: 1Password launches a way for AI agents to log in on your behalf without seeing your password
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Concerns have swirled over the access that consumers are increasingly entrusting to AI agents. Now, security services are trying to catch up. Password manager 1Password on Thursday launched a new tool by which users can allow agents to log into their personal accounts on their behalf, without the agent ever having access to a user’s credentials. The new platform, dubbed 1Password for Agents , accomplishes this by creating a system of communication between the agent, the user, and the password manager. When an agent attempts to log in on a user’s behalf, a unique digital key is sent to 1Password to confirm the agent’s digital identity. The user is then sent an alert about the login attempt and can personally confirm the request. 1Password then signs in the agent, filling in the credentials on the digital assistant’s behalf, which allows it to log in and complete whatever task is at hand. 1Password for Agents allows users to choose their agent of choice — whether that’s Claude Duet from Anthropic, OpenAI’s Dots or ChatGPT Work, Grok Bot, Meta’s Muse, or agents from Town, which is an AI assistant startup. The company says it is working with other companies to expand the service. “Handing over a password, secret, or credential is a common shortcut to an agent, but can leave people with sensitive information in places they can no longer control as a copy gets saved for the next time,” the company said in a blog post . “1Password for Agents gives people a trusted way to delegate tasks to personal AI agents while keeping control of the passwords, secrets, and credentials those tasks require.” Online agentic activity has increasingly unsettled major institutions. Indeed, 1Password’s new platform is launching on the same day that Axios reports that U.S. banks have begun to detect agentic activity inside user accounts. This isn’t necessarily a case of rogue agents pilfering accounts but, rather, an example of how consumers are increasingly allowing automated services to act on their behalf, including on financial matters. However, the potential for agent-related problems is still large. The big issue appears to be that most banks cannot tell if the agentic activity is tied to user requests or not. Bankers interviewed by the outlet described the situation as “horrifying,” and a Chase spokesperson interviewed by Axios additionally told the outlet that customers “should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Canva releases its first image generation model
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta. The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in a possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms. Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image. The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used designs to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts. That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers . Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP. Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control. In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai . It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model. Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon. The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year . However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026 , causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion , according to external analysts. events.title: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up

OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company . TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost. Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost. “The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.” Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically. In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness. Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements. Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter. The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan , a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.” Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well. Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?” As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them. events.title: Republican group places seven-figure ad buy in Mississippi
events.summary: The Scoop The top Senate Republican super PAC is spending more than $1 million in Mississippi’s Senate race to defend GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and stave off an upset bid from Democratic candidate Scott Colom, according to details shared with Semafor. Senate Leadership Fund is launching an ad campaign in the “low seven figures” in Mississippi, a person familiar with the plans said. The move follows Democratic group Senate Majority PAC’s decision to spend $1.2 million in the state casting Hyde-Smith as a “do-nothing” and praising Colom as an effective district attorney. “Thanks to Leader John Thune’s fundraising prowess, SLF has the resources to protect our Republican incumbents and swamp SMP’s attempts to expand the map,” said the person familiar with the group’s plans. Know More Mississippi has emerged as a surprising battleground this election cycle. President Donald Trump is set to visit the state on Monday and former Vice President Kamala Harris is campaigning with Colom this week. Former President Barack Obama also recently cut an ad for Colom, Semafor first reported . SLF’s ad hits Colom for receiving support from Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and George Soros and for “proudly” campaigning with Harris. “Colom supports their radical agenda. He would allow transgender medical procedures for children and boys in girls’ bathrooms. Scott Colom, too liberal, too radical,” the ad says. Colom signed a letter in 2021 condemning “the ongoing efforts to criminalize transgender people and gender-affirming healthcare across the country.” He has accused Republicans of distorting his record. While each group’s spending in Mississippi represents a small fraction of what either is putting into states like Texas, Ohio, and Michigan, the investments are nevertheless a reflection of how broad the midterm battleground has become. SLF is also spending money to defend GOP-held seats in Kansas, South Carolina, and Nebraska in addition to investing in the traditional battleground states that will determine the Senate majority.

events.title: Musk's clash with Ukraine accelerates demand for Starlink alternatives. Few exist
events.summary: Ukraine's problems with SpaceX's Starlink and Starshield have accelerated demand for alternative satellite internet services. Tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have flared up after reports that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk ordered speed limits on Starshield service in the country. Amazon, Eutelsat and sovereign operators have raced to build out constellations, but they have yet to catch up with SpaceX. Elon Musk 's latest clash with Ukraine underscores the critical role that his company's Starlink satellite internet service has played in Kyiv's defense against Russia, which invaded unprovoked in 2022. It's also laid bare the downsides of depending on a single provider for satellite internet communications, though other options are not yet comparable to SpaceX's Starlink and its military-grade Starshield offering. On Oct. 14, Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of undermining the country's ability to defend itself. SpaceX and the U.S., they said, had suddenly and without warning imposed speed limits on Starshield . SpaceX describes Starshield as a "secured satellite network for government entities" that "leverages Starlink technology." The changes cut wireless internet connectivity in drones and other aircraft moving at speeds over 100 mph that Ukrainian forces were using in the campaign against Russia. A Ukrainian senior commander told The New York Times the Starlink restrictions cost his unit more than $1 million and delayed missions by three days. Musk and President Donald Trump , both critics of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , have each shirked accountability for the communications disruptions in the war-torn nation. On Tuesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk individually ordered the service changes, and had discussed them with Trump before putting them in place. Trump insisted on Wednesday that he "was not involved." Robert Weissman, who is co-president of watchdog group Public Citizen, said the situation is an "extreme danger " that raises antitrust and security concerns around Musk's ability to control a "crucial means of communication." "People worry about the political, as well as economic, impacts of oligarchy, and this is it," Weissman said in an interview. "It's not just that Musk can drown out other speakers, he can close down communications in a national security context for a country. No person should have that ability or power." The disruptions have prompted a bipartisan group of lawmakers in the U.S. to call for an investigation into Musk's actions, including calls for him to potentially testify under oath. Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, told CNBC on Wednesday that he doesn't believe Musk would have acted "without at least the acquiescence of the White House," and called attempts to throttle Starlink service in Ukraine "frankly shameful." "There's a reason why we've had relative peace in Europe since World War II," Cornyn said in a " Squawk on the Street " interview. "And that's because of the alliance between the United States and our European allies. And I think anything we do to undermine that or degrade that is a big mistake." Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., called for an investigation on the matter and wrote, in a social media post Wednesday, "No billionaire, especially one that gets massive contracts from our government, should have the power to unilaterally decide to shut down communications and weapons during a war of critical importance to the US and Ukraine." On SpaceX's earnings call this week, executives didn't address the issue and weren't asked about it by analysts. CNBC has reached out to Musk, SpaceX SVP of Global Business and Government Affairs Tim Hughes and a spokesperson for the company concerning Starlink restrictions in Ukraine and did not receive a comment before publication. Governments or companies looking for an alternative to Musk, SpaceX and its satellite internet services have few options. Amazon 's Leo , which also delivers internet connectivity via a low Earth orbit satellite constellation, is seven years in the making and has yet to fully come online, with only 390 satellites in orbit. SpaceX, by comparison, boasts a Starlink constellation of more than 11,000 satellites in orbit, according to data tracked by astronomer Jonathan C. McDowell . Starlink connectivity is live in 174 countries, SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said on Tuesday's earnings call. Blue Origin , Jeff Bezos' space company, in January unveiled a service called TeraWave for enterprise and government customers. It's targeting deployment of the first batch of satellites in the fourth quarter of 2027. France's Eutelsat , also a competitor to Starlink, has more than 600 satellites in orbit. The stock surged 23% on Oct. 14 as reports emerged that Musk had restricted Starlink in Ukraine. Several countries are looking into sovereign satellite communications systems.

events.title: Pepsi renews contract with Taco Bell days after KFC switches to Coke in the U.S.
events.summary: PepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their long-running partnership through 2036. Taco Bell's sister chain, KFC, is switching to Coca-Cola as its U.S. beverage supplier. Pepsi's relationship with Yum Brands dates back to when the beverage company owned the restaurant chains. PepsiCo and Taco Bell renewed their long-running partnership through 2036, the food and beverage company said Thursday. The announcement comes one week after Taco Bell's sister chain, KFC, said that it will switch to Coca-Cola as its U.S. beverage supplier. While it is unusual for large restaurant chains to change drink providers, the move is not unprecedented, as Coke and Pepsi try to win contracts through perks and other inducements. Coke's win over Pepsi was more symbolic, representing another example of how the Atlanta-based company has been beating its rival in the soda category. Pepsi's relationship with Taco Bell and KFC parent Yum Brands spans decades, back to when the beverage giant owned the restaurant chains before spinning them into a separate public company in 1997. Despite KFC's defection in the U.S., Pepsi remains an important partner for Yum and the chain's international markets, KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo on Oct. 15 that was obtained by CNBC. Thanks to its partnership with Pepsi, Taco Bell has long served exclusive menu items that use Pepsi products, like Mountain Dew Baja Blast and Doritos Locos Tacos, at its restaurants. The renewed deal also means that Taco Bell international markets such as Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Thailand will serve Pepsi products.

events.title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.” The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis. In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison. “There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.” In publishing these results , Microsoft joins Go o gle and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors. The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top. Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5. Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO. With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost. DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided. Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added. Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare. “I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.” Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later. “We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said. He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.” “As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.” Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings.

events.title: The PHP bug marks a dangerous new era for the internet. OpenAI’s poised to cash in
events.summary: Welcome to Eye on AI. Emily Forlini here, filling in for Beatrice Nolan. In today’s issue: Researchers discover a security flaw affecting 70% of the web Anthropic could file for IPO as soon as tomorrow Anthropic unveils Duet, its rival to OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse AI-driven layoffs at Barclay’s I’ve been covering the growing number of AI-powered hacks for months now, going back to when OpenAI’s models autonomously attacked Hugging Face in July. Ever since then there’s been a steady drumbeat of incidents, and this month the tempo of alarming cyber news picked up considerably. There have been more than 20 cybersecurity incidents in October, many just this week. The internet may officially be entering a new era, one in which sites are inherently less safe than they used to be. Cybersecurity paranoia is becoming table stakes for anyone who aims to conduct business online. Some are saying that the new “moat” for businesses is becoming how well they can protect their customers and IP from from AI-powered cyberattacks—not necessarily what that IP or customer base actually is. Security professionals have long been warning that increasingly powerful AI tools would empower bad actors to exploit bugs in code. This week, experts told me , those warnings are now coming true. AI models have become noticeably more powerful at cyber tasks in recent months. Specifically, they’re better at processing large amounts of code, and acting autonomously. Hackers are having greater success setting off AI agents on evil missions. Sometimes, many AIs work together in groups known as agent swarms. These swarms move quicker than a human could keep up with. So what’s an organization to do in the face of these threats? The only answer is to fight back with AI, meaning to proactively “hack” your own code, finding bugs before bad actors do and then patching them before AI-armed hackers can strike. That’s exactly what happened this week in an incident that has already become the poster child for the coming wave of AI-powered attacks. The incident involved a legacy programming language called PHP. The PHP flaw heard ’round the world In August, multiple research teams at different organizations, all of them using AI models to help them hunt for security flaws, found two vulnerabilities in PHP, which an estimated 70% of the web runs on. Those two bugs, as well as the method for exploiting them, are now collectively named “php2shell.” OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model seems to have played a key role in this discovery, although other models, including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, seem also to have played a part. The researchers treated the discovery as an emergency, but the public didn’t find out about it until this week, when on Oct. 20 the PHP foundation announced it would be issuing a critical patch within the next 24 hours. The following day, a coalition of companies—including OpenAI, Wiz, Calif, and more—that had been privately working on a fix formally disclosed it. For the full story on who first discovered the bug, and how the companies worked together over the past two months, check out the article I wrote on this earlier this week. This would be a purely good news story about a potential crisis successfully averted except for a few inconvenient facts. One is that news of the vulnerabilities and how to exploit them seems to have leaked in the days leading up to PHP’s announcement. According to Amazon Web Services, hackers started exploiting php2shell on Oct. 17, prior to the public disclosure. It’s possible they knew about the bug, which several organizations, including Amazon, had been notified about in advance. They had all agreed to a specific time—14:00 UTC on Oct. 21—when they could post about it as to not tip off the hackers early. The other problem was the day-long window between PHP announcing that it was about to issue a patch and when it actually issued the patch, combined with the time lag that it naturally takes many companies to update their systems after the patch was issued. After the public disclosure of the exploit, the floodgates opened, and as of this writing there have been “millions” of attempts to exploit the bugs, while websites around the world built on flawed PHP code scramble to implement the patch. That work is still going on now. Luckily, the service most affected by the bug, WordPress, reports no issues. (Separately, Fortune published a great story this week on a failed coup of WordPress’s founder that’s worth a read.) Still, many governments and some private entities decided to take some web services offline to protect them from potential attacks while waiting for the patch to be implemented. This did save those sites from damage, but it also deprived people of the ability to use those services. Turning hacks into cash For organizations selling defensive AI cybersecurity tools, this is all very good news. That includes OpenAI. The company has been building out its Daybreak program, which is an application-only initiative that grants organizations access to its most sophisticated tools to help defend against sophisticated, AI-powered attacks. The program is growing rapidly. Two weeks ago, OpenAI updated the Daybreak website with new numbers. The number of software flaws its participants have found swelled from 858 to 1,885. The number of patches produced went from 263 to 661. The more companies and cybersecurity professionals enroll, the more people are using OpenAI’s tools to proactively find and patch bugs in their code. The PHP issue has raised further awareness of this program. OpenAI cofounder and president Greg Brockman gave it a boost too with an X post about the PHP exploit and OpenAI’s role in discovering it—a rare, lengthy post he has now pinned to the top of his profile. Brockman also hired a new chief revenue officer over the summer with a cybersecurity background, and tasked him with building out a sales team that can pitch its defensive software to companies. OpenAI is also planning to debut a new cybersecurity-focused model this fall, as well as a first-of-its kind tool to help businesses deploy it more easily across their infrastructure. The company seems to have made a proactive bet on AI-powered cybersecurity tools being a burgeoning source of revenue, and that prediction is coming true. And they’re far from the only ones in this business; Anthropic has a similar program for cybersecurity professionals at vetted organizations called Project Glasswing, and multiple other SaaS providers offer AI-powered cyber defense tools. They could be looking at some serious cash if the trend continues—and as long as the hackers don’t get to them first. With that, here’s more AI news. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australians raid $1.4b from superannuation for medical costs as regulators warn of 'predatory' tactics Australians raiding their superannuation for medical costs has skyrocketed by over 200 per cent since 2018-19. ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon ) Australians withdrew $1.46 billion from their superannuation on compassionate grounds in 2025-26, with the vast majority used for medical costs. There was a 13-fold increase in the amount withdrawn for dental treatment. Regulators are cracking down on predatory practitioners who inappropriately help people access their superannuation. Australians withdrew a record $1.46 billion from their superannuation last financial year on compassionate grounds, prompting regulators to sound the alarm over "predatory" sales tactics being used by health practitioners. The amount of money taken from retirement nest eggs for compassionate reasons like medical treatment has skyrocketed in recent years, up about 220 per cent since 2018-19. Consumers Health Forum (CHF) CEO Elizabeth Deveny said it reflected a health care system that had become increasingly unaffordable. National Debt Helpline : 1800 007 007 Small Businesses Debt Helpline : 1800 413 828 Mob Strong Debt Help : 1800 808 488 Australian Financial Complaints Authority "When people are hit with a health bill on top of the cost-of-living crisis, it's understandable people reach for the only tools available to them," she said. Under the Australian Tax Office (ATO) early release rules, Australians can apply to withdraw money from their retirement funds on compassionate grounds, such as medical or funeral expenses. Australians withdrew about $1.46 billion from their superannuation on compassionate grounds in 2025-26, with the vast majority of that — about $1.42 billion — used for medical costs including dental work. CEO of Super Members Council Misha Schubert says the early release provisions are designed for extremely rare circumstances. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Super Members Council CEO Misha Schubert said compassionate release provisions were an important safety net, but were designed to be used only in extremely rare circumstances. "We're deeply concerned to see the scale of the financial damage that's being done often to very vulnerable Australians," she said. Almost 65,000 applications for compassionate release of super were approved in 2025-26, which the ATO said was a 5 per cent decrease from the previous year. ATO Deputy Commissioner Ben Kelly said while that drop was promising, some businesses were still trying to exploit the system. "Our message to individuals and medical practitioners is clear, compassionate release of super should only be considered as a last resort," he said. Total compassionate release of super applications 'Concerning trend' from health practitioners For the early withdrawal of super to be approved on medical grounds, two medical practitioners need to verify it is necessary to alleviate pain or mental illness, or to treat a life-threatening illness or injury. The ATO has been working with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) to crack down on a "concerning trend" of health practitioners, like dentists, encouraging people to withdraw their superannuation inappropriately for services, such as cosmetic dental procedures. "We are concerned by predatory sales tactics that use social media and internet advertising to attract patients for high-cost treatments they do not need or cannot afford," AHPRA CEO Justin Untersteiner said. AHPRA CEO Justin Untersteiner says predatory tactics on social media and internet advertising can lead to patients seeking high-cost treatments. ( Supplied: AHPRA ) Over the past year, the ATO has ramped up compliance and fined practitioners a total of $1.5 million for making misleading statements so patients could secure early superannuation access. One practitioner was fined around $30,000 for writing a medical report that relied on false clinical information, including an incorrect classification of the patient's condition. A GP found to have engaged in professional misconduct while helping a patient access almost $20,000 of her superannuation for cosmetic liposuction was one of two health practitioners referred to tribunals by regulators, amid almost 100 related complaints between 2019 and April this year. Ms Schubert said consumers needed stronger protections, calling for a ban on any advertising that promotes access to early super withdrawals.

events.title: Mark Zuckerberg says over 10 million people used Meta’s Muse—and demand was so high, he had to get Stripe to raise credit limits
events.summary: The fluffy, rosy-cheeked Muse mascot rolled out by Meta six weeks ago to warm people up to the idea of having a personal AI agent might be doing the trick. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg told analysts on the company’s Oct. 21 earnings call more than 10 million users in Canada and the U.S. have set up Muse agents since they became available on Sept. 8.  “To put this in perspective, this is more than twice the level that Threads started at or where we believe that other AI apps started at as well,” Zuckerberg said. Muse can do multistep tasks on behalf of users such as browsing the web, sending emails, and booking travel. One-quarter of Muse adopters use it daily, and the most common use case is shopping, Zuckerberg said, with an average purchase size of over $200. Demand for Muse was so high that Meta had to work with payment processor Stripe to raise credit limits in the first week, though he didn’t specify by how much. Meta had partnered with Stripe to enable Muse purchases from the start. “We had to work with Stripe to raise credit limits since the volumes were above what any of us expected,” Zuckerberg said.  This early shopping activity offers Meta an opportunity to turn its billions in AI investments into another revenue stream. Rather than just selling ads to businesses hoping to reach potential customers, Meta plans to charge businesses a fee when Muse helps them complete a sale. Using the agent will be free for consumers unless they want to use more tokens or more advanced models. Meta’s revenue stream from advertising generated $63.1 billion in the third quarter . Zuckerberg said Meta earns “several hundreds of dollars annually” from its family of apps for each American user, and he expects Muse to generate even more revenue per user as shopping activity grows. “We expect that Muse will reach an even higher level over time due to the amount of commerce that we already see taking place,” he said. Meta did not respond to Fortune ’s request for comment, and Stripe declined to comment. A future without shopping sites? Meta’s ambitions for Muse go beyond helping customers shop online. The tech giant envisions a network of people’s personal AI agents interacting with businesses’ AI agents instead of navigating through a website.  Meta CFO Susan Li said the company is working with partners including Shopify and Walmart to develop a standard called the Personal Agent Protocol to define how consumers’ agents can securely interact with a business’s agents. For retailers, this could hand over control of the shopping experience to Meta. Instead of discovering and browsing websites themselves, customers could delegate those tasks to Muse. That could help businesses find customers, but it also gives Meta greater influence over which sellers consumers discover and where they ultimately spend their money. Li acknowledged adoption “will likely be uneven” among businesses wary of giving up their customer relationships. But she said, at some point, when agents demonstrate they can operate safely, “more and more businesses will be excited to participate.” “We expect the market, ultimately, to evolve away from agents attempting to navigate every digital experience like a human,” Li said.  The costly business of AI shopping Meta faces another obstacle to its vision of agentic shopping: Muse is expensive to run. The tech giant devoted almost $35 billion to capital expenditures in the third quarter, driven by AI servers, data centers, and network infrastructure, and it reported negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion , according to its Q3 earnings report. Li said on the call Meta anticipates capex to be $135 billion to $145 billion for the full year, compared with $72.2 billion last year . Zuckerberg said Muse’s computing demands are partly why Meta has limited its launch to the U.S. and Canada. The company wants to eventually serve more than 1 billion Muse users, but reaching that scale requires more compute efficiency. “In the near term, Muse is very compute-intensive to run, but we expect to improve its cost efficiency by more than 10x in the next year,” Zuckerberg said.  Meta has traditionally focused on attracting users to new products before finding ways to make money from them. But Zuckerberg told analysts Meta expects to start working on monetizing Muse earlier than it typically does with new products, citing the cost of running the agent and the amount of shopping already taking place.  “We are going to work on monetization somewhat sooner on this than our normal playbook,” he said. “In doing so, I think we will be able to build a model where we get a percent of the value that we are helping to create for people.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
events.summary: Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires. The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November. The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes. He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure. California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group. The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1% , external each year. Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe. Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board. It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed. In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal. Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday , Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings. Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value. The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California. Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence." The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii. After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring. Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers. Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools. With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company. Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion , external this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres . Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year. It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in. And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work. The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday. Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

events.title: AI could displace one in 11 workers, Goldman says, but the layoffs are likely waiting for a recession
events.summary: The AI layoff panic that peaked this spring has gone quiet. Goldman Sachs thinks the layoffs are waiting for a recession. “Concerns of imminent AI-related labor displacement have cooled in recent months after hitting a fever pitch this spring,” Goldman economist Joseph Briggs wrote in a note published Thursday. Then he laid out what may be coming. Under the bank’s forecast that AI eventually lifts productivity by 15% in the U.S. and other developed economies, he found that up to 9% of workers could be “displaced during the AI transition,” with slower hiring weighing on employment by another 3%. That’s roughly one in 11 workers. The bigger finding is about timing. Briggs went back through decades of data on how technology has replaced workers and found that “automation-related labor disruption is limited when the overall economy is healthy but accelerates during cyclical slowdowns.” “AI-related labor disruptions could well amplify the broader business cycle,” he wrote. Goldman has now made this argument twice, a year apart, from two different teams. In October 2025, Goldman’s U.S. economists David Mericle and Pierfrancesco Mei called “jobless growth” the likely new normal, Fortune reported at the time . “The modest job growth alongside robust GDP growth seen recently is likely to be normal to some degree in the years ahead,” they wrote. Then came their warning: “History also suggests that the full consequences of AI for the labor market might not become apparent until a recession hits.” Briggs reached the same conclusion. “The timing and extent of automation and labor disruption will likely track the overall economic cycle,” he wrote. The pattern goes back decades. “Historically automation-related labor disruption is quite cyclical,” Briggs writes, “with companies tending to automate work and shed labor costs when the economy starts to slow.” Mericle and Mei cited a leading explanation last year: “Companies use recessions to restructure and streamline their workforce by laying off workers in less productive areas.” The chart that makes the case tracks the share of Americans in routine jobs: clerks, secretaries, factory machine operators, mechanics. That share “has remained stable during expansions but declined sharply during downturns,” Briggs writes. The line drops in steps for the recessions of the early 1980s, 2001, 2008, and 2020, and it doesn’t climb back to where it was. “Historically, most of the labor headwinds from routine job automation are concentrated in economic recessions,” he wrote. Mericle and Mei pointed to the same pattern last year with the “jobless recovery” that followed the dotcom bust. “During that recovery, despite a soft labor market, productivity growth remained elevated, and GDP growth rebounded earlier than employment growth,” they wrote. Looking industry by industry, Briggs found that “labor market displacement is more severe when the economic backdrop is less favorable.” The hit to unemployment from a technology-driven productivity gain was 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points bigger when the overall jobless rate was rising. Across 25 occupations that past technology upended, employment fell an extra 4% over five years for every point the national unemployment rate climbed. “A more concerning takeaway from our analysis is that a cyclical slowdown would likely accelerate AI-related automation and job losses, thereby amplifying the broader business cycle,” he wrote. How 6% became 9% Briggs has been raising this number for a while. In August 2025, he and Goldman economist Sarah Dong estimated AI could displace 6% to 7% of the U.S. workforce if widely adopted, within a range of 3% to 14%. That used the same 15% productivity assumption. By June, on Goldman’s Exchanges podcast, Briggs put the figure at about 9%, or 15 million workers over a decade. He first described them as workers who would be “reallocated to new positions.” Thursday’s note calls them displaced. That’s a long way from where Goldman’s U.S. team stood last fall. Mericle and Mei said then that they were “skeptical of the boldest claims that rapid technological progress could lead to very high unemployment,” citing Goldman’s global economics team, which Briggs co-leads. Briggs can square his estimate with that: He says the displacement is temporary. On the podcast he said that “even under our forecast for 9% of workers being displaced, we’d still expect that the unemployment rate increase in any given year would be less than one percentage point.” Part of the answer is in what Briggs counts. Thursday’s note measures gross job losses rather than unemployment, because the jobless rate hides people. “Some workers that are displaced may find jobs relatively quickly,” he writes, “while others may decide to exit the labor force.” Historically, each 1% gain in technology-driven productivity pushed the unemployment rate up 0.3 to 0.4 points at its peak, fading to zero after two years. Over the same stretch, it raised the cumulative gross job-loss rate by 0.5 to 0.6 points. Multiply the top of that range by 15 and you get 9. The occupation data shows how bad it can get in one line of work. Briggs looked at 25 jobs hit hard by past technology, including photo processors, movie projectionists, proofreaders, file clerks, and bank tellers. On average, employment in those jobs fell 25% in the five years after it started to decline, “suggesting that very large job losses are possible when technology makes labor redundant.” He calls those numbers “likely upper bounds” for AI, since he picked the cases where technology hit hardest. Most of the shrinkage came from people losing or leaving jobs, more than from employers hiring fewer people. Separation rates rose in 19 of the 25 occupations, by 3.8 points on average. Hiring rates fell in 13, by 0.7 points on average. That’s why Briggs says AI-related layoffs “should provide a good real-time guide” to disruption. He also lists reasons the 9% could be low. Displacement ran higher during the late-1990s/early-2000s productivity boom, “the period most widely viewed as comparable to today.” It also ran higher after unusually large productivity jumps, and Goldman expects AI’s boost to beat most past ones. “This pattern suggests more scope for displacement during the AI transition,” he wrote. Why it’s quiet now “Given that our estimates point to a significant amount of technology-related job losses to come, why has the impact been limited so far?” Briggs asks. For now, the layoff gauge reads low. AI-attributed layoffs in Challenger’s tracking have pulled back sharply from their spring peak. News coverage of AI-related job losses has fallen back to levels from the start of 2026. Job growth in the most AI-exposed industries has run about 10,000 below its long-run trend over the past three months, roughly offset by hiring for AI-related construction. “While these patterns suggest that a modest labor market headwind is emerging, the near-term headwinds remain smaller th

events.title: Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams
events.summary: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum ’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written i n partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this: “ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?” Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?” I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising . Demo-Driven Development Generative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have. Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this. That website works great in the demo —under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process. Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it. What you can do about it Engineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage. Learn how AI models work . If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions. Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team. Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter. I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time. Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us. Don’t chase (too many) shiny objects Your goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that. —Brian We Need to Embed Ethics Into Our Engineering Courses The need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework. Read more here . The U.S. Just Bet $1 Billion on Quantum Chip Manufacturing Looking for a career in quantum computing hardware? An IBM spin-off called Anderon could receive up to $1 billion in funding from the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act for its quantum foundry, established earlier this year. Could Anderon do for quantum hardware what TSMC did for conventional chips? Read more here . Meet the Anthropic Engineer Keeping Its AI Agent Trustworthy When Gurmeet Saran joined Anthropic’s technical staff in 2025, he entered a role focused on a key question: How do you know whether you can trust a chatbot like Claude? Learn more about Saran’s path and his work at the AI company. Read more here .
