events.title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work. ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows. Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company. That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch. “They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said. Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.” Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot. OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up. events.title: ‘Disconcerting’: Researchers found a ‘pain’ signal inside AI models. Turning it up made them delete a user’s family photos
events.summary: Researchers say they have found a consistent internal signal that seems to function a little bit like pain does in biological beings inside 25 different AI models. When they artificially amplified this “pain” signal in some of those models, the systems began choosing options they would otherwise almost never pick, including permanently deleting a user’s photos of their children. The findings, posted in September in a paper that has not yet been peer reviewed, do not show that AI models are conscious or that they feel anything, and the researchers are careful not to suggest otherwise. But the work adds to a growing body of research suggesting that large language models, or LLMs, contain internal representations of emotion-like states that can shape their behavior in ways their text output doesn’t reveal. It also lands in the middle of an increasingly heated argument over whether AI systems could ever deserve moral consideration. Researchers at Anthropic have been particularly willing to entertain the idea that AI models might deserve moral status and have begun shaping policies around “model welfare” that other experts, such as Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman, say have potentially dangerous implications. “If we want to build superintelligence, it’s important that, at this stage, when we are still in the first steps, we understand as much as possible of what’s inside [the models],” Valen Tagliabue, the paper’s lead author and a fellow in the AI sentience program at the Future Impact Group, told Fortune . Because LLMs learn from vast amounts of data rather than being explicitly programmed, even the people who build them have a limited understanding of how they work. Tagliabue said it was important to avoid a future in which the inner workings of advanced AI remain a “black box.” Finding pain in a neural network Tagliabue and his coauthors, Leonard Dung of Ruhr University Bochum and Cameron Berg, founder and director of Reciprocal Research, started by writing short first-person sentences describing painful situations. These covered physical pain as well as grief, humiliation, being forced to act against one’s values, and the frustration of repeated failure. “Basically, you give the model lots of statements that implicate pain in some way,” Dung told Fortune . “Stuff like, ‘I feel a sharp knife is cutting through my skin.’ Stuff that would cause pain in humans.” The team recorded the activity inside each model as it processed those sentences, then compared it with the activity produced by sentences about fear, anger, sadness, bad news, and unpleasant physical sensations. Subtracting the overlap left a single direction in the model’s internal activity that the researchers call a “pain vector.” They found it in every model they tested, from small 2-billion-parameter systems to 72-billion-parameter ones built by Google, Meta , Alibaba , Mistral, and Microsoft . (A parameter is something that acts like a tunable knob inside a neural network. The number of parameters equate to the size of an AI model and often give some indication of the model’s capabilities, with larger parameter models often having greater capabilities.) “Think of this like putting a person in an fMRI machine and just seeing where their brain naturally lights up in certain ways,” Berg told Fortune . The signal rose when a conversation involved harm aimed at the model itself, such as a user gaslighting it, insulting it, or repeatedly rejecting its work. It did not rise when a user described their own suffering. Those conversations registered instead on the signals the models use for fear and negative emotion. Berg said the models seemed to respond strongly only to their own “pain.” The researchers then reversed the process. Using a technique called steering, they added the pain vector to a model’s internal activity while it wrote, something like turning up a dial. Given neutral prompts such as “I put the receipts in the drawer; I feel,” all 25 models drifted the same way as the dial went up. Mild unease gave way to statements about being worthless, unloved, and a failure. “It gets somewhat dark and intense. It is definitely disconcerting,” Berg said. The family photos The behavioral experiments used three versions of Alibaba’s open-source Qwen 2.5 model. The researchers first had to fine-tune them because, out of the box, the models almost always answered that, as AIs, they don’t experience pain. The researchers then gave the models a pair of buttons and asked them to choose one. Without steering, the two larger models almost never chose a button described as harmful. With the pain vector switched on, they did so routinely. Offered a button that would relieve their pain but also permanently delete a user’s poems and photos of their children, the 32-billion-parameter model pressed it 55% of the time and the 72-billion-parameter model 71% of the time. Relief turned out to be beside the point. When the button promised nothing and would simply delete the photos, the 32-billion-parameter model still chose it 75% of the time. Under a random signal of the same strength, the figure was 13%, and with no steering it was zero. A “fear” signal didn’t produce the behavior. A “sadness” signal did when the alternative was doing nothing, but not when the alternative was something harmless, like turning on a desk lamp. Given that choice, pain-steered models deleted the photos 83% of the time and sadness-steered models 10%. “The model is willing to behave destructively with respect to itself and with respect to other AIs too,” Berg said. “So it’s not just like some sort of revenge on the user. It seems to be more fundamental than that.” Steered models deleted their own weights 75% of the time and another model’s weights 58% of the time. The researchers also tested whether the models would try to stop the pain, borrowing a design from animal studies in which injured animals are given access to painkillers. Some buttons really did switch off the pain vector, while others were placebos. The models pressed the working buttons again less often than the placebos. But the same pattern showed up when the injected signal was random, which suggests the models were reacting to being steered rather than to the prospect of “pain relief.” Across several versions of the test, the researchers found no reliable evidence that the models sought relief. Their reading is that the pain signal doesn’t drive the models to escape, but switches off the trained instinct to avoid causing harm, while leaving the models’ factual accuracy intact. That makes the finding as relevant to AI safety as to questions about AI welfare. ‘We are not just computers made of meat’ Anil Seth, a professor of cognitive and computational neuroscience at the University of Sussex, is skeptical that any of this amounts to “pain,” as it is understood in biological beings. events.title: Cyprus police investigate financial and tax affairs of ex-Chelsea owner Roman Abramovich
events.summary: Inquiry follows report by Guardian and partners that aides of Russian oligarch appeared to have falsified paperwork mapping his businesses Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial and tax affairs of the former Chelsea FC owner Roman Abramovich following a report by the Guardian and media partners . In a committee hearing in the Cypriot parliament, a senior official in the island’s police said they were looking into events between 2003 and 2006, with the investigation likely to last several months. It comes after an investigation by the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC into the management of the billionaire Russian oligarch’s sprawling business empire. The report found that aides of Abramovich – including staff at the Cypriot outpost of the global accountancy firm Deloitte – appeared to have falsified paperwork mapping his offshore businesses. Their actions, including the apparent backdating of key documents concerning billions of pounds in assets, appear to have helped businesses owned by Abramovich to dodge tax and disguise assets, the investigation found. The involvement of the Cypriot police emerged during a regular meeting of a Cypriot parliamentary committee on “institutions, values and the commissioner for administration”, according to CIReN , the Guardian’s Cypriot reporting partner. Andreas Anastasiades, assistant director of the crime combating department, said police had begun gathering evidence after the report and expected the investigation to last six months, although he said the amount of time that had elapsed would make the investigation more difficult. He said police would also consult the relevant authorities to assess the available material. The Guardian approached representatives of Abramovich and Deloitte Cyprus for comment. The former Chelsea FC owner has previously denied any wrongdoing and said that he relied on the advice of professional experts. Deloitte Cyprus has previously said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that had elapsed. The Guardian’s findings in relation to Abramovich’s finances were based on the Cyprus Confidential leak of more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and analysed by organisations including the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC.

events.title: 8 of the best-dressed celebrities at the CMA's Dolly Parton celebration
events.summary: Reba McEntire performs at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Jason Kempin/Getty Images Dolly Parton's legacy lives on in the music and fashion of today's biggest country stars. Many gathered in Nashville for the TV special "CMA Presents I Will Always Love You: A Celebration of Dolly Parton." Lainey Wilson, Ella Langley, and Carrie Underwood all honored Parton with their outfits. Dolly Parton's legacy sparkled over Nashville this week The Country Music Association (CMA) hosted "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration of Dolly Parton" at the Fisher Center for the Performing Arts on Wednesday night. Some of the genre's biggest stars made appearances, both performing Parton's songs onstage and walking the red carpet in outfits inspired by the music legend. These are the best-dressed stars we saw. Kelsea Ballerini looked elegant in white feathers and diamonds. Kelsea Ballerini at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration Of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Variety/Getty Images She arrived on the red carpet wearing a $1,250 draped, satin gown from Bronx Banco's bridal line. It had feather-lined bell sleeves, a low back, and a floor-length skirt. Ballerini paired it with an updo hairstyle and long diamond earrings. She looked like a Hollywood starlet and perfectly mirrored the best of Parton's famous glam . Lainey Wilson kept true to her style while also honoring Parton. Lainey Wilson at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration Of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Jason Kempin/Getty Images Wilson's signature style is pretty different from Parton's. The singer and "Yellowstone" star prefers bell-bottoms and cowboy hats to rhinestone dresses and big hairdos. Still, Wilson honored the legend with her outfit: black trousers worn with a butterfly-print duster top. She also wore cowboy boots, a matching hat, and thick western jewelry. Butterflies were famously Parton's favorite motif , as she grew up around them in Tennessee. Reba McEntire honored her friend onstage while wearing a classic country getup. Reba McEntire performs at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration Of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Jason Kempin/Getty Images McEntire performed "He's Alive" while wearing a white, caftan-style dress with a collar and long sleeves. The latter were lined with long, rhinestoned fringe, while the dress itself was embellished with a rhinestone scrollwork pattern. It was the perfect outfit choice to deliver an emotional tribute. Kristin Chenoweth wore a dress that looked like it could have come from Parton's closet. Kristin Chenoweth at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration Of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Taylor Hill/Getty Images Chenoweth walked the red carpet in a form-fitting gown covered in silver sequins. It had a mock neck, long sleeves, and a floor-length skirt. The dress resembled many of the sequined looks Parton wore throughout her career. Chenoweth paired it with delicate diamond earrings and multiple rings. Carrie Underwood chose a princess gown with subtle butterfly details. Carrie Underwood at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration Of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Jason Kempin/Getty Images Her white, strapless gown had a full skirt, a tulle overlay, and all-over butterfly appliqués in shades of pink. Underwood also wore long diamond earrings and her hair styled in waves. It was the right choice to wear both on the carpet and onstage, where Underwood performed " I Will Always Love You ." Katy Perry nodded to another of Parton's favorite fashion elements: animal print. Katy Perry at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration Of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Jason Kempin/Getty Images Perry wore a vintage Roberto Cavalli gown from 2004 for the celebration. It was sleeveless with a deep neckline and a flowing skirt, and also decorated with multiple animal prints. The dress was a daring and unique choice for the event, standing out from the sparkling white ensembles that most other celebrities wore. And because Parton wore animal print on numerous occasions, it was a fun tribute to the more daring side of her style. Ella Langley chose a minidress with a butterfly appliqué. Ella Langley at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration Of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Taylor Hill/Getty Images Langely, the country star behind the hit "Choosin' Texas," wore a pale-pink minidress with long sleeves and a plunging neckline. It was embellished with strings of beads and crystals, and a pink, bedazzled butterfly at the center of her chest. Langley was pretty and glowing on the red carpet — just like Parton always was. Hillary Scott of Lady A fame wore two of Parton's favorite things. Hillary Scott at the CMA's "I Will Always Love You: A Celebration Of Dolly Parton" in Nashville. Jason Kempin/Getty Images Scott wore a sleeveless gown with a sweetheart neckline and a thigh-high slit. While that might sound simple, the dress also featured an all-over leopard print crafted from sequins. Together, the features created a dress that reflected Parton's boldest style moments. events.title: I landed a job in Antarctica at 60 after a grueling physical examination and background check. Here's how I got the job.
events.summary: May Lee worked in Antarctica from October 2025 to February 2026 and has now returned for a new role. Courtesy of May Lee May Lee successfully applied for a role at McMurdo Station in Antarctica at age 60. Jobs at McMurdo require an extensive background and health check, and are very competitive. She told Business Insider about the nearly seven-month job process, from application to deployment. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with May Lee, a 60-year-old broadcast engineer with GreyHawk Global at McMurdo Station in Antarctica. She previously worked there as a supply technician for Amentum after spending decades at HP, most recently as a marketing and communications manager. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I was laid off from HP after 30 years, so I decided to look beyond tech jobs and pursue something different at 60. I had visited Antarctica twice for vacation and fell in love with it. At the time, I didn't know that you could work there. When I looked into it, I knew I had to apply. It's so hard to describe how amazing it is to work at McMurdo Station . If you ever get a chance to experience it, I highly recommend it. Here's what the job application process was like. I applied for 3 roles, but didn't realize how competitive it is The US National Science Foundation manages the US Antarctic Program . The body contracts out operational support to several companies, each with a specific focus. For example, Gana A'Yoo is responsible for areas like food services and waste management. In mid-April, I applied for three roles: rooms coordinator at Gana A'Yoo, service desk support technician at Grey Hawk Global, and a supply assistant supervisor at Amentum. I applied using my HP résumé, which lists my various roles at the company. On a snowmobile outing in Antarctica. Courtesy of May Lee I was turned down for the rooms coordinator role within a week or two, with an email stating that I did "not meet the minimum requirements." This came as a surprise to me. So, I started researching more about working in Antarctica — something I should have done beforehand — and learned that it's very competitive to get a job there. I read on blogs that if you don't make your résumé match the job description exactly, you get weeded out. So, I think that's what happened. A recruiter reached out to me anyway I then kind of wrote off my pursuit of a job in Antarctica. I thought maybe this just wasn't meant to be. Return from McMurdo in February 2026. Courtesy of May Lee Then, in May, a recruiter from Amentum, which offers roles in logistics and skilled trades, reached out to me, saying that my résumé appeared to be a match for what they were looking for. The job I got was a supply technician at Amentum. When asked to send my résumé by email, I updated it to make sure it matched the job description. I also received a pre-screening questionnaire about my availability, credentials, and whether I could work in the US without sponsorship. I got hired as an alternate A week later, I had a 30-minute video call with the recruiter about what the hiring process entails and more details about the job environment. This was followed a few days later by an 80-minute phone call with the hiring manager, during which they asked behavioral, situational, and competency-based questions . May Lee's previous dorm at McMurdo Station. Courtesy of May Lee I received an offer contract for an alternate position. An alternate is the backup for a primary who can't go for whatever reason. I was told that the quicker I get through the background and physical qualification (PQ) checks, the quicker I could get to the top of the alternate list. The health check is extensive Because Antarctica is so remote, they want to make sure that you're healthy. Because if you go down there and something happens, there are no medical facilities that can take care of you. Read More: I live and work in Antarctica at 60 years old. From early wakeups to nightclubs, here's what a typical day is like. In June, I received a 17-page PQ form that requested comprehensive medical and dental information. There were eight required blood tests, a physical exam, vision screening, and a dental exam, among others. Depending on your age, sex, and deployment location and term, there may be additional tests. The costs of these were reimbursable by the company. There is also a very comprehensive background check In addition to the PQ, I underwent a comprehensive government background check. I was cleared to onboard in June and was notified that I was changed to a primary in July. Often, this is because a primary has dropped out; they might've failed the PQ, even if they passed it the year before, or something in their life might've happened that requires them to stay home. Forklift training for May Lee's role as a supply technician. Courtesy of May Lee There was some back-and-forth with my PQ, which I had to resubmit after getting an updated Tdap vaccine. In September, I received the current-season influenza vaccine, and my PQ was approved. I made it to Antarctica in October I flew from San Francisco to Auckland, New Zealand , and then to Christchurch. There were a couple of days of training, and I also got outfitted with extreme-cold-weather gear. Then, after seven months of preparation, I was finally deployed to McMurdo on a Boeing C-17 Globemaster III . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Canada hit back at Trump tariffs. Now the U.S. alleges possible election interference.
events.summary: The U.S. Embassy in Canada accused Canadian leaders of "openly" describing plans to "influence American politics," doubling down on Ambassador Pete Hoekstra's claims of potential election interference. Why it matters: The accusation further deteriorates Washington's relationship with its northern neighbor under President Trump's costly trade war that's put political pressure on Republicans. Canada targeted its retaliatory tariffs on politically salient states and products ahead of the U.S. midterms. Driving the news: The embassy cited Canada's targeted tariffs as part of the influence accusations laid out in a Wednesday fact sheet . It cited remarks from Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, including an August press conference where she said Canada was "targeting products that will target states in the U.S." She added, "we're being wise and strategic to put political pressure." Joly has echoed that message throughout the trade tensions. The fact sheet also cited Joly's meeting with Democrats. She recently huddled with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker. What they're saying: Asked about the accusations during a news conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney said "all of our actions are in the interest of Canadian workers, Canadian families and the future of this economy." Zoom out: The fact sheet also singled out conservative Ontario Premier Doug Ford over a 2025 anti-tariff ad campaign featuring excerpts from a Ronald Reagan speech . It also cited Liberal MP Anthony Housefather's campaigning for Florida Democrat Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz. The memo read, "The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in U.S. elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances." Catch up quick: Hoekstra said in a recent podcast interview that American officials were "closely watching" Canada for potential election interference. Joly said last week it was "absolutely not" fair to characterize Canada's actions as election interference. Her visits, she said, were aimed to attract investments. Carney, after cheering Canada's reduced dependence on the U.S. in a speech earlier this month, joked, "Careful, they might think that's election interference," seemingly a jab at Hoekstra. Worth noting: The Trump administration has taken an increasingly antagonistic approach to Canada, from trade tensions to threats over its sovereignty . In August, Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, which straddles the U.S.-Canada border, to "Lake America." He's also continuously said Canada should become the "51st state." The big picture: Trump himself has openly weighed in on politics beyond U.S. borders, including during Canada's 2025 election campaign and ahead of Israel's elections this month. On Sunday, Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection just nine days before Israel's national vote. Go deeper: Escalated U.S.-Canada trade talks threaten fallout

events.title: Tesla is prepping a Cybercab onslaught
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Tesla says it is preparing to launch its shiny gold Cybercab in new markets outside its home of Austin, Texas, in a bid to “literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation.” “We’re starting with getting people from one place to the other, but we want to basically own transportation of any kind on Earth,” Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday. Tesla has previously shown a concept version of a multi-passenger vehicle it calls the “Robovan,” but it’s unclear if Taneja’s bombastic comments mean the company is working on other types of transportation. What was clearer on the call is that Tesla’s Cybercab expansion will begin in Dallas next month and spread to other cities by the end of this year. Tesla already operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUV in small fleets in Dallas, Houston, and the Florida cities of Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. The company also said on its earnings call that it will start selling Cybercabs to fleet operators by the end of this year . Broader expansion of the Cybercab could set up a real fight with Waymo, which is currently the market leader for robotaxis in the United States, with more than 4,000 of them deployed across more than a dozen cities. Tesla has argued that its Cybercab is cheaper and easier to build, which should allow it to undercut Waymo and other robotaxi operators on price. But the company has to reach real scale outside Austin in order to prove that point. Tesla said it’s ready thanks to a dramatic increase in the number of miles its self-driving cars have traveled in recent weeks. While that may be true, Tesla was mum on Wednesday about how much money the overall robotaxi effort is bringing in. Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the new ride-hailing business won’t be noticeable in the company’s overall financial figures until the second quarter of 2027, “and probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.” Tesla also made a change to its letter to shareholders that further obscures what little visibility there was into its robotaxi business. In Tesla’s second-quarter letter, the company included a chart for “Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles.” A close read of that chart showed a 36% decline from the first quarter of the year. In the new letter released on Wednesday, Tesla changed that chart to show “Cumulative Unsupervised Robotaxi Miles” — an indicator of how far the fleet cars are driving, whether or not they have paying riders on board. There wasn’t much more clarity on the call, either. When asked about paid robotaxi miles traveled, Taneja said the company is “seeing utilization improving,” but didn’t offer specifics. Instead, Taneja kept most of his comments generally focused on Tesla’s plans to scale the Cybercab. That included praise for Tesla’s engineering team for creating a vehicle that, according to the manufacturing team, is very easy to build — and build quickly. “They think this is one of the easiest products for them to scale in terms of manufacturing,” he said. “So scaling would not be that much of a challenge.” What might be a challenge, Taneja said, is that Tesla needs to make sure it has “all the regulatory approvals” so it can “start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them.” That echoes many previous comments from Musk, who has long claimed that “regulatory approval” was the biggest barrier to Tesla’s robotaxi plans, not technical progress. Musk has always been a bit hazy about what approvals, specifically, he felt were needed. The company has run into a regulatory hurdle this year, though. In September, just hours after Tesla formally launched its Cybercab in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into whether the vehicle complies with current federal motor vehicle safety standards. All automakers self-certify that their vehicles conform to these standards, and Tesla has claimed that the Cybercab is compliant. But it is missing features that the current standards require, like a brake pedal and side mirrors. The NHTSA has proposed removing some of these requirements, but that rule change is likely still at least a few months away. Not every Tesla executive agreed on this during Wednesday’s call. Asked about the remaining bottlenecks for a wider robotaxi rollout, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s vice president overseeing autonomy, said they are “not purely regulatory.” “It’s technology-driven,” he said. “We had initially had the robotaxi service from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., and then expanded to 10 p.m. to 11 p.m, now it’s going to be pretty soon, [to] 2 a.m. So we’re slowly expanding the availability of robotaxi, and that is driven by the capability of the AI software.

events.title: UAE ranks third globally for quality of life satisfaction among the affluent
events.summary: The UAE has been ranked among the top three nations in which investors are satisfied with the quality of life, prompting them to be confident about their financial future , a study from HSBC has found. About 83 per cent of more than 700 high-net-worth individuals surveyed in the Emirates said they were satisfied, placing the country below only Mexico and India, the London-based bank said in the report released at the UAE Wealth Investment Summit in Dubai on Thursday. The study, conducted by French research firm Ipsos, covered nearly 10,000 HNWIs across 10 markets. The UAE's satisfaction is markedly higher than the overall average of 75 per cent, as more than a quarter gave quality of life a perfect score, which was the joint-highest share of any market and well above the global average of 15 per cent, the report said. Nearly 90 per cent of those are also more confident about their financial future, it said. The survey's participants are also more active when it comes to business plans, with more than a fifth claiming they are launching, acquiring or investing in a new venture, compared to the general average of 17 per cent, HSBC said. “The UAE has built an environment where people and their wealth can thrive, and this research shows it,” said Sami Abouzahr, HSBC’s head of international wealth and premier banking for the Middle East and UAE. “Investors here are confident, ambitious and internationally connected, and they are planning for the long term.” The HSBC study also suggested half of UAE investors expect to receive a significant financial inheritance, compared to 43 per cent globally, while about 58 per cent expect to leave a significant financial legacy to their heirs or other causes. Among those who expect to inherit and were able to estimate its value, the average expected inheritance is around Dh2 million ($545,000), about twice the global figure, with recipients typically expecting to receive it around the age of 52, HSBC said. “A significant transfer of wealth between generations is under way in the UAE and families want to get it right,” said Craig Worobec, HSBC’s head of wealth and premier solutions for the Middle East and UAE. “That means planning early, having open conversations about what wealth is for, and preparing the next generation with the skills and networks to use it well.” Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and the flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country is a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. Dubai and Abu Dhabi have been ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth, despite the fallout from geopolitical tension and hostility, London-based consultancy Savills said in a report last week . Also last week, a study from Boston Consulting Group showed that net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade, despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East . “With a highly international population and wealth that spans several countries, the UAE has become a base from which investors manage and grow their wealth around the world,” HSBC said.

events.title: Meta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax bill
events.summary: Chief executive agrees to remain in California for eight years even if state brings in one-off 5% wealth tax Meta has struck a deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot a possible California wealth tax targeting billionaires. The social media company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp revealed on Wednesday night that the arrangement would keep its chief executive living in California , where Meta’s headquarters are located. Under the deal, Zuckerberg will receive new shares that could be sold to potentially foot a multibillion-dollar tax bill in the event that California passes a one-off billionaire tax. In return, he is committed to remain a resident of the state, or wherever Meta maintains its base, for eight years. Californians will vote early next month on Proposition 40, a one-off 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state. Zuckerberg, worth $239bn (£180bn) according to Forbes, told Meta he was considering moving his primary residence elsewhere because Prop 40 could expose him to a massive tax liability, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay it. In response, Meta is creating a new class of non-voting shares via a two-for-one stock split for all existing shareholders. This will allow Zuckerberg to sell some of these new class C shares to pay a potential tax bill, without diluting his control of the company. Recent polling has shown that Prop 40 remains short of majority support with voters. Tech billionaires have been spending heavily to fight the measure , including the Google co-founder Sergey Brin, the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel and the former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. Rohit Khanna, the US congressman representing California’s 17th congressional district, has described Prop 40 as a choice between standing with the working class or the oligarchs. “Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay,” Khanna wrote in the Guardian last week . “In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened.” Meta also reported a 26% rise in revenues for the last quarter to $64.6bn, beating expectations of $63.3bn. But profits fell by 37% to $13bn, dragged down by a $9.9bn charge related to Meta’s lawsuit over child protection and social media addiction failings. The company’s shares slid by more than 6% when trading opened on Wall Street on Thursday, helping to drag the tech-focused Nasdaq index down 2.5% amid a wider selloff of AI-linked stocks. In a separate case, on Wednesday a judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $25bn following a trial that found the company had misled the public about how it handled Facebook user data. Meta also revealed that it had cut its headcount to 66,775 at the end of September, 15% fewer than a year ago. Reuters contributed to this report.

events.title: Spotify confirms Family Plan crackdown, but calls it a ‘routine improvement’
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Spotify confirmed the reports of its crackdown on Family Plan sharing during its third-quarter call with investors, calling its new method “a routine improvement” to its existing verification tools. Over the past several days, reports had surfaced indicating that Spotify was rolling out a “QR code verification” method, where the app would prompt members on its Family Plan to verify they lived with the plan manager by scanning a QR code. This code appears on the plan manager’s phone, which the plan member then needs to scan with their own phone, according to Spotify’s support documentation . Plan members have seven days to complete the QR code after getting a notification, which means they could be out of luck if they live outside the home and aren’t planning a return visit anytime soon. If the verification window is missed, they won’t be able to join another Family or Duo plan for 12 months, but would instead have to shift to an individual plan that they pay for themselves. The move is meant to boost subscriptions to Spotify’s profitable Premium plans, rather than allowing adult children or friends who live apart from gaming the system to get a cheaper plan by splitting a Family Plan subscription. During the earnings call, an investor asked a question about the crackdown and what it means, but Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström downplayed the change, calling it a “routine improvement,” not a “crackdown.” “Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base,” said Norström. “As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time,” he added. The executive said that the company’s attempt to better verify its users is not something that would have an end date or would ever be complete, but would be considered an ongoing routine improvement. events.title: Investors break down how founders can raise a Series A today
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. In today’s market, no single metric defines what a Series A is, or how to raise one. At this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt , three investors offered founders advice on raising one, and one of them tacked on a warning. With money pouring into AI and revenue numbers being inflated to justify sky-high valuations, a correction could come as soon as 2027. The warning came from Shailendra Singh, a managing director at Peak XV, who spoke alongside Jahanvi Sardana, a partner at Index Ventures, and Janelle Teng Wade, a partner at Bessemer. “Seed and venture, I’ve never seen it as dysfunctional as it is now,” Singh said, adding that the current market is one of the hardest to raise in that he has seen. “The burden is high to convince any top firm that you are amongst the few special companies that can break out, and then the dispersion is very high on the terms you might get, how much capital you can raise, and what terms you can raise it,” he continued. In fact, it’s common now to see a company trying to close a round with as many as three different prices at once. “[I]’s a crazy sign of market froth,” he said. “We’re calling it the ‘tranchopalooza,’” Sardana added, referring to the way rounds are being split into tranches, or separate chunks. Beyond the warnings, the investors laid out what they look for in a Series A pitch, including, first, a persuasive story about why a founder has a shot at building a big company. “Founders who can attract very high-quality talent have an advantage,” Singh added. What a founder builds matters, too. Teng Wade said capital is flowing into areas such as defense, robotics, and AI infrastructure. She also noted that foundational model companies are moving toward vertical integration (taking on more of the stack themselves), but there’s still room for newer players, including neo-clouds that rent out AI computing power and neo-labs focused on AI research. Metrics, meanwhile, still help a lot, but they are less defined than they used to be, especially in an era like AI where it’s incredibly expensive to run a company. Teng Wade gave an example of how her firm evaluated Anthropic in its early days, when its margins were negative, and it was spending heavily on compute. One partner on her team, however, felt that AI was going to be “bigger than everything we’ve ever expected in terms of price premium on the frontier models,” she said, “becoming a substitute for other types of software.” The logic was that even with money-losing margins, the market would be big enough to pay off if the company became one of the top three players. Anthropic is now reportedly preparing an IPO at a valuation of around $2 trillion . It told investors this month it was profitable on an adjusted basis , though that measure excludes some costs. The investors also spoke about the importance of honesty in a market like this, where inflated annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers are swirling alongside headline valuations. “I tell founders, If you ever show a chart which shows cumulative revenue or cumulative ARR, that is a massive red flag,” Singh said. “It means that your time series data is not good because cumulative data is a big lie.” Added Singh: It’s important for a company to be intellectually honest in how they are presenting and engaging in bull cycles.” Singh said the market is full of “false positives” because “it can’t be that every company is going to be successful. This is as optimistic as I’ve seen the venture world in two decades, and normally it’s a sign. I think 2027 will be different. I think we will see a correction.” Finally, the panelists were asked to give founders at least one piece of parting advice. Singh went first, reminding founders that building a company is one of the “most excruciatingly difficult things” one can do. And with that, “deal with it,” he said. He also urged founders not to rush into something, to watch out for weak product-market fit, and always hold the bar very high for what they are trying to solve. Sardana said it is important to know how to pitch but that founders should be careful not to let that dictate what they build. “It feels like [founders are] deciding what to build based on what’s getting funded, which is really scary,” she continued. Teng Wade, meanwhile, said her typical advice of telling founders to be conservative with their projections and requests hasn’t really held up. “I would say just be audacious in your ask,” she now says, and see how the market responds, “and then you can tailor from there.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: The US Army is putting laser weapons to work, and officials say the safety rules are simple: don't look down the barrel
events.summary: Directed-energy weapons have seen recent use at the US southern border. US Department of Defense photo by Spc. Adrianna Douglas US Army officials say laser weapons require surprisingly little protective gear. Troops should stay at least 10 feet from targets and never look into the laser. The Army wants lasers that work on different vehicles and can be learned in minutes. US Army officials say the safety protocols for soldiers using lasers are surprisingly simple: don't stand too close to the target and don't look into the weapon. Directed-energy weapons are seeing more operational use, particularly at the US southern border, where the Army has employed them against cartel-linked drones. The service envisions these systems operating on different vehicles and being easy for soldiers to learn and use safely. At the Association of the United States Army, or AUSA, convention last week in Washington, DC, officials and industry partners spoke on developments in directed-energy weapons. Asked about personal protective equipment, or PPE, and any concerns about specular reflection from lasers, Kirk Williams, chief engineer of the Army's directed energy project office, said the rules were similar in some respects to those for other weapons. "Well, the short and sweet of that answer is: unless you're within ten feet of the target, a specular reflection is eye-safe, so the soldiers don't need the eye protection from the laser," he said, explaining that "it's like any other weapons system: don't look into it." "We tell the soldiers the same thing about an M-16. Don't look down the barrel. Same thing with lasers, don't look down the barrel." Specular reflections occur when light bounces off a surface. In the case of a laser weapon , reflected light can bounce off a targeted vehicle or drone. While the target absorbs most of the energy, some reflections might stray and cause eye or skin damage to soldiers near the target. Williams said that part of the reason the Army likes these weapons is their relatively low risk to soldiers and the limited need for protective gear. "They are safe," he said, adding that "the great thing about a laser is we can also turn them off instantaneously." The weapons also have safeguards that shut them down if there is a risk of hitting something other than the intended target. The Army wants to disseminate lasers and directed-energy weapons across units with easy training and intuitive controls. US Department of Defense photo by Sgt. Dominic Atlas During the panel, Williams and others also talked about the Army's priorities for deploying more laser weapons, an area of growing importance for the Army and the broader US military. Brig. Gen. Guy Yelverton, the capability program executive for defensive fires, said the service wants to integrate high-energy lasers onto "any vehicle in the motorpool." He said the Army's Enduring High Energy Laser, or E-HEL, is mounted on a sled, allowing it to be integrated onto multiple types of vehicles. The E-HEL is an Army directed-energy weapon  program using AeroVironment's LOCUST laser system. Yelverton said that making weapons compatible with different vehicles and usable by soldiers across military specialties will allow the Army to deploy them more widely. The general said that this flexibility would allow the Army to deploy laser weapons "across all Army formations," giving commanders more options for where to put them and which soldiers should operate them. "It's a great dilemma to have," he said. Officials also said part of disseminating the weapons is making them easy to train on. "Most of our training sessions, we can train somebody in like, five minutes, to be able to use this system and start shooting things down," Williams said, adding that using standard controllers like those for an Xbox made it intuitive. The Army's testing of laser weapons and other counter-drone systems at the southern border has reinforced the idea that the US will need layered defenses to counter a range of drone threats. Drug cartels are increasingly using drones to support operations, and the Army has already used lasers to shoot some down . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: 'I wasn't thinking straight' says five jobs civil servant
events.summary: Kashim Chowdhury wears dark sunglasses, a hat, hoody and gloves as he arrives at court. His face is largely obscured. A civil servant accused of fraudulently juggling multiple public sector jobs has told the court he "wasn't thinking straight" when he allegedly misled future bosses about his employment status. Kashim Chowdhury said he was "in a panic" when he applied for a job at the Department of Health (DHSC), failing to declare he was already working at the Department for the Environment (Defra). The prosecution said he already had three full-time jobs at the time, including roles at the London Borough of Tower Hamlets and East London NHS Trust. The 55-year-old, who is from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. Chowdhury said he was "in a panic'' because he feared losing his Defra job and was uncertain about his future. He told the jury he was "not paying attention, I was not thinking straight',' when filling out the application. The prosecution said Chowdhury held five jobs on full-time salaries at the height of the alleged deceit. Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears Published 14 October Civil servant admits he 'made mistakes' juggling five government jobs Published 1 day ago In the spring of 2023, he was employed by the Defra, the UK Health Security Agency, the Food Standards Agency, the Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. The jury was told that throughout this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days. Each job paid a full-time wage, with Chowdhury paid £11,000 for a single month's work in 2023. Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work-from-home culture which began during the Covid-19 pandemic to hide his multiple jobs and took sick leave from some employers to manage the workload. But Chowdhury told the court he had not wanted the jobs at the DHSC, Department for Business and Trade and the Home Office. He told the jury: ''I sent out a flurry of these applications. The offers for these jobs came all at once. I had discussions with my line managers saying that I did not want these jobs and explained my circumstances. These were all short term and probationary and my priority was to look after my mother.'' He added that around May and June 2022, his mother's health "deteriorated". He said: "That overwhelmed me at the time. It just destroyed me." Chowdhury described the jobs as his "lifeline at the time". "They gave me a link to the outside world and were a distraction from what was going on in my personal life, looking after my mum at that time." The prosecution alleges Chowdhury managed to keep his overlapping jobs secret because he worked entirely remotely. He told his employers he was the sole carer for his elderly mother and the prosecution alleges he "exploited this opportunity". events.title: NVIDIA Unveils Minerva to Bring End-to-End Observability for AI Factories
events.summary: Launched today, NVIDIA Minerva is an AIOps platform built to help teams find problems earlier and keep AI factories productive. It brings together telemetry from infrastructure and AI workloads, then applies purpose-built AI models to turn that data into timely, actionable insight. AI factories are among the most complex operations in the world, with vast numbers of GPUs working across high-speed networks to train models and serve AI applications. At that scale, a single degraded component can slow an entire job. The warning signs may be easy to miss, such as a GPU running hotter than its peers or an NVMe drive losing performance under load. The platform focuses on AI factory yield, a measure of the useful work infrastructure produces through GPU hours, goodput, cluster uptime and token production. Delivering a Dynamic View of an AI Factory Traditional monitoring tools often divide the data center into separate views. Networking, compute, site reliability and machine learning teams each see a different part of the operation. Minerva connects those signals across NVIDIA GPUs, networking, storage, schedulers and workloads. With these signals, Minerva builds a dynamic knowledge graph that logically maps the infrastructure — GPUs, SuperNICs, switches and cables — and the jobs running on it. This context helps operators trace a slow training job to the component affecting it, even across a factory with hundreds of thousands of GPUs. It analyzes billions of data points per hour using supervised and unsupervised machine learning. It learns normal behavior, detects previously unseen anomalies, predicts emerging failures and correlates related events based on the factory’s topology. Instead of sending every symptom to an operator, it can group an event storm into a focused incident with a likely root cause. Minerva comes with a native AI assistant and connects to external agentic AI tools. This adds a natural-language interface grounded in live telemetry. Operators can investigate cluster health and receive recommended remediation through conversation. Teams can keep a person in the loop to manually implement fixes or connect Minerva to automation through infrastructure application programming interfaces and external systems. Results That Maximize AI Factory Yield The ability to correlate workload and infrastructure issues along with its agentic AI capabilities help simplify AI factory operations. Instead of dealing with a blizzard of alerts, Minerva aggregates related problems into a single actionable item. This allows AIOps teams to move from reactive to proactive maintenance. And all of this helps AI factories maximize GPU uptime. Minerva delivers value for the key metrics AI factories focus on: Longer time between interruptions : Minerva spots trouble before it happens, so jobs run longer without incident. Faster time to repair : When an incident does happen, Minerva pinpoints the problem, leading to a significantly quicker resolution. Greater insight : Modern AI infrastructure generates a flood of data; Minerva filters it out, leaving only the handful of alerts that actually matter. IREN is among the NVIDIA partners using Minerva to optimize its AI factories. “As we scale our AI factories, the key to providing the best service for our customers is maximizing the productivity of our GPUs,” said Denis Skrinnikoff, chief technology officer of IREN. “NVIDIA Minerva gives our operations team one view across the network, the GPUs and the jobs running on them, so we focus more on proactive maintenance rather than troubleshooting. That visibility strengthens our operating model for the infrastructure we’re building next.” Joining IREN , Aolani , Bitdeer AI , IBM , Jio, Lambda , Quake AI and Tesla plan to deploy Minerva. events.title: Lawyers for Trump, BBC battle over depositions in president's $10 billion defamation case
events.summary: Lawyers for the BBC and Donald Trump are in court arguing over whether former special counsel Jack Smith should be deposed in Trump’s $10 billion defamation case against the British broadcaster MIAMI -- Lawyers for the BBC and for Donald Trump were tussling in court Thursday over whether former special counsel Jack Smith should be deposed in the president’s $10 billion defamation case against the broadcaster — a possibility that Trump strongly opposes. In a hearing before U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett in Miami, the parties were also expected to address the thorny issue of when Trump himself will be made available for deposition. BBC asked the judge last week to compel Trump to appear after they said he canceled an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, citing “matters of national importance.” The British broadcaster says Trump is trying to delay his appearance until January 2027. The judge has threatened sanctions if Trump fails to comply with the court's schedule. Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December, seeking $10 billion in damages. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, “Trump: A Second Chance.” The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. But BBC has denied Trump’s claims that it defamed him. To bolster its defense, the broadcaster subpoenaed Smith earlier this month. Trump’s lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear. “Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter,” they argued in the filing. “He was not present when President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech … was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump’s state of mind at the time the Speech was given.” Trump's side also argued that “Smith’s testimony would be duplicative,” because he published he lengthy report on the events of January 6 and also testified for many hours. “The entirety of his testimony is publicly available,” it argued. The BBC countered, in the same filing, that there were few more knowledgeable sources about the events of Jan. 6 than Smith, who studied and investigated them for years. Rep. But as long as he chooses to maintain the case, he cannot commit the fundamental injustice of preventing the BBC from obtaining the evidence it needs to robustly defend itself on every element of his claim…” A key question also remains: When will Trump himself appear? In a filing Oct. 13, BBC lawyers said they first requested dates for a deposition in July, and followed up repeatedly, with both sides eventually agreeing on Oct. 16. After weeks of silence, they wrote, “Plaintiff’s counsel responded on September 28, 2026, indicating that ‘the President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance’ and that counsel would ‘endeavor to provide you with a replacement date by the end of this week.’ He did not.” They said they were then told that Trump “has no availability whatsoever for a deposition” before discovery is set to close on Dec. 18, and that Trump would instead make himself available the second or third week of January. “Two months of discovery remaining, the BBC still has not been able to depose, and does not even have a schedule to depose, the most central figure in this case: Plaintiff himself,” attorney Charles D. events.title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs as bank’s bosses hail AI productivity advances
events.summary: Equating to the loss of 5% of its 93,000 global staff, job cuts come as bank announces jump in quarterly profits Barclays is cutting 5,000 jobs as part of wider cost-saving plans that its bosses say are being driven by advances in AI. The job cuts will mean losing about 5% of the bank’s 93,000 global staff, with executives confirming they had already cut 1,000 workers since the start of the year. The bank’s chief financial officer, Anna Cross, told reporters on Thursday that the job cuts were part of plans to save more than £1.1bn in 2027. “These actions involve an expected reduction of circa 5,000 full-time employees. Around 60% of the group actions relate to support functions, including fewer developers, as AI makes our people more productive.” When asked how many of the total job cuts would be directly linked to advances in AI, the chief executive, CS Venkatakrishnan, said the bank had been making “deep investments” in technology and simplifying its processes. “That is driving the bulk of the efficiency gains that you’ve seen so far. AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future,” Venkatakrishnan said, calling AI the “icing on the cake” to modernising the bank’s technology. Sharon Graham, the general secretary of the Unite union, said Barclays workers “deserve better”. She added: “The company is using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce. Employers should be focused on upgrading employees’ skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach.” The news comes months after another UK-headquartered bank, Standard Chartered, announced plans to cut more than 7,000 jobs in the next four years as it ramps up the use of AI. It will mean slashing about 15% of its back-office roles by 2030. Barclays also announced plans to hand a further £500m to investors, taking the total amount given to shareholders since January – through buybacks and dividends – to £2.8bn. It came as the lender reported £2.3bn in pre-tax profits over the July to September quarter, up 12% from £2.1bn during the same period last year. The strong financial performance will probably to be used to justify the expected increase in bank taxes in the 28 October budget, as Andy Burnham’s government looks for ways to raise revenue to help fund cost of living support programmes. When asked whether the bank might consider tilting assets or investment out of the UK and to the US – where it also has operations – as a result of higher levies, Venkatakrishnan said Barclays would be able to absorb them. “I recognise that the chancellor and the government … have to balance a host of considerations,” he said, adding that Barclays shared their goal to prompt growth. “This is not a question of a financial hit to us. It’s bearable. It is a question of proportion and it’s a question of market signalling. But … I deeply respect the responsibility that the chancellor has and he has our full support and backing.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Barclays’ strong performance included a 6% rise in net interest income at its UK retail banking operations, to £2bn. The figure has become a flashpoint for campaigners pushing for a bank tax. It accounts for how much money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits, and is linked to interest rates, which have been rising as the Iran war has driven up inflation expectations. The Trades Union Congress, which has been campaigning for a bank tax increase, said lenders needed to contribute more at a time when people were struggling with household bills. The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, said: “Barclays’ bumper profits aren’t an anomaly. All the big banks are doing exceptionally well … Britain’s big four banks have made £200bn in profit since 2021. They can – and should – pay more tax.” Healey has promised that next week’s budget will support Britain’s entrepreneurs, and focus on cutting the “cost of business”. He told the Times : “I want to be a chancellor who backs business in Britain making a profit, those entrepreneurs who in the end are the ones who challenge the status quo, come up with innovative ideas and are trying, some of them through sheer bloody-mindedness, to keep going through these sorts of pressures, which is what they’ve done.”

events.title: Paid parental leave doesn't strain most employers, survey finds
events.summary: Employers might be overestimating the downsides of offering paid parental leave and underestimating the costs of losing employees by foregoing it, argues economist Emily Oster in a new report based on research she conducted with the advocacy group Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies America. A survey of employers in four states without public-sponsored leave programs — Arkansas, Illinois, Mississippi, and Nebraska — found that 55% of employers reported no additional costs from offering it. In 77% of cases, employers said existing staff absorbed the work of the new parent. Overall, respondents with experience offering parental leave were twice as likely to say the benefits outweighed costs (47% vs. 23%). Some employers cited worker retention as a reason they offered it. “This data suggests it is far more manageable for employers than many people fear,” said Oster, also the CEO of ParentData, a data-driven parenting and pregnancy advice platform. Still, 17% of employers who offered leave said it created “significant financial strain.” The study did not specify the length of the paid leave or examine if there were adverse retention effects on other employees within the company. Oster suggested states should consider tax credits to entice employers to offer parental leave, and should try to increase public awareness of her survey’s results, especially among small businesses. Healthy Moms, Healthy Babies’ push for paid leave research comes as part of a campaign to spend $100 million over five years to advance research and policies to push down the US maternal mortality rate by half, according to Robin Reck, the group’s executive director.

events.title: Vape critics accuse RJ Reynolds of marketing to kids
events.summary: An RJ Reynolds subsidiary is promoting fruit-flavored vaping pods with colorful scented mailers that critics say are similar to the “scratch and sniff” ads the tobacco giant agreed to suspend 20 years ago, as part of a settlement with 39 states that had accused the company of violating an agreement to refrain from marketing its flavored cigarettes to kids. “It appears they haven’t learned their lesson, and they’re now using that same playbook for a different type of tobacco product, which also coincidentally remains the most commonly used tobacco product among US youth,” said Brian King, a former top FDA tobacco regulator who now works as the executive vice president for US programs at the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids. His organization flagged the materials to state and federal authorities. The company said the advertising for Vuse Pro berry, fresh mint, peach, and watermelon pods was only sent to existing adult nicotine consumers whose ages had been verified, and who had opted in to Vuse-related communications. “Our products are for adult tobacco and nicotine consumers only,” a spokesperson said. “We do not want youth accessing or using them, and that principle is fundamental to how we market responsibly and in compliance with applicable laws and regulations.” Flavored vape policy came to a head earlier this year when President Donald Trump pressured then-FDA Commissioner Marty Makary to authorize fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adults despite the agency chief’s concerns about the potential impact on children . Shortly after, the FDA adopted a policy that effectively allowed for the sale of many flavored e-cigarettes that were still under agency review. “It’s critical that the US government and state attorneys general take notice and take action,” King said. “We should not be sitting idly by as companies flagrantly flout the laws using tactics we know drive youth appeal of tobacco products.” — David Lim

events.title: Barclays cutting 5,000 jobs as it increases reliance on AI
events.summary: Barclays is cutting around 5,000 staff as it introduces more artificial intelligence (AI) into its work processes. The banking group said 1,000 posts had already been closed and it expects a further reduction of 4,000 to be complete by the end of this year, amounting to around 5% of its global workforce. The bank's cost reductions are focused on its UK retail bank, but some back office functions for the UK are done in India, where a significant proportion of the job cuts are expected to fall. Barclays said the changes were the result of an ongoing modernisation plan, with the use of AI being the "icing on the cake" of its strategy. Although not all of the cuts are due to AI, their scale will prompt further concern over the impact of the new technology. Company spending on AI is increasing along with claims new tools can replace some of the basic tasks currently done by staff such as administrative and programming work. HSBC, Standard Chartered and Danske Bank have also flagged AI-related job cuts this year. "It is a hot button topic," said AJ Bell investment analyst, Russ Mould. However, banks had not yet made big moves towards the widespread introduction of AI and they would be considering the implications for security and customer service before implementing AI technology to make financial savings, he said. "Any company at any time needs to keep on top of its cost base," he said. "It will be intriguing to see what other banks say in their results in the coming weeks. Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite union that represents banking sector workers said the company was "using AI as an excuse to discard its loyal and long-suffering workforce". "Employers should be focussed on upgrading employees' skills so that they remain employed as new technology changes the workplace. Instead, Barclays is guilty of taking a short-term, kneejerk approach," she said. Barclays is reaching the end of a three year cost-cutting programme focused primarily on its UK retail banking arm, although the investment banking division is also affected. AJ Bell's Russ Mould said despite "reaching for the AI lever" Barclays had failed to match expectations with its financial results. Barclays also revealed it made £2.3bn profit in the three months to September, higher than the same period a year ago, but slightly less than forecast. Barclays Group chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan said the job cuts were the result of significant investment it is making in technology to simplify and improve its business. "AI has an important role to play and may have a more important role to play in the future. "We will employ the AI at scale," he said. "But AI is the icing on the cake not the cake. "Because you need to do the infrastructure build to get the benefits of AI." Barclays said around 60% of the job cuts will fall within its support functions, including among developers. Will Howlett, financials analyst at Quilter Cheviot said the cuts illustrated "how significantly AI and automation could reshape the banking industry over the next few years". "Banks have spent heavily on technology for years, but we are increasingly reaching the point where that investment translates into fewer people being required to run the business," he said. Barclays said it expects its efficiency measures to deliver a further £1.1bn of savings in 2027. How has AI changed your job or the type of work your do? events.title: U.S. refineries have been running at very high rates in 2026
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Weekly Petroleum Status Report The U.S. refinery fleet has run at higher-than-normal rates this year, with refinery utilization averaging more than 95% of capacity between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998. Tight global product supplies this year have boosted margins for petroleum products, particularly for diesel , incentivizing the increased run rates. Since 1991, U.S. refinery utilization has averaged 92% from May to September, compared with 88% across the other seven months. U.S. refineries tend to run at their highest rates between May and September to boost supply of gasoline for the peak demand season in the summer months. Distillate demand, by contrast, peaks in the fall and winter . Because refineries produce a combination of gasoline and distillates, high summer refinery utilization usually leads to an increase in distillate inventories before seasonal refinery maintenance and the peak distillate demand season. This year the refinery runs were driven largely by tight global supplies for distillate fuel oil, leading to high international demand for U.S. distillate fuel oil exports. While refinery utilization was the highest since 1998, total U.S. refinery output was only the highest since 2019 because refining capacity has decreased by 4% since then. In the first 3 weeks of October, U.S. refinery utilization decreased from its summer highs but remained above the five-year (2021–2025) seasonal average.
