events.title: Data and AI agents give a lift to TK Elevator service technicians
events.summary: DÜSSELDORF, Germany — Torben Teichmann, a service technician for TK Elevator , arrives at an office building. To do maintenance on an elevator, he dons his hard hat, safety glasses and gloves and takes out the tools he needs to access the parts of the elevator the public rarely sees. In the past, Teichmann might have needed to manually find information: ask around to find the elevator, track down the notebook containing handwritten service notes and search through hundreds of pages of technical manuals. He might have discovered he needed other tools, requiring trips back to his car. Once the work was complete, he wrote up his notes, usually in his car, “and it’s not so comfortable to write there.” Today, however, an agentic AI app, created with Microsoft Foundry and Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models , briefs Teichmann through his phone or tablet about the elevator before he even enters the building. He knows which tools to take with him. He knows which elevator, on which floor, and what the issue is — whether it’s regular maintenance or a service call for a problematic door, for example. On his phone, he can search digital manuals or the previous service history of the elevator. “I love AI. It’s really easy. (…) I’m the boss at the job site and the AI is my buddy that gives advice.” Torben Teichmann, a service technician for TK Elevator. Photo by Max Brunnert for Microsoft. Afterward, another AI voice agent asks him questions about the work he has performed, which he can explain in his own words. The debriefing agent records Teichmann’s answers without requiring any writing or typing. It asks follow-up questions if more detail is needed. The exchange works in both directions. The assistant draws on information collected from earlier visits, while Teichmann’s spoken debrief adds his experience to the record for colleagues who may service the equipment later. In the end, his debriefing notes are essential. Not just for him but for future generations of technicians. As TKE has 25,000 highly qualified service technicians globally, there are significant learnings from other parts of the world Teichmann can draw upon. In turn, his learnings will help colleagues across Germany and in other parts of the world. “I love AI,” Teichmann says. “It’s really easy. The best is it’s information I need now,” he adds, pointing his finger to emphasize the urgency . “I’m the boss at the job site and the AI is my buddy that gives advice.” The agents draw on a digital foundation TKE has developed over the past decade by connecting elevators and escalators to the secure cloud and bringing together the connected-equipment data, service information and technical documentation using Microsoft Azure. Based in Düsseldorf, TK Elevator (TKE) manufactures, installs and services elevators and escalators, called “units” in industry parlance. Once purchased, those units are the property of the building owner. TKE has service contracts to maintain them, much the way an individual buys a car and takes it to the dealer for annual checkups. Units can last for decades, so maintenance plays an important role at TKE, whose 25,000 service technicians care for 1.4 million units globally. The work is largely invisible when everything is running. But when an elevator breaks down, it quickly affects how people move through their day. TKE says its units carry 1.5 billion passengers a day. “Our equipment is infrastructure critical,” says Christian Fongern, CEO of TKE Germany. “Imagine in an airport, in a hospital or in an office, an elevator or escalator is not working. This has tremendous impact on the people in that building. Our utmost target is to keep the elevators running. Uptime is our mission critical statement here, and service is the heart of our business.” Most of the work is regular maintenance; not every service call involves a mechanical failure. Everyday use can also cause problems. For example, physical force applied to elevator doors or buttons, chewing gum deposited under an escalator handrail, all manner of small items (keys, coins, baby pacifiers) falling through the gap by the elevator door. Birds and mice manage to enter and make a mess. Dirt tracked in by so many shoes is one of the biggest problems, clogging the door rails or blocking a sensor. Whether the visit is planned or not, AI agents are intended to make the work easier by helping technicians find relevant information more quickly. TKE began digitally connecting elevators and escalators around a decade ago, using sensors and digital controllers to collect information about how the equipment was operating. From the start, it brought that information together in a central data platform using Microsoft Azure , ⁠⁠ Azure IoT and ⁠ Azure Databricks and built it out further in partnership with Microsoft Industry Solutions Engineering , now called Microsoft Frontier Company . Creating a common data environment was particularly important as TKE added different types of equipment through acquisitions. That meant servicing units made by other manufacturers, as well as introducing its digital-native EOX and HELIX elevators. More recently, generative AI has started to allow the company to draw on information that does not sit neatly in operational systems, including technical documents and technicians’ service notes. “Everything we did before was on structured data,” says Christian Jung, head of digital data and AI foundation at TK Elevator. “It was either IoT data or enterprise data sitting in systems already. But we were not able to leverage data from unstructured sources.” Sensor readings can show what an elevator is doing. But much of the knowledge needed to diagnose a problem may be elsewhere: in a technical manual, a previous technician’s notes or a description of what happened during an earlier visit. Generative AI allows TKE to extract, search and draw connections across these sources. “We were able to give technical guidance to technicians on how to fix a problem,” Jung says. For example, the same models of elevators or escalators in different buildings may get very different usage and service history — useful information when it’s time to maintain or repair a unit. Other context — the location of the unit, the business hours, the specific floor having a problem — can save a service technician significant time and frustration. It’s all the kind of information that generative AI can process easily but that was difficult to gather and share before. Collecting the data was only the first step. TKE created nine digital operations centers, or DOCs, where data analysts and technical specialists look for patterns that could help technicians identify emerging problems or prioritize maintenance. Tobias Lüsebrink heads digital transformation for TKE Germany and works at the DOC in Berlin, where data analysts and technical elevator experts work closely to interpret data and find patterns.

events.title: Brazil's energy course may hold after election, but Amazon at risk
events.summary: Brazil’s energy path could change less than environmentalists expect if right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro wins Sunday’s presidential election. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s administration has celebrated new oil discovery and exploration efforts, marking a difference from some regional leftist allies. Lawmakers from the candidates’ respective parties also found much agreement when debating a critical minerals law that centers domestic value addition earlier this year. One area where the pair may diverge, however, is on the Amazon: Brazilian economist Monica de Bolle said the enforcement of existing environmental laws could weaken under Bolsonaro, whose father presided over the loss of more than 11 million acres of rainforest. A nearly $3 billion takeover of a Brazilian rare earth mining firm by USA Rare Earths—which the US government holds a stake in— also hangs in the balance: Lula opposed it, and will likely try to use a new law to change the terms of the deal if he remains in office, according to de Bolle. — Eugenia Perozo

events.title: Climate talks are failing
events.summary: Tim’s view Climate diplomacy is deeply broken. The latest dire United Nations projection, published on Wednesday, stressed that the ambitions to limit global warming adopted a decade ago in Paris are all but out of reach , absent an urgent economic and political pivot that appears nowhere on the horizon. Blowing past 1.5℃ of warming is inevitable, and even the most far-fetched techniques possible to claw temperatures back down probably won’t return it to that level in the future. Warming is instead on track to reach 2.8℃ this century, the report said. And, perhaps even more alarmingly, the report found that even if all countries fulfill the climate plans they’ve spent the past decade honing through the UN negotiating process — a very big if — warming will only be limited to 2.6℃. Setting adequate goals, nevermind achieving them, is itself apparently impossible. Unsurprisingly, the report lays a lot of blame on the US, which saw its emissions rise more than any other country in the past year. But the bigger consequence of the US withdrawal from the Paris process — which will continue with COP31 in Türkiye in a few weeks — is that its leadership was evidently important in maintaining a strong centralized platform for collective action. Instead, Eurasia Group analyst María José Valverde wrote this week, talks have splintered into a miasma of bilateral one-off deals that, collectively, are no more likely to produce stronger climate outcomes and that render “negotiations increasingly unproductive” and COP summits “progressively irrelevant,” especially as governments and companies grapple with a cascading series of energy crises. Türkiye has a chance to change the course. Ankara’s advantage is that its central goal for the summit — accelerating electrification — is also a key principle of energy security. But it’s not enough, on its own, to put Paris back within reach. Notable China is planning to frame tariffs against some of its clean technology as a major obstacle for global climate action in the upcoming COP summit.

events.title: The internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it? | Chris Stokel-Walker
events.summary: The internet has broken – again. Shouldn’t the tech firms that make billions from it pay to fix it? I’ve been banging the drum about these vulnerabilities for years. It will take more than a handful of exhausted developers to keep us safe P arts of the internet are going dark. In the Netherlands, government websites, including its digital ID login service, have become unavailable. Finland has taken public services offline, and Wikimedia, the organisation behind Wikipedia, has switched off some of its systems too. This sounds like the results of a cyber-attack. In most instances, however, the people running the sites deliberately switched them off because the alternative – keeping them online – was too risky. The future is here, and suddenly much of our digital infrastructure is looking very fragile. The websites were turned off because of two serious security vulnerabilities in PHP , a programming language that is used by about 70% of websites that we can track. Those vulnerabilities in effect gave hackers an open window through which to climb and loot everything within. That could mean an attacker getting into an online shop, stealing customers’ addresses and passwords, or changing its checkout page to harvest card details. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre advised organisations that were unable to update immediately to consider taking their systems offline. It’s very tricky to get people to care about something quite so techy. PHP is a tricky abbreviation – even explaining what it stands for (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) is complicated, because it’s recursive. And how it helps the web work is also difficult to explain: a good analogy is it’s like the back-of-house team in a restaurant: your browser puts in an order, and PHP handles the cooking and delivers the meal. In any case, what matters is that you’ve almost certainly used websites powered by it this week. I’ve been reporting on scares like these in our digital architecture for more than a decade, and the underlying problem barely changes. In 2014, I wrote about Heartbleed , a vulnerability in OpenSSL, the software that helps keep communications across the internet secure. It was up to two men named Steve – working for OpenSSL on a shoestring budget and shouldering an awful lot of responsibility – to keep us from disaster. Twelve years later, it feels like we’re still having the same conversation. Heartbleed wasn’t the end of it. In 2021 I reported on a dangerous flaw in Log4j , a seemingly mundane tool that records what happens inside computer systems. Then three years later we had XZ Utils , a tool for shrinking file sizes used on Linux computers into which someone had deliberately planted a backdoor. In each of these incidents, small teams working for the public good recognised the problem, acted, and averted disaster. Each one of these incidents underscored how we rely on a handful of under-resourced individuals to keep vital parts of the web secure. The PHP Foundation made that point itself this week . Its developers first identified the issue that could bring the internet to a halt in 2024, but it was seen as too expensive and too tricky to fix. The foundation has since admitted the delay was a “structural failure” owing to poor resource levels. This is where AI comes in. In August, researchers working with Calif, OpenAI and Wiz identified how easily the PHP issue could be exploited by using AI tools. And hackers quickly did too. Cloudflare’s chief executive, Matthew Prince, said his company had seen millions of attempts to exploit it already. Automated systems powered by AI can hammer away at weaknesses in an instant, bombarding their human guards with reports that they have to sift through. Researchers documented about 48,000 vulnerabilities across the internet in 2025. We’ve already passed 84,000 in 2026, with more than two months of the year still to go. That’s one every five minutes. Not every one will be as serious as this latest one, which scored 9.2 on a 10-point scale used to measure these things. But we’re facing an onslaught. Which all makes for an uncomfortable reality: we’re going to have more days like these. AI makes it inordinately cheaper to find weaknesses in vast volumes of old code, and repairing them is difficult. A 2025 review by the UK government found that about 28% of central government technology was classed as “legacy” – meaning out of date – while some organisations couldn’t even estimate how much old software they had. In April, ministers admitted they couldn’t give a comprehensive account of what had since been fixed or retired. So we need to fix that. Companies need to know what software they’re using, including the obscure elements they rely on, and who’s responsible for fixing it. That documentation is boring work, which is probably why it’s overlooked. But we’re in a different world now, and it needs to be done. Paradoxically, AI can help with it.

events.title: Tank barrel production returns to UK after 20 years
events.summary: Rheinmetall said the facility had created 100 jobs and it would look to expand its workforce in the future The production of gun barrels to be used on tanks has returned to the UK for the first time in 20 years with the opening of a new manufacturing facility. The UK Gun Hall in Telford, run by German defence firm Rheinmetall, has supported 100 jobs and will make barrels and breaches for large calibre weapons. Defence secretary, Wes Streeting, attended the opening ceremony on Thursday and said Britain was "back in the business of making weapons" for its armed forces. "From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action," he said. "One hundred skilled jobs in world class manufacturing and the return of large calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in 20 years - this is what defence as an engine for growth looks like," Streeting added. The barrels and breaches will be made for both 120m and 155mm weapon systems, including for the RCH 155 and future artillery platforms, according to Rheinmetall. The firm is already involved in the UK's Boxer combat vehicle programme and is upgrading the country's Challenger tanks . Wes Streeting said the opening of the facility would be a boost to Britain's defence capabilities Specialist workers from Telford have been recruited and the firm said it would expand its workforce as production ramped up. Ahead of the factory's opening, staff spent time at a Rheinmetall facility in Germany where they were trained in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production. Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall, said the gun hall was an "important milestone" that would strengthen the country's industrial base "for decades to come". "We are committed to investing in the UK for the long term, expanding our industrial footprint and working together to deliver the capabilities needed for the future," he added. Papperger told BBC Radio Shropshire it was a significant investment in Telford, adding that the firm only had one similar production line in Germany. "At the moment, we have a lot of orders and we need the capacity. Telford has very well-educated people, highly-motivated people," he added. Papperger said the company currently had 1,300 employees in the UK but was looking to build up that number. During his speech at the event, Streeting described Telford as being "synonymous with engineering and manufacturing". "Today is a vote of confidence in our country," he continued, "a statement of intent on our mission to reindustrialise Britain and create good, well-paid jobs across our country." events.title: TSH Resources reports 274 hot spots within estate boundaries after SGX queries over haze
events.summary: Children wearing face masks in Banjarbaru, South Kalimantan province, on Oct 21. TSH Resources operates 36,000ha of planted areas in Kalimantan and Sumatra. SINGAPORE – Plantation company TSH Resources said 274 hot spots were detected within its estate boundaries in Indonesia between Jan 1 and Oct 21, but maintained that none of the fires occurred within its planted or operational areas. The Malaysian plantation group , which has a primary listing on Bursa Malaysia and a secondary listing on the Singapore Exchange (SGX), said all the hot spots were located in community enclaves outside areas directly managed by the company. “The group’s field teams responded to and extinguished these fires, and police reports have been lodged in respect of these incidents,” the plantation group said in a filing with Bursa Malaysia and SGX. Its Oct 22 disclosure was in response to queries from SGX Regulation (RegCo) regarding forest and peatland fires in Indonesia which have caused transboundary haze affecting the region. The company operates 36,000ha of planted areas in Kalimantan and Sumatra, according to its 2025 annual report. The company also disclosed that a fire occurred on Aug 17 within an area of its subsidiary, Bulungan Citra Agro Persada (BCAP). It said the fire originated from a community enclave outside BCAP’s operational area, and was extinguished on the same day. BCAP subsequently lodged a police report and continued cooperating with the relevant authorities. Separately, TSH said it received an inquiry from the sustainability department of Apical Group, one of its customers, on Sept 1 concerning hot spots at another subsidiary, Farinda Bersaudara. TSH said it explained that the incident occurred in a community enclave outside its operational area, and that Apical, a vegetable oil processor, was satisfied with its explanation. The company said it had not received any other formal inquiries or notices from the environmental authorities concerning the recent haze. It added that its operations and activities within its Indonesian concessions had not contributed to the transboundary haze. TSH is among eight agribusiness companies listed in Singapore that have responded to queries from SGX RegCo concerning their operations and possible links to the Indonesian fires. The others are Golden Agri-Resources, Bumitama Agri, First Resources, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri Resources and Olam Group. TSH said it has enforced a zero-burning policy since May 2009, prohibiting the use of fire in land preparation, new planting and replanting activities. The policy also applies to its contractors and suppliers. It added that it had not undertaken new planting on peatland since the end of 2015. To monitor fire risks, the company uses satellite-based monitoring systems to detect hot spots, land clearing and possible encroachment. TSH said it has 123 fire observation towers, 11 drones and 28 firefighting squads comprising 425 firefighters. It spends an average of RM2 million (S$625,200) annually on fire prevention, monitoring and response measures. TSH has continued repurchasing its own shares amid the heightened scrutiny. In a separate filing on Oct 22, the company disclosed that it bought back another 250,000 shares, spending around RM286,577. The purchases brought its cumulative treasury holdings to about 65.6 million shares, equivalent to around 5.1% of its issued shares. In September, TSH disclosed that its 90%-owned indirect Indonesian subsidiary has been fined about RM42 million over the cultivation of land outside the legally approved plantation area.

events.title: War dents Gulf’s protein boom
events.summary: Anyone aiming to boost their protein intake in the Gulf has likely felt the pinch in their wallet lately. Prices are rising everywhere, driven by a global craze to add protein to everything, but this isn’t converting to profits for Gulf food producers, who are grappling with higher costs because of the war. Riyadh-based National Agricultural Development Co., best known for its Nadec dairy brand, doubled sales in its protein segment for a second consecutive quarter, helping lift revenue by 7.8% compared to a year ago. But net profit plunged 72.5% year-on-year because of higher feed prices, shipping costs, and surcharges associated with maritime logistics. Nadec expects the pressure to ease once the “regional operating environment normalizes.” Still, the results show how even businesses with domestic production and strong local demand are struggling with the war’s logistics disruptions. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Mark Carney lands in Turkey to forge a new partnership as Canada looks beyond the US
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has arrived in Turkey for a two-day visit to forge a new partnership ANKARA, Turkey -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Turkey on Thursday for a two-day visit seeking to forge a new partnership as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States . Carney is making the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkey, although he traveled to Ankara in July to attend the NATO summit . He is scheduled to meet with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and other officials before traveling to Istanbul for talks with Turkish business groups as the two countries seek to deepen trade ties. The Canadian prime minister has sought to diversify partnerships and reduce reliance on the United States amid an escalating trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump, marked by U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods, retaliatory measures by Canada and statements questioning Canadian sovereignty. In an interview with Turkey’s state-run Anadolu Agency, Canada’s Ambassador to Turkey, Marcel Lebleu, said this week that the visit’s main purpose was to “launch a strategic partnership through a joint declaration by the two leaders.” Talks would focus on cooperation in energy, nuclear plants, sustainable mining and the defense industry. The two countries would also hold negotiations on a free-trade agreement, he said. Turkey is looking to build a second nuclear power plant on the Black Sea coast, in addition to one currently being built by Russia’s Rusatom on the Mediterranean coast. Mounted cavalry units escorted Carney's vehicle to the sprawling Turkish presidential compound, where a welcoming ceremony was held. Erdogan and Carney then proceeded to a palace building for bilateral talks. On Thursday, Amnesty International called on Carney to raise human rights concerns during his trip. Rep. The mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem Imamoglu , considered a main rival to Erdogan, has been imprisoned for over a year on corruption charges he denies. Hundreds of party members and elected officials have also been detained in a crackdown critics say is designed to cripple Turkey’s largest opposition group. Erdogan's government insists Turkish courts operate independently. “As the judiciary is increasingly used to silence dissent and suppress critical voices, a clear message emerges: speaking out can come at a heavy price,” Amnesty's Turkey director, Ruhat Sena Aksenir, said in a statement. “Canada must not treat human rights as secondary in the negotiations. Sustainable partnerships depend on accountability and respect for the rule of law,” she added. In a sign of improving ties, Canada lifted its ban on the export of weapons to Turkey in 2024. It had imposed the restrictions following Turkey’s military incursions into Syria and over Turkey’s support to Azerbaijan in its conflict against Armenia, including providing equipment that used Canadian-made parts. A statement from Carney’s office said two-way trade between Turkey and Canada increased by 50% in the past five years. events.title: Millions in cheese revenue lost as protest torpedoes Italy's buffalo mozzarella output
events.summary: A truckers' protest in southern Italy has halted the production of buffalo mozzarella, causing an estimated 3 million-euro loss in just 24 hours ROME -- A truckers' protest in southern Italy has halted the production of the famed buffalo mozzarella , causing an estimated loss of 3 million euros in just 24 hours as the milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region and the finished cheese cannot reach customers, an official said. The weeklong strike by truck drivers over the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war has also blocked deliveries of other basic goods to supermarkets and left gas pumps empty in much of southern Italy. The government approved new tax breaks for truckers Thursday, but it was too early to tell whether they were enough to end the protest. The disruption is particularly damaging to buffalo mozzarella because the production of the protected cheese depends on a tightly timed supply chain. Buffaloes have to be milked regardless of whether dairies are operating, while production rules require that their milk be turned into mozzarella within 60 hours. Pier Maria Saccani, director of the Consortium for the Protection of Mozzarella di Bufala Campana DOP, said that about 1 million liters of buffalo milk produced on Wednesday couldn't be turned into mozzarella because of the transport blockade. The consortium oversees production standards and protects the designation of origin of the cheese in Italy and abroad. “Yesterday, no mozzarella was produced,” Saccani said, explaining it was a “3 million-euro block in 24 hours” — a loss of about 3.4 million dollars. Farmers typically have only enough capacity to hold the fresh milk until dairy trucks collect it and cannot store large quantities for extended periods. “So this blockade has obviously caused panic among farmers, who say, ‘Where are we going to put it?’” Saccani added. The dairies making mozzarella cannot afford to accumulate a highly perishable product if trucks are unable to deliver it to customers. Several dairies have remained closed as a result, Saccani said, describing the situation as a “complete production blockade.” Unlike false claims this summer that production of Parmigiano Reggiano cheese was in crisis due to extreme heat, buffalo mozzarella output is indeed in jeopardy. Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say During an extraordinary Cabinet meeting on Thursday, the Italian government led by Premier Giorgia Meloni approved new measures to help truckers and farmers face higher fuel costs, bringing financial aid to those two groups to a combined 540 million euros in tax credits, up from 434 million euros. Some farmers have resorted to feeding part of the unused milk to their animals because they have nowhere to send it, Saccani said, adding that the transport disruption is also threatening supplies of animal feed and diesel needed to keep farms operating. “It’s a very, very complex and delicate situation,” he said. The blockade comes as milk producers and dairies are already confronting higher costs. Saccani said the consortium estimates production costs have risen about 30%, driven by increases in animal feed, diesel, energy, plastic packaging and transportation. The increases have not been fully passed on to customers, he said, leaving producers to absorb much of the additional expense and cutting into profitability across the supply chain. Buffalo mozzarella is an important industry in the Campania region, where the city of Naples is located, and in neighboring areas of southern Italy. Saccani said that in 2025, the production of Mozzarella di Bufala Campana DOP totaled just under 58,000 metric tons, with about 37% of production exported. France is its largest foreign market. events.title: Dubai introduces one frequent flyer mile for each minute in the city
events.summary: The airline points game has been over for years, but the marketing gimmicks refuse to die. Emirates, which has nearly returned to its prewar capacity, is trying to entice more connecting travelers on long-haul flights to make a stop in Dubai. Previous incentives included discounts at amusement parks, hotels, and restaurants, but now it’s adding a sweetener: one frequent-flier mile for each minute spent in the city. The fine print matters, however, as the maximum award is 7,200 points for a five-day visit . While this is a bonus for anyone already planning to come, it’s hard to justify extending a stay, even by a minute. The most travelers can earn converts to a 216 dirham ($59) voucher at Dubai Duty Free, and is nowhere close to a cabin upgrade. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Abu Dhabi lures Eli Lilly, Oura, and Whoop in healthcare push
events.summary: Abu Dhabi is betting big on GLP-1 drugs and wearables as it seeks to retool its healthcare system for preventive care. Mubadala Bio signed a deal with US drugmaker Eli Lilly during the Future Health Summit in the UAE capital this week to package and distribute GLP-1 drugs locally. In April, the UAE became the second country to register Lilly’s weight-loss pill Foundayo, and was an early market for Mounjaro. The Department of Health also launched research projects with two of the hottest wearables brands, Whoop and Oura. Boston-based Whoop will study whether continuous monitoring and coaching can improve markers like cholesterol in adults with obesity and hypertension, both persistent public health challenges in the Gulf. Oura launched Project Cradle, a two-year pilot to see if its ring can flag spontaneous preterm birth in high-risk pregnancies, and will rely on Abu Dhabi’s clinical and genomic records, too. — Kelsey Warner

events.title: The Briefing Room
events.summary: Radio 4 , · 22 Oct 2026 , · 28 mins Will the French accept that changes need to be made to fix their ailing economy? Political paralysis and a debt crisis has led to 5 prime ministers in the last two years. Every attempt at fixing the economic problems is met with outrage and protest. Saturday 17th October 2026 saw some of the worst protests in years, with peaceful demonstrations over the cost of living and school funding descending into an 'apocalyptic hell'. 500 police officers were injured in the violence, 1,500 shops were damaged and an historic 19th century city hall was burnt to the ground in the mass disorder that ensued. But there are some serious economic issues that must be faced head on. France's borrowing costs have just hit a 26 year high, signalling they are not trusted to manage their growing debt. Public spending in France is higher than in many other European countries and a big part of that bill is pensions. Raising the pension age would save the state much needed money but proposals to do so were met with outrage and put on hold. So, has France become ungovernable? Guests: Sophie Pedder, Paris bureau chief, The Economist Victor Mallet, Financial Times, author of Far-Right France: Le Pen, Bardella and the Future of Europe Agnes Poiriet, UK editor, L'Express Producers: Ben Carter, Phoebe Keane, Kirsteen Knight

events.title: AI-related demand powers prices, rents of Singapore industrial space in third quarter of 2026
events.summary: JTC’s all-industrial rental index rose 0.5% quarter on quarter in the third quarter of 2026, while prices picked up 1% on the quarter and 4.2% year on year. AI-related demand kept Singapore industrial rents and prices firm in Q3 2026, even as occupancy slipped to 88.9%, JTC said on Oct 22. JLL and Knight Frank said semiconductor and manufacturing growth supported demand, but lease renewals, cost-cutting and geopolitical tensions limited stronger occupancy gains. JTC expects around 300,000 sq m of new space in Q4 and 1.2 million sq m a year from 2027 to 2030, while investment sales rose to about $2 billion. SINGAPORE – Buoyant growth in artificial intelligence-related sectors fuelled demand for Singapore industrial space in the third quarter, keeping rents and prices firm even as occupancy dipped. JTC’s all-industrial rental index rose 0.5% quarter on quarter, continuing an upward streak of rents steadily rising for 24 quarters since the trough in the third quarter of 2020. Q3 rents were 2.1% higher year on year, the industrial landlord’s report showed on Oct 22. Prices of industrial real estate also continued to rise , climbing 1% on the quarter and 4.2% year on year. The overall occupancy rate eased 0.2 percentage point from the previous quarter to 88.9%, weighed down by tenants vacating older factories earmarked for redevelopment and weaker demand for suburban business parks. JLL South-east Asia head of research and consultancy Chua Yang Liang said global demand for semiconductors supported the growth of industrial rents. “Asia-Pacific economies including South-east Asia countries like Singapore and Malaysia are firmly plugged into this growth driver,” he added. “Consequentially, Singapore’s islandwide industrial property market continues to maintain a stable rental growth trend, mirroring the growth rate of the previous quarter.” Tridiana Ong, head of occupier strategy and solutions at Knight Frank Singapore, indicated advanced estimates showing that Singapore’s economy grew by 5.4% year on year in Q3 2026. The manufacturing sector expanded by 7.5%, reflecting continued strength in activity, particularly from AI-related industries. Still, the quarterly increase in leasing transactions for multi-user factory and warehouse space was “relatively measured”, Ong said. This suggests that much of the demand stemmed from lease renewals and ongoing space requirements, rather than expansionary moves, she added. Chua also noted that ongoing geopolitical tensions are starting to weigh on occupier sentiment, with cost-cutting and space optimisation efforts beginning to impact overall occupancy levels, although underlying industrial demand continues to be firm. Rental growth is likely to remain modest, he said. He estimated that overall, rents may undergo an upside of 2% to 3% for the full year, given stronger near-term economic performance and continual appetite for premium assets. Chua also anticipated prices rising 3% to 4% as capital continues to flow into safe havens such as Singapore, driving further marginal yield compression. Business park rents inched up 0.1% on the quarter, while occupancy slipped 0.7 percentage point to 77.2%. Warehouse space recorded 1 per cent quarter-on-quarter growth in rental and an 89.7% occupancy rate for the quarter. Rents at multiple-user factory spaces, single-user factory spaces, business parks and warehouses recorded a year-on-year uptick of 1.6%, 3.1%, 0.7% and 2.8%, respectively. With office rents in the Central Business District remaining significantly higher and prime office supply limited, business parks could offer possible space solutions even though CBD locations remain favoured, noted Ong. Citing a “good pipeline supply” of new industrial space, JTC said that as at end-September, around 300,000 sq m of such space could be completed in Q4. Between 2027 and 2030, an average annual supply of 1.2 million sq m of industrial space is expected to be completed, of which 59% is single-user factory space with pre-committed demand. This is slightly higher than an average annual supply of new completions of around one million sq m over the past three years. In Q3, JTC awarded two tenders, one for a single-user development at 6 Tuas Avenue 14, and another for a multiple-user development at 5 Tuas Avenue 13, with bids received reflecting “strong market interest in multiple-user sites”, it said. The tender for another single-user development at Jalan Besut was not awarded as the top bid of $500 per sq m per plot ratio did not cross the reserve price. Across the market, total investment sales value jumped from an estimated $1.4 billion to about $2 billion, driven by a few large-ticket deals alongside sales from newly launched strata industrial developments, said Ong.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives on GeForce NOW at launch, bringing a new campaign, multiplayer action and DMZ, high-stakes extraction mode to supported devices . The campaign also gets an enhanced look: GeForce RTX 5080-class performance arrives for Ultimate members, bringing support for ray-tracing features in the cloud. There’s a new way to join the cloud, too: Existing supported Fire TV Stick users can now purchase one-month Performance or Ultimate memberships directly through Amazon, making it easier to sign up and start streaming on the big screen. Plus, Square Enix’s FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE brings cinematic pixel art and strategic battles to the cloud, and The Elder Scrolls Online’s Echoes of Skyrim Season adds the entire Greymoor Chapter free for all ESO Standard Edition owners. It’s all part of six games joining the GeForce NOW library this week. Squad up and answer the call on the cloud. Activision and Infinity Ward’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launches today on GeForce NOW. Members can drop into the trenches in Korea, close-quarter combat in New York, high-octane chases through Paris, night raids in Mumbai and city-wide engagements to reclaim occupied territory. Fight as Private Park, a young South Korean soldier facing live combat for the first time alongside his squad as a routine patrol turns into a desperate fight for survival. Beyond the front lines, operator-turned-outlaw Captain Price is operating outside the system he once served, pursuing revenge through covert missions as the conflict spreads. Multiplayer pairs precise combat with fluid movement, a dozen core 6v6 maps from around the world and battlegrounds that are shaped by the campaign’s global conflict. Loot, fight, negotiate, betray and extract — it’s all fair in the cloud and battleground. Ultimate members can now experience the campaign with ray tracing, powered by newly added GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, handhelds, mobile devices, browsers, supported TVs and more. Transactions are processed through Amazon’s billing system, creating a more seamless path from setup to gameplay. GeForce NOW transforms Fire TV into a powerful PC gaming rig in the cloud. Members can stream supported PC games they already own or purchase new titles from digital stores including Steam, Epic Games Store, Ubisoft Connect, Xbox PC Game Pass, GOG and EA. The library includes thousands of ready-to-play games, including many of the world’s most-played titles and more than 100 free-to-play games. No downloads, installs, patches or updates stand between a new game and playtime. An Amazon Fire TV Stick, the GeForce NOW app and an Ultimate membership are all it takes to level up the living room with GeForce RTX 5080-powered gaming. Square Enix’s FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE launches today on GeForce NOW, bringing the series’ classic roots into a cinematic pixel-art world. Travel with companions bound by fate and uncover the truth behind a force threatening to bring everything to ruin. Strengthen the party with Visions of beloved FINAL FANTASY characters, each bringing unique skills and abilities to battle. Dynamic camera angles and pixelized 3D models give familiar fantasy a fresh perspective. Exploit enemy weaknesses to stagger foes, break their defenses and seize extra turns before finishing the bonus phase with powerful Resonance attacks. Airships, crystals, espers and moogles bring familiar series favorites to a world filled with secrets to discover. GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage in the cloud, leaving more space on supported devices for everyday essentials. Save the inventory management for potions and Phoenix Downs. The Season also introduces Solo Dungeons, reimagining challenges previously designed for groups. Moon Hunter Keep and March of Sacrifices have been redesigned and rebalanced for players ready to tackle their dangers alone. Earn new rewards and take on new challenges at your own pace without needing to find a group. A new Tamriel Tome also launched Oct. 21, offering both free and premium battle pass reward tracks. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles. events.title: Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill
events.summary: When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA . “My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber , a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.” What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options: Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment. Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration. Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report. Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question. Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable. Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule. Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology , who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.” For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits. Mapping Your Way Into Washington Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices. On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research , and investing in STEM education . That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.” Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.” For Jathar’s first congressional visit , organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says. A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour , so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too. “If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.” –Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point? During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls. Shortcuts to Influence Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge. “When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw , designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI , which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI . events.title: Permitting deal draws lobbying blitz as hurdles mount
events.summary: The fragile Senate permitting deal is a major priority across the energy industry, per newly filed lobbying disclosures. Why it matters: The filings reveal behind-the-scenes efforts by powerful interests and companies representing oil and gas, mining, renewables, environmentalists and plenty in between to shape the legislation. The big picture: The bill title (Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act), its acronym (BAAJA) and its bill number appear throughout third-quarter lobbying disclosures. The bill was introduced Sept. 30, the last day of the third quarter. The disclosures, due Oct. 20, offer a window into efforts to influence the legislation during its drafting and negotiations. The lobbying extends beyond groups that specifically named the bill in their filings. Many others with a stake in the bill — like the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Manufacturers — list permitting legislation in other ways. Driving the news: Here's just a small subset of the parties in the arena. Industry groups like the American Petroleum Institute, the Edison Electric Institute, the American Forest & Paper Association, the National Mining Association, and the Data Center Coalition. Green groups including Earthjustice, the Nature Conservancy, and Defenders of Wildlife. Low-carbon power trade groups such as the Solar Energy Industries Association. State of play: The lobbying goes far beyond trade associations, with many individual companies also involved. They range from Chevron and BP to power giants like Duke Energy and Southern Company to geothermal startup Fervo. Industrial and equipment heavyweights like Caterpillar, Schneider Electric and Cummins are there, too. Zoom in: The disclosures also offer clues about which provisions attracted lobbying attention. For example: The National Mining Association identified BAAJA provisions that would change Clean Water Act permitting, including state water quality reviews and limits on lawsuits challenging permits. The Interstate Natural Gas Association of America listed BAAJA provisions affecting interstate natural gas pipelines among its lobbying topics, alongside other pipeline permitting proposals. Threat level: The latest filings land amid new friction over the bill. This week the Interior Department asked a federal judge to allow it to reconsider the Biden-era prior approval of Avangrid's planned New England Wind project off Massachusetts. "This is how you blow up a permitting deal," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) told Axios and other outlets about the latest in a string of Trump team moves against previously approved projects. Yes, but: An administration official cast the federal filing as a procedural move in the case brought by other opponents of the project. "Our filings defend the current government's litigating position," the official said. "We have been very transparent about the need for permitting reform and have also been transparent with Senator Whitehouse's and Senator [Martin] Heinrich's teams on all these legal filings," the official said, citing the two Democratic co-authors. 🆕 The latest: Democratic attorneys general from nine states express "substantial concerns" with the bill in a new letter to lawmakers, Punchbowl News reported this morning. What we're watching: The public advocacy and closed-door maneuvering should reach a fever pitch ahead of the first procedural vote on Nov. 9, and in the days and weeks that follow. The next wave of disclosures, covering October-December, should provide an even clearer look at the interests at play. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

events.summary: Mattel thwarted restive shareholders by inviting one of them to come inside and play. Hours after Semafor reported that investor Southeastern Asset Management was preparing a boardroom fight , the toymaker said it had signed a cooperation agreement with another of its big investors, EdgePoint Investment Group, to put one of the Canadian firm’s top partners on its board. By bringing EdgePoint into the boardroom, Mattel secures an 18% stockholding in friendly hands. That neutralizes the threats brought on by Southeastern and other investors, including John Rogers’ Ariel Investments, which has pushed for a sale. It’s not a failsafe, but a start. Scoreboard: Mattel, 1. Activists, 0. — Rohan Goswami

events.title: Economic worries abound ahead of Brazil runoff
events.summary: Economic worries are feeding voter discontent ahead of Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday, helping the conservative challenger’s prospects. Once defined by the size and strength of its labor movement, the number of unionized workers in Latin America’s biggest economy has shrunk by almost half in the last 15 or so years. That shift is partly explained by the rise in gig work: Almost two million Brazilians now work full-time for transport or delivery apps. The loss of worker protection has fed discontent, with almost 50% of respondents to a September poll saying the economy had worsened in the last year. In response, leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva this week fast-tracked welfare payments as he looks to catch up in the polls. — Jeronimo Gonzalez

events.title: Meta's new class of nonvoting stock lets Zuckerberg fund AI without losing control
events.summary: Liz’s view Why does Meta need to be a player in the AI race? It isn’t Google, organizing the entire internet; or Microsoft, the operating system of corporate America; or Amazon, the backbone of digital commerce. Those companies have an existential stake in the future of websites, software, and shopping. Meta sells ads. AI could transform that business — but the same could be said of Salesforce and JPMorgan, and neither Marc Benioff nor Jamie Dimon is pouring billions of shareholders’ dollars into building frontier models. They’re customers, not manufacturers, of AI. Mark Zuckerberg, however, controls Meta and wants to make it an AI behemoth. Those two facts explain the news, scooped yesterday by Semafor , that Meta is creating a new class of nonvoting stock. It sounds dry. It isn’t. The move lets Zuckerberg issue new shares — to fund acquisitions, recruit OpenAI and Anthropic stars with massive pay packages, or simply raise cash — without diluting his controlling stake in the company he founded 22 years ago. Another motivating factor, according to unusually detailed filings that lay out Zuckerberg’s discussions with the board, was the possibility that he’d be forced to sell stock to pay a potential California billionaire tax. (In the middle of negotiations last month, he told Meta’s board he planned to list his Palo Alto house for sale publicly, a PR nightmare waiting to happen.) Staying at the frontier of AI is expensive, and Meta carries a lower credit rating than Alphabet, Amazon, or Microsoft, limiting its ability to keep borrowing. It has been creative about shifting data-center costs off its balance sheet, but that can only go so far. At some point, it will need to issue new shares. Now it has a way to do so that doesn’t cost Zuckerberg his grip on the wheel. Might shareholders revolt at being handed stock that comes with no say in how the business is run? Nope. Meta shareholders absorbed the snub, and a $25 billion jury verdict in a case stemming from the 2010s Cambridge Analytica episode, by temporarily sending the stock up 2% in after-hours trading Wednesday. Notable Meta had previously made an attempt at creating a similar class of nonvoting stock for Zuckerberg in 2017, but had to scrap it because of its unpopularity with investors.

events.title: The Download: computing’s next leap and permafrost’s climate threat
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. How far can we push computing? On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued. We simply had not built the tools yet. He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size. But that easy descent has now stalled. Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance. Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement.  Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing . —Volkan Gurses This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine: The Impossible issue . Subscribe now to read it in full . It’s also part of MIT Technology Review Explains , our series exploring the ideas shaping technology. Read more from the series .  Three things you should know about permafrost How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it. The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just helicoptered into Alaska’s forests to report on the fires threatening permafrost and their complicated potential climate effects . Here are three things I took away from his reporting . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday. Roundtables: a conversation with the creator of AI-designed viruses Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King offered a preliminary answer by using a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next.  In our latest Roundtables conversation, MIT Technology Review senior AI reporter James O’Donnell spoke with King about his work, being named one of our Innovators Under 35 , and new ways of seeing biology. Subscribers can now watch a full recording of the event . Want to join the next conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 AI has uncovered a decade-old flaw threatening much of the web It found flaws in PHP, the code behind most websites. ( Reuters $) + Governments are urging website owners to patch PHP or take sites offline. ( BBC ) + Exploit attempts jumped from thousands to millions after disclosure. ( Axios ) + Now is a good time for doing crime. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Hackers used Claude and Grok to automate attacks on over 400 banks The AI agents targeted financial institutions in Latin America. ( Information $) + Unvetted AI agents are also accessing US bank accounts. ( Axios ) + Barclays says AI is allowing the bank to cut 5,000 jobs. ( Guardian ) + AI is making online crimes easier. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 The Pentagon has cleared the DHS to test a heat ray weapon It could be used for crowd control at the southern US border. ( CNN ) + It uses invisible energy beams to produce a burning sensation. ( Axios ) 4 A startup says AI-designed viruses have treated their first patient The experimental treatment targets drug-resistant E. coli. ( NYT $) + But the company has not published peer-reviewed results. ( Futurism ) + AI-designed viruses are already killing bacteria. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Japan hopes to return the first samples from Mars’s moons Its spacecraft is now on its way to Phobos. ( Guardian ) + It aims to reveal whether Mars was once habitable. ( Economist $) 6 Meta faces a $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica scandal The company says it will appeal the New Mexico ruling. ( CNBC ) + A Meta share deal has convinced Mark Zuckerberg to stay in California. ( WSJ $) + Until the company remade its stock structure to help him pay it. ( NYT $) 7 A new antimatter experiment could open the door to new physics Scientists hope to spot differences between matter and antimatter. ( Nature ) 8 China’s Unitree is pitching its latest humanoid as a robot bodyguard A promotional clip shows the H2-X disarming attackers. ( SCMP ) 9 Just Eat has apologised for bizarre AI-generated menu pictures Users were unimpressed by the bacon in cola and cheese sushi. ( BBC ) 10 Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do chores Hosts are threatening to strike, but guests are celebrating. ( Wired $) Quote of the day “Now they’ve given everybody a reason not to use Starlink: that Starlink isn’t reliable for national security for anybody but Trump. Maybe he’d turn it off on the United States if he didn’t like policy and he didn’t like the president.”  —SpaceX investor Ross Gerber tells CNN that Elon Musk’s decision to restrict Ukraine’s Starlink access has made the service a liability for every other government that relies on it. One more thing Online harassment is entering its AI era Scott Shambaugh didn’t think twice when he denied an AI agent’s request to contribute to matplotlib, a software library he helps manage. Then things got weird.  In the middle of the night, Shambaugh opened his email to discover the agent had retaliated with a blog post. Titled “Gatekeeping in Open Source: The Scott Shambaugh Story,” the post accused him of rejecting the code out of a fear of being supplanted by AI. “He tried to protect his little fiefdom,” the agent wrote. “It’s insecurity, plain and simple.”  Shambaugh isn’t alone in facing misbehaving agents—and they’re unlikely to stop at harassment. events.title: Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims.
events.summary: Lonnie Rouse was diagnosed with a neurological disorder that medical experts attributed to exposure to chemicals during his work cleaning up the Hanford nuclear site in Washington. Margaret Albaugh for ProPublica Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping and lost several teeth biting into a banana. For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the Hanford Site , a now-decommissioned Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country. Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least 48 potentially hazardous chemicals . The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off his boots.  Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress has acknowledged , based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to workers. Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work. Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers themselves.  By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.  As he watched, the governor signed a bill that was supposed to change his life. Rouse hung onto an old photo of himself cleaning rodent feces while working at the Hanford Site. Rouse packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the site for almost 20 years. Image photographed by Margaret Albaugh for ProPublica For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under the law , agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory illnesses . Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something other than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their claims.  Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.  But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims, Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend approving a single one.  The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals. Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.  The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims. It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.   Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152 workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits. “It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.” After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has taken beyond the two meetings. “Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email. The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’ findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.” The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics. In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts. The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive. DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until the legal process concludes. Rouse’s wife, Melinda, takes his vital signs. Margaret Albaugh for ProPublica In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.  “We were always told that nothing is out here that’s going to harm you — you do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and you’re going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care. “But that’s not what happens.”  “Depleted and Disgusted”   The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the air above. events.title: Tax online sales more heavily to save high streets, Burnham urged
events.summary: Exclusive: British Chambers of Commerce president calls for overhaul of business rates and greater powers for local leaders How Middleton’s revival could inspire struggling towns What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients Andy Burnham has been urged by one of his most senior former advisers to tax internet sales more heavily than in-store purchases to help “level the playing field” for struggling high streets. As the prime minister and his chancellor, John Healey, prepare for their first budget next week, Andy Haldane joined calls for action to stop more shops closing across the UK. In an interview for a Guardian series looking at how Britain can reverse the declining fortunes of towns, the former Bank of England chief economist urged them to launch a realignment of the tax system away from favouring online sellers, alongside a review of business rates and measures to turbocharge devolution. “The balance of tax incentives are strongly skewed towards the digital over the physical, and the large over small, and if you’re serious about high streets that needs somehow rebalancing,” he said. Calling on Burnham to follow through with Labour’s manifesto promise to “replace” the business rates system, Haldane said “some levelling of the playing field” was needed to help smaller operators who faced soaring costs and evaporating demand. “One of the reasons why high streets are dying, and some of the towns, is business rates are punitive for smaller shops,” he said. “This needs to be wrapped up with that more fundamental review of business rates and I’ll hope we see that in the budget. The prime minister has made town centres a top priority after years of decline that have left many hollowed-out, with shops closed, buildings boarded up and once-busy hubs sitting empty. Healey’s budget on Wednesday is tipped to include measures to ease the pressure on these high streets, including a tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay. The measure could raise up to an extra £1bn by forcing them to collect VAT on behalf of large-scale sellers based in the UK as well as those overseas. He is also expected to honour the promise Burnham made in June to take more small players out of the system altogether by raising the rent valuation threshold at which businesses start paying. The Treasury is also understood to have taken an interest in a report by the IPPR thinktank calling for an online sales tax to fund lower high street business rates. Big retailers including Morrisons, Waterstones and the UK’s biggest supermarket, Tesco, have long called for such a move. Labour has already had one business rates shake-up. In April, taxes on warehouses used by online retailers were increased, but the increase on the UK’s most valuable commercial properties also drew other large buildings such as department stores and hotels fuelling calls for further tweaks. Some retailers have warned against a more targeted warehouse tax because many big chains now combine online shopping with a high-street presence. Allen Simpson, the boss of the trade body UKHospitality, said the government had indicated it would ease costs on his sector, but he sensed ministers were wary of US retribution if taxes on big US-based tech firms such as Amazon and eBay were hit, warning that “Trump might hit us with a tariff”. Burnham’s push to revive communities with measures to hand more power and money to local leaders comes as Nigel Farage’s Reform UK seeks to weaponise high-street decline. Research shows public support for his rightwing populist party has grown most in the places where high-street vacancy rates have risen most. Haldane, who is the president of the British Chambers of Commerce, advised Burnham as he prepared to enter Downing Street but did not take a formal position in government. A leading expert in regional economic development who masterminded Boris Johnson’s levelling up plans – before distancing himself from the Conservatives over cuts to local government – he praised Burnham’s agenda to hand more power and funding to local leaders. However, Haldane said a revamp of business rates would be critical to boosting the economies of struggling towns. “That would be a very, very important element of the ‘growth in every postcode’, and making the most of devolution outside the city centric mayoralties,” he said. In his first weeks in power Burnham announced a cut in business rates for pubs, clubs and live music venues from April. Labour has also introduced community ownership funds and launched a £5.8bn “pride in place” strategy to hand more money and power to local leaders to support regeneration. However, retail and hospitality industry leaders argue that Labour has added to the headwinds facing high streets by increasing taxes on employment and adding to other business costs, and have pressed for these to be partly reversed to fund youth job creation .

events.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
events.summary: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday. The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers , the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury , a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago. Mysteries remain Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.
