events.title: Chalmers says investors feel good about Australia despite gloom at home
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Jim Chalmers declares optimism about business investment despite domestic gloom Treasurer Jim Chalmers will highlight strong business investment figures in a speech to investors on Friday. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Jim Chalmers says business investment is on track to grow nearly twice as fast as was forecast in May. On the other hand, Treasury is expecting to forecast higher unemployment and lower economic growth when the mid-year budget update is published in December. The economic conditions are adding to political pressure on the Albanese government. Business investment is booming in Australia despite stubborn inflation and a stagnant economy, according to Treasurer Jim Chalmers, as global investors rush to park their money in what they see as "an island of opportunity and stability" in troubled times. Speaking to a gathering of investors in Sydney on Friday, the treasurer will boast of the warm reception he received in a string of international visits last week and reveal that business investment is growing more than twice as fast as was previously expected. The optimism comes in the midst of a difficult period for Mr Chalmers, who has been weighed down by gloomy domestic conditions and backlash to his tax hikes on wealth, which have angered business lobbies and unsettled some Labor MPs. Though acknowledging what he calls Australia's "fair share of challenges" and revealing that Treasury will forecast higher unemployment and lower growth, Mr Chalmers will frame the investment boom as a bright spot. "I [have] heard the same message over and over: in a world of ratcheting risk, Australia is more and more reliable," he will tell investors at the Citi A50 Economic Forum, according to an excerpt of his remarks seen by the ABC. "You wouldn't be here with your $25 trillion of capital if you disagreed." Investment $50 billion better than expected Mr Chalmers will reveal Treasury now expects business investment to grow faster than 5 per cent this financial year, doubling the May forecast. That forecast will be formally updated in December's mid-year budget update, and while acknowledging that "potential surprises" could change this early figure, Mr Chalmers will say it would amount to an extra $50 billion in extra investment. Earlier this year, Australia's peak business lobby the BCA declared Australia was in the middle of the pack as a global investment destination, more favourable than China, South Korea and France, but less than the United States, the UK and New Zealand. Australian data centre operators have raised a record $35 billion so far this year. Meanwhile, the RBA governor says central banks globally are monitoring the risk of an AI investment bubble. Among the BCA's recommendations was for Australia to streamline the application process for foreign investors, something the government was already progressing. Mr Chalmers will argue it is working, with $278 billion approved so far this year and more than half of all applications now processed within a month by the Foreign Investment Review Board. Investment in data centres for artificial intelligence has been a big factor. The ABC reported in September that Australian data centre investment had reached $35 billion for the calendar year, more than one-10th of the total $278 billion investment. Reserve Bank burnishes inflation concern While this investment will boost Australia's growth figures, it is also one of a handful of factors concerning the Reserve Bank as it grapples with inflation. The bank raised the cash rate to 4.60 per cent last month, above the previous 2024 peak. Markets believe another rate hike in early November is possible. RBA Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser sounded pessimistic in public remarks on Wednesday, saying the inflation outlook was "materially worse" than forecast. RBA warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' As markets put the chance of a rate hike in November at more than 50 per cent, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser warns of a "central banker's nightmare". The unemployment rate hit a five-year high of 4.7 per cent in September. Mr Hauser said it was "a little weaker" than had been expected but did not suggest that this would deter a rate hike, adding: "I stress the 'little' … we need to see some easing in the economy." The economic conditions have added to political pressure on the Albanese government, with usually placid backbenchers increasingly willing to bemoan the government's handling of economic conditions in private commentary.

events.title: Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply
events.summary: Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz Shipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you? Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May. Yemeni Houthis , who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield. Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday. It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely. Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran , oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt. Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf . However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman. Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%. American Airlines abandoned its previous forecast that it might achieve a profit this year as it faced “historic fuel cost pressure”.

events.title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre
events.summary: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland . Now they are all gone. After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River. “It doesn’t end. It goes on and on,” says Mari Annala, an ecologist from the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL), looking at drone footage of the former forest from the perimeter. With 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, Finland has found itself at the forefront of the tech companies’ latest push. As well as its relative geopolitical and geological stability and abundance of land, the cool climate makes it especially attractive for saving on energy costs. Earlier this month, Google was ordered by the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) to temporarily stop work on Muhos and another site about 100km south-east in the village of Otanmäki after it failed to complete the necessary environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land. The news has prompted widespread outcry and a national reckoning over what role, if any, the country should play in the global rush to build datacentres to keep up with rapid AI development. Last week, Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted “on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time”. Muhos and Otanmäki are part of a €13bn AI infrastructure project by Google that has attracted criticism from Donald Trump, who would rather the centres were built in the US and has publicly called for the company to reconsider. It is the biggest ever project of its kind in the Nordic country. The Finnish government, which has presided over deep spending cuts, has encouraged the investment. Last month, when the Google plans were announced, the country’s prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a “top priority” and “the value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment”. He said the Google deal would “deliver lasting benefits for both parties”. But the revelations over Google’s misconduct have prompted public concern over what these deals mean for nearby communities, energy prices for Finnish households and Finland’s natural environment, a national source of pride. The datacentre push is likely to become a key election issue when Finns go to the polls in April. In addition to the 250,000 trees felled at Muhos, Annala estimates that an additional 150,000 trees were felled at Otanmäki. Because the trees have been felled illegally, she says wood from the two sites cannot be sold to wood-processing plants. The move has also prompted questions over why Finland’s renewable energy sources are being used to power international corporations. More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and a fee to compensate local communities for environmental damage. Since the scandal broke, Orpo has described what happened in Muhos as a “cold shower”. Hanna Halmeenpää, chair of SLL’s board, said she had been incredulous when she discovered Google’s law breaking. “At first I couldn’t believe it,” she said. “I have never heard that any company has done anything like this in Finland.” She said the system depended a lot on trust, which she believes Google took advantage of. “They bought the vast land area and they just started to cut it, just like that,” she said. “It’s pure arrogance and it’s amazing.” The speed of developments had shocked the country, she said. “Many people are just watching the news and asking each other: ‘What’s happening now? What can we do about it? And do we have to take all these datacentre projects in Finland?’” Jussi Kangasharju, head of computer science at the University of Helsinki, said that while datacentres brought a limited number of jobs, potentially boosting the local economy, the benefits on a national level were minimal. “Really, for Finland, there are no benefits,” he said. “They are international companies serving international customers. Very little corporate taxes go to Finland. Datacentres ultimately have very little benefit for others except the datacentre operator.” With legislation still playing catchup, there is a rush to get projects under way as fast as possible.

events.title: Coogan, Burnham and the fight to revive Middleton: could it be grist to the mill for struggling British towns?
events.summary: Turnaround initiated by the now prime minister and led by the actor could provide blueprint for other neglected areas Save high street by taxing online sales at higher rate, Burnham urged What makes a good town? Here are five key ingredients T he former England footballer Paul Scholes and the actor Steve Coogan stare out from beside a fish and chip shop in Middleton, near Manchester . Looming over a mural of the pair – and the whole town – is an enormous former cotton mill that powered its economy a century ago. The deafening looms and spindles of Warwick Mill fell silent decades ago, replaced in recent years by TikTok “urban explorers” who share videos of themselves crawling through its abandoned shell. Yet the old building may have life inside it yet: last month Rochdale council wrestled Warwick Mill out of the hands of its absentee owner, a millionaire Chinese businessman, under whom it had been derelict for years. Now the Grade II-listed site is at the centre of plans Andy Burnham believes could turn Middleton, where he was once a trainee journalist , into a blueprint for the future of Britain’s struggling towns. “It used to be good,” said Dorothy Kersh, in the town square with her husband, Ernie, both of them 83. “In the 70s we had a cinema, we had banks. It’s lost character and we’ve hardly got any shops. We haven’t even got a bank now – I never thought NatWest would leave Middleton. It’s just going downhill.” Middleton, a town of about 50,000 people a few miles from both Manchester and Rochdale, is in the type of existential crisis suffered by most British towns. A decade or so ago, locals could find virtually everything they needed in its neat square of grocers, butchers and banks. But a giant Tesco has hoovered up the cash since it opened in 2013, compounding the rise of online and out-of-town shopping. In addition to the loss of all its banks, the town saw the remains of its last post office closed by Modella Capital, the new private equity owner of WH Smith , days before Burnham became prime minister. Now the shopping precinct offers little more than bookmakers, vape shops, pawnbrokers and fast-food outlets. Its geographical identity feels muddled. Middleton was historically in Lancashire but has a Manchester postcode and dialling code, although residents pay their council tax to Rochdale. The region’s lauded tram network does not stop here. “It’s really a dying town,” said Tim King, outside a large post office branch that closed down years ago. “We’ve only got one cash machine and that’s at Tesco, and there’s never any money in it. We’ve lost out on the trams. We haven’t got anything down here, to be honest.” But six miles from the birthplace of the modern co-operative movement in 1844, a community fightback is under way. Months before he departed for Downing Street, Burnham launched a mayoral development corporation for Middleton, giving local leaders power to set lower business rates, acquire underused land and property, and build 1,500 new homes. The body is led by Coogan, the Bafta-winning creator of Alan Partridge, and Rose Marley, the chief executive of Co-operatives UK. Crucially, residents and business owners will have a seat at the table: a survey of 2,000 Middletonians is shaping the agenda of this new mayoral body – with Warwick Mill and other empty buildings identified by locals as an immediate priority. Wearing a hard hat and hi-vis vest during a tour of Warwick Mill last month, Coogan said the Middleton of his childhood was a “thriving” town but that “over the last 35 years there has been a kind of a bank ride” by firms registered in the British Virgin Islands, China and the US: “All that money has been extracted but very little has been put back into the infrastructure.” Coogan said the project was about more than attempting to revitalise his home town. It was a chance to reverse the political and economic malaise that has seen former Labour voters shift to rightwing populist parties such as Reform UK in post-industrial areas across Britain. “There’s a problem in this country which is post-industrial neglect,” he told the Guardian. “The idea, the Blairite approach: it’s called multinationalism, there is nothing we can do, throw your hands up, you’ve just got to see what happens, we can’t help these people . “Leaving that vacuum will mean that the extremists, populist extremists, will fill that gap. That’s the problem with top-down, well-meaning, but disempowering, philanthropic, centralised socialism . People don’t want to receive charity, they want to be empowered .” Coogan is part of a group called Middleton Co-operating, which aims to “rewire the whole of the economy locally” by taking infrastructure and everyday essentials into public control. Its plans include using renewable energy, such as solar panels and small wind turbines, to help power a secondary school and a hospice.

events.title: Trump and an oil shock aren’t enough for Texan drillers
events.summary: The Scene MIDLAND, TX — This should be a glorious era for Diamondback Energy. In the 15 years since the oil company went public, it has leveraged savvy fracking skills and astute acquisitions to grow from a scrappy West Texas driller — its stock ticker is FANG — to a behemoth responsible for about 4% of US oil production. This year, thanks to the surge in oil prices caused by the war in Iran, Diamondback’s second-quarter profits per share more than doubled from last year; Wall Street expects another boost when third-quarter earnings are released in a few weeks. But CEO Kaes Van’t Hof isn’t celebrating. “We don’t like when prices are too high,” he told me. Oil prices north of $100 per barrel — the US benchmark is around $99 this week — “are great for a month or two, and then I get called to Congress and called a price gouger.” High fuel prices could be a decisive disadvantage for US President Donald Trump in the looming midterm elections. As he scrambles abroad for barrels, the Permian Basin — the country’s biggest and richest oilfield, the bedrock of US energy security at a time of unprecedented turmoil in global markets — remains the place where his battle will be won or lost. And indeed, production here is higher than ever. But many Permian drillers are ambivalent about this growth. Diamondback, like its peers, has been hesitant to answer Trump’s repeated calls to “drill, baby, drill”; the company’s latest production target for the year is only about 4% higher than it was before the US-Iran war. Across the Permian, daily production is only 1.5% above where it was when the Strait of Hormuz crisis began in February, despite US oil prices rising 50%. That circumspection is the result of some hard lessons from a century of booms and busts. Despite major engineering strides in driving down production costs, and a wave of industry consolidation that has concentrated resources and decision making in fewer hands, executives like Van’t Hof are less willing than ever to take billion-dollar gambles adding rigs just because the president wants them to. No matter how attractive oil prices look today, many in the Permian believe a price crash is inevitable, either because Trump’s daily “jawboning” keeps futures traders feeling bearish, or because of a genuine security breakthrough in Iran, evaporating consumer demand owing to high prices and the clean energy transition, or the influx of foreign barrels from places like Venezuela. That’s a market reality that Washington often seems to miss: Trump’s overall “energy dominance” strategy relies on companies like Diamondback to drill more, but sets them up for failure if they do too much. “We’re the only business in the country where neither side of the aisle wants you to make money,” Van’t Hof said. “‘Drill, baby, drill’ is basically drill as much as you can to commit economic suicide.” Tim’s view Standing on the site of Diamondback’s newest frack, I began to understand why an unprecedented oil supply crisis has not unleashed a corresponding gold rush in the Permian. Tim McDonnell/Semafor Here, you can hear this vanguard of US oil drilling before you see it: the earth-shaking racket of a dozen semi-truck-sized gas generators, powering more than a dozen equally huge pumping machines, pushing sand and fluids into four brand-new wells. To get these wells pumping, three dozen people, including workers from Halliburton and several other subcontractors, work in round-the-clock shifts for at least a week, using explosives and high-pressure fluids to “fracture” deep shale rock formations along the length of a horizontal well that can run for miles parallel to the surface so oil and gas can be siphoned out. This is the basic technology that revolutionized US oil a decade ago, and made the country by far the world’s top producer. But it was always somewhat odious to oil company shareholders, who found it a money pit that didn’t make sense if crude prices weren’t high. When prices picked up this year, no one expected Chevron or ExxonMobil to suddenly drill more in the US. Their monster capex budgets change direction slowly, and both companies have their hands full with far-flung global drilling adventures. But in booms of the past, small and midsize drillers would have jumped to cash in. The muted reaction to this year’s market spikes reveals a fundamental shift underway for companies in the Permian, from chasing the most lucrative short-term barrels to chasing a kind of financial sustainability capable of returning cash to shareholders after the boom goes bust. The only way to keep up production and stay economically competitive has been to obsess over cost efficiency, Hunter Landers, Diamondback’s senior vice president of well construction, told me as we walked the site: “We’ve been pulling all kinds of rabbits out of our hats to save money and stay resilient.” The core of that strategy is to drill deeper and longer, so that the fixed costs of the fracking operation are spread over more barrels per well. The frack happening beneath us was about half as deep as Mount Everest is high, in a section of oil-rich rock that used to be considered out of reach; other innovations allow for simultaneous fracks, minimizing downtime. Others have different tactics: Brendan McCracken, CEO of midsized driller Ovintiv, said the company boosted its rate of production per foot to the highest in the Permian in part by pushing surfactants — essentially slippery industrial soap — into its wells. Companies are preparing wells that can be brought online more quickly when prices tick up. They’re using AI to scavenge for insights among vast datasets. They’re writing hedge clauses into sales contracts, to shield themselves from price crashes. They’re even sourcing frack sand locally rather than importing it from quarries in the Midwest. And the spate of M&A consolidation that rolled through the region in the past few years — Diamondback completed a $26 billion merger with its rival Endeavor Energy Resources in 2024, for example — means there are both fewer executives around to make rash decisions and fewer underground resources available for less-scrupulous wildcatters to jump on. Kirk Edwards, CEO of the small Odessa-based producer Latigo Petroleum, lived through the bust of the mid-2010s, when reckless growth in US shale triggered a price collapse. “That was horrible,” he said. “Now you’ve got our president saying, ‘Hey, we’re going for $40 oil again.’ Well, that would be catastrophic. So nobody’s going crazy on drilling.” Instead, the name of the game is to create pockets of stability in an inherently volatile business. “We’re all grown up now,” Van’t Hof said. “And I get screamed at less in meetings by investors.” The View From Midland Despite the year’s geopolitical turmoil, there’s a newfound sense of economic stability in Midland that, for the first time in the city’s history, doesn’t seem to depend on sustained high oil prices. events.title: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
events.summary: How did AI discover the internet's massive cyber-security risk? For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet. It took AI to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert. The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites. Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline. Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI. OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory". Cyber-security issue hitting sites worldwide prompts 'millions' of hacking attempts Most people may not have heard of PHP, but they probably interact with it daily. It stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, an open-source, back-end programming language which runs on a web server. Developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, PHP still powers lots of platforms today, including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites. When you visit a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read. It has also been used to write a number of tools for building or speeding up the creation of web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks. According to cyber-security firm Wiz, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. It is maintained by a non-profit called the PHP Foundation , external , composed of individuals and companies which depend on the language and aim to ensure its "long-term prosperity". A group of cyber-security researchers and organisations disclosed two vulnerabilities within PHP this week, which they warned could have the potential to upend sites across the internet. Cyber firms Wiz and Calif said the flaws – coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, with versions of PHP released over the last decade affected. Ryan Austin, a Calif researcher who helped uncover the security issues, told the BBC it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found". Wiz wrote in a blog post , external about its findings that, under the right conditions, hackers could exploit the php2shell issue to take control of affected web servers and steal sensitive data - saying everything built on PHP was left exposed. AI could also make such attacks easier and faster, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC. He estimated the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites. Jill Slay, a cyber-security researcher at the University of Adelaide, said it would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites. The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums. That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure. Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website. Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on Wednesday A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline. Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk. More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said. What happened after the flaws were exposed? The PHP Foundation rolled out patches on Wednesday to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years. "All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said. Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms. The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database. "These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.

events.title: Blockades, checkpoints and court action: fending off Brazil’s biofuel giants in the Amazon
events.summary: After decades of violent displacement and land theft, the country’s quilombola communities are fighting back F or most of his 39 years, Josias Dias dos Santos, known as Jota, has endured degrading cycles of displacement as a quilombola , a descendant of Black people once enslaved on Brazil ’s sugar cane and coffee plantations. He says his and other quilombola families subsisting in the rainforests in Pará, northern Brazil, were first forced out of their settlements by violent loggers, then by ranchers and miners. Yet, they say the worst came with the arrival of the palm oil industry in what is now the country’s most deforested state . Palm oil companies producing biofuels and supplying global customers, subsidised by the federal government, have laid claim to ever larger tracts of traditional quilombola territory over the past two decades. Since then, Dias dos Santos says, the companies have put up mazes of fencing , guard towers and security checkpoints , sometimes cutting communities off from their family cemeteries. Leaders who attempted to speak out for their land rights and against toxic industrial waste were often either jailed or gunned down in ambushes that went unprosecuted. Now quilombolas fear the second round of Brazil’s presidential elections will heighten the threat to the forest and its people. Many say a victory for Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro , would make securing the formal recognition of their land rights “impossible”. Dias dos Santos was barely seven years old when loggers forced his and other quilombola families to flee their homes near an abandoned sugar mill, where their enslaved ancestors once worked. After the loggers came the palm oil industry. With government encouragement , the industry set out to acquire large tracts of land in northern Pará. Today, about 202,000 hectares (500,000 acres), much of it near the Acará River, are used to produce palm oil for biofuels and a wide range of foods. For years, quilombola communities complained that the companies were squeezing them off their traditional lands. They also claimed their families were being affected by a toxic chemical byproduct of palm oil production, which also plagued the Acará River with bloated, dead fish. Quilombola activists who led protests and failed attempts to reclaim land met violent ends. One leader, Artemio Gusmão, was decapitated and dismembered ; another was shot 16 times in the back. “We were frightened,” Dias dos Santos says. Tensions between the quilombolas and the palm oil companies increased in 2020 after Brasil BioFuels (BBF) took over a large operation in the region. It built a complex of fences, gates and watchtowers guarded by private security guards and began systematically filing more than 1,000 police reports accusing quilombolas of making threats, damaging property and stealing its equipment. While many displacement cases in the Amazon end with companies forcing traditional communities off their land, the Acará quilombolas were different. The community acted to reclaim what they said was their land with a human blockade, then established borders that made it impossible for a palm oil company operating there to enter. Behind their own security gates, the quilombolas began reforesting and restoring biodiversity to lands once degraded by palm oil monoculture. They built schools, community centres and hundreds of homes, despite a campaign to evict them. In one incident in late 2021, BBF’s security chief, Walter Romero Ferrari, led scores of armed men to break up a demonstration against the company. Court records say that the armed men tied protesters’ hands behind their backs and used pepper spray on them. Ferrari and another BBF executive were eventually charged with torture (the case is still pending). That event convinced the quilombola community members to pursue more radical forms of resistance: they planned to block BBF’s main entrance, a controversial move that many feared would lead to arrests. On 24 February 2022, Dias dos Santos and others arrived at BBF, padlocked the gate, and refused to move, despite their lack of weapons against armed guards. BBF representatives later accused them of threats, which they deny. The quilombolas declared they would no longer allow the company to harvest palm fruits and insisted they owned the land behind the gate. Over months, accusations of violence and theft arose, but the blockade endured, with the community expanding checkpoints and building infrastructure using income from selling palm fruit. Finally, the courts have not only refused to enforce most of BBF’s land claims, but one key government body has already ruled that the quilombolas have a valid right to much of the land they have reclaimed. They have also rejected eight of nine requests by BBF to lay criminal charges against Dias dos Santos.

events.title: Gulf attracts finance firms controlling $5.8 trillion since war
events.summary: The News Finance firms controlling over $5.8 trillion have established their first offices in the Gulf in the nearly eight months since the Iran war disrupted the region’s economies, a sign that money managers are still betting it will remain a source of new cash. In that time, all the Gulf’s major finance hubs — Abu Dhabi, Doha, Dubai, and Riyadh — have welcomed new investors including Advent, Bain Capital, Capital Group, Man Group, and Singapore’s Temasek. Abu Dhabi has proved to be the most popular destination, both by the number of new office openings and the assets under management of the firms setting up there. That’s a reflection of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds ramping up the pace of dealmaking this year, and the emirate gaining recognition as a booking center for hedge funds. Nearly 20 companies overseeing more than $5 trillion combined have committed to setting up in Abu Dhabi since Feb. 28, with Dubai in second place attracting 10 managers running $670 billion in assets, according to data compiled by Semafor using artificial intelligence analysis of public announcements. Many firms see this as “the moment to demonstrate their belief in the region’s long-term potential,” said Robert Mogielnicki, founder of Paris-based consultancy Polisphere Advisory. Governments and sovereign wealth funds in the region expect to see this commitment demonstrated as “two-way investment corridors,” with foreign capital coming into the Gulf in return for partnerships with regional, state-controlled investors on global deals. Know More For many of those opening in Abu Dhabi, it’s a way to get closer to SWF clients in the region, a long-term bet on the Gulf’s growth, and a potential foothold for further expansion. New Mountain Capital, which manages $60 billion, opened an office in Abu Dhabi earlier this month as a bet it can be a gateway to a region that will continue to generate more wealth than it can invest domestically, despite the current volatility. “We approach our business with a long-term perspective at New Mountain, and our decision to establish a local presence reflects our conviction in the Gulf’s growing importance as a global capital allocator and our commitment to serving the region for years to come,” Adam Weinstein, President and COO said in a statement to Semafor. Abu Dhabi — which fashions itself as the “capital of capital” — uses its wealth to attract foreign investors to the emirate, partnering with global firms on domestic deals and international ones. Mubadala has become the world’s most active sovereign wealth fund this year. “Abu Dhabi’s attraction endures” despite the conflict, said Hasnain Malik, managing director for Emerging Market Equity & Geopolitical Strategy at research group Tellimer. The emirate offers firms “proximity to sovereign investors, tax free jurisdiction, regulatory framework, time zone, and air transport connectivity, in order of descending importance.” Other cities in the region have had less success attracting first time entrants this year. Just two firms announced plans to open their first Gulf offices in Riyadh, although one of those was the $518 billion Singapore sovereign fund Temasek, which said it would open in Abu Dhabi at the same time. Riyadh has attracted the biggest names in global finance to the kingdom in recent years, but most of them already had operations elsewhere in the region first. Only one firm, Silicon Valley-based Activate Capital, has said it will set up regional operations in Doha as part of an agreement with the Qatar Investment Authority. The firm is betting that it can use Doha as a hub for scouting investment opportunities across the Global South. That is indicative of another trend — the Gulf has increasingly become a location for finance firms looking for new markets to drive growth across the wider region. That’s part of what lured Capital Group, which manages $3.3 trillion, to open in Abu Dhabi this year. “Establishing a presence in Abu Dhabi is an important step in our long-term strategy to accelerate growth globally,” said Benno Klingenberg-Timm, Head of Abu Dhabi Office and Head of Institutional for Europe and Asia, Capital Group. “The current geopolitical environment does not change that long-term commitment.” Notable The Middle East has faced significant challenges from the Iran war, but its financial systems have continued to operate and Abu Dhabi has evolved into a global financial powerhouse, according to sovereign wealth tracker GlobalSWF. Still optimistic about its growth potential, Dubai’s financial center started work on a $1.4 billion new district , Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Snowy 2.0 to cost 12 times more than initial budget with further delays
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Review finds delayed Snowy 2.0 hydropower project could cost up to $25b Snowy 2.0 has been plagued by setbacks since it was announced in 2017. ( ABC South East NSW: Floss Adams ) A major review of Australia's biggest renewable energy project has found it could cost up to $25 billion, which is about 12 times the original price. Snowy 2.0 was initially set to cost $2b and come online in 2021. The project is now expected to be delivered in 2029. The cost of delivering Australia's biggest renewable energy project has doubled since the last estimate and is now set to become fully operational a year later than expected, according to a major review. Snowy Hydro has released its much-anticipated cost reassessment for the Snowy 2.0 hydropower project, revealing it could cost up to $25 billion, with first power expected in early 2029 and the project to be fully operational later that year. While the Commonwealth-owned company has set a target cost of $22 billion, it is allowing for an additional $3 billion to be spent on the project if required. Snowy 2.0, which started being built seven years ago, had an initial budget of $2 billion and was originally expected to start operating in 2021. Those figures were revised as part of a project reset three years ago , which projected first power would be delivered in late 2027. It was expected Snowy 2.0 would be fully operational a year later, at a cost of $12 billion. Dennis Barnes was appointed Snowy Hydro chief executive in 2023. ( ABC News: Isla Evans ) Late last year it was announced the project's contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV) would conduct a "line-by-line reassessment", which has now been released three months later than initially expected. Snowy Hydro chief executive Dennis Barnes said he was "incredibly disappointed" with the update. "We had a project that was stalled and had billions of dollars of claims on the table in 2023," he said. "I'm pleased we've got progress. Progress doubled in the first year after the reset. "What I'm disappointed about is obviously the resultant costs of the progress we're making." Dennis Barnes says more people are now working on Snowy 2.0 than what was expected in 2023. ( ABC News: Isla Evans ) Mr Barnes said the "design immaturity" that was faced before the 2023 reset had contributed to the latest cost blowouts. "We've understood that we're going to need a lot more people for a lot longer to deliver this job," he said. "This job is 80 per cent people costs. We've got 5,000 people on the job now working across multiple work fronts and that's obviously a lot more than we thought in 2023." The review found 65 per cent of machine tunnelling and 90 per cent of cavern excavation had now been completed and work to build the underground power station was underway. While Mr Barnes said the project was in its "strongest position yet", he could not rule out further cost blowouts beyond the most recent targets. "There's never any guarantees with mega projects. We're doing a world-first thing in many respects in really complex conditions," he said. Snowy 2.0 is designed to underpin Australia's electricity security and affordability over coming decades, as the country transitions away from fossil fuels. Based in the New South Wales Snowy Mountains, the project will link two dams through about 27 kilometres of tunnels and include an underground pumped hydro station the size of the Sydney Opera House. The project will act like a giant battery, pumping water upstream when electricity is cheap and releasing it back downstream to generate power when demand is high. Snowy 2.0 will store excess power from wind and solar and deliver it to the grid when needed. ( Supplied: Snowy Hydro ) It has a total capacity of 2,200MW and is expected to power three million homes for a week, the equivalent of about 26 million household batteries. Unlike batteries, pumped hydro offers long-duration storage, meaning it is designed to be a renewable energy insurance policy during days when there is limited sun or wind. But Snowy 2.0 has been embroiled in controversy since it was announced by former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull in 2017, including cost blowouts, missed deadlines, scrutiny over safety issues and contractor disputes. A major setback came after one of the initial three tunnel boring machines, Florence, got stuck in early 2023 for 11 months after hitting soft ground and creating a sinkhole. The National Audit Office gave Snowy 2.0 a glowing review in 2022 but the most recent audit , released earlier this year, found "significant deficiencies" in the management of the project.

events.title: Saudi Arabia's Humain expands Nvidia deal with 84MW AI computing plan
events.summary: Saudi Arabia's Humain has expanded its partnership with US chip maker Nvidia to develop up to 84 megawatts of artificial intelligence computing capacity, including infrastructure for an unnamed American customer, as the kingdom accelerates its push to become a global AI hub. The agreement, announced at Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin on Thursday, covers about 27,000 advanced graphics processing units (GPUs), with deployments beginning later this year and further capacity planned for 2027. The expansion builds on a partnership announced in May 2025 during US President Donald Trump 's visit to Riyadh, when Nvidia unveiled plans to supply Humain with hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips over five years. The initial phase involved 18,000 Blackwell processors, part of a broader plan to develop up to 500MW of AI computing capacity over five years. The first phase of the latest agreement will comprise 14MW of Nvidia's Blackwell HGX B300 systems, equivalent to about 6,000 GPUs, with deployment starting in the fourth quarter. The infrastructure will support Humain Cloud customers, including AI companies, government entities and businesses. A further 70MW of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin infrastructure, representing about 21,000 GPUs, is planned from mid-2027. Of that, 50MW will be dedicated to advanced AI workloads for an unidentified US client, with deployment targeted to begin in June. The remaining 20MW will support Humain Cloud, with deployment expected to begin in July or August. The companies said the Vera Rubin projects remain subject to final agreements and deployment plans. GPUs are powerful processors used to train and run AI systems. Blackwell is Nvidia's current generation of AI chips, while Vera Rubin is its successor, designed to handle more complex workloads faster and more efficiently. “We are moving quickly to bring the next generations of Nvidia-accelerated computing into Saudi Arabia at meaningful scale,” Humain chief executive Tareq Amin said. Launched in May 2025 and chaired by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Humain is owned by the kingdom's Public Investment Fund and plans to develop about 3GW of data centre capacity by 2030 and more than 6GW by 2034. Saudi Arabia is competing with the UAE to attract AI investment. In Abu Dhabi, G42, OpenAI and Oracle are developing Stargate UAE , a 1GW computing cluster that forms the first phase of a planned 5GW UAE-US AI campus, with Nvidia also a technology partner. Both Gulf countries depend on US export approvals to obtain advanced AI chips, making Washington's technology restrictions an important factor in their expansion plans. The latest announcement comes days after Saudi Arabia postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference from October 26-29 to next year. This followed a Houthi attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 10 that killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300. Mr Amin was among the speakers scheduled to attend gathering, which has become a major platform for announcing investment agreements involving Saudi Arabia's technology and infrastructure sectors. The FII Institute says the annual conference has helped to secure $250 billion in signed agreements and investment pledges since its inception.

events.title: Meta’s Ad Sales Are Suffering Now That Europeans Can Pick Less Personalization
events.summary: Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what advertisements they see. Advertising revenue in Europe continued to decelerate in the three months through September, the company said on Wednesday, underperforming its global figures. In the region, advertising revenue grew 18 percent year-on-year, slowing from the previous two quarters and lagging the 33 percent growth seen in the US and Canada. Though Meta did not explicitly blame the introduction of the Less-Personalized Ads model on Wednesday, chief financial officer Susan Li had previously warned “we’re seeing the impact of less personalized ads offering in Europe now that it’s fully rolled out, and that may be an additional headwind,” in July’s second quarter results follow-up call. The preceding two quarters had seen advertising growth fall from around 40 percent to 24 percent; in the US and Canada, it had accelerated from 30 percent to 31 percent. “We believe the EU’s free, personalized advertising option is contributing to the European slowdown,” Dominic Ball, equity research director at market analysis firm Rothschild & Co Redburn, told WIRED. Meta began to offer Instagram and Facebook users the LPA option at the beginning of this year, after EU regulators ruled that it was breaching its Digital Markets Act obligation to give consumers the choice of an equivalent service that uses less of their personal data and hit the firm with a €200 million fine. Sales growth has slowed in the region since the start of the year, when Meta rolled out the option. The European Commission said that charging EU users who did not want their personal data used for personalized advertising for an ad-free service—a measure Meta introduced in the EU in November 2023—did not satisfy this. Meta does not disclose how many people have chosen each option. LPA uses 90 percent less data than personalized ads, Meta says, with ads shown based on what a person sees in a particular session on the site, plus some data points like their age, location, and gender. It leads to poorer returns for EU advertisers, it warned in a response to the EU’s ruling. Less-personalized ads are less efficient, leading to fewer transactions, and more ads being closed due to being irrelevant or repetitive, it said. Indeed, the price advertisers were willing to pay per ad in Europe is not growing as fast as in the US and Canada, Wednesday’s results showed. Li told investors on Wednesday the company has “a lot of runway” to increase ad conversions and efficiency, as it is “continuing to find ways to either enhance the actual performance of the recommendation engine.” Rothschild & Co Redburn’s Ball believes the company will be able to use AI to improve its ad targeting in Europe despite working with fewer personal data signals. Investors were keen to understand how this fits into Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse , launched last month, questions about which dominated the call. Li said the company is seeing high commercial intent from people using Muse—asking for product recommendations, researching alternatives, and comparing options—which will allow them to eventually tap into the advertising market with that product. events.title: Young Americans are losing faith in the future — and Trump
events.summary: Data: Harvard Youth Poll, Fall 2026; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios Nearly two in three U.S. adults younger than 30 who plan to vote in next month's congressional midterm elections say their main motivation is to oppose President Trump and his policies, according to a newly released Harvard Youth Poll . The big picture: Seventy-seven percent of respondents disapprove of the president's handling of the economy, including about half of young Republicans. And just 9% say the U.S. is headed in the right direction — the lowest in the survey's history. Why it matters: Economic populism is driving emotions, along with concerns about war, AI, billionaires, deportation tactics, social policies and corruption. Majorities of respondents support Medicare for All, a wealth tax and bans on congressional stock trading. What we're watching: Just one in three Americans ages 18-29 say they'll definitely vote — a substantial drop from 40% who said so in 2022. Notably, most of that drop is driven by Republicans. Only 34% of Republican respondents said they'll definitely vote, down from 46%; 50% of young Democrats say they'll definitely vote, essentially unchanged. Just 22% of independents they'll definitely vote, down from 26%. Data: Harvard Youth Poll; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios Zoom in: Topping the list of what young people consider serious threats to their long-term financial security: rising prices and the cost of living (79%), followed by the power of large corporations (68%) and trade wars (68%). Nearly half said their household is struggling to make ends meet or getting by with limited financial security. By the numbers: 63% say their votes for U.S. House or Senate will be cast in opposition to Trump, while 14% say they're motivated by support of the president and 17% say he's not a factor. Two-thirds disapprove of the job Democrats are doing in Congress; 74% disapprove of congressional Republicans' performance. Stunning stats: For the first time in the poll's history, the share of young adults who said they expect to be worse off than their parents (27%) slightly exceeded the share who said they expect to be better off (25%). The difference was within the poll's margin of error, but the longer-term trend is striking. In fall 2021, 39% expected to be better off than their parents, while just 17% expected to be worse off. When Harvard first asked the question, only to college students, in 2003, 74% believed they'd be better off than their parents. In this recent poll only 28% believed it. When asked if they're more hopeful or fearful about America's future, fear (69%) outweighs hope (26%) by more than two to one. What they're saying: "At the beginning of adulthood, younger people should be able to see a path from hard work to a secure life, and the big question is whether that promise still holds," John Della Volpe, director of polling at Harvard Kennedy School's Institute of Politics, said in a conference call with reporters Wednesday. Methodology: The Harvard Youth Poll was conducted Sept. 30-Oct. 7, 2026, by the Harvard Public Opinion Project (HPOP) with Ipsos' KnowledgePanel®. It is based on a probability-based sample of 2,024 18-to-29-year-olds. The margin of sampling error is +/-2.61% for results based on the entire sample of adults; +/- 3.19% for the sample of registered voters; and +/-4.30% for the sample of those who plan to "definitely" or are likely to vote.

events.title: Robinhood picks DIFC for Middle East debut and targets 2027 launch
events.summary: US financial services platform Robinhood is expanding to the Middle East, with the Dubai International Financial Centre becoming its regional headquarters. The company said on Thursday it had been approved by the Dubai Financial Services Authority to offer trading and custody services across all 10 asset classes approved by the regulator, including equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds and investment tokens. “The DIFC is one of the world’s most important financial hubs, and our expansion there brings us closer to building a global platform that enables anyone, anywhere to own the highest quality financial assets,” said Vlad Tenev, chairman and chief executive of Robinhood. Robinhood plans to start offering its products in the region in 2027, giving investors access to a wider range of global financial assets. The company said its Dubai operations will be led by Salah Kaddoura as senior executive officer and president of Robinhood Mena . He will oversee the expansion of the regional team. "Our belief is that Robinhood’s arrival will open up increased access to the market for retail investors," he told The National . "Our expansion is driven by three key factors: demographics, innovation, and strategic regulation." “From our new home in Dubai’s premier financial hub, we’re looking forward to building Robinhood’s regional presence and expanding access to the global financial ecosystem for a new generation of investors,” Mr Kaddoura added. The move comes as Dubai strengthens its position as a financial centre , attracting international companies seeking access to the region’s growing investor base. The number of companies at DIFC grew at a record pace in the first half of this year, despite uncertainty over the Iran war, as the emirate’s financial hub continued to attract banks, wealth and asset managers, and hedge funds from around the globe. DIFC, one of the fastest-growing onshore financial hubs of the broader Middle East, North Africa and South Asia region, registered 2,318 new companies in the 12 months until the end of June, marking a 30 per cent annual increase, the regulator said in July. Global companies that set up their regional offices at DIFC during the first six months of the year include Allianz Trade Middle East, Arrowpoint Investment Partners, Bank of Canada, Blue Mountain Capital, Citadel, Gordian Capital, ICICI Prudential Asset Management, JP Morgan International Advisors, and Varenne Capital Partners. Arif Amiri, chief executive of the DIFC Authority, said Robinhood’s decision to establish its regional headquarters in Dubai reflected growing demand for technology-driven investment services across the Middle East. “With its proven ability to broaden participation in financial markets, Robinhood is well positioned to contribute to the continued development of the region's investment landscape and to connect a new generation of investors with opportunities across global markets,” he said. DIFC is among the key planks of Dubai's growth ambitions and is aligned with the Dubai Economic Agenda, the initiative known as D33, which aims to double the size of the emirate's economy to Dh32 trillion ($8.71 trillion) over the next decade and establish Dubai among the top three global cities. Dubai is also pursuing a Dh100 billion expansion plan for the second phase of the the financial centre, called DIFC Za'abeel District, which on completion will boost overall capacity to 42,000 companies housing 125,000 professionals across more than 1.5 square kilometres of floor space. Demand for office space continued during the first six months of this year with DIFC Square, which has 600,000 square feet of space, becoming 100 per cent pre-leased before completion. events.title: Hackers are turning web browsing into a spyware trap
events.summary: Hackers are finding new ways to infect iPhones with spyware — even when victims never click a malicious link — according to new research shared with Axios. Why it matters: Software once used to spy on politicians, journalists and other high-value targets is becoming a tool for everyday cybercriminals looking to steal cryptocurrency and login credentials. Driving the news: Researchers at iVerify and Report URI said Thursday they've uncovered two campaigns in which criminal groups with suspected ties to China exploited online advertising infrastructure and legitimate websites to deliver iPhone spyware. In one case, iVerify found that a financial institution employee's iPhone was infected after they scrolled past a professional soccer advertisement on Instagram. The ad automatically triggered an attack that stole the person's login credentials and searched their cryptocurrency wallets. In another, Report URI uncovered a campaign affecting nearly 8,000 legitimate websites after hackers purchased roughly 630 expired domains that those sites still relied on. The attackers used those domains to redirect vulnerable iPhone visitors toward spyware designed to steal their credentials and cryptocurrency. How it works: Both campaigns exploited tools that load automatically as people browse the internet, eliminating the need to trick victims into clicking malicious links. In the iVerify case, malicious code began running as soon as the Instagram advertisement appeared on the victim's screen. The attack checked the iPhone's operating system before deploying a compatible exploit. In the Report URI campaign, attackers purchased expired domains once used to host legitimate website features, such as chatbots and analytics tools. Thousands of websites were still loading code from those domains, allowing criminals to quietly redirect visitors toward malicious software. Threat level: The findings show how cybercriminals are building an infrastructure for delivering spyware through everyday online activity, rather than relying on traditional phishing attacks or targeting specific individuals. Both methods also allow attackers to selectively target vulnerable devices. Advertising platforms can narrow audiences based on interests and device characteristics, while malicious website code can identify a visitor's operating system before selecting an attack. The big picture: Cybercriminals are increasingly weaponizing spyware to exploit mobile phones, whose security (whether on an iPhone or Android) has often been seen as ironclad. Last year, iVerify uncovered evidence of the first spyware campaign targeting iPhones in the U.S. and the European Union. Last week, researchers at the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab uncovered the first public confirmation of zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads — targeting at least 45 devices within international news network Al Jazeera. Rocky Cole, co-founder and chief operating officer at iVerify, told Axios that spyware is now "the fastest proliferating threat to mobile devices at the current moment." The intrigue : "They're either Chinese or they definitely want us to think that they are," Scott Helme, founder and CEO at Report URI, told Axios about the groups behind the campaigns. What to watch: Researchers warn that the growing availability of sophisticated spyware is forcing consumers to rethink how they protect their phones. Cole and Helme both emphasized keeping mobile operating systems updated, since the attacks depend on exploiting vulnerabilities in specific software versions.

events.title: Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
events.summary: Hugging Face’s New AI Model Lets You Chat With DNA The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop. Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return. Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes. “We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X . Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.” Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion . (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.) DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works. Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch. Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA. The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications . Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time. One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy . If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm. Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says. The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are. events.title: Making the case for context-aware AI
events.summary: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes. For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know. The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling. This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents. Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis. Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized. Two words for you: context matters. My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis. Welcome, Devavrat. Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here. Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises. The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision. Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can’t just do that in a vacuum. And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come. Megan: Right. events.title: Three things you should know about permafrost
events.summary: How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.   The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two in-depth stories about permafrost. His reporting took him to the boreal forests of Alaska, where he helicoptered into the wilderness to learn more about how this material could affect our climate both now and in the future. I’d recommend you give both of James’s stories a read. There’s this feature about efforts to tackle the intensifying fires that are threatening permafrost, as well as this look at how researchers are trying to understand the complicated tangle of potential climate effects. Here are three things I took away. Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere. While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age. That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years. But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change. Those emissions form a feedback loop, accelerating warming further. The steady rise in global temperatures has already shrunk the footprint of the Arctic permafrost by about 12% since 1850, and the pace has been picking up in the last 50 years. The wild thing is, only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost. And none of them include the abrupt thaw and collapse that can happen after events like heat waves and fires (more on those fires in a moment). There are efforts to make sure future UN reports reflect the growing science, but for now, all this means that we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm. Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss Fire is a natural part of boreal forests’ life cycle, but they’re getting more intense because of climate change. And crucially, fires can accelerate the thawing of permafrost. By the end of the century, this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide. Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada and Alaska is generally to let wildfires burn as long as they’re not threatening human habitats. But some researchers say we should explore fighting these fires to save the carbon trapped in the forests and the permafrost beneath them.   Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, essentially highlighting areas where fires are most likely to spread and which areas are home to certain types of permafrost that would release the most emissions. (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost. Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form from the late Pleistocene era.) That’s all just the beginning—once we figure out potential targets, the question is what to do about it. Some suggest setting more prescribed fires, something Indigenous groups have done for thousands of years, partly to reduce the danger of massive blazes. Or resources could go to early detection and efforts to put out fires before they grow. The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere. We know that permafrost thawing can release greenhouse-gas emissions and drive climate change. But there are complications.   One particularly big wrinkle: Other effects from permafrost thawing and fire recovery might counteract the carbon lost from those events. For example, as temperatures warm, plants can gradually move north and take hold where they couldn’t have before. Those plants soak up carbon from the atmosphere as they grow, at least partly locking away what was emitted. Researchers are working to better understand this ecosystem. And the more we learn, the more complicated the picture looks. How much carbon is lost from permafrost, and how much a given area will recover its carbon, depend on a huge array of factors. How severe are the fires that have accelerated local thawing? What’s the local climate and environment? And what kind of permafrost is at stake? The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand.  This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .
