events.title: Ballot Rejections Soared in Rural Counties After USPS Reduced Mail Service
events.summary: Jacque Laird, elections administrator for Adams County, Washington, prepares ballot envelopes for delivery to voters at a third-party processing center that sorts mail, Direct Mail Enterprises, in Spokane. Adams County was one of the eastern Washington counties that saw a spike in the number of mailed ballots being rejected for arriving too late after U.S. Postal Service changes. Rajah Bose for ProPublica In early August, election workers north of Spokane, Washington, went across the street to the post office to check for late mail-in ballots. It was three days after the primary and they were expecting no more than a few dozen. Instead, their mailbox was brimming with envelopes — more than 500 of them, each a vote that wouldn’t count. The sight was “jarring,” said Auditor Lori Larsen, a Republican who oversees voting in Stevens County. Across the region, other election officials were getting similar jolts. In the 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots came in late, compared to about 600 in 2022, the previous midterm primary. In recent weeks, concerns about mail-in voting disruptions have focused almost entirely on President Donald Trump’s now-shelved plan to sharply restrict who can vote by mail .  But a ProPublica data analysis shows that delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures have endangered the validity of ballots cast in rural areas, not only in Washington, but across the country. Over the past three years, as mail volume continued to plummet and annual deficits ballooned, the Postal Service started consolidating the processing of first-class mail at larger regional plants instead of at smaller hubs closer to local post offices. Then, in a little-noted switch that mostly took effect after the 2024 election, the agency cut the frequency of mail pickups in half at many post offices 50 miles or more from these processing plants, from twice daily to once. The changes often added a day or more to delivery time and, most importantly for ballots, pushed back postmarking, which doesn’t happen until mail reaches the regional centers.  In this year’s primary, the effects of the cuts were clearest in five states that make detailed data on mail-in ballots available: Washington, California, Ohio, North Carolina and Oregon. All have or recently had grace periods allowing ballots to count if they come in after Election Day as long as they’re postmarked by the deadline. In these states, the number of ballots rejected for arriving late soared in counties affected by the service changes compared to 2022, ProPublica’s analysis showed.  Rejection rates in counties where services were cut doubled or tripled from what they were four years ago, dwarfing any increases in counties where postal pickups remained as they were, our analysis showed. In urban Spokane, for example, the number of ballots rejected for being late actually dropped this year. Across the five states, the delays have had the most substantial effect in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, ProPublica’s analysis shows. In Washington, Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, a Democrat, said he sees the service changes directed by Republican appointees leading the Postal Service as a way to undermine mail-in voting.  “I don’t think they realized how much it was going to affect their voter base,” he said, adding that Washington has “a lot of rural Republican voters.” Rates of Rejection Due to Late Ballots Were Higher in Counties with Reduced Mail Service Note: The chart shows the four states where data on all returned absentee ballots was available. Data from North Carolina and Washington tracked absentee ballots returned by mail. Data from California and Ohio tracked absentee ballots returned by any method, including drop boxes. Sources: California secretary of state, North Carolina State Board of Elections, Ohio secretary of state, Washington secretary of state. Ken B. Morales/ProPublica Postal Service leaders say such delays are less likely in the Nov. 3 general election because of “extraordinary measures” the agency puts into place for these votes, when there’s typically far more turnout. They have circulated a memo to the nation’s more than 30,000 post offices saying that for the 10 days before the election, managers should separate completed ballots from other first-class mail and deliver those intended for local election offices the day they come in. At an Oct. 15 news conference, Postal Service leaders emphasized the agency’s longstanding recommendation that voters mail ballots back at least a week before their states’ deadlines, while defending the agency’s ability to fast-track ballots through the system.  “We work to identify and address issues quickly,” said Amber McReynolds, chair of the Postal Service board of governors, “so ballots can continue to move swiftly from election offices to voters and from voters back to election offices.” Election consultants, researchers and former Postal Service officials told ProPublica that the guidance for the upcoming vote gave more detailed directions on how to expedite ballots. They said they hoped the agency’s special measures would limit delays, but some said mistakes were likely.  “I don’t think we can say with any kind of conviction that there will be no ballots rejected,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer of the National Association of Election Officials. “It isn’t a question of ‘if,’ but a question of ‘how many.'” A pilot program instituting the delivery changes in 18 regions before the 2024 election ran into problems. An audit by the Postal Service’s inspector general found that agency staff in these areas sometimes didn’t handle ballots correctly, mainly because instructions weren’t clearly communicated. (A Postal Service spokesperson said “learnings from the pilot” have been applied as the program has expanded.) After this year’s primary, reports by media outlets noted that mail-in ballot rejection rates were higher than in the past, but ProPublica’s analysis shows these increases were directly connected to Postal Service changes. Research published in September by the Brookings Institution also found this connection, projecting that if the pattern held in the general election, tens of thousands of mail-in ballots could be rejected. At least seven closely contested congressional districts — including Washington’s 3rd, California’s 22nd and North Carolina’s 11th — are in areas that were affected by service changes in the primary, ProPublica found. Elena Patel, who conducted the Brookings analysis, said service changes may still imperil mail-in votes in the general election. “I think there remain risks to ballots,” she said, adding that the Postal Service’s plan for the general election “depends on flawless execution.” Mail

events.title: Philippines surprises with jumbo interest-rate hike as inflation surges, peso slumps
events.summary: Protesters marching along a Manila street to press for a rollback in oil prices and removal of value-added and excise taxes. The Philippine central bank raised rates by 0.5 points to 5.5% to fight rising inflation and support the peso, which hit a record low. The BSP warned of more action if needed. It said higher oil prices, transport fares and a possible El Nino dry spell are adding pressure. Inflation hit 7.2% in September, far above the 3% target. The bank kept its 2026 forecast at 6.1% and lifted 2027 to 6%. MANILA – The Philippine central bank delivered an outsized interest-rate hike and signalled readiness to tighten further to rein in resurgent inflation and support a peso that has sunk to a record low. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) increased on Oct 22 the target reverse repurchase rate by a half-point to 5.5% as expected by only one of 25 economists in a Bloomberg News survey. Twenty-four predicted a less aggressive, quarter-point hike. Broadening price pressures and upside risks to inflation requires a “strong” response, the BSP said in its statement. “Such a decisive response will make monetary policy appropriately restrictive. This will contain second-round effects and firmly anchor inflation expectations.” “The BSP stands ready to take further monetary policy action as necessary to ensure the timely return of inflation to the target,” it added. The nation’s benchmark stock index ended 0.7% lower after the decision, snapping five straight days of gains. The Philippine peso continued its decline on Oct 22. The move underlines how drastically the inflation threat has built up for the Philippines, which must now confront the possibility of a severe El Nino dry spell , while still reeling from the impact of the global oil shock. The Philippine peso also hit a fresh historic low on Oct 22 after breaching the key psychological level of 63 per US dollar for the first time last week. The weakened currency risks fanning inflation as the nation relies heavily on imports for fuel and food supplies. The monetary authority has now increased borrowing costs by a total of 125 basis points since the Iran war broke out early in 2026, even as the Philippine economy is growing at its slowest pace since the pandemic. Still, the inflation outlook has hardly improved. The BSP kept its forecast for 6.1% inflation in 2026, while significantly raising its estimate for 2027 to 6% from 5.4% previously. The gauge is only seen to moderate to 3.3% in 2028. “The forecasts were worse than we thought,” Governor Eli Remolona said in a news briefing after the decision. “There was a bit of a sense of urgency to try and dampen these inflationary pressures.” Price pressures are building up as renewed fighting in the Middle East drives up global oil prices, while transport fares have been raised. The biggest risk ahead is a possible severe El Nino dry spell that could hit farm production, according to the governor. Bank of the Philippine Islands lead economist Emilio Neri Jr, who was the only one to correctly predict the decision, said the jumbo rate hike reinforces the BSP’s inflation-fighting credentials. Consumer prices already surged 7.2% in September from a year earlier, reversing four months of deceleration. That brought the year-to-date inflation average to 5.4%, well above the central bank’s 3% target. The governor expressed concern about peso weakness and its impact on imported inflation, even as he said the BSP would not deplete its reserves to defend a specific level of the currency. He added that domestic economic activity should recover by the first quarter of 2027, supported by improved government spending. While the central bank has left the door open for more rate hikes, Pantheon Macroeconomics’ Miguel Chanco said further tightening is not a done deal for the BSP’s December meeting. “Incidentally, today’s larger-than-expected adjustment could’ve been motivated as a front-loading of what would’ve been another uncontroversial 25-basis point hike in the last sit-down of this year,” he said. events.title: Gulf economies to contract 4.8% this year with sharp recovery in 2027, IMF says
events.summary: Gulf economies are set to shrink 4.8 per cent this year as the Iran war disrupts energy exports and weighs on non-oil activity, before rebounding 9.1 per cent in 2027 , the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday. The forecast marks a sharp reversal for the six-member Gulf bloc, with the IMF cutting its 2026 growth projection by 6.8 percentage points from the 2 per cent expansion it expected in April, according to its Regional Economic Outlook released in Dubai on Tuesday. The Gulf region posted growth of 4.5 per cent last year. “While some economies have remained relatively resilient, others have experienced severe disruptions, leading to a substantially weaker regional economic outlook since our April forecast,” Jihad Azour , director of the IMF's Middle East and Central Asia department, said at the report's launch at the Dubai International Financial Centre. “This conflict has disrupted energy production, shipping, tourism, trade, and confidence. And the burden of this disruption has fallen most heavily on oil-exporting economies, directly affected by the interruption of energy production and transport,” he said, calling the war a “severe shock” for oil importers. There is divergence between the Gulf countries, with Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar the most affected because of the drop in hydrocarbon production and exports. Their economies are projected to decline by 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, this year. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are “less affected”, with contractions of 3.9 per cent and 3.3 per cent, respectively, while Oman's economy is projected to grow by 4.1 per cent this year. The sultanate's geographical location, as well as focus on non-oil reforms in recent years is backing its economy, Mr Azour said. The wider Gulf's contraction for this year is similar to the level experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when the bloc's GDP shrunk by 4.9 per cent. While the primarily reason for the drop in growth has been due to the oil sector, the bloc's non-oil economy is also forecast to contract by 0.8 per cent this year before returning to 4.5 per cent growth in 2027, underscoring the wider economic fallout from the conflict. Oil and gas production among Gulf exporters directly affected by the conflict plunged from 33 million barrels a day in February to about 19 million in May, with Qatar's output falling as much as 86 per cent, the fund said. Exports have since staged a partial recovery. Gulf crude shipments rose to more than 75 per cent of prewar levels in September, the International Energy Agency said. Oil prices are now projected to average close to $96 per barrel in 2026 and $87 per barrel in 2027, compared with $82.20 and $76, respectively, in April, with the forecast peaking at about $110 per barrel in late 2026 before declining steadily, the IMF said. The conflict is also eroding the Gulf's financial buffers. The IMF expects the bloc's current-account surplus to narrow to 1.3 per cent of gross domestic product this year, from 5 per cent in 2025, while its combined fiscal deficit widens to 2.3 per cent of GDP from 0.8 per cent. Inflation is projected to rise to 2.7 per cent. The diversification of trade routes and investment in resilience have significantly helped Gulf countries weather the shock from the war. While the fund anticipates a sharp rebound in Gulf economies next year, the forecast hinges on an end to hostilities and the gradual resumption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in early 2027. Saudi escalation Saudi Arabia, which has been facing an increasing number of attacks by the Yemen's Houthis, has the capacity to handle the impact of conflict, Mr Azour said. “The Saudi economy has during this war has been able to redirect flow of oil, use infrastructure that is on the Red Sea, and therefore the impact of the shock on Saudi comes … second after Oman [which has seen the least impact from the war]. This is a country that is less affected,” he said. “Of course, the recent tension we saw it's having impact on their economic activity. But overall, for a country that is still exporting five to six million barrels a day, with the depths of the market that they have and the strong internal demand, their capacity to withstand the shock is high,” he added. Looking ahead, the biggest downside risk is the “obvious one on the horizon … the risk of another escalation in fighting”, said Hasan AlHasan, senior fellow for Middle East Policy at the International Institute for Strategic Studies. Speaking at a panel discussion on the IMF report, he stressed that geopolitics now “occupies centre-stage in present economic performance but also in future economic planning”. Touching on the Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia, he stressed that the region has the resilience to deal with the escalation, but urged for regional integration. “I think what this will depend on is the extent to which countries in the region are able to resolve their differences, and we're seeing very positive signs and encouraging signs in that direction,” he added. Also speaking at the panel, Monica Malik, chief economist at Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank, said the Gulf economies have withstood the pressure well, and a big part of that is for energy exports to reach the market. “What is very important is that the region has entered this shock in a very strong position,” she said. “If we look at growth, really since the pandemic, you've seen multiple sectors performing well, multiple economies performing well. The resilience has not only come from looking to diversify the economy, but also from the fiscal side.” While there are uncertainties over how things get resolved and how quickly things normalise, “but given the reforms we've seen, given the balance sheets, given the focus of governments, I'm optimistic on the longer term and medium term outlook”, Ms Malik added.

events.title: Trump turned the government into an investor. Democrats have shopping plans, too.
events.summary: The News As President Donald Trump continues buying government stakes in private companies, the rest of Washington is starting to appreciate the power of his new tool. The Trump administration has so far announced 43 equity stakes in firms producing everything from minerals to semiconductors, 36 of which were negotiated without explicit legal authority — and more are yet to come . The administration may be negotiating even more stakes under the radar, since SEC filings for unrelated deals mention the possibility of warrants . Unwinding the administration’s investments would prove legally and politically difficult — but Democrats likely won’t want to, at least not right away. They’re already weighing how to use equity stakes for their own ends, signaling that Trump’s government intervention in the private sector may be the start of a permanent trend. “The Trump administration’s approach to government equity stakes has completely lacked transparency and accountability,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., told Semafor. “While this is something future administrations may want to consider, it’s clear that to actually serve Americans, it would require a totally different approach.” Thanks to the precedent Trump has set, a future Democratic president could reap multiple benefits from equity stakes in private companies. Among them, as former Biden administration officials suggested: reining in the AI industry, shrinking defense spending, boxing China out of critical sectors, and pressuring gun and oil companies. Even demanding an equity stake as a condition for government assistance — whether it’s a loan, grant, or other federal permit — is a powerful tool that’s now more readily at the White House’s disposal, no matter which party controls it. “We’re through the looking glass,” said Democratic strategist and former Biden administration official Doug Farrar. Van Hollen isn’t the only 2028 Democratic contender who’s focusing on overseeing Trump’s deals rather than discontinuing them. In a statement to Semafor, California Gov. Gavin Newsom trolled Trump as “THE LEADING SOCIALIST OF OUR TIME,” crediting him with unlocking “A BOLD NEW ERA OF GOVERNMENT-RUN BUSINESS … WITH HIS GLORIOUS GOVERNMENT TAKEOVERS.” The next president may well also have more power to purchase equity stakes; legislation moving through the Senate would give the Pentagon explicit legal authority to do so. “The sky’s the limit, because the pattern’s been set,” said Tad DeHaven, who helps track the equity stakes at the Cato Institute. Know More Some Republicans don’t want any administration making forays into the private sector with public money. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, recently introduced legislation that would require the government to dissolve any equity stakes after eight years. “Whether it’s President Trump or somebody else like Bernie Sanders who might be president someday, I don’t trust the federal government being a long-term investor in American companies,” Husted told Bloomberg TV. But no one else has signed on to his bill. And some progressives are already embracing taking stakes. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced this month that his Economic Development Corporation, helmed by Biden’s former FTC chair, Lina Khan, would invest $30 million in a quantum technology lab in exchange for 15% of its profits. Already, “the [Trump] administration keeps gaining footholds in the industries that make up the supply chain for the AI buildout,” said Farrar, who worked for Khan at the FTC. “That could be an important point of leverage for a future president of either party — but especially a Democrat who wants to seriously regulate this industry.” Sanders, one of the left’s leading critics of the AI industry, went a step beyond profit-sharing by suggesting this summer that its companies surrender half of their stock to the government. “The Trump administration has opened up Pandora’s box with this approach to state capitalism,” said Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Biden and Trump administrations. Some Democrats fear Trump could sell off his equity stakes following the next presidential election. Others pray their party, as it prepares to take back at least some power in Washington, can dig into Trump’s equity stakes without creating too much pressure for a selloff after he leaves office. Any future Democratic president would seek to “figure out a way of imposing some sort of governance scheme over all of these equity interests that strikes the right balance,” said Bharat Ramamurti, the former deputy director of the Biden White House’s National Economic Council. “I hope there is not an overreaction to one of [Trump’s equity stakes] not panning out, especially because many of the other ones may end up being quite successful for taxpayers,” Ramamurti added. “And you’ll be making a losing financial decision if you decide to cut all of that off.” Room for Disagreement Given that Trump has built three campaigns around his skills as a dealmaker, the White House has plenty of reason to argue that his opponents won’t use his playbook. In a statement to Semafor, White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton appeared skeptical that a Democrat would hang onto Trump’s existing stakes. “Through voluntary equity investments in willing companies, the Trump administration has partnered with the private sector to rebuild America’s industrial base,” Middleton said, adding that “it’s justifiable to doubt that Democrats will want to build on President Trump’s legacy to revitalize American industry and strengthen our economic independence.” Eleanor’s view It’s easy to envision a future Democratic president using Trump’s model to advance a more progressive agenda, as Mamdani already has in New York. But one Republican asset that Democrats will have trouble replicating is the man who’s largely responsible for the Pentagon’s investments: Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg. The Cerberus cofounder has faced remarkably few obstacles in Trump’s Washington, where the GOP-controlled House, Senate, and White House have stayed mostly out of his way. As one former Pentagon official who worked on its equity stakes put it to me: “It is extraordinarily unlikely that [a Feinberg analog] exists in Democratic politics and that they will have that level of political capital.” Notable Senate Armed Services Chair Roger Wicker, R-Miss., recently told Semafor that the Pentagon “must regularize” its equity stake purchases “to render this approach sustainable over the long term.”

events.title: Singapore oil product inventories fall to three-week low
events.summary: Combined onshore oil product inventories were at 38.134 million barrels in the week ended October 21, Enterprise Singapore data showed. Singapore’s oil product inventories fell to a three-week low at 38.134 million barrels, driven by weaker light and middle distillate stocks, Enterprise Singapore data showed. Light distillates dropped to 10.971 million barrels and diesel and jet fuel fell 20% to 8.31 million barrels, while traders expect North-east Asia diesel exports to stay firm into November. Residual fuel stocks rose 4.5% to 18.86 million barrels after six weeks of falls, but high freight costs may limit arbitrage flows as East Asia stays well supplied. NEW DELHI – Oil product inventories held in Asia’s key fuel trading hub Singapore declined to a three-week low, government data showed on Oct 22 , driven by a fall in middle and light distillate stocks. Light distillate inventories, including naphtha and petrol, fell to a three-week low of 10.971 million barrels in the week, the data showed. Naphtha total imports fell about 29% on week to around 122,000 metric tons (~1.09 million barrels), as no shipments from the Middle East or India arrived. The top supplier was Russia at 74,000 tons, followed by Malaysia at 44,000 tons. Singapore did not export naphtha in the week. Petrol imports tanked by about 61% to 125,000 tons (about 1.06 million barrels) during the period, while exports climbed about 49% on week to roughly 724,000 tons. Outbound petrol volumes were led by Malaysia at about 180,000 tons, followed by Indonesia at around 166,000 tons. Petrol inflows were led by China at nearly 77,000 tons. Meanwhile, stockpiles of middle distillates retreated in the week to Oct 21, after hitting near six-month highs in the previous week, the data showed. Inventories of diesel and jet fuel fell 20% week on week to 8.31 million barrels, hitting a four-week low. Looking ahead, diesel exports from north-east Asia, particularly from South Korea, are expected to remain firm going into November amid steady spot sales volumes, traders said. Singapore’s residual fuel inventories rebounded for the first time after sliding for six consecutive weeks, the data showed. Residual fuel stockpiles rose 4.5% week on week to 18.86 million barrels (2.97 million tons) in the week to Oct 21, though remaining below September ’s average of 19.89 million barrels a week. Total fuel oil imports into onshore tanks rose 74.9% to above 965,000 tons in the week, with the UAE as the top supplier, followed by Thailand and Brazil. Meanwhile, total exports more than tripled to over 440,000 tons, with most of the volumes headed for China. East Asia appears to be amply supplied in October, with higher volumes coming from most key exporting regions, LSEG shipping data showed, though some trade sources said that high freight costs may hamper arbitrage flows in the coming months. events.title: Can Germany overhaul its economy before AfD grows stronger?
events.summary: Can Germany overhaul its economy before the AfD grows stronger? Conflicts, rising costs and Chinese competition are testing Germany's economic model like never before. Which new sectors could revive growth and contain the far-right AfD, whose support has grown larger than ever? Germany's export-led economic model faces unprecedented strain just as support for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party reaches a new peak. Chinese rivals are steadily eroding the market share of major German industrial players, while persistently high energy prices, elevated labor costs and excessive red tape are adding to the structural crisis. After two years of contraction, real GDP edged up only 0.2% last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office, Destatis. Exports to China fell 9.7% in 2025, with German vehicle and part shipments plunging by a third. While there are signs the German economy is turning the corner, the government's latest forecast of 1.3% growth in 2026 is still modest compared with the pre-COVID boom years. The AfD is currently polling ahead of all other political parties in Germany. The country's many economic challenges have been a major factor in the right-wing populists' rise. Germany's domestic intelligence agency sees reliable indications that the AfD is right-wing extremist in its entirety. The party has vowed to put Germany back on a growth path by ending the transition to renewable energies, lowering taxes and renegotiating European Union treaties, while also reforming welfare and sharply restricting immigration. Merz seeks growth via advanced tech As Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition searches for a fresh growth strategy to fend off the rise in populist politics , the government has set out its high-tech agenda focusing on six priority sectors. These are artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, microelectronics, biotechnology, clean energy (including nuclear fusion) and climate-neutral mobility. Irene Bertschek, head of the Digital Economy research unit at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW), argues that Germany's research in these "key enabling technologies is very strong, particularly in the area of climate-neutral technologies." Yet, the results are often commercialized abroad, Bertschek told DW, with the United States leading in AI and China closing the gap quickly. A report published Monday by the Made for Germany initiative — a group of 147 companies and investors — builds on the government's plan, estimating that these and other new technologies could attract up to €4.1 trillion ($4.6 trillion) in investment by 2035. Realizing that potential, however, will depend less on today's industrial giants, like Volkswagen, Siemens and BASF. "It will not primarily be the established companies that conquer these new fields, but innovative newcomers — startups," Oliver Falck, director of the ifo Center for the Economics of Innovation and Digital Transformation, told DW. The task, Falck said, is to create the right conditions for startups to emerge, including proximity to top universities, access to private capital and enough freedom to experiment. He argues for state financing during the early-stage "valley of death" — the risky phase between research and commercial viability when private financing is often scarce. Investors circle future growth sectors There are clear signs this shift is already happening. Data from Deutsche Bank and startupdetector, a German startup database and market intelligence platform, show more than 3,000 startups were founded in Germany in the first half of 2026, up 88% from the same period last year. One-third of the new ventures have an AI focus. Venture-capital investment soared 44% to €5.8 billion in the first half of 2026, with firms such as Neura Robotics and drone manufacturers Stark and Quantum Systems benefiting. US investors, meanwhile, are increasingly buying up Germany's famed Mittelstand — its traditional small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) — with an eye on their specialized technology. "The German Mittelstand is highly innovative. Now it is essential to invest in key technologies such as artificial intelligence and to tap into the potential that arises at the intersection with established technologies," Bertschek stressed. The expert, who is also chair of the German government's Commission of Experts for Research and Innovation (EFI), thinks SMEs should make better use of their huge amounts of production data and collaborate with AI startups to help those young firms grow. Another idea for accelerating the shift to new high-tech sectors comes from Sven Gabor Janszky, chairman of the Leipzig-based futures-research institute 2b AHEAD. He argues that Germany needs special economic zones to help catch the next wave of economic growth. "For a few specific technologies, you lower the regulations, you recruit ambitious workers and pump money into these zones," Janszky told DW.

events.title: "Stop whining": What Vance's take on Ohio ad controversy means for 2028
events.summary: Vice President Vance 's call for fellow Republicans to "stop whining" about Vivek Ramaswamy's controversial attack ad in Ohio's race for governor showed a key part of his political mindset ahead of his expected run for president in 2028: Never back down. Why it matters: Channeling President Trump, Vance has shown contempt for what he sees as the old-guard GOP's reflex to cave under pressure from Democrats and the media. He thinks too many Republicans sacrifice allies to make controversies go away, and that giving critics a political scalp only encourages them to demand another, according to people familiar with his thinking. It's an approach with some risk — namely whether Vance, entering a critical period in his political career, has the political muscle to get away with Trump's no-apologies approach. Driving the news: Vance on Wednesday defended Ramaswamy amid bipartisan outrage over an ad featuring the estranged mother of Ramaswamy's Democratic opponent, Amy Acton . In the deeply personal ad, Acton's mother calls her daughter a liar, and says Ohioans shouldn't vote for her for governor. Not mentioned in the ad: Acton and her brother were removed from the mother's care as children after Acton accused her stepfather of sexual abuse. Her mother sided with the stepfather, leading to an estrangement that has lasted nearly 50 years. Appearing at a campaign stop for Ramaswamy in Ohio, Vance showed little concern about the criticism over the ad. Vance said he was "disgusted" by fellow Republicans criticizing it, telling them to "stop whining." Asked whether the ad was appropriate, Vance said it was "not really my concern," and that politics is tough. The other side: The backlash has included Republicans and Democrats who believe the ad crossed a moral line by exploiting Acton's traumatic childhood. "I would not have run that ad," Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, who appeared alongside Vance and Ramaswamy at a campaign rally Wednesday, told the AP . Former UN ambassador Nikki Haley called Ramaswamy "a bad guy," adding: "It's a shame he continues to get away with it." Acton told CNN that she hopes her story of recovering from abuse inspires others, and that she "was not stunned" at "the antics of an out-of-touch billionaire," referring to Ramaswamy. Behind the scenes: Vance's refusal to denounce allies dates to his 2022 Senate campaign in Ohio. During a March 2022 debate, Vance refused to condemn then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) for appearing at a rally organized by white nationalist Nick Fuentes. "She is my friend, and she did nothing wrong ... I'm absolutely not gonna throw her under the bus," Vance said then. In the final days of Ohio's 2024 Senate primary, Vance aggressively defended GOP candidate Bernie Moreno amid a controversy over an adult dating website account linked to Moreno's work email. As vice president, Vance has refused to disavow his friend Tucker Carlson amid accusations of antisemitism — even as Carlson's relationship with Trump was fracturing. After racist and antisemitic messages surfaced in a leaked Young Republicans group chat, Vance declared on X that he wouldn't join the "pearl clutching." During a December 2025 speech at a Turning Point USA event, Vance rejected political "purity tests," declaring: "I didn't bring a list of conservatives to denounce or to de-platform." What they're saying: "There is nothing JD has more personal disdain for than weak Republicans who reflexively kowtow every time the Dem-media demands a scalp," a source close to Vance told Axios. "It drives him crazy to see the cucked reaction from some establishment operatives and politicians in the GOP, who he views as nothing more than useful idiots for the left." The intrigue: Some Republicans see Vance as influenced by Trump and Vance's mentor, tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who has embraced a similar no-apologies mantra. "The president's refusal to kowtow to the left is one of the things JD admires most" about Trump, the Vance source said.

events.title: Scoop: Unvetted AI agents are accessing U.S. bank accounts
events.summary: Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios. Why it matters: AI agents are becoming a nightmare for America's banks, making their way into banking systems faster than financial institutions can respond. The difficulty in distinguishing between a human and an unauthorized bot is forcing banks to block the technology and rapidly rewrite their terms of service. Driving the news : Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others are racing to contain agent risks. Some are aware of unauthorized access, people familiar with the issue said. These are generally situations when an agent or AI assistant accesses a human's account with the user's permission and login credentials. Even if permitted by the user, this goes against the guidelines of most banks requiring that humans log in to their own accounts. This presents significant security risks : banking executives fear the steps agents with login access might take, especially if a user has granted purchase authority or the ability to shift funds. In other instances, some banks have tracked activity when agents — programmed to fulfill requests or complete tasks on a user's behalf — contact call centers or appear to take actions independent of user instructions, the people said. What they're saying: Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances. State of play : The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said. Morgan Stanley has begun blocking third-party agents from accessing its platforms, sources familiar with the decision said. JPMorgan , Bank of America and Citi are also restricting agents . A Chase spokesperson said customers should not give their usernames and passwords to anyone. A Morgan Stanley spokesperson said the bank hasn't observed instances of "rogue AI agents accessing our platforms." Zoom out: Most banks have authorized or are moving in the direction of allowing read-only access , which should allow agents to see customer financial information without taking action. Banks already grant such access to third-party apps like Quicken for budgeting and other activities. Reality check: Several industry and bank executives told Axios they recognize the need to find a middle-ground with AI agents. Customers will want to use these agents going forward, which banks recognize. But for now, the risks of being too permissive are too high. Threat level: Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said. One bank executive told Axios they struggle to differentiate between agents, as well as whether an agent has been authorized by a user or has gone rogue and gained access to a customer account. What we're watching: On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure. But money isn't necessarily enough to solve this problem, one source said, because of how quickly the technology is developing and revealing new weaknesses in real time. Banks are investing in preventing worst-case scenarios, but they are also preparing for when those could happen, including with "day after" scenario planning that would allow them to quickly secure or restore customer access, sources said. The bottom line: The rapid pace of AI advancement is becoming a security nightmare for America's financial institutions.

events.title: Sexual Assaults on Campus No Longer Scrutinized as Closely Under Trump’s Education Department
events.summary: Shoshana Gordon/ProPublica The civil rights arm of the U.S. Department of Education has dramatically scaled back investigations involving schools and colleges since the second Trump administration began, even as complaints continue to pour in, a ProPublica analysis of newly obtained records found. The analysis shows how severely the department’s Office for Civil Rights has retracted from its mission, launching an average of about 100 new investigations a month — 1,839 total from Inauguration Day in 2025 through July 2026. The OCR launched an average of 310 new investigations each month in 2024 during the Biden administration, according to data previously obtained by ProPublica. Under President Donald Trump, the OCR abandoned the public-facing list of schools it was investigating and the reasons for those investigations , including claims of discrimination based on race, sex and disability. ProPublica sued the department to obtain internal case data. The government subsequently provided records of the OCR’s actions in the first 18 months of Trump’s return to power, and we are publishing the data so the public can search the cases. events.title: Trump administration divided over housing order
events.summary: The Trump administration is at odds over an executive order targeting housing affordability, people familiar with the talks told Semafor. The White House has grappled with how to address the cost of living ahead of the midterms, which are less than two weeks away. A six-section draft viewed by Semafor would make it easier for some homeowners to “proactively” cancel their mortgage insurance; create an interagency task force on manufactured housing; allow more homeowners to refinance without title insurance; and direct the Agriculture and VA departments to lower interest rates for single-family home loans. Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte is pushing for Trump to sign it as soon as this week, some of the people said, while others in the administration are pumping the brakes. Housing groups have expressed concern over some proposed changes, the people said, which they warn could wind up boosting prices. The White House and Pulte did not comment. “It’s definitely on everyone’s radar, and I think people are really just hoping that it’s not something that’s done for theatrics; that if it is done, it’s more real and has substance to it,” one industry representative said of the executive order. “I mean, people aren’t against stabilizing housing costs, right? But they just want it done in a cautious and safe way.” Scotsman Guide earlier reported on the talks. — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Norway’s wealth fund slightly cautious on stocks, incurs $38 billion loss in third quarter
events.summary: The country’s sovereign wealth fund is the world’s largest single investor, owning on average 1.5% of all listed companies globally. Norway’s US$2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund reported a 278 billion kroner loss in the third quarter, after rising interest rates hurt its fixed-income holdings. Deputy CEO Trond Grande said the fund had been “slightly cautious” on equities and some Big Tech stocks, with only small underweights and no plan to change for now. The fund, the world’s largest single investor, said AI stocks were highly volatile. It warned any setback in the technology could hurt markets, though it did not see a systemic risk. OSLO – Norway’s US$2.3 trillion (S$2.94 trillion) sovereign wealth fund said it had been “slightly cautious” on the equity markets and some of the larger Big Tech companies, after it reported on Oct 22 a loss of 278 billion kroner (S$37.9 billion) for the third quarter. Investing the Norwegian state’s revenues from oil and gas production, the fund owns on average 1.5% of all listed companies globally, making it the world’s largest single investor. “We have been public that we have been a little bit cautious on the equity market overall and a little bit cautious on some of the bigger technology names,” deputy CEO Trond Grande told Reuters after the results. “In the bigger scheme of things, that’s just smaller underweights.” The fund must follow a benchmark index set by the Finance Ministry, with equities tracked against the FTSE Global All Cap index, meaning it has a small margin of manoeuvre to deviate from that index and go underweight or overweight on some stocks. The fund’s return underperformed the benchmark by 0.18 percentage point in the quarter. Grande said the fund had been slightly underweight on some tech stocks for “quite a while” and had no plans, for now, to change. The tech sector as a whole accounted for 23% of the fund’s total holdings as at June 30, according to fund data. “We are happy with how we have the fund structured just now ... but this is something that we constantly review. So nothing is carved in stone,” he said. Overall, there had been quite “a lot of volatility” in the ecosystem of AI stocks, ranging from model labs and data centres to the energy providers and the chip manufacturers, he said. “Should there be a backlash or should there be an accident that kind of holds back the penetration of the technology, that certainly would hurt the equity market,” he said, adding he would not describe the risk to markets as systemic. In the third quarter, the fund posted a return of minus 0.5% on its global investments due to rising interest rates hitting its fixed-income portfolio, which accounted for 25.8% of its overall holdings in the period. Overall, the fund is invested in some 7,100 companies as well as bonds, property and renewable energy projects. REUTERS

events.title: Barclays to cut 5,000 jobs in AI-fuelled push to lower costs
events.summary: The bank reported third-quarter earnings on Oct 22 that missed several key estimates. Barclays said it is cutting 5,000 jobs, or about 5% of total headcount, as part of a “technology-enabled” effort to reduce costs as it adopts artificial intelligence across the bank. The bank reported third-quarter earnings on Oct 22 that missed several key estimates. Barclays’ bond traders suffered the biggest slump on Wall Street during the quarter, taking the shine off a strong performance on the equities desk. Revenue from fixed income and currency trading fell 19% compared with a year earlier to £1.01 billion (S$1.7 billion), behind analyst expectations compiled by Bloomberg. That meant the equities traders, who posted a 47% jump in revenue, almost matched that revenue haul with their best performance since at least 2009, the year after Barclays acquired the North American business of Lehman Brothers. The bank said the fixed-income result reflected lower client activity in rates and credit, and “further adversity in September due to the macroeconomic environment”. On a call with reporters, chief executive C.S. Venkatakrishnan said the performance in FICC was “somewhat disappointing”. “We will employ AI at scale,” Venkatakrishnan said on the call. “But AI is the icing on the cake, not the cake.” Barclays cut about 1,000 jobs in the first six months of 2026, with the remaining due before the end of the year. About 60% of the job cuts are coming within support functions, including among developers. Barclays employed about 93,000 people globally at the end of 2025. The London-based bank said it was “structurally reducing” costs to “generate capacity for investment”. It is focusing on simplifying the organisation and increasing efficiency, driven by AI, according to a presentation. The bank cut £201 million of costs in the three months through September, and plans to cut about £300 million more in the final quarter of the year. Barclays’ retail bank could not do enough to overcome weakness in the investment bank, with the British retail unit broadly stable and the US consumer arm also roughly flat year on year, missing estimates. The bank stuck to its targets for the coming years, with operating expenses largely as expected in the quarter, and announced a £500 million share buyback. Investors have been watching the bank’s cost control after it reported disappointingly high expenses in its half-year earnings, despite a fresh cost-cutting programme announced in February. Peers including JPMorgan Chase & Co, Goldman Sachs Group and Bank of America saw similar trends across fixed income desks, where revenue fell as much as 17% year on year as they dealt with the impact of rising interest rates, which can push down the value of existing debt and crimp demand from clients to transact. Overall, the Barclays investment bank slightly missed expectations with total income of £3.13 billion. “With one quarter to go before the end of our original three-year plan, we have either achieved or are on track to achieve all of our 2026 group targets. We are confident in and committed to the 2028 targets that we laid out earlier in the year,” Venkatakrishnan said in a statement. British lenders are bracing themselves for a rise in taxes on their earnings as part of the Labour government’s budget next week, which would use the proceeds to fund cost-of-living relief for households. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Why both parties are welcoming Trump in Iowa
events.summary: The News SIOUX CITY, Iowa — President Donald Trump will touch down on Thursday in Iowa, the site of perhaps the tightest Senate race in the country. Strangely enough, both candidates are welcoming him. Only one, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, will be at his rally on Thursday, but Democrats are banking that Trump’s presence helps them due to his unpopularity. “It’s good. … He needs to see what the policies, like the tariffs and the war in Iran, cuts to healthcare, have done to a state like Iowa,” Democratic candidate Josh Turek said in an interview. A couple hours away in Greenfield, Hinson denied any tension between her and Trump, despite her recent calls for him to end the Iran war and stop cutting deals with Russia’s Vladimir Putin. “President Trump knows where I stand,” she told Semafor. “I nag him a lot to get priorities for us all the time.” At an event on Tuesday in Des Moines, she disclosed that Trump recently called her right after she dropped off her kids. “Ashley, it’s your favorite president. How’s it looking, how are you feeling about the polls?” Hinson recalled Trump asking her. She said she asked how a deal to export more soybeans was coming together. Know More The Senate race is absolutely everywhere in Iowa, which is also home to three competitive House races and a governor’s race (Democrat Rob Sand is now favored to defeat Republican Zach Lahn). The Senate race appears to be the one Republicans are most worried about. Trump will swing through Iowa twice in October, a sign that Republicans need him to juice turnout in a state he flipped that hasn’t flipped back to Democrats. The radio ads are inescapable, the TV spots are relentless, and Trump’s visit puts an exclamation point on a race where the National Republican Senatorial Committee and the RNC are both spending millions in coordinated advertising on behalf of Hinson. The top Senate GOP super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, is also spending money to counteract Turek’s competitiveness. “You know what that means. They wouldn’t be coming unless they knew that this race was winnable for us,” Turek said. Democratic groups are spending a lot on Turek as well, identifying his race as a top pickup opportunity in a cycle where Democrats need to net four Senate seats to retake the majority. Hinson said Trump’s visit will help remind Iowans why they voted so strongly for him in 2024, the third straight cycle the state backed him. “Look back to where things were two years ago, before we had President Trump securing our border,” she said. “Iowans found the choice that they have in this election: somebody who wants to again go back to those policies of two years ago or move our country forward and continue working.”

events.title: Oil jumps US$2 on escalating Middle East tensions
events.summary: Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran, in eastern Saudi Arabia, on Oct 14. Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia have stoked concerns over further disruptions to crude supplies. Oil prices jumped after more Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia raised fears of wider Middle East conflict and crude supply disruption. Brent crude rose US$2.82 to US$111.64, while WTI gained US$2.24 to US$99.39. US stocks fell, but distillate stocks rose. The US plans to withdraw some family members from missions in the region. Iran warned of a wider response, while Russia and Ukraine peace talks may resume by November. SINGAPORE - Oil prices rallied over US$2 (S$2.55) a barrel on Oct 22 after more Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia stoked concerns over a broader escalation of conflict and further disruptions to crude supplies from the world’s key exporting region. Brent crude futures climbed US$2.82, or 2.59% to US$111.64 a barrel at 6.26am GMT, close to a five-month high. US West Texas Intermediate crude gained US$2.24, or 2.31%, to US$99.39. “Oil prices remain well bid, with ICE Brent back above US$110 per barrel this morning following additional deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia,” ING analysts said in a note on Oct 22. The US State Department plans to withdraw family members from a number of other US missions in the region, US officials told Reuters. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis struck several targets on Oct 21 with at least one person killed and eight more wounded at a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oil field. Explosions were also heard in Sirik in southern Iran, Iranian media reported on Oct 21, saying the nature and origin of the explosions were unknown. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said on Oct 22 that four vessels involved in illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf were simultaneously hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Oct 21. The IRGC added that three more vessels collided with mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and warned the US military that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. Supply disruption continued to impact global inventories. US crude stocks fell by 3.06 million barrels to 412.5 million barrels last week, the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) said on Oct 21, compared with analysts’ expectations in a Reuters poll for an 820,000-barrel draw. Distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, rose 1.68 million barrels in the week to 104.3 million barrels, versus expectations for a 1.16 million-barrel drop, EIA data showed. The Trump administration is offering to loan up to nearly a third of the one-million-barrel US emergency heating oil reserve, the Department of Energy said on Oct 21, seeking to contain prices that have surged on diesel shortages owing to the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin hosted US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Oct 21 for talks on ending the war in Ukraine amid Washington’s latest push to stop Europe’s bloodiest conflict since World War II. The Kremlin said Putin had agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine by as soon as November. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he supported the talks and hoped they would start as soon as possible. REUTERS

events.title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
events.summary: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs. What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning. As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind. Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip. And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade. A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more. “You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention. Matching storage to the AI data life cycle Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn’t fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer. This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage   What this means for how AI gets budgeted For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators. Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished. A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand. Building for economically scalable capacity Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it. What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives. Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales. There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget: What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it? Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing? If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse? Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence. That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after. This content was produced by WD. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

events.title: Affordable home scheme went from 'blessing' to 'disaster', buyers say
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ACT affordable home scheme dubbed a 'disaster' as Canberra buyers wait years to move in Tash Lawther at the Whitlam property she has been waiting years to move into. ( ABC News: Lily Nothling ) Some people who bought townhouses off the plan as part of the ACT Suburban Land Agency's Affordable Home Purchase Scheme say they have been waiting years to move in. Some say they are also locked in contractual disputes with the builder about the properties. The Suburban Land Agency says it recently sent its own inspector to the properties in Whitlam to examine quality and completion issues. It was spruiked as a scheme to allow low and middle-income earners to purchase their first home in Canberra, but almost five years after signing on, some participants are yet to move in. Instead, some buyers say they have been left stranded as they grapple with incomplete works while locked in contractual disputes with the builder. "It's the sense of powerlessness — it's supposed to be a home, the place you feel safe and comfortable in, and this house is going to be a reminder of the years waiting. "I do feel like ... maybe it wasn't possible within the price-capped contract." The ACT Suburban Land Agency’s Affordable Home Purchase Scheme was set up to provide affordable properties in the fast-growing new suburbs of Whitlam and Taylor. Canberra resident Tash Lawther has been locked in contractual disputes with the builder of her Whitlam property. ( ABC News: Lily Nothling ) Ms Lawther was initially excited when she was selected, via a ballot, to purchase land and a three-bedroom one-bathroom townhouse in Whitlam for about $440,000 in December 2021. "It was a little bit of good news to share after a couple of really hard years post-COVID and just a little bit of joy for everybody to get excited about," she said. Participants were advised construction would start in 2022 and would be completed in 2023. Instead, the project was overshadowed by lengthy delays before work finally began. Suburban Land Agency chief executive Adam Davey says some of the homes are taking "extraordinarily long" to finish. ( ABC News: Robert Baird ) Suburban Land Agency chief executive Adam Davey said the ACT government had been providing rent assistance to 11 buyers for about two years as works dragged on. events.title: Beyond The EPE Budget: Building The Next Generation Of Computational Lithography
events.summary: At the recent SPIE Photomask Technology + Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography conference, an expert panel discussed the growing importance of edge placement error (EPE). I had the pleasure of joining moderator Jed Rankin of IBM and fellow panelists Hans Stiepan of Carl Zeiss SMT, Ezequiel Vidal-Russell of Micron Technology, Jo Finders of ASML, Il-Yong Jang of Tekscend, and Vivek Balasubramanian of Applied Materials. Together, we brought perspectives spanning OPC and EDA, mask technology, lithography systems, materials, and metrology. One point quickly became clear: EPE is no longer a narrow lithography metric. It is becoming a system-level measure of how well our industry can translate design intent into a manufacturable, high-yielding device. The mask, scanner, resist, etch process, metrology, OPC, and downstream integration all contribute. Each discipline can optimize its own part, but a collection of local optima does not automatically produce the best device—even if everyone arrives with an excellent slide explaining why their part is already optimized. EPE has become a system problem As pitch scaling becomes more difficult, tighter control of placement, variability, and pattern fidelity becomes one of the main paths to continued scaling. The challenge is that EPE is an unbounded budget. Mask three-dimensional effects, absorber profile, sidewall angle, critical-dimension uniformity, registration, scanner behavior, resist variability, etch, stochastic effects, process-induced stress, and even wafer or die bonding can all move an edge or change its electrical consequence. Yet the audience survey delivered a wonderfully familiar verdict: OPC was viewed both as a major source of EPE and as the leading place from which future EPE reduction would come. In other words, OPC was cast as both the villain and the superhero. Jed leaned into the joke, asking what Ezequiel and I would need from the rest of the industry to carry that superhero burden. By the final poll, confidence in OPC had risen to 58 percent—prompting the prediction that I might appear next time in tights. I am happy to accept the confidence; the cape may be negotiable. The EDA challenge: Stop treating residual error as one big bucket Today, many effects that are difficult to isolate are absorbed into empirical corrections, rule tables, or an “etch” term. This is pragmatic and often necessary in production, where repeatability, runtime, yield, and schedule outweigh a perfect explanation. Ezequiel captured the dilemma well: after seeing the poll, he was not sure whether the OPC community should feel encouraged or concerned. The audience clearly expected OPC to take care of every systematic and correctable effect—and, where possible, reduce sensitivity to the uncorrectable ones too. That is an impressive job description for any superhero. But even OPC needs good physics, good data, and a process window; it cannot leap an inaccurate model in a single bound. As tolerances shrink, the effects we sweep into the correction bucket become large relative to the remaining process window. EDA must therefore represent the real manufacturing system more completely: not an idealized mask with uniform properties, but pattern-dependent mask profiles, realistic metrology behavior, scanner effects, process variability, and the interactions among them. Not more data, better data More data alone is not the answer. We need data that is physically meaningful, sufficiently repeatable for manufacturing, and connected to the patterns that matter on the wafer. A single SEM image contains far more information than one extracted CD. Contours, profiles, roughness, placement, local geometry, and pattern context can all inform better models. At the same time, no fab can measure everything. OPC and process models should help identify the patterns with the highest wafer sensitivity, rank the hotspots, and translate that sensitivity into mask and wafer metrology requirements. This closes a critical loop: modeling guides measurement, measurement improves modeling, and both focus resources on yield-relevant problems. AI must be paired with physics and validation I believe artificial intelligence will deliver one of the largest future gains in EPE reduction. Machine learning can capture residual systematic behavior that is difficult to model directly, while agentic systems can coordinate optimization across traditionally separate domains. But semiconductor manufacturing cannot rely on an unexplained black box. A model that reports zero EPE without showing why it is trustworthy is not production-ready. The path forward is explainable AI anchored by rigorous simulation, validated against appropriate metrology, bounded by known physics, and monitored for the conditions in which it can safely be applied. Agentic systems should solve defined engineering problems Agentic AI should not be turned loose across the ecosystem with the assumption that it will discover a global optimum on its own. Adoption will begin with well-defined problems: reducing global CDU, selecting robust mask geometries, optimizing source and mask together, prioritizing metrology, or connecting pattern variation to electrical impact. For each problem, we must define the objective, the data required, the knobs the system may turn, the physical constraints, and the validation criteria. Confidence will grow locally, and successful agents can then be connected into broader workflows. EDA must connect EPE to power, performance, area, cost, and yield Our customers do not sell EPE; they sell products defined by power, performance, area, cost, and yield. Some EPE limits are hard geometric boundaries: exceed them and a structure shorts, opens, or fails. Other errors occupy a gray zone where their importance depends on device behavior. EDA has an opportunity to bridge that gap by bringing electrical simulation, stochastic analysis, lithography, mask optimization, process modeling, and design technology co-optimization into a common decision flow. The goal is not simply the smallest geometric error everywhere. It is the right allocation of process margin where it creates the greatest product value. Fig. 1: Process simulations using stochastic modeling techniques can predict process characteristics that lead to electrical problems with a design before reticles are built. Collaboration is the path from local to global optimization Foundries and IDMs sit at the center of this opportunity because they see the complete manufacturing flow and hold the data that connects mask, scanner, process, device, and yield. EDA providers need deeper partnerships with them, as well as with mask makers, metrology suppliers, and lithography equipment providers. Those partnerships must enable secure, purposeful sharing of data and context—not data collection for its own sake. events.title: PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload
events.summary: For decades, silicon characterization has been built around Process, Voltage, and Temperature, or PVT. We characterize devices across process variation, sweep voltage and frequency, control temperature, generate SHMOO plots, and establish the operating envelope of the silicon. That methodology remains fundamental. But today’s high-performance processors are increasingly systems in their own right. An AI accelerator may contain thousands of compute elements, distributed SRAM, high-speed SerDes, PCIe and Ethernet interfaces, multiple clock and power domains, advanced packaging, firmware, operating systems, compilers and application software. Two devices operating at exactly the same voltage, frequency, and temperature can behave differently depending on what they are being asked to do. This suggests adding another dimension: PVTW: Process × Voltage × Temperature × Workload Frequency can be swept within this characterization space to determine operating margin. The objective is not to replace traditional ATE characterization with System Level Test. It is to combine the electrical precision and control available from ATE with the realistic operating environment available from SLT, while retaining the ability to use either independently. One platform, two capabilities, three modes One way to implement PVTW is through a hybrid characterization architecture integrating ATE resources and SLT capability. There is no reason to recreate resources that already exist in ATE. Existing ATE infrastructure, including older generation platforms, can provide programmable device power supplies, individual rail control and measurement, variable frequency clocks, digital stimulus and capture, ATPG and structural content, parametric measurements, and conventional SHMOO characterization. SLT provides something fundamentally different: the application environment. The processor can boot firmware and an operating system, load drivers and runtime software, and execute deterministic workloads designed to exercise specific parts of the architecture. For an AI processor, those workloads might emphasize compute, SRAM, external memory, PCIe, Ethernet, or chip-to-chip communication. Other workloads could intentionally activate several simultaneously to create realistic system stress. The architecture therefore provides three modes. ATE mode performs conventional electrical, structural, and parametric characterization. SLT mode executes controlled system workloads. Combined mode uses ATE resources to control and measure electrical conditions while the device executes an SLT workload. Combined mode is where PVTW becomes particularly interesting. From conventional SHMOO to workload SHMOO Consider a conventional voltage and frequency SHMOO using ATPG or appropriate functional content. At a controlled temperature, establish the operating boundary. Now boot the processor, establish a deterministic workload, and repeat the sweep. Start with a compute-intensive workload. Repeat with SRAM, external memory, PCIe, and Ethernet-intensive workloads. Finally, create combinations that deliberately generate simultaneous compute, memory, and I/O activity. Suppose an ATPG SHMOO indicates that a device operates correctly down to 0.72 V at a particular frequency, while an SRAM-intensive application begins producing errors at 0.76 V. That 40 mV difference is not simply a disagreement between ATE and SLT. It is characterization information. Something about the workload is consuming margin. Is it SRAM timing? Clock distribution? IR drop? Simultaneous switching noise? A thermal gradient? Power delivery? Or an interaction among several subsystems? Characterization requires control There is an important distinction between testing and characterization. Booting Linux, running an AI workload, and observing whether the processor crashes is useful testing. Characterization requires controlled variables, repeatability, and the ability to deliberately move the operating boundary. Hold workload, temperature, and frequency constant while sweeping a selected voltage rail. Then hold workload, temperature, and voltage constant while sweeping frequency. Change temperature and repeat. The hybrid architecture can go deeper. Hold I/O and memory rails constant while margining the core rail during a compute workload. Then margin a memory-related rail while executing a memory-intensive workload. We can begin creating subsystem-specific workload SHMOOs that connect: Workload → Subsystem → Electrical Margin From workload failure to electrical debug Consider a device that passes Wafer Sort and Final Test but develops errors after a sustained application workload. Cooling reduces the failure rate, while increasing the core voltage does not eliminate the problem. Telemetry indicates that most errors are associated with the same memory interface or byte lane, although the failing addresses move. The device does not necessarily have to leave the characterization platform. SLT mode can expose the system behavior and help isolate the subsystem. The platform can operate in ATE mode to investigate electrical and structural characteristics using programmable power, clock control, ATPG, functional patterns, and parametric measurements. Or both capabilities can operate together. The workload can reproduce the marginal condition while ATE resources manipulate selected rails and clocks. The three modes therefore answer different questions. SLT exposes the behavior. ATE investigates the electrical and structural characteristics. Combined mode characterizes their interaction. This creates a tight engineering loop: Create workload → Observe marginality → Isolate subsystem → Characterize electrically → Modify conditions → Repeat workload → Establish correlation → Determine root cause For me, that is the interesting possibility behind PVTW. SLT no longer needs to be viewed only as a downstream production screen. Combined intelligently with ATE resources, it can become part of a controlled silicon characterization environment. But this leads to another question. If two devices both PASS, are they actually equivalent? That is the subject of Part 2: Beyond Pass/Fail: Characterizing Silicon Margin with PVTW. The post PVTW: Extending Silicon Characterization From PVT To Real-World Workload appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .
