events.title: Chip Scaling Moves Beyond The Transistor
events.summary: Key Takeaways: The semiconductor industry reached $1 trillion years early, but keeping pace with demand now depends on systems integration as much as transistor scaling. Packaging, photonics, power, and test are converging into one optimization problem, which means improving any one of them can move the bottleneck somewhere else. AI is shifting from the workload the industry serves to a tool it uses, and the open question is how much engineering and manufacturing authority it will be given. When SEMICON West gathered in San Francisco in 2023, the semiconductor industry was forecasting a path to $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2030. Three years later, the industry has already blown past that number. SEMICON West 2026 returned to San Francisco with a sold-out exhibit floor, more than 30,000 attendees, and an industry confronting a different question: How does it keep up with the growth it once aimed for? SEMI’s own projections show how steep that curve has become. In his opening keynote, SEMI President and CEO Ajit Manocha forecast a market of more than $2 trillion by 2030, and potentially $3 trillion by 2035. At the SEMI Market Symposium, the association projected 300mm fab equipment spending of $149 billion this year, rising to $227 billion by 2029, with construction beginning on 20 new 300mm fabs or production lines in 2026 alone. AI infrastructure is driving much of that growth, but electrification, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and industrial automation are adding semiconductor content, as well. What makes the current expansion unusual is the growing complexity of the systems those chips will enable, not the almost insatiable demand for chips. “We’ve started talking about how to re-engineer engineering because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections,” said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys . “That’s at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what’s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack?” Across presentations, panels, and discussions on the show floor, several issues kept converging around that problem. Advanced packaging is becoming part of system architecture. Photonics is moving closer to compute, while bringing new manufacturing and test challenges with it. Test, inspection and metrology have to follow more complicated assemblies and manufacturing histories. And AI is moving from something the industry builds to something it uses to design and manufacture. None of these technologies is new, but each is becoming harder to optimize independently, and that may be the clearest indication of what the industry will be working on in the coming years. Scaling becomes a system-level challenge The shift was apparent in conversations ranging from transistor scaling and HBM to advanced packaging, optical interconnects, and cooling, where improving any one of those can move a bottleneck elsewhere. More compute increases pressure on memory bandwidth and power delivery. Moving memory closer reduces data movement but concentrates heat. Disaggregating a large die can improve yield and allow functions to use different process nodes, but it creates more interfaces that have to be connected, powered, cooled, and tested. “Packaging is no longer simply the place where semiconductor innovation ends,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&D at Intel Foundry . “Increasingly, it’s the place where system innovation begins.” That makes memory, data movement, power delivery, and thermal management part of the architecture rather than downstream considerations. “The challenge is not to co-optimize one component,” Immaneni said. “It is to co-optimize across the system from end to end between silicon, packaging, and platform.” Nitin Deshpande, Marvell’s vice president of advanced packaging, made a similar point during imec’s pre-show ITF USA program. “The package is really becoming a system where the compute, the memory, the interconnects, the power, the cooling, all of these things come together.” Making those pieces work together is only part of the challenge. Larger, more heterogeneous packages still have to become high-volume products with acceptable yield, reliability, and cost. “We can have very cool concepts, but if we cannot scale these into high volumes, if we cannot have a high-yielding, reliable process with a supply chain that can provide the parts in time, everything that we do cannot be converted into a business,” Deshpande said. Patrick Vandenameele, CEO of imec, noted that AI infrastructure can keep growing by adding accelerators and racks, but adding hardware isn’t scaling in the traditional semiconductor sense. “These data centers are true engineering marvels,” he said. “But at the same time, this is not what we semiconductor people call scaling. It looks a little bit more like multiplication.” That distinction helps explain why so many separate topics at SEMICON West kept leading back to the same place. The industry isn’t abandoning transistor scaling. It’s adding another level above it, where performance depends on how effectively different technologies can be combined into a functional system. Fig. 2: Redefining a system. Source: SEMI AI moves from assistant to operator AI was nearly impossible to avoid at SEMICON West, but the conversation is shifting. Machine learning has been part of design, process control, and defect classification for years, and generative AI added natural-language access to complicated tools and data. Agentic AI goes further, allowing engineers to hand an agent an objective and let it invoke other tools, models, or agents to reach it. “We started from an assistant copilot to generative capability to now what we’re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome,” said Synopsys’ Ghazi. The appeal of agentic AI becomes clearer when looking at the size of the spaces engineers are being asked to optimize. “The space that we’re optimizing in has exploded,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research . “We’ve now gotten to a place where the parameter set is intractable.” A current Lam etcher, for example, can have a potential recipe space on the order of 10 23 possibilities, which is well beyond what any engineer can explore manually. “That’s really where AI is coming to the rescue,” Fried said. “It’s the ability to get through massive multi-parameter dimensional spaces, massive sets of intertwined sensitivities between a much larger parameter space, and a much larger spec space.” Acting on what AI finds is where the discussion gets more complicated. Flagging an unusual process signature is different from letting an AI system alter a recipe, and predicting equipment degradation is different from stopping production. events.title: How Self-Aligned CFET Technology Could Extend CMOS Scaling Beyond 10 Å
events.summary: As their dimensions continue to shrink, conventional gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors may face growing challenges, such as leakage, mobility, resistance, and manufacturing variability. A proposed self-aligned complementary field-effect transistor (SA-CFET) architecture addresses these constraints by vertically stacking N-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (NMOS) and P-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (PMOS) devices and using self-aligned modules to improve density and manufacturability. What is a CFET? A complementary field-effect transistor (CFET) is a transistor architecture that vertically stacks NMOS and PMOS devices. This configuration can reduce cell area, increase effective channel width, and improve electrostatic control compared with side-by-side device layouts. With SEMulator3D , the Semiverse Solutions team used digital twin process modeling to show that the self-aligned architecture can support static random-access memory (SRAM) and logic cells while delivering a 0.0094 μm² SRAM bit cell, a 52.7% area reduction compared with N3 technology, and at least a 10 nm overlay window across critical contact layers. Why transistor scaling beyond 10 Å is difficult Many experts believe that the currently most-advanced transistor architecture, silicon GAA nanosheets, may begin to have physics and manufacturing issues past the 10 angstrom (Å) node. These challenges include: Source-drain tunneling and increased leakage current as the gate length shrinks Mobility issues, surface scattering, and manufacturing issues as the channel thickness is reduced Contact and parasitic resistance issues as the transistor size decreases Manufacturing variability that may seriously impact yield beyond the 10 Å node With these challenges, it is becoming increasingly difficult to scale down the nanosheet device area or enhance device density by simply shrinking the active area, gate, or metal patterning pitch. Why CFET matters for sub-10Å scaling CFET architecture stacks PMOS and NMOS vertically to achieve significant area reduction, enhanced performance through larger effective channel width, and improved electrostatics. 1,2,3,4 However, CFET architecture faces its own critical integration challenges: metal gate isolation complexity and contact crowding that can cause electrical shorts or open circuits. These issues intensify at smaller dimensions, requiring innovative solutions for scalability. How the self-aligned architecture works To address these challenges, we propose a SA-CFET architecture with three key self-aligned modules: SA-BPR (buried power rail), SA-CT (contacts), and SA-TSV (through-silicon via). These process modules enlarge the edge placement error window and mitigate contact crowding, improving process margin. The architecture uses non-metal gate cut design and middle dielectric isolation (MDI) for work function split. 5 SA-CFET maintains compatibility with N3 specifications (42-nm CPP, 21-nm metal pitch), transforming overlay-sensitive steps into self-aligned processes for better manufacturability. Fig. 1: Key integration loops of the SA-CFET. Design implementation: SRAM and logic cells The SA-CFET design can be used to successfully build 6T SRAM cells and logic standard cells (NOT, NAND, NOR) with no metal gate split required within any single fin, simplifying the process flow. The complete interconnection network, validated through digital twin (process) simulation, demonstrates complex routing capability while maintaining self-aligned benefits. Fig. 2: 3D interconnection network architecture showing SRAM and logic cells (NAND, NOR, NOT) with complex routing validated through digital twin simulation. Performance results SA-CFET achieves a 6T SRAM bit cell area of 0.0094 μm²—a 52.7% reduction versus N3 technology 6 and 19% reduction versus state-of-the-art A7 CFET designs. Process robustness validation shows at least a 10-nm overlay window for all critical contact layers with no open/short failures, confirming robust process margin. Fig. 3: SRAM bit cell area comparison showing 52.7% reduction versus N3 technology. Fig. 4: Overlay window validation confirming robust process margin across critical contact layers. Conclusion This article describes an innovative self-aligned CFET architecture that employs multiple self-aligned processes. Using this architecture, we designed a process sequence for both a 6T SRAM device and for logic standard cells using digital twin (process) modeling. We found the proposed architecture shares similar or even more relaxed design rules compared to current or conventional semiconductor manufacturing. It also provides an area reduction from both existing N3 devices and state-of-the-art CFET architectures. More importantly, it avoids many of the scaling issues found in existing nanosheet architectures, achieving enhanced performance through larger effective channel width and improved electrostatics at smaller nodes. We believe that this work demonstrates a potential architectural solution to support CMOS scaling for transistors at 10 Å and beyond. References Subramanian et al., “First Monolithic Integration of 3D Complementary FET (CFET) on 300mm Wafers,” 2020 IEEE Symposium on VLSI Technology, Honolulu, HI, USA, 2020, pp. 1-2. events.title: Stacked-Die Multi-Chip Architectures: The Tradeoff Between Scaling And Power Delivery
events.summary: By Kaladhar Radhakrishnan, Nicolas Butzen, and Vishal Javvaji The semiconductor industry has embraced multi-chip and stacked-die architectures as the primary path for continued performance scaling. As monolithic designs become more difficult and costly to advance, chiplets, advanced packaging, and 3D integration enable higher levels of performance, bandwidth, and functional integration for AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. Yet the success of stacked-die, multi-chip architectures has exposed a growing power delivery challenge. As more compute resources are integrated into a package, there is a sharp uptick in current density and the number of independent voltage domains, placing unprecedented demands on shared power delivery resources. To address these challenges, we discussed in our recent power delivery white paper how Intel Foundry is moving voltage regulation closer to the load. By enabling higher-voltage power distribution, integrated voltage regulators (IVRs) reduce current density in the package, provide higher regulation bandwidth, and reduce reliance on large decoupling capacitor networks. Intel Foundry’s portfolio spans package-integrated magnetic inductors, fully capacitive IVR chiplets, and advanced package integration technologies, providing multiple paths to improve power integrity, efficiency, and scalability. System-level consequences of stacked-die architectures Advanced packaging delivers significant gains in performance, bandwidth, and integration density. However, consistently distributing power through increasingly complex packaging and interconnect structures introduces new challenges in maintaining power integrity across the package. One consequence is voltage droop. As AI workloads generate rapid swings in current demand, the power delivery network must respond instantly. When it cannot, voltage can briefly fall below target levels, potentially impacting performance. To maintain reliability, designers often add voltage guard bands and operating margins. While effective, these safeguards can limit silicon from reaching its optimal efficiency and performance. Multi-chip and stacked-die architectures also intensify the tradeoff between signal density and power delivery. As more compute tiles, memory interfaces, and die-to-die links are added, routing congestion increases, creating additional resistance, tighter voltage margins, and growing power delivery constraints. Moving power delivery closer to the load As current density continues to increase, the industry is moving toward architectures that bring voltage conversion closer to the point of consumption, reducing power delivery losses while improving responsiveness to rapidly changing workloads. Intel Foundry is advancing several complementary technologies designed around this principle. FIVR with CoaxMIL: Intel was an early pioneer of fully integrated voltage regulators (FIVRs), which moves the last voltage conversion stage onto the processor. By shortening the distance between the regulator and the load, FIVR helps reduce distribution losses and improve transient response. To support rising current densities, Intel developed CoaxMIL, a magnetic inductor technology that delivers significantly higher current density than earlier approaches while requiring less area (see Figure 1). For customers building next-generation AI and HPC devices, this translates into improved power conversion efficiency, faster response to workload changes, and more efficient use of valuable package real estate. The result is greater performance potential without proportional increases in power delivery complexity. Fig. 1: CoaxMIL magnetic inductor technology. C2VR: Intel Foundry’s continuous capacitive voltage regulator (C2VR) takes voltage conversion in a different direction. Rather than relying on traditional inductors, C2VR uses high-density capacitor technology to achieve efficient voltage conversion in an extremely compact form factor. Because capacitors are integrated directly onto the voltage regulator chiplet, C2VR can deliver both high efficiency and exceptionally high current density. It can also respond rapidly to sudden current demands, helping minimize voltage droop during the bursty workload transitions common in AI accelerators. For customers, the benefit is improved power integrity, tighter voltage control, and a scalable solution capable of supporting future multi-kiloamp workloads. IVR chiplet architectures: These dedicated power management chiplets allow voltage conversion to be positioned closer to the compute die than traditional motherboard-based regulators. The primary advantage of IVR chiplet architectures is flexibility. Architects can position voltage regulation where it delivers the greatest benefit, whether on the landside, embedded within package layers, or beneath compute dies. This flexibility allows architects to optimize power delivery for specific applications while reducing distribution losses and improving overall efficiency. In advanced stacked-die systems, these architectures also open the door to vertical power delivery schemes that reduce distribution distance and improve power integrity. The future of power delivery As AI systems continue their rapid evolution, power delivery is becoming as critical to performance scaling as transistor and packaging innovation. The next generation of data center architectures will require a portfolio of solutions that move power conversion closer to the load, improve efficiency at extreme current densities, and maintain stable operation under increasingly dynamic workloads. Intel Foundry technologies are important building blocks, helping ensure that future compute platforms can continue scaling performance without being constrained by the power delivery network. This blog is the second in a two-part series on power delivery innovation. Part 1 explores how data center energy trends are affecting chip power delivery. Nicolas Butzen is a principal engineer at Intel. Vishal Javvaji is a process integration manager at Intel Foundry. events.title: What Breaks When Packaging Moves From Wafer To Panel?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Moving advanced packaging from wafer to panel changes more than available area. Processes developed around wafer geometry, handling, and equipment have to be reconsidered at panel scale. Larger panels amplify dimensional change, warpage, and process history, making what happens at one manufacturing step increasingly important to the next. The most economical manufacturing flow may use different substrate formats at different stages rather than carrying one large panel through the entire process. Moving advanced packaging from wafer to panel sounds, at first, like a geometry problem. Large AI and HPC packages are increasingly rectangular, while the 300mm wafer underneath them is still round. As the package size grows, more of that expensive processing ends up around the circle’s edges where nothing useful can be built. A panel gives that area back. It can fit more large packages into the same process cycle, and unlike a wafer, its dimensions don’t impose the same hard limit on the size of a square or rectangular package. For advanced packages that keep getting larger, the economics are difficult to ignore. But the semiconductor packaging sector has spent decades learning how to process wafers, not panels. Equipment, materials, recipes, handling systems, and process controls were all developed around the geometry and mechanical behavior of a round workpiece. “The risk of doing the assembly on the 600mm panel is high, and I don’t think we have all the equipment today to run the process,” said Teck Chong Lee, technical director of advanced fan-out development for HPC applications at ASE , in a recent presentation. “One of the options is, once you complete the interposer in large format in 600, then you divide it into four pieces to run the assembly and the C4 process. This is a much lower-risk approach.” The economics behind that compromise are substantial. In the same study, a 5.5×-reticle-size interposer produced 9 units on a 300mm wafer, compared with 16 on a 300mm panel. A 600mm panel divided into four 300mm pieces produces 64, while processing the full 600mm area intact raises that to 72. In pure utilization, the intact panel produces 8 times as many units as the wafer, a gain well beyond the roughly fivefold difference in raw area, because the rectangular panel wastes almost nothing at its edges. The flow therefore takes the area advantage where it can use it, then gives some of it back before assembly because the manufacturing infrastructure isn’t ready to follow the larger format all the way through. That compromise exposes the larger transition underway. Moving packaging from wafer to panel isn’t simply making the process bigger. It is discovering which parts of the process were dependent on the wafer dimensions all along. The process was built around the wafer The utilization advantage grows as the package does. In one comparison, Intel Foundry used a 510 × 515mm panel and showed that a roughly 4× reticle package would produce about 10 units on a 300mm wafer and approximately 48 on the panel. Eventually the wafer imposes a harder geometric limit, since the largest square that fits on a 300mm wafer is only about 210 × 210mm. “For certain form factors, we believe a wafer is more economical,” said Tarek Ibrahim, senior principal engineer at Intel , in a conference presentation. “However, when you go beyond a certain form factor, you can see quickly that the panel becomes more effective, mainly because you can get more units out of a panel. Because of the way AI is heading and the need for a very large system, panels became an obvious choice for scale.” Fig. 1: Intel’s Tarek Ibrahim discusses substrate scaling for heterogeneous integration. Source: Semiconductor Engineering The economic crossover doesn’t mean the manufacturing process crosses over with it. Much of the equipment and process knowledge used in advanced packaging was developed for a round wafer, and changing the shape and scale of the substrate changes what those processes have to do. Over time, many of those wafer-specific assumptions became invisible because the workpiece underneath them rarely changed. What looked like a requirement of the process was often just a requirement of the wafer. “At wafer level, it’s a single-sided process,” Ibrahim said. “On panel, it’s actually a dual-sided process. Managing the process at that panel scale with the right uniformity and the right Cpk [process capability index] is definitely a challenge.” Part of the challenge is that familiar wafer processes don’t always transfer cleanly to a larger rectangular surface. Spin coating, for example, relies on radial symmetry, so a rectangular substrate produces uneven film thickness toward the corners while most of the dispensed resist is thrown away. In a 600mm panel flow, photoresist is instead deposited by slit or slot-die coating across an active area of roughly 586 × 586mm. Lithography also changes, with maskless direct imaging displacing the conventional wafer stepper in many panel flows. Those differences propagate into the materials and equipment surrounding the process. Fine-line RDL on glass panels is pushing toward new photoresists and application methods, tighter overlay control, and equipment that can maintain temperature and process uniformity across a much larger area. Large hot plates become a development problem of their own. As line and space moves from roughly 5µm toward 2µm and below, processes that historically belonged farther back in the packaging flow begin demanding something closer to front-end precision. The awkward part is that the panel can’t simply inherit the front-end equipment built to provide that precision. Much of that infrastructure assumes a round 300mm wafer, while traditional substrate equipment was designed around different feature sizes and process tolerances. Panel-level packaging is landing somewhere between the two. The result is less a scaled-up wafer flow than a new manufacturing process being assembled from pieces of several older ones. The panel solves an increasingly expensive geometry problem, but it also exposes how many coating, exposure, handling, and uniformity assumptions were tied to the wafer that came before it. Yield decides how big is useful The simplest argument for a larger panel is that more packages fit on it. The real economic question is how many good packages come off. That matters more as the value assembled onto the workpiece rises. A panel carrying logic and HBM can contain tens of thousands of dollars of known-good silicon before some package-level failures become visible. At that point, even a small yield loss can erase the savings created by processing more area at once. “There’s so much money in chips going onto a wafer or panel that a tiny yield hit, and the loss of some of that super-expensive silicon, will just blow all the benefits from a larger scale that you had right out the window,” said Mike Kelly, vice president of chipl

events.title: Foundries And OSATs Increasingly Overlap
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Foundries have been doing backend work for advanced packages. OSATs are now taking that on. This particularly affects 2.5D and panel assembly with new equipment and materials. Hybrid bonding is mostly a foundry activity now but will likely move to OSATs as well. Foundries and outsourced assembly and test (OSAT) houses have traditionally had distinct lanes, but the lines are blurring as OSATs acquire select foundry capabilities and foundries return some of the jobs they have taken from OSATs. “We’re at this bridging point where the IDMs and the foundries are doing more of what OSATs can do, and the OSATs are also trying to get much closer to what the foundry does at the back end,” said Raghu Nayak, head of sales at Zeiss. OSATs will never compete with foundries on advanced nodes and front-end wafer fabrication. But for backend activities, where dimensions aren’t as demanding, OSATs are acquiring capabilities that replicate what foundries can do. The biggest areas of overlap are 2.5D integration and panel assembly, with hybrid bonding likely to move there as well. The change affects equipment and materials. “We are seeing the migration of lithography-related materials and processes from traditional wafer fabs into advanced packaging environments,” said Poupak Khodabandeh, chief business officer at Brewer Science . “As advanced packaging increasingly relies on fine-pitch redistribution layers (RDLs), OSATs and packaging organizations are using materials and process flows that historically would have been associated with wafer fabrication.” “The industry has traditionally operated in silos across equipment, front-end fabrication, design, packaging, and test,” said Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco . “We need to connect those disciplines so teams can use shared, physics-grounded insight to make faster, better-informed design decisions, while also providing greater manufacturing flexibility — especially at the backend.” It used to be “to each his own” Foundries and OSATs have taken on complementary duties for many years. Foundries fabricate the silicon chip, while OSATs put the chip into a housing and test the final product. A vast array of EDA tools and fab equipment makes what the foundry does possible, while OSATs have worked more with tools that originated in the printed circuit board (PCB) world. Two industry trends are challenging this status quo. The first is the development of advanced packaging. It’s no longer enough to put a chip on a substrate, wire it up, and pour molding compound over it. This doesn’t minimize the effort required to do those basics well, but they’re very different from what advanced packaging requires. “Advanced packaging is becoming more lithography-intensive,” said Khodabandeh. “The industry’s push toward higher interconnect density for AI, HBM, chiplet architectures, and heterogeneous integration is driving the adoption of wafer-fab-style patterning processes within packaging facilities. RDL fabrication is a good example, where increasingly sophisticated lithography is required to create finer features.” Intel Foundry works both sides of the aisle, with foundry and packaging capabilities. “When you do fine pitch bumps, the bump count goes up quite a bit compared to coarse pitch,” said Ravi Mahajan, fellow at Intel Foundry . “So you have to figure out things like embedding [bridge dies such as EMIB]. You have to figure out alignment and equipment precision.” For them, they can attempt these things on either side of the divide. Foundries have been heavily involved in 2.5D packaging, but a second industry trend is making that more difficult — a lack of capacity. Foundries can’t make all the chips their clients want, so they’re prioritizing and allocating. That may mean turning away some business they would otherwise entertain, likely in backend and legacy processes, since foundries will focus on newer-node silicon processes they are uniquely capable of. The OSATs are ready to pick up those processes. These are lower-resolution processes that foundries have historically employed but for which OSATs share capabilities. Legacy-node builds can spill over to assembly houses, especially since advanced packaging requires tooling consistent with those older technologies. Although this overlap largely affects older processes, as constraints continue, even more aggressive technology, which foundries have often packaged (or done the first packaging steps) themselves, may be offloaded. “With further volume restrictions, both legacy-node and leading-edge products are shifting toward OSAT packaging,” said Thomas Uhrmann, vice president of sales at EV Group. Three primary tasks These market dynamics have driven three primary assembly-related processes from foundry to OSAT: 2.5D packaging, panel packaging, and eventually, hybrid bonding. 2.5D packaging in a manner resembling TSMC’s CoWoS (chip on wafer on substrate) involves mounting one die atop another. When the base is an interposer, this is 2.5D. When it’s another active die, it becomes 3D. Typical processes place the top die, already singulated, on a bottom die on a wafer that hasn’t been diced up yet. Once the top die is in place, the bottom wafer can be diced, with the stack-up headed for a package. One fast-growing area that needs this technology is photonics. “Customers are coming to us asking if we can do electrical die to photonics die or wafer attach,” said Gerard John, senior director in Amkor’s Chiplets/FCBGA Business Unit. “We take this module, dice it out, and then attach it to a substrate. That’s a new trend we are seeing, and we can do that.” It may, however, bring some tough new requirements. “This is a big challenge because now you have the optic side of the wafer or die,” added John, and this needs active alignment to attach fibers and test them. Panels, meanwhile, have grown to the 500 mm range per side, but moving to a smaller size actually helped. “Several OSATs had early development lines for panel-level packaging, mainly targeting large panels with 500 mm dimensions,” explained Uhrmann. “TSMC’s decision to move to panel-level packaging with 310 × 310 mm 2 , which is a format closer to classical 300 mm round process tools, has enabled traditional wafer-based equipment manufacturers to scale up for high-performance materials and resolution, rather than PCB equipment manufacturers to scale down.” Meanwhile, some assembly houses are doing hybrid bonding. But for high volume, it largely remains a foundry task, owing to the challenges the process presents. As hybrid bonding loses its novelty and becomes standard, it represents another task that foundries could hand off to OSATs. How are you paying for that? events.title: Elon Musk’s dream merger is a nightmare for SpaceX shareholders
events.summary: The blowout news from SpaceX’s Q3 earnings wasn’t the rocket and AI giant’s outstanding performance that far exceeded even analysts’ elevated expectations, but Elon Musk’s revelation that SpaceX and Tesla are weighing a merger. On the call, held the evening of Oct. 20, Musk declared that his two signature holdings have each named “special committees” composed of independent directors to explore a union. Musk’s statement confirmed Wall Street’s long-held view that the deal was highly likely, and now—given that Musk effectively controls both companies and loves the concept (though as a “conflicted party” can’t serve on the committees), the tie-up looks all but inevitable. The prospect of a SpaceX-Tesla combo got rave notices from the research crews covering both companies. In most cases where the acquirer is en route to paying what amounts to a humongous P/E, its stock falls. Not this time. Investors applauded both enterprises, sending Tesla up 3.4% the day following Musk’s statement and SpaceX ahead 7.8%, adding $155 billion in market cap. At first glance, their already tight kinship, and sundry overlapping businesses, suggest that a SpaceX-Tesla makes sense. SpaceX buys Tesla Megapack batteries and Cybertrucks, Tesla invested $2 billion in xAI, bought by SpaceX in February, and they share ownership of the much-feted chip project Terafab. Not to mention that the deal would clinch Musk’s long-harbored vision of running a single colossus as a kind of Berkshire Hathaway of AI-driven tech. The wizard freed to blend these two great elixirs of innovation? What’s not to like? A close examination of claims made for the deal, especially assumptions on its supposed advantages in bolstering the finances of both companies, points to an extremely risky wager that must perform never-before-seen heroics to reward shareholders. It’s the ultimate buy the leap of faith, it’s about the vision, not the numbers, never bet against Elon scenario, set against the sobering numbers. Let’s explore four frequently made arguments for what would prove the largest and, so far, probably the most universally praised merger in the annals of capitalism. SpaceX-Tesla would be accretive to SpaceX shareholders The idea is that while SpaceX profits are just starting to accelerate, adding Tesla’s earnings, generated from its bedrock EV and battery sales, would immediately raise the former’s earnings per share. In fact, it’s technically true. If the pair combined now, that’s how the math would work. The problem: The addition to SpaceX’s GAAP profits per share would be minuscule, and since SpaceX’s bottom line is growing and Tesla’s is dropping, the deal if done a year or two from now would prove extremely dilutive for the Starlink provider. What stands out when you examine what SpaceX would pay versus what earnings it would get is how shockingly expensive the transaction would be. One big question: How much of a premium would SpaceX offer over Tesla’s current price? As Rajat Gupta of J.P. Morgan points out in a report on the likely merger, that number in most tech acquisitions is 30% to 35%. So let’s posit 30%. Right now, Tesla’s market cap is $1.52 trillion; tack on 30%, and the transaction would cost SpaceX $1.98 trillion. SpaceX’s valuation stands at $2.14 trillion. We’re looking at almost a merger of equals. SpaceX would need to issue the equivalent of 92% of its current shares outstanding to capture Tesla. Hence, SpaceX’s count would zoom from 13.1 billion to 25 billion shares. SpaceX would be awarding nearly half of its future earnings to Tesla’s shareholders. And what is it getting in return? We don’t know what the robots and self-driving cars will deliver, but we do know that Tesla booked just $3.28 billion in GAAP net profits over the past four quarters. Since SpaceX had a $1.5 billion loss over that period, the pro forma deal, as of today, would be “accretive” in the sense that buying Tesla would make the combined company slightly profitable. But SpaceX would just go from earnings per share that are a minuscule negative to a tiny positive. What’s important is the amount SpaceX is paying for those earnings and puny accretion. It would be getting $3.28 billion in profits in exchange for stock worth $1.98 trillion. That’s $600 for every $1 in extra earnings. To make matters worse, Tesla’s profits have been tanking while SpaceX’s bottom line is taking off. In Q3, SpaceX reversed the three prior quarters of deficits by registering $4.4 billion in GAAP net profits, enough to lower its four-quarter loss to that $1.5 billion. In other words, profits are trending the right way, big-time. Via a merger, SpaceX would go from owning 100% of those fast-rising earnings to just over 50%, and getting what is for now a minimal contribution from Tesla. On the accretion argument, it looks like a bad outcome for SpaceX shareholders. But overall, this would be a good deal for SpaceX, right? Even if SpaceX didn’t buy Tesla, its valuation so dwarfs its earnings that only by achieving stupendous growth in revenues and profits can it deliver shareholders an even decent return. In May, David Trainer of New Constructs provided a mathematical reckoning that at its current valuation of $2.14 trillion, SpaceX would need to be generating around $300 billion in profits on sales of roughly $1.6 trillion by 2035 to provide a competitive return. That’s a tall order, to put it mildly. The profits number would be almost a quarter more than what Alphabet makes now, on over three times its revenues. The rub: A Tesla acquisition simply gives SpaceX a far steeper hill to climb, one that gets almost twice as steep sans much help from Tesla. If SpaceX shoulders a 30% premium, the combined companies would start life at a market cap of $4.12 trillion. (That’s SpaceX’s current $2.14 trillion plus the $1.98 trillion paid for Tesla.) SpaceX 2.0 would edge Alphabet ($4.0 trillion) and Microsoft ($3.9 trillion) to rank as the third-most-valuable enterprise in America behind only Nvidia ($5.3 trillion) and Apple ($5.0 trillion). By Fortune’ s estimate, using Trainer’s methodology, SpaceX would need $550 billion in profits and around $3 trillion in revenue to ring the bell by 2035. That $550 billion target is over twice what Alphabet amasses today. Once again, if Tesla were bringing already big and fast-rising profits to the table, the task wouldn’t be nearly as difficult. But it’s just the opposite. The EV-maker is providing exceedingly slender profits that have already declined from $15 billion in 2023, and $5 billion in 2024 to a run rate that’s a third below the figure of just two years ago. Tesla would help SpaceX with what it needs most: Lots of cash flow to pay for its big, pricey AI adventure Much of the attention on SpaceX’s financials focuses on its incredible cash burn that’s chiefly financing its ambitions in AI, or what it now calls “Super Intelligence.” In the first nine months of this year, SpaceX pocketed $13.1 billion in cash from ope

events.title: AI power demand underestimated, say 81% of energy executives
events.summary: More than eight in 10 energy industry decision-makers expect artificial intelligence to drive electricity demand beyond current forecasts, raising concerns about whether there is enough global infrastructure to power the rapid expansion of data centres. A global survey commissioned by Adipec , Abu Dhabi's annual energy conference, found that 81 per cent of energy industry insiders believe AI-driven electricity consumption will exceed existing projections, with 32 per cent expecting demand to be significantly higher. Only 3 per cent expect demand to fall below current forecasts, according to Adipec's Global Energy Report 2026, released on Thursday. Those surveyed included executives from energy companies, technology providers, investors and industry suppliers. The findings come as technology companies accelerate investment in energy-intensive data centres, creating opportunities for power producers while putting additional pressure on electricity networks. The International Energy Agency expects data centres to consume about 950 terawatt-hours of electricity by 2030, roughly double the 2025 level, according to figures cited in the report. The growth in data centre power demand has become an increasingly important consideration for energy producers and governments. At Abu Dhabi Sustainability Week in January, Dr Sultan Al Jaber , Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc , said global electricity requirements from data centres could increase fivefold by 2040. The report's findings build on the “power is knowledge” message that was the theme of discussions at Adipec last year, as The National reported. The relationship between AI and electricity remains a central focus of this year's event, which will take place at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi from November 2 to November 5. Technology companies reign The expansion of AI is also expected to change the balance of influence within the energy industry. About 43 per cent of respondents believe technology and AI companies will gain the most influence over the sector, compared with 15 per cent who selected governments and regulators. Financial institutions were also selected by 15 per cent, followed by international oil companies at 14 per cent and national oil companies at 9 per cent. The findings reflect the increasingly close relationship between AI and energy , as technology companies become major drivers of investment in electricity generation and infrastructure. For oil and gas companies, the shift is creating new commercial opportunities. While gas and liquefied natural gas growth currently ranks as the biggest commercial opportunity for oil and gas insiders, AI-driven efficiency is expected to take the top position over the next decade. About 27 per cent identify AI-driven efficiency as a leading opportunity in 10 years, while 25 per cent cite supplying power for AI and data centres. The report also found that 81 per cent of oil and gas insiders believe adopting AI will become essential to remain profitable over the next decade. The findings are particularly relevant to the UAE, where Abu Dhabi is developing a 5-gigawatt AI campus that will house the Stargate UAE computing cluster, expected to cost more than $30 billion . However, a quarter of energy insiders believe the industry is unprepared for AI-driven electricity demand, with grid delays among the biggest obstacles. At Adipec last year, Dr Al Jaber called for “massive” energy investment to meet growing requirements. The Adipec report, conducted by global strategic communications consultancy Kekst CNC between August and October 2026, surveyed 1,832 energy industry decision-makers across 78 countries and included 17 executive interviews. Its findings reflect industry expectations rather than independently verified demand forecasts.

events.title: Children in care to get £10 a week savings
events.summary: The States of Guernsey said about 40 people in care will be eligible for the scheme. A new government savings scheme will set aside £10 a week for children in care for them to access when they turn 18. Established by the States' Children and Family Community Services and Guernsey Community Savings, it is designed to give young people a financial foundation when becoming an adult. The States said the scheme will apply to children from entry into the care system and 40 will benefit immediately. Associate director of children services Lucy Cook said the savings accounts would support young people by "helping them to access opportunities that might otherwise be out of reach." The States of Guernsey said the transition to independent living for people in care can bring "significant financial pressures, from setting up a home to managing everyday living costs". "Having savings of their own can offer greater choice, security and confidence as they take this important step," it said. The States will pay a one-off fee to allpay, a payment services company, to establish the scheme. The charity Guernsey Community Savings will then open and manage the accounts, and work with each young person and their social worker as they approach their 18th birthday. At 18 years old, they will have the choice of opening an account with Guernsey Community Savings or transferring their savings to an account of their choice. Cook said children in care deserve the opportunity to "look ahead with confidence and hope for their future". "This initiative is about giving our care-experienced young people a stronger foundation and recognising our commitment to them as corporate parents. "We want every child in care to know that they are valued, supported and encouraged to achieve their full potential." Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Chief executive of Guernsey Community Savings Joe Brown said children from care are "particularly vulnerable to financial exclusion when they reach adulthood". events.title: Singapore security robotics firm Kabam to cease operations on Nov 20
events.summary: Kabam Robotics co-founders Kelvin Wee (left) and Benjamin Chia with their robots which can patrol and inspect facilities such as malls. Kabam Robotics, a Singapore security robotics firm, will stop business on Nov 20. It apologised to customers and asked those with open cases to contact it before then. The closure reason was not given. It is unclear how many staff or customers will be affected, though LinkedIn lists 54 employees and the firm has major clients such as Aetos, Certis and Changi Airport Group. Kabam was founded in 2020, later merged with Cognicept Systems, and had more than 150 robots deployed. Its shutdown comes as Singapore pushes to grow its robotics sector through programmes like RoboNexus. SINGAPORE – Home-grown security robotics company Kabam Robotics will cease business operations from Nov 20, according to an e-mail sent to its customers. In the e-mail seen by The Business Times, Kabam’s management apologised for any inconvenience caused and thanked customers for their support over the years. “We sincerely appreciate the trust and support you have placed in Kabam over the years. “It has been our pleasure to work with you, and we are truly grateful for the opportunity to serve your business,” the company said. It added that clients requiring assistance with existing matters should contact it before Nov 20. The reasons for the closure were not disclosed. It is unclear how many employees will be affected or what will happen to the company’s existing customers and robot deployments. Kabam’s LinkedIn page lists 54 employees associated with the company. BT has reached out to Kabam for comment. The company did not immediately respond. The company counts local security services firms Aetos and Certis among its clients, as well as Changi Airport Group, JTC Corporation, Amazon Web Services and Mandai Wildlife Group, its website showed. Its products include artificial intelligence-powered security robotics and management software for video surveillance and autonomous patrolling in indoor and outdoor facilities. The company is a majority-owned subsidiary of Singapore-based precision engineering company Patec Group, which is listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange. It was founded in 2020 as Patec’s robotics venture and then merged with fellow local robotics start-up Cognicept Systems in 2022. BT reported in 2023 that more than 150 of Kabam’s robots were deployed globally and in Singapore, including at Jewel Changi Airport, Paya Lebar Quarter Mall and Toa Payoh HDB Hub. The company’s planned closure comes amid Singapore’s considerable efforts to develop its robotics industry. It was among the first six companies supported under RoboNexus, an accelerator programme piloted by Singapore’s National Robotics Programme in September 2024. The programme was officially launched in March 2025 to support local robotics start-ups through tailored mentorships, business development support and global market access. Kabam was among two robotics companies that tapped the programme’s research and talent pipelines at the product development stage. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: China moves to set global standards for brain-computer interface technology
events.summary: As Beijing prioritises development of the technology, a China-led committee aims to dictate how it is built China has taken a major step in spearheading the standardisation of brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, as it now chairs the secretariat of a subcommittee jointly overseen by two key international organisations and lists the technology applications as a national development priority. The China-led subcommittee, known as ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 43, was set to formulate global standards regarding the communication and interaction between brains and computers that are applicable across application areas, according to abstracts on both websites of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC). The committee, chaired by Yu Yuntao, a former department head with the China Electronics Standardization Institute, has already published several standards, including the BCI vocabulary, data format for non-invasive brain information collection, reference architecture and use cases. “The [Chinese] government is betting on this industry, among others, as one that has the potential to become the next EV sector,” said Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at Eurasia Group.

events.title: KPMG ban on government work extended after 'serious ethical failings'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Ban on KPMG getting government work extended to February after audit leaks scandal Topic: Accounting and Auditing Services KPMG is under the spotlight for "serious ethical failings". ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February. Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into KPMG and found the way the Big Four firm had handled a whistleblower's complaint revealed "serious ethical failings". KPMG CEO John Sams and chairman Michael Ebeid say they are working on a plan to make "lasting change" and hope to win back the government contract. The federal government has extended its ban on accounting firm KPMG bidding for new government work until at least the end of February, following a review that found "serious ethical failings" by its leadership and some of its senior partners. Ian Watt was commissioned by the Department of Finance to conduct an independent review into the Big Four firm, following allegations its audit partners misused client data then mishandled a whistleblower's complaint about it . In response to Mr Watt's review, which was handed down today, the department said it has agreed with the firm to a further extension to the pause on KPMG bidding for Australian government work until February 28, 2027. During this period, KPMG will provide the department with an implementation plan and the first of its quarterly progress implementation reports. The department also needs to ensure that "KPMG is engaging constructively with the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) and the Tax Practitioners Board (TPB) reviews, and is committed to addressing any recommendations that have been made by those organisations". Dr Watt said in his review the way the accounting firm had handled the whistleblower's complaint revealed "serious ethical failings by some senior members of KPMG" and "significant cultural concerns within KPMG". Dr Watt noted the review was focused on the leadership and culture of the firm "that had been warned on previous occasions about weaknesses in ethical culture, speak-up confidence and accountability, but did not deal with them with the rigour and urgency required". Firms raise doubts about KPMG's integrity In the wake of the KPMG audit leak scandal, executives from Macquarie, Westpac, Optus and Dexus cast doubt on their faith in the auditor. He said since March, KPMG has undergone significant change, with a new chair and a new CEO, and a number of senior personnel having left the firm. Dr Watt said the firm had also commissioned several reviews to understand the root causes of the events. "As was often observed during review interviews, trust takes time to build, and while transparency builds trust, lack of transparency damages it." Dr Watt said his report should not be read as a judgement on every member of KPMG. "Virtually all of KPMG's staff had no involvement in the events that occurred," he said. KPMG CEO John Sams and its chairman Michael Ebeid said they accepted the findings and recommendations of Mr Watt's review. John Sams says the firm is working to revamp its internal culture. ( Supplied ) "The report lays bare our failings and highlights the hard work that we must do to address them," they said in a statement. The firm had appointed Kerry Schott to provide independent oversight and said "while we are making important progress, we know that changing culture takes longer than changing individual roles, structures or controls". "Confidence in KPMG's suitability for Commonwealth work must be earned through evidence of effective, lasting change," the statement said. Call to overhaul code governing bids Dr Watt also recommended the department of finance strengthen the Commonwealth's supplier code of conduct, including tougher sanctions for suppliers breaching their obligations and more reporting pathways for potential unethical behaviour. Whistleblowers need better protection Without whistleblowers, Australians would be kept in the dark about major corporate scandals, but evidence suggests the experience of raising alarm bells can destroy their lives. Several states and territories have also banned KPMG from taking on public sector work pending the outcome of Dr Watt's review, or their own reviews. They are working through their responses to the findings. Greens finance and public service spokesperson Senator Barbara Pocock said a small extension of the freeze on KPMG contracts was not dealing with the issue.

events.title: Woman 'scared to turn heating on' due to oil cost
events.summary: Roslynn Garner-Gatley says she relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water A woman has said she is frightened to put her heating on because the cost of domestic oil has nearly doubled. Roslynn Garner-Gatley, 76, lives in a three-bedroom semi-detached cottage in Yealmpton, south Devon, with no gas supply and relies entirely on oil for heating and hot water. She said her oil tank held 1,000 litres (220 gallons). About six months earlier, she bought 500 litres (110 gallons) for £317 plus VAT but, when she contacted her supplier for a current quote, she was told the same amount would cost £600 plus VAT. Garner-Gatley said: "I did not expect at my age after working for 50 years to be in a situation where I am terrified of putting on the heating because of the price of it." The cost of filling her heating oil tank has nearly doubled Garner-Gatley said she had started going to bed earlier to keep warm while watching television and had recently begun using a hot water bottle and bed socks as evening temperatures dropped. She said instead of keeping hot water on a timer, she only switched it on when she needed it for washing, cooking or bathing before turning it off again. She added that people living in rural areas who depended on oil had "no choice" but to buy it. She said: "After working all my life I didn't expect to be constantly worrying about how to keep warm at my age. It is really quite frightening." Heating fuel costs have risen by up to 82% since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, according to Minster for Energy Consumers Polly Billington. Earlier in October, the government promised better regulation of the sector . Ministers said they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things went wrong. Minimum order levels set for some customers would also be reviewed, they added. A spokesperson for the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, said: "We have pledged £53m in support for vulnerable households on heating oil, while helping people switch to clean heat with Boiler Upgrade Scheme grants worth £9,000. "We are also reforming the heating oil sector, holding suppliers to account and giving consumers confidence that they will get a fair deal." Cornwall Council and Devon County Council have money available for households struggling with increasing heating oil costs from their crisis resilience funds, which are provided by the government. Cornwall Council said it had issued payments of £300 to 1,386 households, a total spend of £415,800, which would double after a decision was made to award a further £300 to the same households. The Devon fund, worth about £8.4m a year, is available through district councils, and is targeted at low‑income households facing an "essential cost they cannot afford". Plymouth City Council and Torbay Council also have their own crisis resilience funds. Have you been affected by the issues raised in this story? events.title: 'I can't afford to heat my home on my pension'
events.summary: Teresa Goubert said the cost of heating had become so expensive that she could not afford to heat her home this winter Some pensioners say they are going to bed early, wearing extra layers and using hot water bottles because they cannot afford to heat their homes this winter. Teresa Goubert, from Guernsey, who uses electric and oil heating, said: "I'm trying to keep it off as long as possible because it's got very expensive and I just can't afford to do it [heat home] on my pension." The States has proposed a 19% increase in the means-tested winter fuel allowance to £50.48 a week. It will be debated in November. Tina Bury, Employment and Social Security President, said: "The fuel allowance is quite a broad brush approach and obviously everyone's needs are different in this area." Listen to the latest news for Guernsey Ms Goubert, who receives the allowance, said: "The first £70 of it is standing charges, so you're only getting sort of £100... just over £100 for your month, which is nothing at the moment." "I'm putting blankets on me and then if I get too cold, I go up to bed, you know, just put more blankets on up there. That's the only solution." Islander Katina Jones, who lives with her husband, said they waited as long as they could before turning the heating on. "Once I make a cup of tea, I use the extra hot water in a hot water bottle to use just to keep us warm." Sheila Cornelius, who lives in an over-55 housing development in the island, said: "It's not very good because I don't believe in being cold so of course all my money, most of it goes on there. "Luckily I've got some nice thick clothes that I can wear instead of having the heating on full, you know, [I] can't afford it." Gareth Wordingham, from Guernsey Electricity, said: "The standing charges this year only went up by 3% so it wasn't a large proportion of the increase itself. "We buy our electricity in international markets, years in advance, so that smooths the price that we pay or our customers' pay. "We have to balance between the smaller customers and also those larger customers who might be equally vulnerable, a family with children, could be equally strapped for money." Nick Crolla, head of marketing for fuel suppliers, Rubis Channel Islands, said: "Since August, we've seen prices increase by up to 30%. "We are really seeing that we're not shielded from the volatile international market. "If customers are concerned about the cost of heating oil, the best thing is to come speak to us, we have payment options to help the customer ease the volatility of the oil prices." Bury, said the committee could respond if heating oil prices increased sharply over winter. "Should we get to the depths of winter and there's a massive spike in costs of oil, for example, we do have the ability to react to that," she added. events.title: 'An £8k service charge left me unable to pay bills'
events.summary: Callum Maddern says he is still straddled with debt after facing a huge increase in his bills A housing association has defended the charges faced by its leaseholders after many complained of huge bill increases to pay for maintenance. Callum Maddern, who lives in Bath, said he had seen his service charge increase six-fold to more than £8,000 per year after Curo said vital work needed doing on his accommodation block. "I didn't have enough money to put the heating on," he said. "I had water on my sink and coffee tables that was freezing. I'd be lying in bed and I could see my breath." Curo, which says it does not make any money from the contributions, said it was "trying to work with residents to prepare them for these bills". Man jailed for 'cruel' attack that killed pensioner Published 1 day ago Community ownership could restore city landmark Published 1 day ago Student who murdered uni housemate jailed for life Published 1 day ago When Maddern bought his flat in 2023, the annual service charge was about £1,300 per year. He was told there was £5,000 in what is known as a sinking fund to cover any necessary works. But the following year, he received a bill for £8,000 to go towards fire safety work and new windows. "Originally I thought there was some kind of mistake," he said. But when he queried the charge, Curo confirmed it was accurate. Maddern describes "constant delays" in his attempts to reach out to Curo and negotiate. "They were totally uncaring," he said, adding he was told he could sell his property and pay the fee that way. Maddern said he ended up selling possessions and taking out loans to pay for the work. While he said he knew that as a leaseholder he had a responsibility to contribute towards maintenance costs, he questioned why everything suddenly had to be done in a three-year period. "If new windows are needed, absolutely that must be scheduled in. But to have everything in the space of three years, surely that is not a good approach," he added. Andrew Snee, director of housing and support at Curo, acknowledged the way charges had been communicated could have been better and said he wanted to apologise "if our correspondence has caused any concern or upset". But Snee denied the company could have managed the costs better, describing the situation as a "perfect storm". "The cost of living is increasing, the cost of contracts is increasing, at the same time we've got increased legislation around property safety and fire safety, which has to be a good thing but it does come at a cost," he said. "We are being as honest and transparent as we can to deliver these costs in as caring a way as we can. Keep talking to us." Ken Pearson says Curo have a responsibility to prepare leaseholders for large bills Ken Pearson owns his flat in a different block elsewhere in Bath. He says his sinking fund contributions dropped to £124 per year when Curo took over his building, but then increased dramatically to £1,767 when a new roof was needed. "We were only being prepared for the new roof when it was a matter of urgency because two flats upstairs had leaks," he said. "We should have paid over a longer period." Pearson took Curo to a tribunal over the sinking fund increases and lost his case, but now believes there needs to be a change in the law to ensure that landlords prepare leaseholders better for expected works. "Curo have failed us and need to be held to account," he said. "They have not picked up that there was this financial catastrophe coming along." In response, Snee said: "I think sinking funds have been managed as well as we can in today's world with all of the pressures on costs and contracts." He added: "If you've been building a sinking fund up and decoration has taken place, that would have potentially drawn quite a lot out. "Then if you're looking at a roof replacement in four to five years' time, not only are you looking at paying for that you're also starting from zero." The government is working on a new law that would ban the use of leasehold for most new flats and create a new right for leaseholders to request improvements. events.title: Is an 'AI war' complicating your job search?
events.summary: Sheeraz Gulsher says there are "huge worries" about AI I have lost track of the number of people who have told me they have applied for hundreds of jobs, only to be met with rejection after rejection. Often, they said it felt like a human had not even looked at their applications. There are lots of different types of recruitment tools. Some match candidates to jobs, others grade and screen CVs. Employers use them to save time sifting through applications, but there are growing concerns that these tools could be biased. I want to find out how fair AI recruitment tools being used to help decide our futures really are - and what happens when we click "apply". What is the 'AI war' in recruitment? There are concerns about the increasing use of AI in recruitment A London-based non-profit organisation, People Like Us, is raising awareness of people's legal right to challenge automated decisions when they disagree with the outcome. A survey conducted by Censuswide among 2,000 UK workers who had applied for at least one job in the past 24 months found that 75% were unaware of their right to challenge an automated rejection. Sheeraz Gulsher, CEO of People Like Us, is leading the campaign called Reject the Rejections, which calls on employers to improve transparency and accountability in the use of AI and automated recruitment systems. He describes the current situation as an "AI war", with candidates "resorting to AI to bolster their applications" while "employers are dealing with huge amounts of applications". Gulsher said: "We can't say for certain that every company is operating its automated or AI systems without bias. That's why we're calling for companies to audit these systems, publish the results and have them independently assessed. "In our research, we found guidance from the Information Commissioner's Office , external stating that people subject to certain automated decisions have the right to request a human review. We're trying to remind people of that right, as many simply aren't aware of it." The research also found 70% of ethnically diverse jobseekers had altered or concealed information on their CVs, including their country of origin, religion or name, out of fear that recruitment software or AI tools would reject their applications. This compares with 57% of white candidates. Would people ask for a human review? Vivi says she needs feedback as a jobseeker Business consultant Vivi, who lives in Lewisham, was made redundant earlier this year. She says she has applied for so many jobs that she's given up and started her own company. "There's one instance where applications closed on Friday and I got a reply on a Saturday morning basically saying that I should work on my skills and come back in six months. But it was so obvious that nobody had assessed my skills." If she had known she could ask for a human to review her application, she might have done things differently. "I would definitely go back and ask for a human to look at my application and if it is a 'no', that's fine, but feedback helps me as a jobseeker." Hema, 49, from Surrey, is an HR and talent professional who has worked internationally across multiple sectors. She was made redundant in June and has since tracked more than 100 job applications and recruitment opportunities. "A lot of them have been automatically rejected within 24 to 36 hours." She added: "I've always landed a job in 10 applications, so to be nearing 100 is completely out of this world." While she is "hesitant" about asking for a human review in case she jeopardises her application, she believes "a human recruiter can see the fuller picture". "If you've got an in-house recruitment team, they know the culture, they can see the type of language that you're using in your CV, in your cover letter, during a phone screen." Of the 425 recruiters CV-Library spoke to, about 90 said they used AI in the CV screening stage. Alec Stanwell, director of marketing, believes there is a "perception gap". "Candidates almost universally believe that employers are using AI to screen their CVs, filter them and to screen them as they go through the process and that is happening but nowhere near as much as candidates think it is. "That perception gap is a problem because candidates are now writing their CVs, and applications, through the lens of 'an AI bot is going to be reviewing this rather than a human'. He adds this is a problem because recruiters are seeing all CVs look the same because "they're all written by AI, or polished by AI". He says this creates a "perfect storm" because AI is then more likely to be used to filter through a large volume of applications. "We're going to end up with computers hiring computers, but we're actually in the world of hiring people." Is there evidence of AI hiring bias? In the four years to December 2022, Stanford researchers analysed four million job applications processed by an AI hiring tool , external .

events.title: Leading European Financial Services Organizations Embrace Open Models to Build Proprietary Intelligence
events.summary: At GTC Berlin, banks, payment companies and financial data providers are showing what production-scale intelligence looks like — built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, powered by open weight models and running on their own infrastructure. Revolut is rebuilding its technology stack on a single foundation model PRAGMA , powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing. Using the NVIDIA cuDF toolkit and Dynamo-Triton software on NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs , Revolut is scaling PRAGMA in production, servicing an initial 80 million customers and engineered to scale 3x. “Revolut processes billions of transactions — the opportunity was always there, but the question was whether foundation models could operate at that scale and across domains. PRAGMA answers that,” said Pavel Nesterov, head of AI at Revolut. “Built in collaboration with NVIDIA, it’s the clearest proof yet that the gap between a research breakthrough and a production banking system can be closed.” Training on Accelerated Infrastructure Starling Bank , the first bank to train an agentic model on U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure, has developed “Starling Intelligence” — the intelligence layer that underpins its AI capability — on Civo’s U.K. cloud using the bank’s own transaction data. Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM , a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable intelligence — accelerated with NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs and improving efficiency across bank-wide use cases. SBS launched a banking sovereign intelligence platform so banks can run generative and agentic models without their data leaving their own walls. Open Models at a Fraction of the Cost Open weight models give European financial institutions proprietary intelligence built on data they own, at costs they control. NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform is the engine running beneath them. Neobank bunq’s agentic assistant Finn now runs on open weight models. Powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, deploying on Nebius matches the quality of leading closed models at 60% of the cost per answer. NatWest is building technology designed to recognize the full range of British accents, dialects and financial terminology, developed with NVIDIA’s speech models, including Nemotron 3.5 ASR. Modulr is building specialized models for distinct parts of payment operations, based on the NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B open model. Santander is an early adopter of the new NVIDIA Kumo family of open weight foundation models for structured financial data, using them to build specialized intelligence for core banking workloads. Accelerated Computing Transforms Financial Research LSEG is working with NVIDIA to help financial institutions analyze large volumes of historical tick data up to 10x faster with the Polars GPU engine , accelerated by NVIDIA cuDF on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs. RavenPack built a dataset generation pipeline on Bigdata.com that takes a plain-language research hypothesis and returns a labeled, backtest-ready dataset — running on a fine-tuned NVIDIA Nemotron model. Investors can use these datasets to identify, analyze and visualize market trends. Speeding Data Pipelines to Improve Fraud Detection RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs and NVIDIA cuDF help accelerate data processing across multi-terabyte-scale, siloed, regulated sources, compressing the time from data to decision for fraud and other scenarios. HSBC provides near-real-time client insights that support customer processes and on-demand decision-making while minimizing risk and fraud, powered by 5x faster data processing on Starburst Enterprise’s GPU Engine . Stripe , a global provider of programmable financial services, sees 42x faster data pipelines and 92% cost savings for its Stripe Radar fraud-detection platform with NVIDIA GPU-accelerated Ray Data in offline testing. This enables Stripe Radar’s machine learning pipelines to continuously optimize model training and improve fraud detection. Learn more about NVIDIA accelerated computing in financial services .
