events.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
events.summary: Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together . Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes." The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed. With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever. Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together. "In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group. During Tesla's earnings call on Wednesday, Musk said he had nothing further to add about the prospect of a merger but quipped: "I feel like I'm tap-dancing through a minefield." Musk said that calling the merger a certainty would be "overstating" things. Tesla reported a slight drop in third quarter sales which came in at $28.05 billion compared with $28.1 billion at the same time last year. The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said. Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects. Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations. The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers. Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year. Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car? But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions. Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors. He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said. But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added. "There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said. SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%. Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine. In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said. Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models . Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus. Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3 Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said. "The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added. The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights. The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January. The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year. The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider. A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said. "The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said. However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.

events.title: Airbnb hosts can no longer make guests strip beds and wash dishes under new rules
events.summary: Washing and putting away dishes are examples of chores that Airbnb says guests should generally not be asked to do Airbnb has changed its rules to limit what property hosts may ask guests to do - including when it comes to cleaning. The updated guidelines state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and can also add other "reasonable" requests. Airbnb states that guests - who are required to pay a cleaning fee - should not be asked to complete tasks normally done by a cleaner, including washing dishes and stripping beds. The new rules will apply to all reservations booked on or after 20 November on the accommodation marketplace. "House rules help guests understand what hosts expect, but we've heard from our community that they can be confusing, onerous and hard to manage," Airbnb told the BBC. "So, we've redesigned them to make them easier to discover and clearer to set, alongside a new policy that keeps requests reasonable, with no surprises." According to the new requirements on the Airbnb website, hosts are generally not allowed to ask guests to complete tasks that "require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes". The company said it may grant exceptions in some circumstances. For example, guests can be asked to limit shower time if there are local drought-related water restrictions. A property's rules will be displayed to guests more prominently moving forward and will appear in the guests' reservation reminders. Contracts will only be allowed in limited circumstances, including when required by law or homeowners association rules. While a host will not be able to impose fines, they remain in control of their house rules and requests, the company said. If a host's request does not follow Airbnb policies, the issue will be flagged and the owner can appeal if they disagree. Guests have for years complained about unreasonable tasks they we required to complete before departure, especially as they are required to pay cleaning fees. TikTok videos from Airbnb hosts Cassie and Jon that show them closely inspecting their rental property in the US state of Georgia after guests leave have gone viral recently for their attention to detail. One video from the couple, for example, accuses guests of "disrespecting the house rules" for leaving a television remote out of place. They have been criticised for their strict rules and high standards but said in response that their content had been misinterpreted Their videos have inspired other content creators to parody stringent hosts. events.title: Mine on tropical island plans to pump pit water into ocean
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts South32 plans to pump water from Groote Eylandt mine pit into ocean The Groote Archipelago is home to several Anindilyakwa communities and the GEMCO manganese mine. ( ABC News: Erin Parke ) South32 wants to build pumps and pipelines on Groote Eylandt to take up to 80 gigalitres of water per year from the mining pit to the ocean. The plan has the support of traditional owners and environmental approval, and comes as the company tries to address massive water management costs. Further consultation is required as the infrastructure would be partially built on Aboriginal-owned land. South32 plans to spend $100 million to pump water from its Northern Territory manganese mine into the ocean as it battles to keep the site open. The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) has faced huge financial challenges due to ongoing flooding in its pits on the remote island, and the company is planning redundancies. GEMCO, majority owned by South32, plans to construct about 12 kilometres of pipelines to take up to 80 gigalitres per year from the mine and discharge it into the island's Milner Bay. The plan has the support of traditional owners via the Anindilyakwa Land Council (ALC), and it has environmental approvals from the NT government. Traditional owners expect the mine to close in the early part of the next decade. The new water infrastructure would be in place for the rest of the mine's life. Mining operations on Groote Eylandt filled with water from Cyclone Megan in 2024. ( Supplied ) It is understood South32's production costs have nearly doubled due to excess water management, and it needs to cut about $129 million out of the business. In its quarterly report, released this week, the company said all production forecasts for next financial year were dependent on the infrastructure being built. Production for 2025/26 was also below initial forecasts. In a statement, an ALC spokesperson said it had been discussing the plan with GEMCO and the NT Environment Protection Authority (NT EPA) for more than three years and had confidence in the environmental plans in place. Further consultation is required because the infrastructure extends beyond GEMCO's mining leases and into Aboriginal-owned land. Work cannot begin without traditional owner consent. "The ALC is satisfied with the NT EPA's response, and this coupled with the other environmental practices are designed to meet the traditional owner expectations that risk for environmental harm is minimised," the ALC spokesperson said. An NT government spokesperson said it wanted the mine to continue operating and that the plan had been approved with strict environmental conditions. "GEMCO is one of the Territory’s most significant mining operations and a major employer and contributor to the Groote Eylandt economy," the spokesperson said. "The ALC acts for the traditional owners, and on Aboriginal land its consent is a legal requirement. Those discussions are continuing. "The NT government has supported these discussions where appropriate, while respecting that the agreement is required between independent parties." The MV Anikitos crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt due to Tropical Cyclone Megan. ( Supplied ) A South32 spokesperson said the water would be clean and it would work to "safely and effectively manage elevated water volumes". "GEMCO currently manages excess water through a range of pathways, including bush discharge and riverine discharge … water is also used at processing facilities and for dust suppression," the spokesperson said. "The excess water disposal project is intended to become GEMCO’s primary pathway for managing excess water." The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in 2024, but it is understood heavy rain in multiple wet seasons was also a factor. South32's website says it is the world's largest producer of manganese, a key alloy in the production of steel and aluminium.

events.title: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
events.summary: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday. During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California, home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026. Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, The Wall Street Journal reported at the time. His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing. Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments in AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control. All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.” Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. A number of California companies have left for Texas , Nevada, and other states in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax. But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models . In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes. events.title: White House to Politico: Retract stories or face "consequences"
events.summary: The White House counsel's office warned Politico in a Monday letter that it had 48 hours to retract or correct recent stories about alleged staff drama, or it would suffer unspecified consequences. That deadline expires Thursday. Why it matters: The White House demand threatens to escalate already tense relations with Politico specifically and, more generally, the press corps that covers President Trump in Washington. Politico, CNN, and MS NOW are already banned from covering Trump in the Oval Office and on Air Force One because the president does not like their coverage. Trump blocked all three outlets from the White House grounds as well, but a judge on Oct. 13 restored their access. CNN threatened legal action Wednesday to regain access to Air Force One and the "pool" of television networks that accompany the president. Zoom in: In his letter to Politico, White House Counsel Will Scharf singled out three stories concerning White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles despite "on-the-record refutations" or contrary evidence supplied by senior staff and even the president. Oct. 15: In a story headlined " Trump's ice maiden is under fire ," Politico Playbook reported that Trump was considering a replacement for Wiles. Trump called it "fake news." Oct. 16: Politico Playbook wrote that the prior day's story had caused a "freakout" and that the president "blew up" over it. A White House spokesman called it "unbelievably stupid and false." Oct. 16: In a story headlined " Susie Wiles helped set up Fox interview ahead of press secretary's exit ," Politico insinuated the chief of staff set up Katie Zacharia to fail in a Sean Hannity interview on Fox the night before. The White House and Fox News denied the reporting. And White House officials provided text messages to Politico before publication showing Zacharia — not Wiles — set up the interview, which the New York Post reported the following day. "Politico has not corrected or retracted its false reporting. Instead, a Politico reporter confirmed that Politico declined to remove Ms. Wiles from the story because she was the 'hook' for the story — a legally fraught and alarming admission to say the least," Scharf wrote. What they're saying: Scharf wrote that "freedom of the press is not a professional exemption from accountability. I therefore demand that Politico immediately correct or retract these publications, issue a prominent and public apology to the President of the United States and to Ms. Wiles, and remove the false reporting from your digital archives." Otherwise, he wrote, the White House would conduct an "immediate review of Politico's relationship with the White House, and, of course, consideration of all other appropriate and available legal remedies." A Politico spokesperson did not return a message seeking comment. White House officials fault the new management at Politico for pushing its reporters to engage in what Scharf called "gossip-peddling." The letter was addressed to global editor in chief Jonathan Greenberger. Zoom out: Trump has had an ongoing love-hate relationship with the press. He is available to reporters for far more question-and-answer sessions than any recent president, but he's quick to anger and threaten press bans for coverage he doesn't like. Early in his second term, Trump banned the Associated Press from the Oval Office and Air Force One access after it balked at calling the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. A federal judge reinstated AP's access months later. The New York Times reported this week that Trump has mused about removing the press entirely from the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room and building a swimming pool there. What's next: Scharf would not specify what consequences Politico faces, but a White House official said "all options are on the table" and described Trump's counsel as "uncharacteristically enraged." Trump is highly litigious with media organizations and, advisers say, his appetite for launching lawsuits hasn't diminished. Some advisers outside of the Trump White House noticed that administration officials may be telegraphing another avenue to attack Politico as a malign foreign influence because it's owned by a German company, Axel Springer. "Politico is a foreign-op designed to interfere in American politics and meddle in our elections with disinformation and misinformation," White House Communications Director Steven Cheung wrote on X Saturday.

events.title: Calls for rent cap to stop WA's spiralling rental market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tenant advocacy groups say cap on rents across Western Australia well overdue Veronica Johnson has felt the brunt of rent increases in the Kimberley region. ( ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne ) West Australian housing advocacy groups are calling for an urgent cap on rental prices after a report finds two-thirds of people would struggle with a $20-a-week rental increase. The Make Renting Fair Alliance says "runaway rents" have outpaced both inflation and wage growth. The WA government has ruled out capping rents, arguing the move could reduce investment in rental housing and hurt tenants. Rent increases would be capped annually across Western Australia under a new plan pushed by housing advocacy groups. The "Cap Still Fits" report, released today by the Make Renting Fair Alliance, argued Perth tenants could save almost $33,000 over the next five years with a 2 per cent cap on rental increases this year. Regional renters could save about $30,000 based on an average rent of $710 a week, according to the report. Tenants in metropolitan suburbs Churchlands, Scarborough and Fremantle could save the most, with renters in regional locations like Karratha, Exmouth and Port Hedland tipped to save up to $58,812 over five years. The Make Renting Fair Alliance says "runaway rents" have outpaced both inflation and wage growth. ( ABC Kimberley: Gareth McKnight ) Alliance spokesperson Kate Miller said stabilisation of the rental market was long overdue. "Rent shouldn't be a free-for-all where renters are expected to cough up infinitely," she said. "We need a system that gives renters and landlords certainty and stops housing costs from spiralling further." Financial counsellor's 'rental nightmare' It is a situation Broome financial counsellor Veronica Johnson is all too familiar with, for both professional and personal reasons. Working regularly across the Kimberley to help the region's vulnerable residents with monetary problems, she was recently "looking down the barrel" of homelessness herself after her lease ended. Ms Johnson had rented a unit in the town, about 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, since 2021, with rent jumping from $480 to $740 a week over that period. Veronica Johnson says without assistance from her employer she was facing potential homelessness. ( ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne ) The only suitable option was an almost identical unit in the same complex, but on a different floor, at $1,000 a week. "We're looking at exactly the same unit in the same complex," she said. "That's over a 100 per cent increase and I can't imagine any mortgages would be that much. "People are shocked to find someone that is actually representing people and assisting people can no longer actually be able to afford to live here." There are calls for a cap in WA to nullify soaring rental prices. ( ABC Kimberley: Vanessa Mills ) Ms Johnson was only able to afford the rent after her employer chipped in to help. After more than a decade of consideration, the WA government introduced a swathe of rental reforms in 2023 , including restricting landlords to one rent increase a year. But it stopped short of rental caps or freezes, arguing substantive change could have unintended consequences on the rental market. Maiy Azize says renters are being forced to make "dire" choices. ( Supplied ) But renter advocacy group Everybody's Home argued increases as low as $20 a week were increasingly unaffordable for the average tenant. Spokesperson Maiy Azize said a separate survey of 1,100 renters, home owners and people in temporary housing found rising costs had tenants at their absolute limit. "Even these amounts that can seem small really add up (after) years of relentless rent increases," she said. "Fuel costs have really gone up in the last couple of years, the cost of food has gone up … [and] electricity bills." Ms Azize said tenants were too afraid to report maintenance issues, fearing it could result in higher rent orleases not being extended. Critics warn of unintended consequences Real Estate Institute of WA president Rob Mandanici said caps offer short-term protection for current renters at the expense of those looking for somewhere to rent. "Rent caps might sound appealing, but they come at a significant cost to the broader rental market," he said. "A cap may benefit existing tenants, but it does nothing to address the underlying shortage of rental homes. "Instead, it risks discouraging investment, driving rental property owners out of the market and making an already difficult situation worse.

events.title: Airbnb Hosts Are Furious They Can No Longer Make Guests Do Their Chores
events.summary: Airbnb hosts are melting down over a new policy banning them from making guests complete tasks that “would typically be performed by a cleaner,” like “stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes.” The change, which applies to all bookings made on or after November 20, quickly sparked outrage after it was announced in an email to Airbnb hosts on Wednesday. Many began fuming online about losing the right to make their guests clean up after themselves. “As hosts, we have a responsibility to protect our investments, our homes, and, in many cases, our personal living spaces,” one person wrote in Airbnb’s official forum for hosts. “The problem is that Airbnb increasingly expects hosts to accept the risks while limiting our ability to protect ourselves.” “Airbnb is like an abusive partner,” wrote one user on the Reddit community r/airbnb_hosts. “I'm alive long enough to recognize how truthful those few words are,” another person replied . “Until and unless I see substantive changes, I'm finally out.” A different self-described host declared that going forward, the kitchens in their rentals will be “stripped down to only bare essentials.” Many guests, meanwhile, are celebrating. For years, travelers have complained about having to pay hefty cleaning fees as part of their Airbnb bookings, only to be required to complete a list of chores before checking out. “The guest experience has become total ass,” one person said in a subreddit for Airbnb hosts. “Clean dishes and run in the dishwasher. Strip the beds, put all linen in the laundry room. Take out all garbage, put in garbage can, take to the curb. Honestly, knock it off.” Airbnb noted in its Wednesday announcement that hosts can’t get around the new policy by putting cleaning tasks in the “Requests” section of their listings instead. Airbnb spokesperson Simon Letouze tells WIRED that hosts can still make “reasonable” requests, such as asking guests to put dirty dishes in the sink. Other examples Airbnb cites include asking guests to take short showers in areas with drought-related water restrictions, or telling them to place trash in bear-proof containers. In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted what they claimed was a screenshot of their failed attempt to edit their property’s “Requests” section. They tried to ask guests to wash and air-dry dishes, put dirty towels in the laundry room, and take trash to a dumpster at an RV park they could find using a map on the refrigerator. But they realized they couldn’t hit Save. Airbnb's interface had underlined and highlighted the requests in red and displayed a pop-up that read “Guests shouldn't be asked to do this task.” Hosts also can’t circumvent the new policy by giving guests a printed list of rules and asking them to sign it when they check in. On November 20, Airbnb is also banning hosts from requiring guests to sign separate contracts, with limited exceptions for local legal requirements, longer stays, or accessing “an optional amenity” like a “golf cart rental.” If one of these situations applies, hosts have to mention it in the dedicated section of their listing. Airbnb adds that it “doesn’t help enforce the terms of these contracts.” Hosts who violate either policy, Airbnb warns, may receive warnings, or in severe situations, have their listings removed or be banned from the platform entirely. In a Facebook group for Airbnb hosts, one person posted a letter they claimed to have sent to company executives, demanding the ability to set their own “common-sense expectations” for guests. They encouraged others to send their own versions. Another asked if they should raise their prices, while a third called for hosts to organize a platform-wide strike. “Even if we all unlist our properties for just a day or two, we can send a powerful message,” they wrote. “Airbnb built its empire on OUR properties. It’s time we reminded them who actually holds the power.” Some hosts haven’t given up on finding a way to ignore or get around the changes. On Reddit, one person said they would simply move their rules to other sections of their listing, like “Guest Access.” (Airbnb did not immediately respond to WIRED’s inquiry about whether this would work.) Another person said they would give the guests a “house manual,” require the guest to read it, and provide a “codeword” as proof. (Several pointed out that this is not only unenforceable but against current Airbnb policy.) “First sentence of my requests section will now state ‘Here are my house rules!’” another person said , though it’s unclear whether Airbnb’s interface will allow this. They named “not smoking” as an example of one of their house rules, but Airbnb has said it enforces host-imposed smoking bans. events.title: Trump administration wants to reconsider permit for offshore wind project
events.summary: The Trump administration is asking a federal judge to let it reconsider a major federal permit granted for a large offshore wind farm, making it the fourth project the Republican leadership has targeted in recent months WASHINGTON -- The Trump administration is asking a federal judge to let it reconsider a major federal permit granted for a large offshore wind farm, making it the fourth project the Republican leadership has targeted in recent months. The Interior Department wants to reconsider its own approval for the “construction and operations plan” for the New England Wind project off of Massachusetts. The plan was approved in 2024 during the Biden administration. The Justice Department said in a filing Tuesday the court should remand the permit, sending it back to Interior, because the plan was approved despite major adverse impacts. The developer, Avangrid, declined to comment Wednesday. Construction has not begun. The Trump administration is using executive orders, agency actions and the courts to try to stop the development of offshore wind, an industry and technology that President Donald Trump has attacked as “ugly” and unreliable compared to fossil fuels such as coal and natural gas. It started buying back offshore wind leases after federal judges blocked its efforts to stop construction on five major East Coast projects. U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat, warned that the administration now risks derailing a legislative effort to speed up permitting reviews for new energy and infrastructure projects. The Senate reached a bipartisan deal in September on a permitting bill, which has not yet been voted on. “This is how you blow up a permitting deal,” he said in a statement Wednesday. The Interior Department also wants to reconsider its prior approval of the construction and operations plan for Revolution Wind, a wind farm for Rhode Island and Connecticut that has finished construction, and for the Maryland Offshore Wind Project, which has not yet begun construction. In August, a judge granted the administration's request to reconsider the permit for the stalled New Jersey project Atlantic Shores. That project had been halted soon after Trump returned to office because co-owner Shell walked away from it . Last year, a federal judge said the Trump administration could reconsider the permit granted to the Massachusetts project SouthCoast Wind days before the president’s inauguration. Pasha Feinberg, an offshore wind strategist at the Natural Resources Defense Council, said the Trump administration’s attacks on offshore wind are escalating at a time when Americans are struggling with surging utility bills. The National Ocean Industries Association, which represents offshore industries including oil and wind, said it's concerned about the uncertainty that comes with reopening federal approvals for offshore energy projects, particularly those already under construction or in operation. The plans for New England Wind call for up to 129 wind turbines that could supply as much as 2,600 megawatts of clean energy to power more than 900,000 homes each year. Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say Its federal approval was challenged in court by ACK for Whales, a group of Nantucket, Massachusetts, residents who say they are concerned about the negative impacts of offshore wind development. The lawsuit in District Court for the District of Columbia contends that the federal government failed to comply with numerous statutes. The federal defendants in the case filed a motion Tuesday stating that remand of the permit is warranted, so Interior could make a new decision. The government also told the court in 2025 it wanted to reconsider New England Wind’s approval. Interior said Wednesday that the latest filing complied with a briefing schedule, and was not announcing a policy change. It says its position on offshore wind has remained consistent throughout this administration. Avangrid built another wind farm, Vineyard Wind, off the coast of Massachusetts in a joint venture with Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners. Construction finished in March , making it the first project to reach this stage during Trump’s time in office. Vineyard Wind was one of the projects the administration tried to halt construction on , citing concerns over national security. McDermott reported from Providence, R.I. events.title: AI uncovers massive flaw in web's foundational code
events.summary: Security officials are sounding the alarm over two critical vulnerabilities in a programming language used to run millions of websites, marking one of the most consequential cybersecurity discoveries yet made with AI . Why it matters : The bugs, which researchers found partly with an OpenAI model, proves AI can uncover critical flaws humans missed for decades — raising the stakes for defenders racing to fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them at machine speed. What they're saying : Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, a global connectivity and internet security company, said the company saw thousands of attempts to exploit the flaws in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X. What's happening: There are two problems hackers could easily exploit in an open-source programming language known as PHP that's used on nearly 70% of all websites . Government officials from the U.S. to Japan are warning companies to apply a patch to fix the bugs, or consider taking down their sites to avoid an attack. OpenAI touted the role its model played in discovering one of the vulnerabilities, which allowed PHP researchers to create a fix. Between the lines: Security researchers have been skeptical of AI-generated vulnerability reports, many of which have turned out to be minor bugs or false alarms. But the PHP discovery could force the cybersecurity community to reckon with the reality of AI threats. "It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post Wednesday. Threat level: If exploited, the PHP flaws would allow malicious hackers to take control of vulnerable web servers without needing a password or other credentials. Since PHP runs under a wide variety of internet applications, that access could allow hackers to take over websites, steal sensitive information and tamper with a website. Some website owners took their sites down earlier Wednesday, including certain services at Wikipedia and 4chan , until they had time to patch their systems. "These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," researchers at Wiz wrote in a post. The big picture: AI-driven bug discoveries are shining a light on the fragility of the modern internet, which is heavily reliant on a slew of open-source software powered by volunteers . The two flaws in PHP existed for decades, but demonstrated that it was possible for a hacker to exploit them required "an exceptionally complex chain of steps," researchers at Wiz added. "Defenders have always relied on the gap between 'vulnerable' and 'exploitable' to buy time to patch," Michael Leland, field CTO at Island, said in an email to Axios. "That gap is rapidly closing." What to watch : Cybersecurity defenders are on guard for what could be a wave of incidents where websites and organizations are hacked using these two vulnerabilities in the next few weeks. events.title: ATO criticised for 'not going in to bat' for millions of Australians underpaid super
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Workers say ATO not doing enough to recoup unpaid superannuation Pauline Devin and Angela Noack are still trying to recover thousands in superannuation their former employer never paid. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) Workers and industry experts are calling on the Australian Taxation Office to be more proactive in responding to unpaid superannuation claims. Data shows one in four workers are underpaid super, and only 15 per cent of that is recovered by the ATO. The ATO says it is serious about ensuring employers are paying super. One in four Australian workers are underpaid superannuation by their employers, amounting to about $6 billion each year, with independent reports showing only about 15 per cent is ever recovered by the tax office. The figures come as no surprise to Pauline Devin and Angela Noack, who were underpaid about $5,000 and $3,000 respectively in super while working at a Brisbane dental clinic two years ago. Early last year, the oral health therapists filed separate complaints with the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), and the regulator found in their favour in April. Millions of Australians have discovered they haven't been paid all of their super. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) But 18 months later, neither have seen a cent returned to their super fund or received any further information from the ATO. "All I ever used to get was, 'No, we can't give you any information because it's an invasion of privacy'," Ms Devin said. "I wasn't asking for financial details or anything like that. "I just wanted to know when I could maybe, possibly, think about getting that superannuation paid to me." The long wait and lack of information from the ATO has left Ms Devin and Ms Noack feeling helpless. Angela Noack says the ATO doesn't "seem to be really going in to bat" for her. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) "I have come to the conclusion I'm probably not ever going to get my super paid from [my employer] at this point, and the ATO don't seem to be really going in to bat and doing anything about recovering that either," Ms Noack said. "The ATO is just useless and hopeless." Pauline Devin says the situation has left her feeling like she's stuck in limbo. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) The ATO declined the ABC's request for an interview, but a spokesperson said in a statement it was "serious about ensuring employers comply with their super obligations and dedicates significant resources to educating employers, undertaking audits and debt recovery actions after liabilities have been raised". The spokesperson also reiterated the ATO's position that "tax secrecy and privacy laws limit what the ATO can disclose to employees" and said where the tax office collected unpaid super on behalf of employees, it advised them accordingly. Funds hire private firm to recoup super Industry Fund Services collects unpaid super on behalf of three super funds, in a role similar to the ATO's regulatory responsibilities. But the firm's executive manager of super recoveries Natalie Lister said the organisation took a more "proactive approach" to super debt recovery. Natalie Lister says her team specialises in recovering unpaid super. ( ABC News: Scott Jewell ) "We'll use digital communications, SMS, email … outbound calls and that's where our specialist team really come in … and [get] an understanding of the employer's situation and working with them to actively resolve it," she said. "If we don't have any success early on, we then have escalation processes, so we'll follow up with … what we call a final demand call and then at that point, we will actually threaten to take legal action." Ms Lister said in most cases, the digital communication and phone calls were enough to successfully engage employers, with only about 10 per cent of cases escalated to the "final call and letter of demand". She said the firm had for years used data provided by its super fund clients to contact employers who were not paying super, avoiding the need for employees to discover and then flag the discrepancy themselves. "We'll try and contact the employer as soon as we can to find out if there is any super payments overdue," she said. "Our experience has largely seen that the ATO, if they are going to intervene, it's much further down the track." Payday super needs to be 'backed in action' On July 1, the ATO introduced payday super , meaning employers are now required to pay workers their super at the same time as their wages. Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert said the reform was a game-changer for the industry because it offered workers and the ATO real-time visibility of their super.

events.title: Scoop: Senate Republicans fear Mississippi is in play
events.summary: Senate Republicans are weighing three last-ditch spending moves that would have been unimaginable six months ago: a cash infusion for Mississippi and even more money for South Carolina and Kansas. Why it matters: It's been 94 years since Kansas elected a Democratic senator, 44 years for Mississippi and 28 for South Carolina. But panic is spreading through the Republican Party. "The wall has broken. The enemy is inside the fort," one national Republican political operative told Axios. "We are now fighting hand to hand." The Senate map, which once looked impregnable for Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), is now full of vulnerabilities. Democratic challengers are polling within the margin of error in more than half a dozen deep-red states, according to internal GOP polls. The other side: "We're nervous about Alaska. We're nervous about Michigan. We're still going to hold the Senate at the end," said another operative. Zoom in: Two weeks ago, when Senate Leadership Fund decided to take out a $5 million "insurance policy" in South Carolina, operatives took a hard look at Idaho, South Dakota and Mississippi. At the time, they concluded they didn't need to spend any money in those states, according to a person familiar with the matter. But Senate Republicans are now reviewing the Mississippi race and may need to spend there to protect Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith from a surprisingly competitive bid by Democratic district attorney Scott Colom . Senate Majority PAC, the main super PAC for Senate Democrats, announced a $1.2 million investment in the race on Tuesday. Zoom out: In early June, SLF started to reinforce a Midwestern red wall to protect the GOP majority, reserving $28 million in TV advertising in Ohio and $11 million in Iowa . Those investments have ballooned to $93 million in Ohio and $53 million in Iowa. After an initial $5 million buy in South Carolina, SLF's spending has increased to $8.5 million, according to AdImpact. And a super PAC linked to Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) is spending another $500,000 in South Carolina. SLF, which is linked to Senate GOP leadership, has earmarked $14 million for Kansas, and has spent nearly $12 million there so far. "No Republican seat is safe this cycle," another operative told Axios. What we're hearing: Some GOP Senate candidates do, in fact, appear safe this cycle. Republicans aren't overly concerned about Sens. Ashley Moody in Florida or Mike Rounds in South Dakota. The intrigue: The National Republican Senatorial Committee raised $31.4 million last month, but its coffers appear to be drained. It took out a $20 million loan as it spends aggressively on its coordinated campaign strategy. SLF ended September with $155 million in cash on hand, according to its FEC filing. The group has spent or reserved $169 million worth of video ads since Oct. 1, according to AdImpact. Even President Trump promised to unload another $100 million before Election Day in a Tuesday post on Truth Social, bringing the total from his super PACs to $400 million. The bottom line: Republicans can still maintain their Senate majority, but none of the polling is giving them a great deal of confidence that they will do so.

events.title: Poll shows big lead for South Dakota Republican Rounds
events.summary: Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota leads in his Senate race by more than 20 points, according to a new poll shared first with Semafor, a sign that any blue wave in November will have its limits. Rounds is trouncing independent candidate Brian Bengs 57% to 36% in the deep-red state, according to a new poll conducted in mid-October by Quantus Insights. That’s a larger lead for Rounds than many surveys have previously shown; some surveys even showed Bengs with a slight lead. South Dakota is one of three states, including Idaho and Nebraska, where Democrats have coalesced behind an independent Senate candidate. Nebraska is the most competitive of the three races. Bengs lost to Senate Majority Leader John Thune in 2022 as a Democrat, but he insists if he wins he’ll create an independent caucus and not align with Republicans or Democrats.

events.title: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
events.summary: A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties Wednesday after a jury found in September that the social media giant misled users about their data privacy. Why it matters: The penalties come nearly a decade after the Cambridge Analytica scandal first broke and signal that Big Tech can face significant financial consequences for misleading users about their privacy. Driving the news: Judge Francis Mathew determined the penalty amount Wednesday, handing New Mexico a win as the only state to take its claims to trial after 48 others settled. Mathew concluded New Mexico was entitled to $219.5 billion based on the state's maximum $5,000 penalty multiplied by 43,899,720 violations. He reduced that to $25 billion. What they're saying: "This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," C.J. Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, told Axios in an emailed statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge." Catch up quick: In September, a New Mexico jury said Meta had committed 43 million "willful violations" of the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act. Mathew found that Facebook's privacy controls failed to give users meaningful control over their data and that third-party app developers could access their information through the platform's systems. Mathew found Mark Zuckerberg knew users didn't understand how data privacy works, and exploited that, noting that the CEO had once written that users "probably don't understand their current privacy settings or care about who sees their updates." Zuckerberg also wrote that the company should give users "a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don't encourage it." Zoom out: The suit followed reporting that revealed data firm Cambridge Analytica had harvested data from more than 50 million Facebook users to craft political ads during the 2016 election. After the scandal, Facebook promised more transparency, but the court found Meta failed to consistently inform users when their data was misused. events.title: Sydney Southwest Metro set to open after 130yo train line replaced
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sydney's Southwest Metro line to open to commuters at end of the month The conversion of the T3 Bankstown Line between Sydenham began in September 2024. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) An open date has been set for the long-awaited Southwest Metro after a two-year project to replace the 130-year-old line. The first driverless service is expected to depart early morning on Friday, October 30. It is hoped the new service will cut travel time with connections including from south-west Sydney to the CBD. The long-awaited Southwest Metro extension now has an opening date, after extended works to replace the 130-year-old train line. NSW Premier Chris Minns said the $23 billion project would officially open with the first service departing at 4:31am on Friday, October 30. The new metro offering will connect south-western suburbs to the Sydney CBD, North Sydney and north-western suburbs. From next Friday, the NSW government said passengers would have access to trains every four minutes during weekday peak hours in places including Bankstown, Punchbowl, Wiley Park, Lakemba, Dulwich Hill and Marrickville. "The new Metro will deliver 50 per cent more passenger capacity than the old T3 Bankstown Line it replaces, along with faster journeys and direct connections to more jobs, education and opportunities across Sydney," a spokesperson said. The opening was delayed until 2026 due to the project's complexity and industrial action. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) They also said services would run every five minutes during the day, and every 10 minutes in the evenings and on weekends. On the first weekend, between October 31 and November 1, services will increase to accommodate increased interest. Mr Minns said it was an investment that would "make a real difference" to communities for "generations to come". "This is about giving people in south-west Sydney the same fast, reliable public transport connections that other parts of our city enjoy," he said. Buses replaced trains on the south-west line for more than two years, and pink-coloured buses became a regular sight on major roads between Sydenham and Bankstown. It meant some commuters faced lengthier travel times. Mr Graham says the time for pink buses is over. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) Transport Minister John Graham said communities "have been very patient" and the wait for the new line to open "will be worthwhile". "The pink buses have really played a big role moving people around, but the time for them is over," he said. "We know this has had an impact, though, on communities, on passengers, on businesses as well. "There's no easy way to upgrade the line in this way; it has taken time. Now it's here, I think people will immediately see the benefits." Mr Graham said the new line will transform the way people travel around Sydney. "You won't need to check the timetable, you'll simply be able to turn up at the station and jump on a metro within minutes," he said. The pink Southwest Link buses will continue to operate on the opening day and weekend. Station improvements and line upgrades The new metro line runs from Sydenham to Bankstown. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) About 48,000 trips are expected to be made across the metro line on a typical weekday during the 8am and 9am peak. Upgrades include platform screen doors, new lifts and station upgrades, updated customer information systems and enhanced security technology along the line. Improvements have also been made at stations to improve accessibility for prams and people living with a disability, with accessible lifts at Wiley Park, Dulwich Hill, Hurlstone Park, Punchbowl and Canterbury for the first time. The T3 Bankstown Line between Sydenham and Bankstown ceased operations in September 2024 to convert the 130-year-old heavy rail line to a metro line. The Sydney City and Southwest Metro station under construction at Martin Place in 2020. ( ABC News: Rachel Pupazzoni ) The conversion deadline was pushed back due to industrial action and complexity issues. It was initially meant to take 12 months. It is the final stage of Sydney's M1 Metro North West and Bankstown Line, which will connect Bankstown to Tallawong along a 66-kilometre stretch. The state government has warned passengers there may be "minor teething issues as services get underway".

events.title: Meta plans nonvoting shares, eyeing more stock sales to fund its AI dreams
events.summary: Meta plans to introduce new non-voting stock, the company announced, which suggests it’s likely to lean heavily on new share sales to fund its AI buildout. The plan, earlier reported by Semafor, will allow the company to issue new stock — for acquisitions, to lure top AI talent, and to pay for chips — without diluting Mark Zuckerberg’s control. Alphabet made a similar move in 2014, executing a 2-for-1 stock split that introduced non-voting shares alongside super-voting shares, which allowed the combined control of co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin to remain at just over 50%. That made it easier for the company to issue $85 billion of new stock earlier this year to pay for AI investments; half of the new shares carry no voting rights . Big tech companies have historically been able to balance out the new stock they issue by buying back shares in the market. But they have paused stock repurchases as the cost of their AI investments mount, and now find themselves as net issuers of shares, which risks diluting insiders’ stakes.

events.title: Will an AI-cloned free tool spell the end of expensive software?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts An AI-cloned free tool is being dubbed 'the end of software' Some developers want to use AI tools to break the power of big tech and "take back the internet". ( Getty: Malte Mueller ) It is being called "the end of software" and the dawn of a new era of AI-powered piracy. New AI tools are disrupting the tech industry, making it relatively easy and fast to clone an existing piece of software and replicate its features. Earlier this month, a small team of developers used AI tools to create near-identical, free versions of two commonly used products: Microsoft Office, with programs such as Word and Excel, and Adobe Creative, which includes Photoshop. A licence to use Adobe's Creative Suite costs more than $1,000 per year, but the cloned version is free. ( Supplied: Artcraft ) Around the same time, a different tool called Reverse Engineer Anything that helps developers use AI to deconstruct and replicate features in other pieces of software shot to the top of trending projects on software repository GitHub. For some, this new generation of tools will disrupt software in the same way MP3 file-sharing networks in the late 1990s changed how we listened to music and watched movies, replacing CDs and DVDs with streaming. But whether this will give more power to users or further concentrate power in the hands of AI companies remains to be seen. 'Set the clock back' to the 1990s internet Brandon Thomas is one of the developers who recently announced they had used AI tools to copy the Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative suites. A 15-year veteran of the US tech industry, he sees himself fighting a "war" for the future of the internet. In the 1990s, "Everything [online] was nerdy, hackable and weird," he told the ABC. "Everything in this era could be inspected, copied, shared with friends, remixed. It was amazing." But over time, the internet became more standardised and bland. Spaces for innovation and personalisation, like Geocities or Myspace, were replaced by closed ecosystems that tightly controlled user access. This is "enshittification", a term coined by writer Cory Doctorow in 2022 to describe the perceived decline of online spaces. Social media platforms like Facebook initially attracted users with clean, chronological feeds and personal connections, then pivoted to intrusive ads and sponsored content. Search engines became crowded with sponsored ads and affiliate-marketing spam, pushing out organic search results. Software makers shifted to subscription-only models with automated billing and predatory cancellation fees, in some cases worth 50 per cent of the annual contract. The cloned version of Adobe Photoshop, Photocraft, has similar features and layout. ( Supplied: ArtCraft ) For some, AI is part of the problem, as "slop" content floods online spaces. But for Mr Thomas, AI is the solution. "AI flips the tide of this war in a way legislation never did," he said. ABC staff targeted in sophisticated cyber attack AI tool saves time but makes errors in police trial AI data centre company cold calling about buying land, inquiry told Tech giant shares plunge 40pc after delays to Melbourne data centre "We can build anything, even triple-A video games and operating systems. "This is the most excited I've felt for the future in a long time. "I think we have a great opportunity to take back the internet from the monopolistic platforms that became rent-seekers and behaved badly to us as users and customers." How AI is making software easier to copy Think of a piece of software like a cake from a bakery. To copy the recipe, you could break into the bakery and steal the list of ingredients (the source code), for which you would be quickly prosecuted. Or you could reverse engineer the cake by tearing it apart, tasting it, and studying it under a microscope. This is known as "decompiling". You can then bake the cake based on what you learnt. Each time you bake the cake, you tweak the recipe so the result more closely matches your description. Queensland University of Technology (QUT) digital economy expert Marek Kowalkiewicz said AI dramatically sped up this process. "[AI-powered reverse engineering] is not very different from having a bunch of human software developers doing the same thing, but it's way faster and cheaper," Professor Kowalkiewicz told the ABC. Experts say AI's dominance of the US market brings risks all of its own. Reverse Engineer Anything, the viral tool on GitHub, dramatically streamlines the reverse-engineering process by allowing a user without coding skills to replicate features from other software at no cost.

events.title: Investors eye proxy fight at Mattel
events.summary: A big Mattel shareholder is preparing to mount a proxy fight at the toymaker and push the company toward a sale, according to people familiar with the matter. Southeastern Asset Management has been considering whether to nominate new directors at Mattel as part of a proxy fight, the people said. The activist has been pushing the company for months to sell itself, following double-digit sales declines in Fisher-Price and other key segments, as well as profit-margin pressures. The issues became more acute after Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz left to join Skydance: Mattel shares, which are down 15% so far this year, dropped by 5% on the news of his replacement, former Condé Nast CEO Roger Lynch. The stock rebounded following a Wall Street Journal report that the company had drawn takeover interest by Authentic Brands Group. Southeastern’s plans could change, the people cautioned, and no decision has been made. It’s unlikely the activist could secure full control of Mattel’s board, but a proxy fight would serve as a referendum on the direction of the company. Under Mattel’s bylaws, an investor can only nominate two directors, except in specific circumstances. Separately, Ariel Investments, another big Mattel shareholder, has told other investors that it believes a change needs to happen at Mattel, according to another person familiar with the matter. In a recent CNBC appearance, Ariel founder John Rogers said the company should sell itself, an unusual posture for a famously management-friendly investor. Mattel said in a statement that it engages with all shareholders but declined to comment further. Ariel and Southeastern didn’t respond to requests for comment.

events.title: Offshore wind farms can enhance maritime security, report says
events.summary: Offshore wind farms can enhance maritime security through greater co-operation and surveillance technology, a new analysis says. The report from the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) in Washington said that although offshore wind infrastructure has become more prevalent in recent decades, too little progress has been made in looking at how it could benefit national security. “By planning for dual-use capability from the outset, the United States can turn energy infrastructure into a force multiplier for national security, one that strengthens surveillance and warning in an increasingly contested maritime environment,” the CSIS report said. The analysis pointed out that in recent years, maritime and subsea infrastructure have become increasingly important – and also vulnerable to attack. “Subsea cables, which carry roughly 95 per cent of the world’s internet traffic, are particularly vulnerable to disruption,” the report said. In May, undersea internet and data cables were damaged in the Red Sea, causing connectivity problems for users in the Middle East, India and Pakistan. The cables were eventually repaired and most experts said that they had probably been severed by accident, but the incident still put subsea cable vulnerability in the spotlight. CSIS's report indicated that the proliferation of aerial drones, autonomous naval tools and unmanned underwater vehicles were also putting maritime security and subsea infrastructure in a more vulnerable position. It added that, concerningly, drone threats no longer come from state actors, but also from gangs and drug traffickers. The report concluded that if private offshore wind farm developers and governments could reach a consensus on how to best equip turbines with surveillance, sensors and data tracking tools, the end result could be “enhanced maritime domain awareness”. It highlighted the addition of surveillance systems to wind farms in and around Norway, Belgium, Poland and the UK. During a round-table discussion on Wednesday, Allegra Dawes, an energy security fellow at CSIS, said greater co-operation in enhancing offshore wind farms for maritime security could create a “force multiplier” effect, particularly for the US. “I think it gives guidance on the technologies that can actually create a stronger national security environment and also a stronger infrastructure backbone for energy,” she explained. Doug Wolfe, chief technology officer for Mighty Waves Energy, added that artificial intelligence could also be used along with the surveillance-enhanced wind turbines to bolster security on several levels. AI, he said, could help automate a lot of different maritime security workflows, while also helping to better understand what's happening under the sea. “It could very quickly characterise and detect whales, different types of whales and frequencies and all of those kinds of things,” he said.

events.title: Celebrating the educators shaping the future of learning
events.summary: Meet the educators shaping the future of learning Teachers and schools hold a special place in students’ lives. They help students discover what excites them, believe in their potential, and imagine who they might become. Through a deeply human partnership among educators, students, and families, education builds knowledge, confidence, and dreams for the future. Today, we celebrate those who have earned advanced recognition within our Microsoft Elevate for Educators community this year: over 54,000 Expert and Fellow educators, more than 1,100 Showcase schools, and 20 inaugural Beacon schools and systems . Together, they join a community of more than 100,000 educators who learn from one another, build their skills, and open new possibilities for every learner to thrive. As teaching and learning evolve, teachers and school leaders are defining what responsible innovation means for education. Microsoft is committed to supporting their expertise and judgment, so technology strengthens students’ curiosity without replacing their thinking. Supporting educators means giving them opportunities to learn, too. Microsoft’s latest AI in Education report finds that 88% of educators surveyed have used AI for school purposes, yet 53% have not received training from their institution. And 66% want training monthly or quarterly. Educators are asking for ongoing professional learning and clear guidance to put it into practice. In partnership with leading education organizations worldwide, Microsoft Elevate for Educators provides a global peer community, professional learning, practical resources, and a pathway that recognizes educators and schools as they progress. It reflects Microsoft’s investment in the people and institutions that help students excel, building skills and widening opportunity for every learner. So many of us can name a teacher who helped us see ourselves differently, or a school that gave us a sense of possibility. Behind those moments are people doing extraordinarily demanding work. Microsoft Elevate for Educators is our way of saying: you matter, your work matters, and you deserve a place where others understand the challenges, have creative solutions, and can help you be your best. Celebrating educators leading the way As educators progress through Microsoft Elevate for Educators, they build skills, strengthen classroom practices, and put Microsoft for Education tools to work. Experts advance classroom innovation, while Fellows build on that experience to mentor peers and lead change beyond their own classrooms. We celebrate the 2026–2027 Microsoft Elevate Expert Educators and 2026–2028 Educator Fellows for their commitment to learning and supporting one another. Schools at the frontier of technology implementation Schools can also progress through Microsoft Elevate for Educators and earn recognition for strengthening teaching and learning. Microsoft Elevate Showcase Schools demonstrate excellence in technology integration, exploring new ways to use digital tools to support educators and enrich learning experiences. This year, we welcomed our first-ever Microsoft Elevate Beacon Schools and Systems . This new designation recognizes leadership at scale through strategic technology planning that brings tools, people, and practices together to extend innovation across entire school systems. Together, Showcase and Beacon Schools are at the frontier of technology use in education, showing how emerging tools can expand what is possible for learners. By sharing what works and what doesn’t, they can help other schools turn innovation into practice. Spotlight: A culture of confidence in Australia What happens when educator learning and innovation becomes a whole school effort? At Canterbury College, a K12 school in Queensland, Australia, Microsoft Elevate educators share their learning through collaboration and teacher meetups. Teachers use Microsoft Copilot to personalize resources and help students explore independently. The biggest change that we see is that there is confidence in doing something new. And in a school, that’s everything. With leadership supporting teachers to learn and share, their growing confidence is strengthening teaching across the school. Feeling inspired? Your journey can start today. Educators can begin as Explorers and schools can join as Pathfinders at any time of the year. From day one, you’ll build skills, connect with peers, put new ideas into practice, and develop a portfolio toward advanced recognition. The next application window for Expert Educator and Showcase School recognition opens in November . We celebrate the educators, schools, and school systems whose ideas and generosity inspire others and bring new possibilities to classrooms worldwide. events.title: Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect
events.summary: IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect . He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028. Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors , received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes. Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals. Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces. Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs. At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November. Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management. Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents. Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD ’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM , engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon . An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011. He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee . events.title: Longer fire seasons mean almost half of Australian homes face bushfire risks
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supercharged fire seasons cost Australia $6b annually as El Niño summer looms Bushfires could cost Australia almost $182 billion over the next three decades. ( ABC News ) New modelling reveals bushfires will cost Australia $6 billion a year, with a single major event costing almost $30 billion. Fire seasons are now 21 per cent longer, with 5.6 million households exposed to bushfire risk. Large parts of Australia are bracing for a hotter and drier summer due to El Niño. As Australians prepare for a summer influenced by what is likely to become the strongest El Niño on record, a new report reveals billions of dollars are being spent tackling bushfire seasons supercharged by climate change. The modelling, commissioned by Emergency Leaders for Climate Action (ELCA), found the country's fire seasons have lengthened by 21 per cent since 1979 due to warming global temperatures. The longer seasons will cost the Australian economy $6 billion each year over the next 30 years, with a majority being spent on harm to health and wellbeing, ahead of damaged businesses and lost homes. ELCA's Greg Mullins, a former Fire and Rescue NSW commissioner, said the high costs come as climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, squeezes fire seasons closer together. "The fire seasons are longer, they're overlapping between states and we're getting catastrophic fire weather," he said. "Previous studies only looked at insured costs, which were far less, but costs across the economy are huge; in 30 years that's $180 billion." Black Summer highlights cost of extreme fires The ELCA report found half of Australian households are exposed to some bushfire risk, at 5.6 million, while major events, such as the Black Summer fires, cost almost $30 billion. And between 2003 and 2020 more than a million Australians had lived in a home within one kilometre of an active fire front. The 2019/20 bushfires tore through about 45 per cent of the Snowy Valleys Council (SVC) local government area (LGA), killing one person and destroying almost 200 homes. There were almost 9,000 livestock fatalities within the LGA and 400,000 hectares of land burnt. Nearly half of the Snowy Valleys region was burnt during the Black Summer bushfires. ( Supplied: James Hayes ) The local council spent more than $50 million on direct recovery, which included road repairs and managing damaged and fallen trees. SVC's manager of technical services, Glen McGrath, said the region was still recovering from the event more than six years later. "You look at the softwood industry, they had a very large impact and it takes 20-plus years for softwood or pine tree to grow and be harvested and processed through the local industry processes, so they won't be coming back online until 2040 or thereabouts," he said. "There's still a number of houses that weren't rebuilt after the fire, so there's widespread impacts and recovery efforts still." Research has found the Black Summer bushfires cost Australia's tourism industry almost $3b , while the Insurance Council has found the event accounts for about $2b of the $2.58b in bushfire claims since 2019. Preparation key ahead of high-risk summers While no two events are the same, El Niño often brings hotter and drier conditions to southern and eastern parts of Australia. Despite 2026 shaping up to become Australia's wettest El Niño year on record , drier than average conditions are starting to persist across parts of the country's east. "In the last three months since El Niño has been active, we've seen drier-than-average conditions along much of the eastern seaboard," senior climatologist at the Bureau of Meteorology Felicity Gamble said. "Extending from central Queensland through to south-east Queensland, down the New South Wales eastern seaboard and across southern Victoria and Tasmania." Greg Mullins says the burning of coal, oil and gas is supercharging bushfire seasons. ( ABC News: David Sciasci ) There are concerns that unusually hot temperatures, combined with an increase in baseline warming due to climate change, could increase the risk of "flash droughts" this summer. "When we get heatwaves, vegetation gives up its moisture very quickly … so things can very quickly turn into drought-like conditions and that drives fires," Mr Mullins said. The ELCA report found better preparation can prevent millions of dollars in bushfire damage. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) Given the typical "lag effect" seen during an El Niño, there is speculation next year could become the hottest on record globally, leading to a particularly bad fire season in 2027/28.
