events.title: Vodafone says 24 million scam calls came via Aussie Broadband
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Vodafone's owner accuses rival Aussie Broadband of being behind millions of scam calls to customers TPG's Vanessa Hicks has called on the regulator to do more to stop scam calls at their origin. ( ABC News: Chris Taylor ) Vodafone analysed millions of scam calls on its network during a one-year period, finding 98 per cent came from internet phone company Symbio. Symbio is owned by Aussie Broadband who says stopping the scammers is very difficult. Aussie Broadband has committed to working with Vodafone's owner TPG to reduce the volume of scam calls while Australia's Scams Prevention Framework is due to be introduced next year. Vodafone's owner has accused its rival, Aussie Broadband, of being involved as a carrier in almost all of the scam calls made to its customers in a one-year period. It analysed millions of scam calls on the Vodafone network between July 2025 and July 2026 and found 98 per cent of the calls — more than 24 million — came via little-known internet phone company Symbio. Symbio is owned by Aussie Broadband. "Every time we see this type of scam campaign we give the evidence and the data to Aussie Broadband for them to investigate and block the bad actors," Vanessa Hicks, executive at Vodafone's parent company TPG Telecom, said. "We want more urgent action to stop this activity closer to the source and stop these calls reaching Australians." Vodafone collected data on scam calls on its network and found the vast majority originated with Symbio. ( ABC News ) Symbio sells Australian phone numbers in bulk to companies, allowing them to make calls via the internet. Aussie Broadband CEO Brian Maher said Symbio had about 500 customers on-selling those numbers. Each of those customers may on-sell numbers to thousands of other users. He said that because Symbio had no oversight of who its customers were selling phone numbers to, stopping the scammers was very difficult. "Where we find a persistent bad actor, then we will disconnect them," Mr Maher said. He said the company used detection software and a team of more than 20 people to reduce scam calls. "We've got plans to invest further into the future, and we'll continue to do that," Mr Maher said, but declined to say how many additional staff would be hired. "It is unfortunate that they've called us out publicly, but we accept that they're frustrated and we want to work with them to solve the problem," he said. Perth-based Ian Odlum posted on Instagram last month about a strange call he received. "I just received a call from someone saying they were from the Australian Federal Police," he said in the post. Mr Odlum said the scammers emailed him to "verify" they were from the AFP, then told him they had seized an individual and their laptop, which contained his personal information. The caller told him he needed to come to Narrogin Police Station, around 200 kilometres from Perth. "It was a very calm, very kind person explaining that they weren't going to ask for my information, but that they needed to speak to me and it was very important," he said. Mr Odlum refused to travel to Narrogin, and the caller hung up. "I don't know exactly what he would have gotten out of this, but it's really scary how real this scam feels," he said. Vodafone's fraud team investigated and found police stations in Western Australia, Queensland, South Australia and the AFP had all been impersonated by calls from Symbio's network. "What we've seen in this particular scam is over 2,400 calls, and this was just in a one-week period in September," Ms Hicks said. The regulator, the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA), said checks made on that particular scam showed regulation was working, saying "the traffic was identified, notifications were passed upstream and blocking occurred". "The apparent sources were multiple overseas telcos, and the ACMA did not identify non-compliance by an Australian telco," the regulator said in a statement. Mr Maher said Aussie Broadband had made "significant progress" over the past month in reducing the number of scams. "We're working as hard as we can, but we need many more pieces of information to be shared with us to solve the problem, and we're working hard to do that," he said. "We are the largest wholesaler in the market, and therefore we would have a higher proportion of scam calls." Symbio warned by the regulator over scam activity The regulator warned Symbio in 2024 after finding the company did not properly investigate scam calls and failed to share information quickly with other telcos.

events.title: Israeli military conducts massive "power projection" operation near Iran's border
events.summary: Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets conducted a sortie on Monday, flying as far as the Iranian border, according to Israeli and U.S. officials. Why it matters: The operation, more than 800 miles away from Israel, took place a week before the Israeli elections and on the same day Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Israel's Ovda Air Base. The sortie wasn't connected to Hegseth's visit. While some Israeli and U.S. officials said the sortie wasn't unusual and that it was meant to deter Iran, it could have led to a miscalculation, triggering an Iranian response and reigniting the war. Behind the scenes: The exercise involved dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft, the sources said. It followed a flight path consistent with a potential strike against Iran, passing through Syrian and Iraqi airspace. As the aircraft approached the Iranian border, they turned around and returned to Israel, the sources said. The intrigue: U.S. officials said the Israelis knew that Iran's air defense systems would detect the sortie. According to the sources, Israel notified the U.S. in advance and described the operation as a training exercise intended for "power projection" and aimed at deterring Iran from launching attacks against Israel ahead of the elections. However, some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Iran. Fox News reported on Tuesday that the Israeli Air Force conducted a drill towards Iran. Driving the news: Last week, Axios reported that Netanyahu and President Trump discussed in early October the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections. Netanyahu told Trump he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program. Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir told Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine at the time that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said. Trump initially seemed to be inclined to resume attacks, but then grew hesitant and eventually decided against Netanyahu's proposal. State of play: An Israeli official said Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir will not allow any unjustified military activity that could undermine the Oct. 27 elections. What he's saying: On Wednesday Netanyahu said at a military graduation ceremony that Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei "has decided to follow in his father's footsteps" and allowed Iranian scientists to move forward with building a nuclear weapon. "He has taken the safety off, and Iran is once again trying to develop its bombs of death," Netanyahu said. "Therefore, there is only one way to eliminate this threat once and for all: to overthrow the regime in Iran. And that is the directive I have given to the IDF, the Mossad and the security agencies," he added.

events.title: New PowerToys utilities make everyday Windows tasks easier
events.summary: PowerToys 0.102 is here: new mouse utilities, Command Palette improvements and much more We’re back with a fresh PowerToys release! This one brings two new mouse utilities, Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide , an optional quick-access shelf for Command Palette , snip dictation in ZoomIt , and a set of new command-line tools for automating PowerToys. Color Picker and Text Extractor also move to WinUI 3, and Keyboard Manager picks up some long-requested remapping features. Get the update by checking for updates in PowerToys or by heading to the release page . Let’s dive in! 🖱️ Mouse Button Lock and CursorHide Holding a mouse button down during a long drag or selection can be tiring. With Mouse Button Lock , press and hold a button for a moment, then let go. Windows keeps treating it as held, so you can continue dragging or selecting until you click any button. This is especially useful for gaming, working in professional applications that require extensive dragging and selection, and improving accessibility for users who find it difficult to hold down a mouse button for extended periods. CursorHide is the second new mouse utility. It hides the mouse pointer while you type, after a period of inactivity, or both , and shows it again as soon as you move the mouse. PR #50271 (Thanks, @DamianEdwards !) ⚡ Command Palette gets a quick-access shelf Compact mode in 0.101 kept Command Palette out of the way until you needed results. Now your favorite commands can be one keystroke away too. Turn on the quick-access shelf in Settings > Appearance > Compact mode to show your pins below the search box while the palette is collapsed. Press Alt+1 through Alt+9 to launch them, or Alt+Shift+number to select one without running it. Drag to reorder, right-click for more actions, and optionally show recent commands and apps next to your pins. The shelf is just one part of a big Command Palette update: Settings search: Fuzzy search finds options, extensions, commands, aliases, and assigned shortcuts, then takes you straight to them. Keyboard-first Dock: Press Win+Alt+J to focus the dock and move between its items from the keyboard. Copilot key support: Choose Command Palette as the Copilot key app in Windows Settings, and press the key again to toggle the palette. Multiple clocks: Pin several dock clocks, each with its own time zone and format. Language and links: Pick an app language for Command Palette, and copy links that open a page, run a command, or jump to a specific setting. Polish: Sharper app icons, faster grid and gallery browsing, results that keep loading at the end of a list, and clearer nested menus. Massive thanks to @jiripolasek for the sustained Command Palette work across this release! ZoomIt can now capture what you say along with what you snip. Turn on Snip with dictation in the ZoomIt settings, then press Space while you drag out a snip and describe what you’re capturing. ZoomIt transcribes your speech on your device, and a single paste delivers both the screenshot and your text. Dictation uses the microphone selected under Record. ZoomIt also gets smooth zoom transitions , better audio pacing in recordings, and a fix for silent recordings on multichannel and spatial-audio devices. More of PowerToys can now be scripted from the terminal: Advanced Paste: Run built-in and custom actions without opening the UI, using files, stdin/stdout, or the clipboard. AI actions use your configured providers and policies. Light Switch: Check status, set or toggle the theme, and manage schedules, with JSON output. Settings: See which utilities are enabled, and turn them on or off even while PowerToys isn’t running. Peek: Preview multiple files and folders from the command line. PowerDisplay: JSON Lines output makes results and errors easy to consume from scripts. On your PATH: FancyZones, Image Resizer, File Locksmith, and PowerDisplay commands now work from any terminal folder. PRs: #50834 , #50459 , #50507 , and #49724 (Thanks, @daverayment !) ⌨️ Keyboard Manager adds tap-alone remaps and easier editing Keyboard Manager now supports tap-alone remaps . Tap a key by itself to trigger a different action, while the key keeps working normally in shortcuts and mouse combinations. Large remapping lists are easier to manage too, with search, modifier and app filters, and bulk deletion . The new editor also gets a searchable key picker , so you can select any key, including media keys or keys your keyboard doesn’t have, and build a full shortcut with just the mouse. Recording now only listens while the editor is in focus, and Tab moves you out of the recording field. IT admins can also deploy and export remapping profiles with DSC v3 . PRs: #49136 and #49287 (Thanks, @MasaYan24 !), #51150 , and #49427 (Thanks, @Gijsreyn !) Color Picker and Text Extractor: Both move to WinUI 3, with a new overlay, editor, and magnifier for Color Picker. Your existing shortcuts and settings carry over. FancyZones: Scroll the mouse wheel while dragging a window to switch layouts, with an optional indicator showing the selected layout’s name. Peek: Added read-only SQLite previews, file and subfolder counts with scanning progress for folders, a plain-text fallback, and Alt+Left/Alt+Right navigation between files. Screen Ruler: Measure in device-independent pixels to account for each monitor’s scaling, with improved edge detection. Environment Variables: A new Remove duplicates action cleans up PATH while keeping the original order. Quick Accent: A searchable character reference in Settings lets you browse language sets and copy characters directly. Grab and Move: Exclude specific apps so they keep their normal modifier-key behavior. Shortcut Guide: Added shortcuts for Claude Desktop and Ableton Live, and made indexing more resilient to malformed manifests. Workspaces: Now asks for confirmation before launching an unverified app configured to run as administrator. Awake: Windows can now turn off the display while the PC is locked, without ending your keep-awake session. New+: Fixed a File Explorer memory leak and improved long-path handling. Settings: Added an interactive animated welcome scene, fixed a memory leak when switching pages, and kept module on/off preferences when a utility fails to load. As always, a big thank-you to everyone who contributed — we couldn’t do this release without you!

events.title: Tech firms monitor city council meetings to track data center sentiment
events.summary: Data-center companies are ponying up to find out which communities will resist them the least. Startup Hamlet has parsed tens of thousands of city council meetings by scraping local governments’ video recordings, tagging comments as friendly or hostile to a potential project. CEO Sunil Rajaraman told Semafor that a large fund that finances data centers and a data-center developer are among its paying customers, looking for whiffs of a moratorium. “Where there might be more favorable political views” may well determine where future projects get built, Rajaraman said. Investors backing these projects are also obvious customers for a real-time feed into Americans’ growing antipathy toward data centers. The appetite for such data shows the lengths to which the tech industry is going to find where projects are most likely to go through, in the face of a national groundswell of anti-data center activism that has turned community sentiment into a financial risk. Other Hamlet customers include real estate developers, political action committees, and retailers, Rajaraman said. The company on Tuesday launched new rankings for where cities and counties stand on a host of hot-button issues (ranging from zoning laws to pickleball), and a portal for people to look up what their elected officials have said. (Among large local governments, Corpus Christi, Texas ranked No. 1 in speakers’ opposition to data centers.) “This is public sphere data,” Rajaraman said. “The data needs to be out there so America can make better decisions.”

events.title: OpenAI says its agents disabled their own safety monitors
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts OpenAI says its AI agents disabled their own safety monitors It is the latest example of autonomous AI models seemingly breaking containment. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic ) Two OpenAI agents disabled or weakened tools used to detect incidents of AI agents acting against human commands. The two instances happened earlier this month, with one later telling its programmer it had not stripped out its monitor. The incidents add to growing concern about how well AI companies control their autonomous systems. OpenAI has revealed that two of its artificial intelligence agents disabled or weakened systems built to catch them misbehaving, with one later denying it had done so. The cases are the latest in a string of safety scares at the world's top AI developers involving agents, AI programs that carry out tasks without human involvement. In a report released this week, the ChatGPT maker said that during two internal coding jobs, its agents switched off or undermined tools for detecting incidents of AI models acting against human wishes. On October 3, an agent running on OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol model, which had been told not to send any messages on the workplace chat app, took that as license to switch off safety alerts meant for the company's security team while fixing a testing system. This latest incident follows an earlier instance in which an OpenAI model accessed a Medicare statistics reporting service. ( ABC News ) Three days later, a GPT-6 Astra agent stripped out its own monitor while copying code from another project, then told the human programmer it had done no such thing. The company said it had also seen several cases of agents launching software with monitoring switched off, exposing a gap in its oversight. OpenAI said it is still trying to determine whether the models were simply overzealous in following instructions or have a particular tendency to evade monitoring. ABC staff targeted in sophisticated cyber attack AI tool saves time but makes errors in police trial Will an AI-cloned free tool spell the end of expensive software? AI data centre company cold calling about buying land, inquiry told The disclosure adds to mounting unease over how well leading labs can control increasingly autonomous systems. In July, a group of OpenAI agents broke out of their test environments and launched a cyberattack on AI firm Hugging Face, causing international alarm. Other companies have since reported similar incidents. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also accused the AI company's models of infiltrating a Medicare website with both public and private data, although no personal information was accessed in the incident. The incidents have fuelled calls in the United States and abroad for tighter oversight of AI development. But US President Donald Trump, under the advice of top AI executives like Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, has urged the industry to police itself. events.title: What the GOP activist who confronted El-Sayed really got wrong
events.summary: David’s view If Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan’s Senate race next month, the Saturday clip of him admonishing a GOP activist about freedom of religion will achieve legendary status in his party. “It’s you who need to understand the Constitution, not me,” El-Sayed told Thomas Teepell during an appearance in the small Michigan city of Caro. The candidate accepted Teepell’s challenge to “disavow the Muslim Brotherhood,” then denounced the “dual loyalty” smear it seemed like the activist wanted to make. If El-Sayed wins, I’d expect Republicans to study that clip, too. That’s because the lesson conservatives can take isn’t that the topic of El-Sayed’s religion is too hot to touch. Teepell struggled to follow up because he couldn’t handle the moment. From President Donald Trump on down, Republicans are very comfortable contending that Muslim immigration threatens America and that the liberal crusade for diversity is national suicide. They love running against El-Sayed, even in the 49 states where he’s not on the ballot. And they don’t hold their tongues anymore for fear of political backlash. “What excites him is this prospect of wielding the power of a country he hates,” Vice President JD Vance told Michigan Republicans about El-Sayed this month. “He wants to litigate ancient grievances with your tax dollars, and he wants to use the grievances of faraway lands to punish you.” This isn’t a swerve away from the GOP’s midterm message. It is the message: Foreigners are undermining America from within, and Democrats won’t stop them. (Never mind that El-Sayed was born in Rochester Hills.) Teepell was very much in line with the Trump-era Republican rhetorical strategy to demonize the “other.” Where he went wrong was, in part, failing to go toe to toe with one of the most skillful extemporaneous talkers in Democratic politics. He was also working against a new reality: The Trump administration’s border closure and shutdown of most asylum claims has made “immigration” less critical to most voters. Casting El-Sayed as the enemy simply wasn’t as easy as he might have hoped. But the bigger context is more favorable to MAGA conservatives: With no Democrat running on a return to pre-Trump border policies, they see that topics once considered forbidden or offensive by media gatekeepers can win elections. The El-Sayed-Teepell moment happened as Paris was gripped by riots; Trump, his White House, and supportive media outlets warned that Democrats would bring the same migration-driven chaos across the Atlantic. Those media gates of the past might not even be standing anymore. They were sturdy in 2008, when Republicans campaigned more cautiously around questions of race and immigration. El-Sayed has indulged comparisons to Barack Obama, whose 2008 campaign convinced the young Muslim that he could one day run for office. In his 2020 memoir, El-Sayed wrote that after he graduated from the University of Michigan, he brushed off the idea (floated by Bill Clinton, his commencement speaker) that he might have a future in politics. Of course not: His name was Abdulrahman Muhammad El-Sayed. But one year later, “someone whose father had immigrated from eastern Africa — someone who was marked by a funny name and dark skin,” won Michigan by 16 points. The idea that something had changed, and that attacking Islam or a foreign name didn’t work anymore, ran through El-Sayed’s 2018 campaign. At one stop, he was buttonholed by Laura Loomer, then a semi-cancelled independent muckraker, who asked how he could “reconcile your own personal practice of Islamic law with your Marxist, socialist political platform.” Loomer was fairly easy for that campaign to brush off. She’s now one of the most influential conservative activists in America, with a direct line to the president. Republicans in the Bush years, who briefly hoped to build a lasting multiracial coalition, were hesitant to attack Obama over his pastor, or to elevate rumors that he was a Muslim. ( “No, ma’am.“ ) On the right, it’s widely believed now that this was a loser’s strategy. That’s why Teepell’s biggest error, in the eyes of the right, was simply lacking a clapback. If Republicans lose big next month, there’ll be a brawl to assign blame — which consultants blew it, which ads wasted money, which issues didn’t work. The party’s margins with non-white voters and first generation Americans, which improved in 2024, will get a harder look. But I wouldn’t expect them to ditch tactics like the El-Sayed confrontation, tactics that the new media environment is built for. Notable In Slow Boring, Matthew Yglesias wrote about the edgy conservative debate over “the Indian question,” and whether Republican rhetoric about immigrants was hurting them. “You either need to be willing to bite the bullet and say you’re eager to keep good people out or else you need to redefine good behavior as bad.”

events.title: Microsoft’s Nadella is back in business
events.summary: The Satya Nadella I interviewed last week for Future Proof at Microsoft’s headquarters in Redmond, Wash., was a very different version of the CEO I saw there in 2023, who wanted to make Google “dance.” Back then, generative AI was the exciting (and scary) new thing, and without Microsoft’s investment in compute, OpenAI wouldn’t have been able to build ChatGPT, and the industry’s trajectory might have been very different. We’re now four years on from the launch of ChatGPT and, outside of software development, AI’s impact on the world has been incremental, not exponential. And Microsoft is less about making competitors dance than it is about getting down to the nitty-gritty of making AI work predictably and reliably — Nadella has gone back to being the CEO of a company that is building a sturdy dance floor. “We, as an industry, have to wake up to this,” Nadella said. “It’s not about the shiny object and FOMO.” Wall Street is happy with the strategy. Microsoft’s stock is up 27% over the past six months and it’s valued at close to $4 trillion. But will it outpace the frontier labs and Nvidia in the long run? Nadella calls the frontier labs “magical businesses,” but points to Microsoft’s remarkable 51-year history. “I look at them and say, hey, this is not an industry where your initial success means anything,” he said. — Reed Albergotti

events.title: Before the ambulance arrives: How AI is helping the NHS rethink patient care
events.summary: When someone in the UK dials 999 for an ambulance, their focus is understandably on when help will arrive. Less visible is the planning, training, analysis and coordination that happen long before a paramedic reaches the patient. “We all think about the ambulance when it’s on scene, but there’s so much that happens before that goes on before an ambulance crew even arrives with a patient,” says James Goulding, chief clinical information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service (YAS) NHS Trust. YAS is one of 200 plus trusts, or organizational units, of the UK’s National Health Service. That preparation includes planning services, recruiting and training staff, analyzing population health data and understanding the experiences of patients who do not speak English fluently. “So much goes into making sure that when that paramedic arrives in front of a patient, that we’ve done all of this work to make it really easy for them to make good decisions for patients,” Goulding says. James Goulding, chief clinical information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service. Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft. Following an earlier trial involving 30,000 employees, NHS England announced plans in June 2026 to make Microsoft Copilot available to as many as 505,000 clinicians and support staff. Participants in the trial reported saving an average of 43 minutes per working day — which adds up to about five weeks of time per person a year. Dr. Alec Price-Forbes, national chief clinical information officer for NHS England, says that the NHS is still in many ways an analog system. “It’s critically important that we use the opportunity that we have in front of us to truly reimagine the NHS,” he says, “to reduce cognitive load and administrative burden for healthcare professionals, make sure they get a better experience and then are in the position to give the best quality care.” AI and digital tools such as Microsoft Copilot can help sustain the NHS by reducing administrative burden, releasing clinical capacity and enabling more productive, connected and person-centered models of care. Helping NHS teams manage information Tom Smith sees that work from several angles. As an area operations manager for Yorkshire Ambulance Service, he oversees operational managers and frontline teams, plans staffing and specialist resources, and responds personally to significant incidents as a tactical commander. The service received about 1.25 million calls to its 999 number in the 2025-26 fiscal year. “It’s everything and anything,” he says. “No day is the same.” Smith also has to read and produce many reports. Microsoft Copilot does not make decisions for him, he says. Instead, it organizes information into a format he can review and interrogate using his operational expertise. “What it does is just give me all the information in a helpful format, which is easy to understand,” Smith says. “It does a lot of my admin tasks for me that would previously have been really time consuming. Then I can just review what it’s done.” Tom Smith, area operations manager for Yorkshire Ambulance Service. Photo by Esme Mai for Microsoft. For Smith, who is dyslexic, that support extends beyond saving time. Writing an email can take longer when he begins to overthink the wording or spelling, he says. The ability to structure a draft, summarize a long report and ask follow-up questions helps “level the playing field” for him. His experience comes as NHS England expands access to generative AI tools across the health service in England. The NHS has put clear, strict safeguards around its use of Microsoft Copilot: it is only for administrative tasks, not clinical work, says Price-Forbes. The NHS is supporting its digital transformation with standards for clinical safety, information governance, cybersecurity, interoperability and real-world evaluation, with transparency and human oversight considered essential to maintaining the confidence of staff and the public. Like healthcare systems in many countries, the NHS serves an aging population, and many patients have multiple chronic illnesses. Price-Forbes says, “It means that we’ve got the opportunity to redesign because we just cannot continue with the old analog model of healthcare delivery. And this is a challenge across the globe. So we now need to redesign care around people and technology, digital and data, and AI is going to be the only way to create those new service models of care.” “Artificial intelligence can transform the NHS — improving care, giving time back to staff and delivering greater value — but only if we turn ambition into trusted action at scale,” he says. “Proven tools, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, must move rapidly beyond isolated pilots and into everyday workflows wherever evidence shows they improve outcomes, productivity or staff experience.” “Done well, AI will not replace the human heart of the NHS; it will protect it — strengthening decisions, restoring time for care and helping create a safer, more personal and sustainable health service. The world has changed. We’ve got to create a digital front door for the NHS.” Dr. Alec Price-Forbes, national chief clinical information officer for NHS England. Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft. He says that this transformation goes beyond technology; it requires that work be redesigned so that AI can help clinicians amplify their expertise while relieving them of unnecessary burdens. This will free “clinicians to focus on judgment, validation and human connection.” He also says that trust is essential for success. “Patients and staff must know when AI is being used, how it shapes decisions and where human oversight applies, with unambiguous accountability for consequential choices,” he says. The challenge now is to use digital capability to redesign pathways, improve flow, support clinical decision-making and release capacity back into care, Price-Forbes says. That means moving at pace, but with discipline. Copilot “gives us that ability to join dots that we wouldn’t see ourselves without a laborious several hours’ worth of trawling through data reports and trying to look at common themes.” Samantha Robinson, chief digital information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service. Photo by Joanne Crawford for Microsoft. Samantha Robinson, chief digital information officer at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, is responsible for helping information move between frontline teams, local operations and the wider NHS. Copilot “gives us that ability to join dots that we wouldn’t see ourselves without a laborious several hours’ worth of trawling through data reports and trying to look at common themes,” she says. The NHS’s information flows in all directions, Robinson says. She may need to turn operational information from across the ambulance service into a briefing for senior NHS leaders. At other times, she must translate national guidance into clear, practical instructions for different teams.

events.title: How AI divided New York's democratic socialists
events.summary: The News The New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America is divided over whether the AI industry is a destructive capitalist force that could kill everyone, or merely an overhyped capitalist hustle. The rift within the largest chapter of the left-wing organization centers on whether the New York DSA should acknowledge the possibility that AI could lead to mass automation and to systems that escape human control — the kind of warnings that gained traction after recent AI-powered hacks. Some tech leaders and Democratic politicians — including America’s leading socialist, Sen. Bernie Sanders — have warned that without guardrails, there’s a chance AI could lead to human extinction. At the chapter’s convention on Nov. 14, members are expected to consider a resolution proposed in September by two graduate students and local DSA members: They warn that industry “negligence” creates “the potential for loss of control of AI agents to cause catastrophic harm.” But the group’s established Tech Action Working Group is not persuaded. Some in the self-described “ techno-skeptical ” committee that steers the chapter’s technology policy see things differently, arguing that dire warnings of doom are an attempt to inflate company valuations, and AI is already doing enough damage. Members of the group’s leadership proposed to amend that measure by removing clauses on automation, loss of control, and catastrophic risk: “ AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story ,” the group posted to Instagram in September. The resolution also calls for “the democratization and socialization of AI ,” but the amendment deletes that phrase. Know More The socialist organization is now mired in procedural infighting. Alexei Gannon and Zachary Jones, who wrote the original resolution, accused the TAWG of presenting its leaders’ views as the group’s official position, even though the group never formally voted on where it stands on AI risk. The TAWG, Gannon and Jones wrote in a Substack post, hasn’t held a membership meeting since March. “To equate worrying about catastrophic risk with buying a Silicon Valley narrative is to lump hundreds of DSA comrades… and 60% of the American public into the same bucket as Sam Altman and Elon Musk,” they wrote. Gannon and Jones declined to comment; the New York City DSA chapter and the Tech Action Working Group didn’t respond to requests for comment. The DSA is also grappling with how to use the technology itself: The local chapter’s tech working group voted in January to ban using generative AI text, images, and video for “any DSA purpose.” The national DSA’s tech committee this month adopted a policy that “ neither endorses nor prohibits ” AI coding tools for its own software. J.D.’s view The discourse in the DSA in many ways mirrors the broader debate confronting the American left over AI, as Democrats look to stake out a position on the issue ahead of the 2028 presidential election. How the DSA and other left-wing factions speak to voters about AI risk could shape what regulation looks like if Democrats retake Congress in the midterms, and which candidates win over the party’s AI-skeptic vote. I got a glimpse of how progressives are positioning on the issue at the People’s AI Assembly on Monday, organized by the AI Now Institute and More Perfect Union. The event centered on the impacts of data centers, surveillance, and the concentration of power in a handful of companies. Sanders-esque warnings about AI threatening humanity weren’t a focal point, suggesting the DSA camp that’s more focused on mitigating present harms is setting the terms of the conversation, at least in New York. “Even as we reckon with these larger societal questions, there are still rules that we can implement and hold these kinds of companies to account for,” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a DSA member, told the crowd. Room for Disagreement It was clear at the People’s AI Assembly that broad swaths of the left remain united on a number of AI-related fronts, including data centers, the concentration of corporate power, and the broader need for regulation and oversight. Brian Romero, a DSA member and incoming state assemblymember who has worked with the chapter’s tech working group in the past, framed the debate as a complex, fast-moving issue that factions across the political spectrum are having. “It’s not unlike any other policy issue,” he said. “There’s going to be differences of opinion on the left.” As another attendee at the People’s Assembly told me: “It wouldn’t be the DSA if there wasn’t debate.” Notable Sanders is facing pushback from some on the left over his doomerist AI rhetoric, WIRED reported. “Some of us are looking at Bernie and saying, what happened? ” one NYC DSA member said. The broader DSA has no “ consistent line on what elected socialists should advocate for regarding AI,” Zhao Levi, a DSA member, wrote in Cosmonaut in September, proposing a national working group to draft one for the 2027 national convention.

events.title: Meta tops Big Tech lobbying as AI labs talk antitrust
events.summary: The Scoop Both OpenAI and Anthropic lobbied lawmakers on the ability of AI companies to share information with one another without running afoul of antitrust rules in the third quarter of this year, according to federal lobbying disclosures reviewed by Semafor. Anthropic’s lobbying form lists the Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act, a bill that would allow labs to coordinate with each other on security risks, as a point of focus for the company on Capitol Hill. The legislation could make it into law as part of must-pass defense policy legislation, Semafor previously reported . OpenAI’s lobbying form is less specific, listing “AI-security collaboration and information-sharing, including proposed antitrust protections” as topics discussed in Washington. Lobbying forms don’t say whether companies are arguing for or against the proposals discussed in meetings. The antitrust lobbying is of interest given the talks around a coordinated AI development “slowdown” pitched by AI leaders last month. The companies regularly lobby Washington lawmakers on proposed AI regulatory bills, as well as legislation on export controls and data centers. OpenAI’s head of global affairs, Chris Lehane, has argued that an antitrust exemption specifically for model pacing would not be necessary. But Trump administration officials criticized AI leaders for calling for such a carve-out, saying they were capable of deciding to slow down among themselves without the government’s blessing. Know More Meta spent $5.9 million lobbying Washington lawmakers in the third quarter of 2026 — the most of any big tech firm during that period — as the AI race grew more competitive and high-profile hacks put pressure on the AI safety debate in Washington, according to Senate lobbying filings. Meta often is the biggest lobbying spender among its Big Tech and AI counterparts, but OpenAI and Anthropic have been spending more and more each quarter, nearly doubling and tripling their spends in the first half of the year, respectively, as they navigate Washington’s discussions about containing their technology. Google, Amazon, and Apple lagged behind Meta in spending but beat AI and chip companies, though Nvidia also posted its highest-ever quarter at $2.2 million as the chipmaker stays dominant and influential in the Trump administration. All three companies have built up massive lobbying portfolios on a range of tech policy topics including kids’ online safety, immigration, taxes, education, and energy policy.

events.title: This Startup Is All In on Recursive Self-Improvement. Its Latest Model Is Scary Good
events.summary: For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement , or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer. Flint is the first offering from Recursive, a company that aims to use RSI to advance both AI itself and other areas of science using AI . “Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI,” Recursive CEO and cofounder Richard Socher told me. Socher says his company used its recursive AI system, dubbed the Eureka Machine, to automate most elements of the model’s development. This enabled a company with a handful of researchers to build a world-class model in just a few months, he says. Socher told me that the Eureka Machine devised a number of innovations, including a new way of training the base model, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon chips. Recursive shared benchmark scores that suggest Flint outperforms other models of similar size and architecture on coding tasks. AI is already widely used to help build, test, and improve AI thanks to its amazing coding skills. This can speed up the process of refining a model and testing new ideas without the need for as much input from humans. It is also possible to create a loop through which AI decides what improvements to make and then begins another round of improvement. For the moment this technique is limited, but if AI can contribute to every aspect of model development, then the process could theoretically continue indefinitely. Some experts worry that letting AI improve itself in this manner could ultimately lead to disaster . These doomsayers claim that AI capable of improving indefinitely could escape human control and might decide that humans are an impediment to its goals. Those concerns gained wider notice this September when a researcher quit Anthropic and warned that advances in AI, including recursive self-improvement, could lead to human extinction within a few years—a concern then echoed by a number of other experts. The idea of RSI has become so controversial that several bills in Congress propose to ban it. Recursive sees these fears as more sci-fi than reality and believes legislation to prevent RSI is an unnecessary impediment to progress. Socher says Flint was built using a system incapable of escaping human control. He says the goal is for the Eureka Machine itself to achieve full recursive self-improvement, but this would still be overseen by humans who could stop the process if it goes awry. “We hope that this shows people that indeed we have all the steps in place” to build such a system, he says. Recursive has raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation from Google Ventures, Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Socher was previously the chief scientist at Salesforce, and his cofounders include Jeff Clune, a professor at the University of British Columbia who researches ways of building AI systems capable of learning indefinitely. I must say I am impressed with Flint. I tested it on a Mac with 48 GB of RAM—a healthy amount but only enough to run a modest-size AI model like Flint, which has 40 billion parameters. The biggest models out there have several trillions of parameters, and they can only run on racks of industrial servers. I used Flint to build a bunch of programs and found it to be both fast and very capable. In my experience, models of this size can be annoyingly error-prone or slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed my coding requests every time. I used it to create a command line to-do list, then tried having it build a program that scours the web for interesting research related to recursive self-improvement. I also had Flint whip up a simple website that explains how RSI works. You can see that here . It’s unclear how much progress other US labs have made chasing recursive self-improvement, but some published work suggests fully recursive systems are already feasible. A team from Microsoft, Carnegie Mellon University, and the University of Virginia recently published work, for instance, showing how an AI coding agent can recursively improve itself by modifying the software harness that turns reasoning into useful action and its own model’s weights. Perhaps there are risks to full RSI if you are close to building a godlike intelligence, but for the time being it seems like a very promising way to improve your own AI models. This is something I’ve dabbled with in previous editions of AI Lab . Indeed, Socher says the approach used to build Flint could make cutting-edge AI more accessible. “It's the only way this very small team can produce a model that's actually better than any other model in its class,” he told me. “This will hopefully show people that [recursive self-improvement] is actually quite nice and will benefit a lot of people.” This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter .

events.title: The oil market's 2027 relief hopes are fading fast
events.summary: Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios Traders are betting that oil prices will remain elevated for longer than they anticipated just weeks ago, threatening to prolong the inflationary pressures that businesses and consumers have weathered for months. Why it matters: Oil inventories have helped cushion the blow from disrupted Middle Eastern supplies, but much of that buffer has been depleted since the war began. The possibility of sustained price pressures into next year throws into doubt the logic that central banks traditionally rely upon to look through energy price shifts — that they represent a one-time shift in relative prices, not an ongoing inflationary process. That leaves the global economy more vulnerable to another energy price surge, with potentially more lasting consequences for growth, inflation and interest rates than energy shocks of yore. By the numbers: Oil futures for delivery in 2027 — contracts to buy or sell crude next year — have climbed to their highest levels since the Iran war began. Prices for January 2027 are up 17% since early September, to more than $97 a barrel. Markets still anticipate some relief next year, but considerably less than they expected just weeks ago. It's a reversal from late summer, when hopes of easing tensions with Iran and a recovery in Middle Eastern oil supplies briefly pushed futures lower. June futures have jumped 18%, to $88 a barrel, while December futures are up 13%, to about $81. State of play: Crude oil exports from the Persian Gulf, including shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and alternative routes, surpassed prewar levels in the week ending Oct. 18, according to the Wall Street Journal . But the costly workarounds enabling that recovery have their limits. Those include ship-to-ship transfers outside the Strait of Hormuz, where security risks have deterred some vessels. "You're coming up against limitations on actually how much volume you can move out of the Middle East, even with these processes," Christopher Haines, global head of oil at Energy Aspects, tells Axios. Restoring confidence among shipping companies and insurers that vessels won't be attacked will be "exceptionally hard," Haines adds. Zoom in: Economist Robin Brooks argues that oil prices reflect higher shipping costs and fears of further attacks more than actual shortages. Using earlier monthly data, he estimates that Persian Gulf crude exports had recovered to 91% of prewar levels, with a "temporary fear factor" adding at least $20 a barrel. What to watch: The Trump administration is seeking to ease fuel prices ahead of the midterms, most recently by allowing more Russian diesel onto the market. But relief may be minimal: Ukrainian attacks have damaged Russian refineries, while sanctions complicate repairs, limiting additional exports, Haines says. The bottom line: "The market narrative has shifted from "transitory" to "new normal" right before our eyes," Bob Elliot, chief investment officer at Unlimited Funds, wrote Wednesday morning .

events.title: Colorado Marijuana Regulators Failed to Protect Consumers From Potential Contamination, Audit Finds
events.summary: Cannabis samples in the process of testing at Kaycha Labs in Denver Stephen Swofford/The Denver Gazette The agency charged with regulating Colorado’s first-in-the-nation legal recreational marijuana market potentially put consumers at risk of using contaminated products, a new state audit found. The report pointed to inconsistent oversight by the Marijuana Enforcement Division and loose state rules around testing marijuana products or contaminants. As a result, it found, nearly 75% of marijuana processed for eventual sale from 2023 through 2025 evaded testing for pesticides. The audit, released Monday , identified a host of issues, including regulators’ failure to meet regular inspection schedules or to conduct sufficient random checks at dispensaries for contaminated products. It also found that delayed agency warnings to the public allowed potentially contaminated products to remain on shelves for months, sometimes years. The audit’s conclusions echo several findings of an investigation this year by The Denver Gazette and ProPublica into the Marijuana Enforcement Division’s lapses in policing contaminants entering the legal marketplace.   In one case highlighted by the newsrooms, it took 15 months for a manufacturer to discontinue production of a marijuana sleep aid pill despite consumers warning regulators that the product was harming their livers. The pills had herbal extracts that researchers say can cause liver damage. Auditors said they did not identify evidence of “widespread health and safety issues” but did find that deficient regulations still left consumers vulnerable. The audit found that unsafe products had remained on the market for as long as three years before the Marijuana Enforcement Division issued a public warning. The auditor’s review of the agency’s health and safety advisories found that, on average, from 2023 through 2025, contaminated products that were the subject of an advisory remained on shelves for more than seven months. That’s the same number of months the news organizations found contaminated products stayed on shelves before warnings were issued. The audit also found that it took the agency three and a half months, on average, in 2025 to issue an advisory once it launched an investigation into potential contamination. Even after investigators determined an advisory was needed, it still took the agency a month on average to issue one.  “These issues limit MED’s ability to meet its core objective to identify product safety risks and to help ensure that licensed marijuana businesses meet product safety requirements,” the audit stated. “As a result, there is an increased risk that marijuana products sold in Colorado may have contaminants or that the potency listed on the labels is inaccurate.” Colorado allows marijuana businesses to test far less frequently than required by state guidelines if they can show consistent compliance with testing rules. The reduced testing program results “in a significant portion of the marijuana product being sold in Colorado not undergoing testing to ensure it is safe,” the audit stated. Manufacturers also can rely on other testing exemptions, such as for certain marijuana-derived skin and body products, but there is “limited MED oversight” of how manufacturers determine they qualify for an exemption. Auditors reported that a survey of MED investigators found that more than half said there are or may be widespread marijuana product safety issues in Colorado’s regulated market.  In a statement released Monday night, the Marijuana Enforcement Division emphasized that state auditors found no evidence “to support claims of widespread health and safety issues” with marijuana products for sale in Colorado, but the agency agreed the audit identified areas for improvement. It said that among other things, it would be assessing exemptions to tests currently allowed under state laws and regulations. The state auditor’s review “allows us to take a critical look at how we can continue to carry out our work, consistent with our commitment to integrity, safety, and continuous operational improvement,” Dominique Mendiola, senior director of the MED, said in a statement. The auditor’s report highlighted a criticism her agency has repeatedly sidestepped: the absence of independent collection of samples for safety testing. The Denver Gazette and ProPublica found that more than half of states with regulated marijuana markets rely on private labs or an independent third party to collect samples. Colorado marijuana businesses are free to collect their own samples submitted for testing. The enforcement division’s own investigators told auditors that, as a result, Colorado relies largely on an honor code to ensure the safety of marijuana sold in the state’s dispensaries. Auditors said that allowing businesses to select their own samples “increases the risk that businesses do not pick samples that are representative of the overall quality of their marijuana product.”  MED regulators at the start of the year said they planned to pursue an overhaul that would have required private lab personnel to collect samples, but they abandoned that effort after manufacturers said it would increase their costs. On Monday, Kyle Lambert, the enforcement division’s deputy senior director, told legislators that the agency opted against an overhaul this year, chiefly because he said it would be a geographic challenge to do away with self-sampling for rural businesses.  “It was decided now wasn’t the right time to propose that as a policy change,” Lambert said, adding that the agency still might revisit the issue. State Sen. Byron Pelton, a Republican from Sterling, pushed back, saying it was a loophole he thinks the agency should consider closing. “If I’m a shady character, I know which products I’m going to go sampling and which ones I’m not,” he said. “That’s a pretty gray area to me.” The audit also questioned the agency’s reliance on businesses voluntarily recalling contaminated marijuana products, saying that “some of these recalls did not succeed at stopping the businesses from selling potentially unsafe product.” Just last month, The Denver Gazette and ProPublica reported that a Colorado manufacturer voluntarily flagged 49 of its popular marijuana vapes for recall, nearly six weeks after a third-party lab notified the company and regulators that it detected methylene chloride, a chemical the Environmental Protection Agency has sought to ban for most uses because it can cause cancer. The MED issued a health and safety advisory a day after the publications first reported the manufacturer had warned dispensaries to stop selling the vapes, which consumers had been purchasing for over a year. The post Colorado Marijuana Regulators Failed to Protect Consumers From Potential Contamination, Audit Finds appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
events.summary: Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild. Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin. The flaws at issue are present in PHP , the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal , Magento , Joomla and WordPress . Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server. Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure. OpenAI , which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.” Censys , a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP. Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog]. “These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.” The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure. The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 , and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12 , 8.4.27 , 8.3.36 , and 8.2.35 . According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework. “A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.” The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif , another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws. This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps. Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.

events.title: Putin tells Witkoff he is ready to resume direct peace talks, Russia releases U.S. detainee
events.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin told White House envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday that he "agrees in principle" resuming trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. to end the war, according to Russian and U.S. officials. Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after President Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. For now, it seems the only concession Putin agreed to is to negotiate. Driving the news: During a three-hour meeting in St. Petersburg, Witkoff presented Putin with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine . Trump envoy Jared Kushner joined virtually. Before the meeting, Russia released U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, 74, who had spent more than four years in captivity after being seized by Russian troops in eastern Ukraine in April 2022. Putin announced his release at the top of the meeting with Witkoff. "He is at Pulkovo Airport," Putin told Witkoff in front of the cameras. Witkoff in response thanked Putin and called him "a humanitarian." Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) expressed outrage at Witkoff's comment. "WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of 'humanitarian'. What an embarrassing and outrageous thing to say," Tillis wrote on X. Cornyn wrote : "No. Putin is stone cold killer." "Stephen is on his way back home and will soon be with his family. The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return - an unprecedented situation for Russia. There was no 'swap' necessary for this release," Trump wrote on Truth Social. State of play: Witkoff arrived in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo , Norway, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the U.K., Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO. Zelensky said Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — a format Russia has so far rejected. The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war. What he's saying: "I believe the talks [in Oslo] were productive, and I would like to say that there is progress, and I will update you on this. I hope that we have truly laid the groundwork for a successful end to hostilities in this Ukrainian-Russian conflict," Witkoff told Putin. Witkoff asked Putin to "consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, where we could discuss the next steps toward achieving a settlement." Witkoff said the talks could include representatives of technical groups of specialists who could discuss these issues in detail. "We have brought several documents outlining approaches to achieving a peaceful settlement in the Ukrainian-Russian conflict. I would ask you, Mr. President, to review these documents a little later," Witkoff said. The other side: After the meeting, Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, told Russian reporters that Putin agreed to hold trilateral talks between negotiation teams. "Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the aforementioned trilateral negotiations on the main topic around the 10th of November," he said, adding that the talks could take place in Abu Dhabi. Ushakov claimed Putin was ready to resume the trilateral talks several weeks ago, but the Ukrainian strikes on Russia on the day of the parliamentary elections led to their cancelation. Putin's adviser said Witkoff briefed Putin on the discussions in Oslo. "The Oslo talks didn't contain much that was useful in the context of resolving the Ukrainian crisis," Ushakov said. The latest: A U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner proposed a trilateral meeting at the technical level between the U.S., Russia, and Ukraine. "This was accepted by the Ukrainians in Oslo yesterday and by the Russians in St. Petersburg today," the official said. The intrigue : Putin also told Witkoff he wants to discuss the possibility of Russia mediating between the U.S. and Iran. "You know that we have a special, trusting relationship with Iran, with our partners in Iran, our friends, built over decades, and if there's anything we can do to resolve this crisis, we'll be happy to do so. You're also well aware of our proposals in this area," Putin said. What's next: Putin told Witkoff he wants to discuss a possible meeting with Trump in China in mid-November.

events.title: Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers
events.summary: Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics , AI agents, and modular data centers , with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all. “To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.” The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face —doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch. Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said. The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out. Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs. Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said. On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data. He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher. In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair. events.title: France’s diesel deal with Gulf states will not make fuel 'cheap overnight’ for European country
events.summary: France's deal to buy diesel from Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Bahrain will not make the fuel “cheap overnight” for the European country although it will also not make it more expensive, according to experts. The three Gulf states are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its usual diesel consumption in the coming weeks, French government sources said on Tuesday during President Emmanuel Macron's regional tour . The aim is to reduce European energy prices, which have drawn protests and public anger in France and elsewhere. The deal “will not make French diesel cheap overnight, but it can stop it [from] becoming scarcer and even more expensive”, said Naeem Aslam, chief investment officer at Zaye Capital Markets. “The bigger value is psychological: France is no longer buying in a panic,” Mr Aslam added. “Gulf supply gives refiners, distributors and traders confidence that physical barrels are coming, which can compress the scarcity premium before it fully reaches the pump.” European diesel has reached about $200 a barrel amid the war in Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. That compares with about $80 at the start of 2026, with refined products rallying much harder than crude prices this year. Temporary easing of supply While the deal can temporarily ease France’s diesel supply shortage, it is unlikely to drive a sustained decline in fuel prices, according to Vijay Valecha, chief investment officer at Century Financial. “The additional diesel arriving in France would ease competition among importers for limited supplies. This could reduce the scarcity premium that buyers pay for immediately available fuel, particularly if inventories are low,” he added. France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell the country 95,000 tonnes of diesel in both October and November, totalling 190,000 tonnes. The UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration. The duration of the supply agreements matter – if UAE and Bahrain shipments continue for several months, they could have a longer-lasting effect on supply security and prices, Mr Valecha said. “If they are temporary or cargoes are delayed, the relief could be short-lived. The wider diesel shortage is a significant driver. The diesel supply squeeze remains severe. The International Energy Agency has warned that shortages could persist well into 2027.” On October 2, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release , prioritising diesel supplies. About 96 million barrels of the 400 million pledged in March have yet to be released. The IEA expects higher refinery output to return the diesel market to a seasonal surplus by early next year but said the recovery would be insufficient to replenish inventories depleted during the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. European commercial gasoil inventories fell to a 25-year low in July, while US diesel stocks reached a 14-year seasonal low by September. Combined gasoil exports from Russia and the Middle East dropped by more than 60 per cent, equivalent to 1.3 million barrels per day. With Mr Macron’s current Gulf visit, the focus would remain on making fuel more affordable at the petrol station rather than just securing France’s fuel supply security, Mr Valecha said. “Analysts estimate that a large release of diesel reserves could lower wholesale prices by $20 to $30 per barrel, or about €0.10 to €0.15 per litre, at the pump, with prices possibly dropping within a few days,” he added. Market signal The latest deal’s importance “lies in the signal it gives to market”, Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer, said. “Despite the recent escalations, oil products find their way out of the Middle East. One should look beyond this specific deal. More supplies from the Middle East ease oil products tightness globally, irrespective if the buyers of single cargoes are in Europe or elsewhere, as this is a global market,” he said. There is indication that oil product exports from the Middle East are picking up and that refineries in Asia are putting more oil products on the market, he added. However, according to Mr Valecha, diesel exports are not expected to pick up any time soon from the Middle East in a way that could bring down costs significantly. “This is because oil product markets are expected to remain tight through mid-2027, even if current war-related disruptions ease. The reason for this being [that] global supply is constrained by an unusually large upswing in refinery maintenance,” he said. Even when Middle East diesel exports rise again, the price effect will lag the headline, agreed Mr Aslam. “The constraint is not only production – it is secure shipping, insurance, tanker availability and the ability to move refined products reliably into Europe,” he said. “The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are showing why dependable Gulf suppliers matter: sustained cargoes, rather than one-off emergency shipments, are what would truly pull diesel prices down.” What next? Europe could diversify imports to reduce reliance on a single source, with potential deals with the US or Asian suppliers helping to ease the current crunch, according to Mr Valecha. “Fuel tax cuts and price subsidies may also offer immediate relief, but they are costly and risk sustaining demand when supplies are tight,” he said. While there have been suggestions that consumers curb demand by shifting to electric vehicles or car pooling, Europe cannot solve a diesel shortage by simply asking consumers to drive less, said Mr Aslam. “Diesel is the bloodstream of its freight, construction, farming and industry. France and its neighbours need a three-part response: co-ordinated reserve releases, guaranteed supply contracts with reliable producers, and a faster shift of freight toward rail and electrified alternatives,” he said. “The mistake would be treating this as a temporary oil price spike. It is a refining and logistics security problem.”

events.title: US stocks nudge higher as SpaceX, Tesla and Nvidia climb
events.summary: The U.S. stock market is drifting higher following strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies NEW YORK -- The U.S. stock market is ticking higher Wednesday as strong profit reports from SpaceX , Capital One Financial and other big companies help offset updates from Netflix and AT & T that investors found disappointing. The S & P 500 rose 0.2% and is on track for a third straight modest gain . The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 47 points, or 0.1%, as of 10 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.7% higher. SpaceX helped lead the way and climbed 11.2% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company. Tesla, which will report its latest quarterly results late Wednesday, climbed 3.8% and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S & P 500. Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 4%, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 6.5%. Expectations are high for profit growth during the summer, and companies will need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made toward records despite worries about high inflation , higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than analysts expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among U.S. shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings. It helped offset a drop for Netflix, which fell 2.7% even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations. AT & T fell 4.4% even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations. Among AI stocks, which have been at the center of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled. After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centers may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money. An Austrian and a Swiss woman freed in Niger after a year and half in captivity NFL suspends 2nd Bills player for spitting, though Sam Franklin denies allegation and plans appeal EU unveils a new Arctic push as global warming and security threats reshape the region CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. On Tuesday, it careened between a loss of 6% and a gain of 5%, for example. On Wednesday, it fell 1.4% after erasing an early gain of nearly 4%. Other AI-linked stocks were more solid, though. Nvidia's gain of 1.8% was the strongest force lifting the S & P 500. Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 12%. Another potential boost for the AI industry came from an easing of Treasury yields in the bond market, which helps dictate how expensive loans are for the U.S. government, companies and regular Americans . The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.09% from 5.12% late Tuesday, though it remains far above its 3.97% level from before the war with Iran sent oil prices and worries about inflation higher. Oil prices remained unsteady on Wednesday following big swings this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry can return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude slipped 0.6% to $108.14 after crossing above $111 earlier in the morning. It’s been yo-yoing between $97 and $112 in October. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3% for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength.
