events.title: Telehealth Giant Hims Wants to Test Every Dude for Low Testosterone
events.summary: Talk of testosterone deficiency is hard to escape these days, with podcasters and politicians obsessing over how to avoid a “low T” lifestyle. As the hormone’s cultural salience deepens, demand is growing. In a timely move, telehealth giant Hims just launched a testosterone replacement therapy service for cisgender men. The direct-to-consumer juggernaut will offer two types of injectable treatments, as well as an oral pill option that can be sent to patients after they take an at-home capillary blood test. Peter Stahl, a urologist and a senior vice president of men’s health at Hims, wants to “cast as wide a net, and get as many people tested, as possible.” Hims, which started out selling erectile dysfunction medications, has expanded into women’s health and grown from a startup to a publicly traded company serving 2.9 million customers since it launched in 2017. Offering testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, is both a new phase for the health platform and a doubling down on men’s health care. “When we first started, we didn't have the capabilities to take care of a complex condition like testosterone deficiency,” Stahl says. “We've finally grown up.” The company will compete with a wide array of online clinics offering testosterone therapy, many of which have cropped up in the past few years using turnkey telehealth services to launch quickly. Many of these services market the medication as a lifestyle enhancer or anti-aging solution. Stahl sees testosterone deficiency as a medical condition that’s “really underdiagnosed” and “really misunderstood.” Testosterone became a controlled substance following the 1990 Anabolic Steroids Control Act, and for decades, taking it has carried an association with muscle-obsessed gym rats. “That created a lot of stigma,” he says. Older research also showed that testosterone therapy came with cardiovascular risks, though more recent findings suggest those concerns were overestimated. Testosterone levels have become a MAGA fixation. This fall, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth announced a mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for most male troops in the US armed services. Texas Republicans have been hurling the phrase “low T” as a masculinity-questioning insult in a hotly contested Senate midterm race between Ken Paxton and James Talarico. A survey of 2,000 American men this summer commissioned by Hims indicates that they are increasingly willing to talk to one another about testosterone treatment, but the stigma persists around taking medication to address low levels. Because testosterone is a controlled substance, it can’t be dispensed like many other treatments popular with digital clinics. Unlike GLP-1s and estrogen-based hormone replacement therapy , which are now often prescribed by clinicians after patients simply fill out a quick questionnaire , TRT requires "synchronous" care. That means any would-be users have to have a video chat with a clinician before getting a prescription, and for ongoing monitoring. “It's important to remember that testosterone therapy can cause infertility, and you don't give it to someone trying to conceive,” says urologist Mohit Khera, the director of Baylor College of Medicine’s Laboratory for Andrology Research at McNair Medical Institute. Khera sees telehealth TRT services as promising ways to expand access to the medication, “as long as it’s monitored appropriately.” While laboratory testing can show whether testosterone levels are below thresholds set by groups like the American Urological Association to indicate potential issues, diagnoses aren’t made based on bloodwork alone. Instead, clinicians assess labs along with patients’ symptoms and medical history. Common symptoms of hypogonadism (the technical term for the diagnosis) include sexual dysfunction and muscle loss. Stahl calls it a “powerful biomarker” for understanding someone’s health. “Quite frankly, it’s underutilized,” he says, noting that men with low testosterone have a 35 percent increased risk in overall mortality. The test doesn’t require a standard blood draw. Instead, Hims will send patients a Tasso blood collection device, a round single-use wearable that sticks to the upper arm and punctures the skin with microneedles to collect a small sample. (It may sound suspiciously like Theranos , but Tasso devices have a solid track record .) From there, the patient sends the collection off to a lab that will conduct an analysis of a broad selection of 21 different biomarkers to assess health, including triglycerides and thyroid hormones as well as testosterone. Based on the results, a patient might be prescribed a compounded injectable testosterone, a commercially available injectable testosterone, an oral pill—or something else entirely, if their testosterone levels are not low. Stahl sees hormone testing as a way to persuade otherwise-reticent men to go see a doctor.

events.title: "I am giving you money!" Nvidia's CEO wants every country to build its own AI
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is crisscrossing Europe with a multibillion-dollar checkbook and a grand ambition: Make his company the indispensable backbone of the global AI economy. Why it matters: As fears of an AI bubble rattle Wall Street, Huang is working to spread the boom beyond the U.S. and China — courting governments, bankrolling startups and cultivating massive new markets for Nvidia's chips. The big picture: The godfather of AI is trying to single-handedly build a new market for Nvidia chips, betting that governments and institutions around the world will want their own, highly customized data centers running open models. If it works, it could shore up demand for Nvidia chips just as another big group of customers — neoclouds — appear financially shaky. Driving the news: Part showman, part salesman, Huang has spent the past week preaching the gospel of AI across Europe ahead of a keynote Wednesday at Nvidia's flagship conference in Berlin. In France, Huang announced investments in four startups and joked, whisky glass in hand , that he's "the biggest VC in Europe." President Emmanuel Macron welcomed him to Paris, while France's economy minister compared the AI revolution to the Gold Rush. In Britain, Huang channeled Oprah Winfrey while announcing stakes in five startups. "I am giving you money! And I am giving you money! And I am giving you money!" he shouted from the stage of a converted London church. In Sweden, Huang unveiled a supercomputer backed by the country's industrial elite, likening Nvidia's technology to a "time machine" capable of compressing years of scientific research into days. In Germany, Huang challenged Chancellor Friedrich Merz to loosen Europe's regulatory instincts. "There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," he warned Monday. "Give Germany a chance. Give this industry a chance." Zoom in: At the heart of Huang's global strategy is "sovereign AI" — the idea that every nation should build and control its own AI infrastructure, data and models, rather than depend on U.S. or Chinese tech giants. In addition to roughly $10 billion in investments in Europe, Nvidia is helping build national AI ecosystems across Saudi Arabia, South Korea, India, Malaysia and Africa. For Huang, the prize is a vast new class of customers, including entire countries that see AI infrastructure as an economic and national security imperative. Between the lines: Huang's global offensive comes at a precarious moment for the AI industry, with Wall Street increasingly questioning whether the technology's enormous promise can justify its astronomical costs. Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave and other "neocloud" providers have plunged, fueling fears that the companies borrowing billions to buy Nvidia's chips may struggle to pay their debts. Investors are also scrutinizing a circular flow of money in which Nvidia helps finance the very companies buying its products, raising questions about how much demand is self-sustaining. What to watch: Huang has emerged as the AI industry's chief cheerleader during periods of market turmoil, countering predictions of a bubble with assurances that demand is still accelerating. His Berlin keynote offered another chance to calm investors by arguing that the next wave of AI spending will come from governments treating the technology as a national necessity, not a speculative bet. Nvidia announced a number of initiatives oriented around the "AI factories" theme at the Berlin event, including a design for modular computing pods that can be quickly deployeds, and a "full-stack" option to offer "sovereign" AI solutions by combining the company's chips and a new family of open-weight models. The bottom line: Countries racing to secure their independence in the AI age may find themselves more reliant than ever on one American company. events.title: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
events.summary: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another editor from the project has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

events.title: Offering cash for votes is quite common – but here’s why it doesn’t work
events.summary: President Donald Trump's offer to pay out $5,000 checks if Republicans win belongs to a long political tradition of cash for votes. AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein Politics is about the distribution of power and money. So it comes as little surprise that many politicians campaign on the material benefits that citizens can expect if those candidates win. President Donald Trump has been no different in this respect. He has promised voters, among other things, a “ DOGE dividend ” using money saved by cutting federal jobs, rebates from tariff revenues , and a diversion of money currently used to subsidize health insurance companies directly to Americans. But his pledge to give US$5,000 to every U.S. citizen if Republicans retain majorities in the House and Senate in the November 2026 midterm elections had a different dimension. This offer wasn’t a rebate for taxes paid or a subsidy for an impacted constituency. Instead, it was tied to an electoral outcome. That brings it closer to vote buying, which raises concerns from a legal point of view . For this to actually happen, it needs congressional approval – and Republican legislators haven’t taken action. But Trump has yet to rescind the idea, which could cost over $1 trillion. So it’s time to ask whether it could make a difference in the midterms, where margins are tight in key races . I’m a political scientist who has studied for the past decade vote buying in countries around the world. Cash for votes may seem like a straightforward way to win support, but my research shows that offering people money rarely changes their vote. Why vote buying rarely works The practice dates back to ancient Rome and was a staple of American political machines from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in New York City, Chicago and states including Georgia, Missouri, New Jersey, Ohio and Virginia. By diverting public money for partisan purposes, local power brokers cultivated relationships with particular constituencies, such as newly arrived immigrants . Institutional reforms, including the professionalization of government bureaucracies at the federal and local levels, slowly constricted these political machines until the last holdout in Chicago succumbed by the late 1970s. But in recent decades, vote buying has surged in new democracies, with politicians in at least 73 countries offering cash, food, clothes, building supplies, medical care or legal advice for votes. If vote buying is so common, it stands to reason that it must work. But a survey of recent research shows otherwise. On average, I have found that the vote-buying attempts across 10 countries and 57 elections around the world have had no detectable influence. Why are the electoral returns so poor? For vote buying to work, the value of the benefits people receive has to outweigh the factors pushing them toward an opposing party. As in the U.S., voters around the world make their choices based on considerations such as their own partisanship; issue preferences; the performance of the incumbent party; the perceived competence of the candidates; and more. Very few voters in any electorate are truly indifferent . As long as those factors together outweigh the value of the benefits that people would receive to switch, vote buying fails. And that’s what typically happens, as I explain in my new book, “ Against the Machine .” The importance of competition There are three specific reasons why vote buying usually flops. First, local competition creates vigorous campaigns that amp up partisan sentiments. These sentiments influence voters’ responses to electoral gifts. If you already like the political machine, you interpret its gifts as a sign that it cares about your welfare. But if you strongly identify with an opposing party – and therefore are a potential target of vote-buying efforts – you interpret gifts as an attempt to manipulate your vote and deprive you of basic political rights. This calculation is one reason why vote-buying attempts can backfire, as a vivid example from Mexico shows. In 2018, two vote brokers working for Mexico’s conservative National Action Party were accosted by local voters in Nuevo Laredo. Angry residents stripped the brokers down to their underwear and painted them with the party’s blue color from head to toe, decorating them with the words “ Vote for the PAN for 500 pesos .” In Mexico’s 2018 election, the PAN party, whose flags are pictured here, ran into opposition in Nuevo Laredo due to its vote-buying attempts. AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell The second reason vote buying often fails is that competitive elections make it difficult for party machines to identify the best voters to target. Strong opposition identifiers react negatively, but weakly opposed voters might trade their vote for a payday. The trouble is that even if local vote brokers can pinpoint these voters before the election, they’re also among the most susceptible to the influence of standard campaigning. That makes them moving targets : Their changing preferences mean that machines end up inadvertently paying voters who either don’t need gifts to vote for them or would need more to actually change their decision. Finally, even when voters who are good targets get these benefits, they often look for an escape hatch to vote their sincere preferences anyway. The secret ballot provides one if they trust that it’s truly secret. It turns out that people are acutely aware of who’s watching them vote. When they see poll watchers only from the party machine, they worry that their votes could be discovered by spies, cameras or by other means. But when they also see poll watchers from an opposing party, they believe that ballot secrecy is preserved and that they can vote sincerely without punishment. Taken together, these reasons have led me to optimistically conclude that the effectiveness of vote buying depends not on the party machine’s prowess but on the strength of the parties that oppose it. Bringing it home Vote buying has a checkered recent history in elections around the world, but could the “Trump dividend” swing the midterms? I see that scenario as unlikely. Partisanship, a core element that makes people resistant to vote buying, is very strong in the U.S. electorate . There’s no need to pay committed Republicans, while committed Democrats will see the offer as a bald monetization of politics that can deepen their antagonism. The design of Trump’s offer also makes it likely to flounder. Promising to pay everyone gets around the targeting challenge, but it also creates what social scientists call a “free-rider problem.” At issue is that people tend to behave in selfish ways. If they expect a certain outcome anyway, they’ll make a decision based on self-interest. For example, independents and less committed Democrats who could be swayed by a $5,000 check might think they can avoid feeling like a sellout if they vote sincerely but they will still get paid as long as others switch their vot

events.title: The permitting bill enters a critical stretch
events.summary: Data: Columbia University Center on Global Energy Policy; Table: Ben Geman/Axios The push to pass a sweeping permitting bill is gaining powerful allies and encountering fresh resistance as Congress prepares for a post-midterms showdown. Why it matters: It's the most important energy bill in a long time. Cutting hurdles for projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors. But some environmentalists say it badly weakens crucial protections in the name of speeding reviews. Driving the news: A new, interactive analysis out on Wednesday projects potentially huge time savings if the bill becomes law. Transmission projects could see the biggest acceleration, per Jack Andreasen Cavanaugh, a researcher with Columbia's energy think tank. He based it on historical data about a large number of specific projects, then estimated how much quicker they would have proceeded under the bill. Columbia's Center on Global Energy Policy doesn't have an institutional position on the bill. But founding director Jason Bordoff, a prominent voice in energy policy circles, is urging environmentalists not to oppose it. State of play: A who's who of economic and national security officials spanning six presidents (including Trump) are linking arms behind the bill in a new letter to Capitol Hill leaders. What's next: The effort goes beyond signatures for some of the former officials, according to letter organizer Arnab Datta of the Institute for Progress, a nonpartisan think tank. "Some folks are engaging beyond the letter itself with stakeholders across the board, and some have made themselves available for members briefings or conversations," he tells me via email. Catch up quick: The letter from 19 officials includes Biden-era Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen and Trump 1.0 Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, among five people who held the job. The list also features Trump 1.0 Secretary of State and CIA boss Mike Pompeo, and Leon Panetta, who had top Obama-era defense and CIA gigs, to name just two others. Friction point: The last 24 hours has also brought new signs of simmering opposition to the bill, or at least parts of it, adding to existing concerns among tribal leaders and some green groups. Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) posted on X that it would be "tone deaf if Congress makes it easier to build data centers." That drew pushback from backers who emphasized provisions to ensure data center companies cover grid costs. What we're watching: The Edison Electric Institute, a powerful group of for-profit utilities, still hasn't weighed in. But David Pomerantz, who's with the progressive Energy & Policy Institute obtained an Oklahoma Gas & Electric document criticizing the transmission provisions. The bottom line: The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bipartisan permitting bill immediately after lawmakers return from recess. events.summary: Ghana plans to ban exports of raw mineral ores by 2030 to boost domestic processing, its president said, reinforcing a broader push by Africa’s resource-rich countries to capture more value from their minerals. “Investors must understand the processing obligations associated with access to our resources,” President John Dramani Mahama said at a mining conference in Accra. The country is Africa’s largest gold producer and also mines manganese, bauxite, and diamonds. The global race for minerals used in clean energy and advanced technologies has intensified competition between China, the US, and Europe for African supplies. Ghana’s proposed restrictions would put it alongside countries such as DR Congo, which restricts exports of copper and cobalt concentrates. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: JPMorgan closes in on Nigeria merchant banking license
events.summary: JPMorgan is on track to secure a merchant banking license in Nigeria after making a $38 million statutory deposit to the country’s central bank, Bloomberg reported. If successful, the New York-based lender, which has been bullish about Nigeria’s prospects , would add considerable heft to the investment banking sector as the country seeks to attract more foreign capital. The move to acquire a Nigeria license is part of the bank’s Africa expansion, including the appointment of an investment banking lead for sub-Saharan Africa this year, and opening offices in Nairobi and Abidjan. It comes as Nigeria’s securities regulator this week unveiled a 10-year plan to grow the country’s capital markets, including a target to raise annual diaspora investment to $10 billion, from $4 billion. It also comes on the heels of the Dangote refinery’s IPO that is aiming to raise at least $1.6 billion by the time it closes. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Africa doesn’t have to 'pick sides' between US and China
events.summary: Washington may want countries in the developing world to pick sides between the US and China, but they are doing everything they can to avoid falling into permanent camps, the head of the UK’s development finance body told Semafor. “Geopolitics is complicating the world of development finance,” Leslie Maasdorp said during a Semafor World Economy Global Leaders Dinner in Bangkok. He added that even as Western-led development finance bodies, such as his British International Investment, implicitly espoused a differing set of values from China’s, prioritizing clean power made it impossible to remove Chinese firms from supply chains given their dominance of the sector. His remarks stand in contrast to those from the head of the US Development Finance Corporation, who told Semafor last month that Washington was, at least in the tech arena, looking to expand infrastructure aligned with the US. “ Not building on US-friendly rails would be madness ,” he said. — Prashant Rao

events.title: Today in the UK, I saw how the Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust is using Copilot to cut down on administrative work and make better use of its data, and ultimately provide a better experience for medical personnel and patients. [Read more]
events.summary: Today in the UK, I saw how the Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust is using Copilot to cut down on administrative work and make better use of its data, and ultimately provide a better experience for medical personnel and patients. It's an early example of what's possible as NHS England expands Copilot to as many as 500,000 clinicians and support staff across the country. Read more: https://lnkd.in/gj8h5e4Z The time a crew spends on paperwork is time taken off patients, so cutting admin quietly adds capacity without hiring anyone. What stands out in the Yorkshire example is how much patient-facing care depends on work done well before an ambulance arrives. It would be interesting to see whether Copilot reduces the need to re-enter or reconcile information across handoffs, not just the minutes spent drafting. That’s where an administrative gain could become a measurable operational one. At our recent GrandResolve roundtable, participants said sharing specific success stories is what makes AI adoption believable, and this article delivers. I especially liked the datapoint on Tom Smith , a dyslexic operations manager at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, who uses Copilot to structure drafts and summarize reports, which helps "level the playing field." Congratulations to the Yorkshire Ambulance Service team. This is what leadership in AI looks like. Others in this thread ask where the saved time goes. Your team answers it with a metric, not a minute count. Per Microsoft’s write-up, the trust uses Copilot to organize its data on conveyance to emergency departments, targets 50%, and reports a move from 60% to 56%. That is the standard for every leader rolling out AI: name the operational number it must move before you scale. Copilot stays on administrative work, humans review the output, and accountability stays where it belongs. Well done, and thank you, Satya, for sharing it. 🔎 I don’t want to be pessimistic, and I’m not generally a pessimistic person. If the goal is simply to reduce administrative work and give healthcare professionals more time and attention for their patients, that’s great. But the pessimistic side of me wonders: will AI only assist healthcare professionals and free up their time, or will it also be trained to do their jobs and eventually replace them? Again, I really didn’t want to say this, but I think it’s a fair question. #RACinform view: Rollout optics ≠ runtime reality. Current signals are pilot‑stage and curated; not enough operational data exists to demonstrate sustained impact across NHS workflows. A more honest framing for frontier deployments is a closing caveat: “Early days — we are monitoring real‑world effects.” This preserves integrity, avoids premature claims, and keeps the focus on runtime evidence rather than executive narratives. It would be interesting to know the KPI improvements related to staff/patient experience before vs. after copilot adoption The figure that stood out for me is not the 43 minutes a day. It is Yorkshire's conveyance to ED moving from 60% to 56%. That is an outcome metric, not a productivity one, and it is the kind of evidence that justifies scale. From the architecture side, going from 30,000 to 505,000 users is where the real work starts. Two things I would put in the blueprint early: 1. Enforce the admin-only boundary in the design, not only in policy. Once Copilot summarises operational reports, the line between administrative and clinical drifts quickly. Sensitivity labels, DLP and scoped data sources should hold that line, reviewed against the clinical safety case. 2. Fix the data plumbing before the prompts. Copilot can only "join the dots" Samantha Robinson describes if the underlying data is integrated and correctly permissioned. At half a million users, oversharing in SharePoint and Teams becomes the main risk surface. Trust at this scale is an engineering property as much as a cultural one. Curious how NHS England will track outcomes like conveyance alongside time saved as the rollout grows. Satya Nadella great to see Microsoft and the NHS England advancing AI adoption in healthcare. While this is a great start LLMs alone are challenged to solve systems-level healthcare problems. Consider EMS as an example. Ambulance dispatch, patient acuity, and anticipated arrivals are early signals in a much larger operational digital twin. Those signals should inform downstream decisions around ED capacity, patient arrival, admission, physician initial assessment (PIA), bed availability, and ultimately emergency department length of stay (EDLOS). Optimizing one workflow does not necessarily optimize the system. Reducing administrative burden is valuable, but the transformational opportunity lies in connecting data, predicting downstream bottlenecks, and orchestrating decisions across the entire patient journey. I see the same challenge across healthcare supply chains, where fragmented systems and disconnected decisions directly affect clinical capacity, operational efficiency, and patient throughput. The next frontier of healthcare AI isn’t simply making individual tasks faster. It’s making the entire health system work smarter, as one integrated ecosystem. My annual letter: Building the frontier ecosystem Satya Nadella 1d The Infinite SaaS Factory Satya Nadella 2w How do we build a frontier intelligence ecosystem? events.title: UK inflation rise to highest in almost a year as Iran war drives fuel prices higher
events.summary: Inflation in the U.K. has risen to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to drive up fuel prices LONDON -- Inflation in the U.K. rose to its highest rate in almost a year as the Iran war continues to ratchet up fuel prices, official figures showed Wednesday, cementing market expectations that the Bank of England will raise interest rates next month. The Office for National Statistics said consumer prices rose by 3.5% in the year to September, up from 3.1% in August. That's the highest reading since October last year, and above the 3.4% that most economists had been expecting for the month. The increase takes inflation further above the Bank of England's target rate of 2%. Prices across the transport industry were the biggest contributor to higher inflation last month, particularly at the pump. Overall, motor fuels soared by 30% in the year to September, up from a 23% annual rise in August. Fuel costs have been soaring because of the Iran war and the ensuing bottlenecks in the Strait of Hormuz , which have squeezed global oil and gas supplies. Treasury chief John Healey said his budget statement next week will aim to give businesses and families “some breathing space” from the upward march in the cost of living. Retired detective charged in possible road rage killing on George Washington Bridge Students and teachers march through Greek capital to protest cost of living UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change Whatever measures he comes up with to keep a lid on rising prices, economists expect the Bank of England to increase interest rates at its next meeting on Nov. 5. Last month, rate-setters held the bank's main rate at 3.75% but gave a big hint that they were ready to hike soon. “With inflation increasing, the pieces are falling firmly into place for a November rate rise," said Suren Thiru, chief economist at ICAEW. Most economists expect an increase in the bank's main rate to 4%. Other central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank , have raised rates recently. Interest rates in the U.K. had been trending downward from a 15-year high of 5.25% until the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. events.title: Apple iPhone Duo hands-on: Your productivity will hinge on this
events.summary: Apple , this had better be good; you made us wait more than seven years for this to unfold. At long last, the company has introduced the iPhone Duo , its first entry into the foldable device category, and first major hardware release under new boss John Ternus. And, on a personal note, I've never seen my peers this hyped for a device. The National gave the device a spin and ran through its features. Here are our initial thoughts. The lowdown The passport-sized iPhone Duo, when folded, gives you a 13.7cm (5.4-inch) display. Open it up and that digital real estate stretches to 19.3cm (7.6 inches). And it's now Apple's thinnest smartphone, at only 5.2mm when open. The power and camera control buttons remain in their usual slots on the right while it's closed or open in landscape mode. But from here, things get shaken up quite a bit. The volume buttons are now on top, and switching to portrait mode while unfolded brings them to the left for more familiar control. Meanwhile, the USB-C charging port, while still at the bottom when folded, switches to the left side when unfolded, which is a little odd as we're used to that on the right. But there are two notable omissions: there is no Action Button, which is customisable and (probably) most commonly used as the silent toggle No Face ID Face ID – repeat, no Face ID. Instead, a Touch ID, nestled on the power button, makes its return. Skipping the Action Button and Face ID will need some getting used to, particularly the latter, but Apple says key stuff like transactions and verifying your identity will still be seamless – you'll just need your fingers instead of your eyes. Also, battery percentage and carrier details won't be readily visible on the homescreens. Instead, you have to swipe down from the top-right, like the iPhone X. The latest, smaller version of Dynamic Island is also present, but now it now appears on the top right. As for the crease, it is virtually invisible. Apple hasn't released a figure for fold-unfold durability, though the Duo has ceramic shield protection for scratchproofing and is rated IP68 for dust and waterproofing. There are four cameras – the main 48MP Dual Fusion system, the 12MP Centre Stage camera on the cover and the under-display camera on the inner display. You can choose from two colours, night sky and star white, with the former our winner. (It would've been better if there was a defining option like lavender or our all-time favourite, cosmic orange.) By now we know that the Duo's prices in the UAE range from Dh8,499 to Dh13,599, and there are extended shipping times due to overwhelming demand. First steps The iPhone Duo has a clean feel: opening and closing feels reliable, and the sturdy hinge ensures it will stay in place without any wobble or movement. Multitasking is a key feature that allows you to do more with fewer swipes and taps. For example, you can have your email on one side and photos on the other, and you can just drag an image as an attachment. Let the Duo sit L-shaped and you'll be able to do some easy stuff. If you're in the camera app or a streaming service like Netflix, controls will be on screen below for easier navigation. The camera also has a new feature that automatically takes pictures without having to control it; trigger the function, let the main cameras face you and it will track subjects and take pictures from time to time, which you will know when the torch briefly lights up. It also acts as a good teleprompter, which creators and on-camera people will find useful. Apple says apps have been and are being optimised to work with the Duo, and a sign that an app has been updated is when you see controls on the right side. It's also optimised for popular apps such as WhatsApp, Instagram and Slack, to make work, play and creation easier. While we don't have the full list, updates for popular apps are expected to be rolled out on Friday, when the device finally becomes available in stores. While we haven't fully tested it, Apple guarantees battery life on a par with the iPhone 18 Pro, meaning it should, according to our own tests , make it through more than a day and a half. There are two batteries in the Duo, although according to Apple, they work as one, discharge as one and do all things together. The Duo is compatible with the USB-C version of the Apple Pencil. At this point, it is unclear if and when other models of the company's stylus will follow the same path. Initial verdict We're still not sure how much of the iPhone Duo's bigger display we'll be using, considering it has specific purposes and the front screen is big enough to perform most of our tasks. We're foreseeing we'll be using the front display for work and communication, and the bigger one for entertainment and gaming. If the overwhelming orders are any indication, Apple's iPhone Duo is poised to do well. The device feels refined, but its biggest draw may be its seamless integration into Apple's ecosystem. That's a compelling selling point for those who usually find foldables cumbersome or complicated, if they're willing to splash the cash.

events.title: Carriers reroute Riyadh flights to airport four hours' drive away
events.summary: Saudi airlines are turning to Al Qassim, about a four-hour drive from Riyadh, as an alternative to the capital while its airport remains closed following a deadly Houthi attack almost two weeks ago. The kingdom’s main flag carrier, Saudia, is offering tickets to Riyadh via Al Qassim, with a bus connection to the Saudi capital. Riyadh Air, Public Investment Fund’s startup airline, is also giving passengers booked on flights to Riyadh the option to fly to Al Qassim. Riyadh airport is now open to traffic with prior permission, but passenger flights have yet to resume and most airlines have canceled services until anywhere from next week to next year. Local airlines have moved planes parked at Riyadh airport to other locations while the airport remains a Houthi target, suggesting that travel to the capital is not expected to resume soon. — Matthew Martin

events.title: SpaceX and Tesla mega-merger under discussion
events.summary: The News Elon Musk’s companies, SpaceX and Tesla, have begun exploring a merger that would create a $3.5 trillion corporate giant spanning key sectors of cutting-edge technology. Musk argued that combining the companies would allow them to deepen cooperation on chip design, robotics, software, and other technologies ; both firms’ share prices rose following the announcement. Liz’s view The outlines of MegaMusk Inc. are starting to emerge, where special committees of SpaceX and Tesla directors will now have to bless the merger. Combining the two would bring the tech and infrastructure parts of Musk’s empire together (the Wall Street pitch) and a hyperconcentrated bet on the billionaire’s inventions, politics, and personality (the actual pitch). Musk already rolled up X, xAI, and SpaceX, whose June IPO paved the way for the Tesla deal. Many of Musk’s projects already bleed into each other — the new Roadster has SpaceX thrusters — and Musk’s employees often work interchangeably across his companies, so there’s some business and governance sense in formalizing what’s already happening. But it’s clear Musk is again using Tesla’s shareholders — and its massive retail investor base — to fund his other exploits, just as he did in 2016 when Tesla bailed out his cash-strapped solar company, SolarCity, and, more recently, when he reallocated Tesla talent and GPUs to xAI. While Musk says he’ll recuse himself from the decision, his companies’ boards don’t have a history of pushing back. Tesla Chair Robyn Denholm told Semafor last year she was skeptical of Tesla investing in xAI; four months later, it invested $2 billion . And a combo would further strengthen Musk’s control over Tesla: Super-voting shares give him roughly 84% of the vote at SpaceX, compared to 20% at Tesla, where every share has equal voting weight. Notable The SpaceX-Tesla tie-up has its own strong logic, one early SpaceX investor told Bloomberg: “Combined, it would be the only company owning the full physical-AI stack … No competitor has an analog .”

events.title: Mecca draws Indonesian sovereign wealth fund investment
events.summary: Opening up real estate ownership in Mecca and Medina to foreign investors could help deliver a boost to investment into Saudi Arabia, after Indonesia’s sovereign fund Danantara completed a 2 billion riyal ($533 million) deal to purchase a hotel and development plots. That agreement is the first time a foreign state has acquired property in Mecca, one of the holiest sites in Islam, and opens the door for further sales to Muslim-majority states, Faisal Shaker, chief executive of Thakher Development, owner of the development sold to Danantara, told Semafor. The company is the master developer behind Thakher Mecca , less than a mile from the Grand Mosque in the city. Sales of another Mecca development called Mathabah will also be launched next year, Shaker said. As part of its plan for sales to foreign investors next year “transactions we aspire to close will not be less than the deal we just announced,” Shaker said. “We are in discussion with multiple stakeholders and different parties from different parts of the world.” Investment into the two cities is “driven by faith and not by cycles,” Shaker said. Saudi Arabia opened Mecca and Medina real estate to Muslims abroad and selected foreign institutions in January. Saudis are still the majority buyers, but Gulf investors are also pouring money into the two cities, Shaker said. Danantara is also considering investing in Medina , Asharq Bloomberg reported. A key part of Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s strategy to grow non-oil income is more than doubling religious visitors to the kingdom to 50 million by 2030 from about 20 million last year.

events.title: Hungarian police arrest Orbán-era central bank governor on suspicion of fraud and abuse
events.summary: Hungarian police have taken former Central Bank governor György Matolcsy into custody BUDAPEST, Hungary -- Hungarian police arrested the country's former Central Bank governor on Wednesday, a significant step in the new government’s pursuit of suspected financial abuses during the rein of Viktor Orbán , whose government has been accused of widespread corruption. Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote in a post on Facebook that the former governor, György Matolcsy, who had also served as finance minister, was in custody, without providing further details. Since taking office earlier this year, Magyar’s government has prioritized investigating suspected financial abuses committed by Orbán-era officials. The arrest followed a statement from Hungary's Central Prosecutor's Office earlier in the day, saying it was “carrying out coordinated investigative actions" in several locations in connection with a Central Bank-related investigation into criminal misappropriation of funds. It did not mention Matolcsy by name but said more details about the case would come later. Matolcsy led Hungary’s central bank from 2013 to 2025, after serving as Orbán’s minister of economy from 2010 to 2013. He was long one of Orbán’s closest economic allies, and has denied any wrongdoing. Matolcsy's lawyer, Pál Bátki, told Hungarian news outlet Telex that the former governor was detained on suspicion of economic fraud that caused significant financial damage and using a forged private document. A criminal complaint was filed last month on suspicion of embezzlement, negligence, fraud, and abuse of office while Matolcsy was governor. The complaint came after the central bank audited past real estate investments that it found to have been purchased for inflated prices, causing significant financial damage to the bank. It was unclear whether Matolcsy's detention was related to the real estate purchases or the endowments to the bank's foundations. In an exclusive interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday, Magyar said it was clear that “certain members of the previous government as well as oligarchs, businessmen and family members connected to them committed serious crimes, typically corruption crimes, both with national funding and EU funding.” His administration in July launched the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, which holds investigative and prosecutorial powers to pursue cases of misused public funds. events.title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Introducing: the Impossible issue We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue . We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood , build cities on the moon , and attain cognitive immortality . We investigate AI’s ability to say no , a bionic eye that can restore sight , and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years . This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride. Subscribe now to read the full print issue . Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month. The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation. Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration . —Tereza Pultarova How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time. The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead. events.title: Microsoft empowers more than 330,000 Volkswagen Group employees with Copilot
events.summary: October 21, 2026 Category: Company News Microsoft empowers more than 330,000 Volkswagen Group employees with Copilot Microsoft Copilot brings secure, AI-powered assistance into employees’ daily workflows and business processes Microsoft Source | 3 minutes Editor’s note — Oct. 21, 2026 — This press release was updated to reflect that the Microsoft AI Tour has been renamed the Microsoft Frontier Tour. REDMOND, Wash. — Oct. 21, 2026 — Microsoft Corp. on Wednesday announced that Volkswagen Group has now equipped more than 330,000 employees across the company with Microsoft Copilot, helping its workforce increase productivity, accelerate decisions and improve knowledge-based processes across the organization. “The real value of AI comes from making it available at scale in everyday work,” said Sophie Vassarotti, Head of Group Data and AI, Volkswagen Group. “With Copilot, we are bringing secure and trusted AI support to our employees, helping them work more efficiently and make better-informed decisions.” Volkswagen Group’s broad-scale deployment of Copilot is the latest step in the Group’s deliberate, phased approach to AI adoption. The organization’s phased rollout began with providing employees with broad access to AI-powered chat via Copilot Chat, for which Volkswagen saw upwards of 300,000 monthly active users on the platform. Today, employees are leveraging Copilot with Work IQ for more advanced productivity scenarios, embedding AI even more deeply into the most business processes — spanning from engineering to production, procurement and sales. In addition, more than 26,000 agents have been active across the Group over the past month alone, scaling AI-driven productivity gains. “By bringing Microsoft Copilot to more than 330,000 employees, Volkswagen Group is putting AI directly into the flow of work — helping people boost productivity, accelerate decisions and focus on higher-value tasks,” said Agnes Heftberger, Chair of the Management Board of Microsoft Germany. “Volkswagen shows how companies can evolve AI from a personal productivity tool into a foundation for future AI innovation.” In addition, Microsoft and Volkswagen Group intend to expand their collaboration and further scale the Intelligent Data Foundation, the Group’s unified data ecosystem, on Microsoft Fabric, to make trusted data easier to find, understand and use across the entire company. Note to editors The collaboration will be featured at the Microsoft Frontier Tour in Cologne, Germany, on Oct. 22, 2026. Sophie Vassarotti (Head of Group Data and AI, Volkswagen Group) and Rupert Stuetzle (GM, Manufacturing and Mobility, EMEA, Microsoft) will present “How Volkswagen Group is building group intelligence in the Age of AI” at 9:00 a.m. CEST (Lab 3 | Hall 1). Microsoft (Nasdaq “MSFT” @microsoft) creates platforms and tools powered by AI to deliver innovative solutions that meet the evolving needs of our customers. The technology company is committed to making AI available broadly and doing so responsibly, with a mission to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more. events.title: AI is getting better at hacking power and water systems, new research shows
events.summary: The world's most advanced AI models are suddenly capable of blueprinting cyberattacks on critical services like power grids and water systems with alarming success rates, according to new research . Why it matters: Critical infrastructure operators are running out of time. Top-tier frontier models are dangerously adept at mapping out attacks, new research from cybersecurity company Frenos shows, and it's only a matter of time before freely available AI models make such hacks easier to execute. "It's a clock that is moving faster than we've ever seen," Steve Swick, former top security executive at American Electric Power, told reporters during a briefing. Driving the news: Researchers at Frenos tested 10 AI models on their ability to plan attacks against industrial systems, such as the software that monitors water treatment processes. Three out of 10 models tested successfully constructed attack plans in roughly 90% of attempts. Performance varied widely: Three models the researchers considered to be at the frontier of capabilities succeeded in just 17.9% to 31.9% of attempts. The strongest foreign open-weight model succeeded 36.2% of the time, while the strongest U.S. open-weight model succeeded just 5.2%. Frenos did not disclose the names of the models tested. Zoom in: The research included nearly 17,000 tests, including 2,520 attempts to construct complete attack plans. The models received information about potential targets and were tasked with piecing together the steps needed to achieve specific objectives. The big picture: Critical services like water systems and manufacturing plants have long been targets for nation-state adversaries and cybercriminals. Many operators face staffing and budget constraints. Testing and upgrading their systems can also risk disruptions to essential services that they can't afford. Unlike traditional corporate networks, industrial systems can be sensitive to unexpected traffic and commands. Even an unsuccessful attack attempt could disrupt essential operations. Threat level: Once attackers gain access to an industrial network, AI could help them quietly map out systems and identify weaknesses without the same time constraints facing human hackers, Frenos co-founder and CTO Harry Thomas said. "AI doesn't have the problem with patience," Thomas said. "It doesn't need to eat. It doesn't need to sleep, and it doesn't need to use the restroom." Paul Shaver, head of operational technology at cybersecurity firm Armadin, added that AI agents can already conduct reconnaissance and analyze large volumes of data without necessarily triggering security alerts. The intrigue: Thomas said the researchers used a relatively simple setup to guide the models through their tasks. More sophisticated tools that provide additional context and feedback could improve their performance. "A more capable harness could have given these AI models more of an edge," he said. What to watch: Several initiatives — including from the White House , frontier AI companies , and cybersecurity organizations — have cropped up in recent weeks to help lower the costs and provide resources for critical infrastructure organizations. events.title: OpenAI brings its frontier models to rival Google Cloud
events.summary: OpenAI is bringing its AI models and Codex coding tools to Google Cloud , expanding its reach to customers of all three major U.S. cloud providers — including companies that are also among its fiercest AI rivals. Why it matters: The move underscores a growing recognition that winning the enterprise AI race isn't just about building the smartest models. It's also about making those models available wherever businesses already run their software and store their data. For OpenAI, the agreement offers another way to reach corporate customers without requiring them to establish a separate relationship with the ChatGPT maker. For Google, it means selling a competitor's AI models alongside its own Gemini offerings, potentially capturing business that might otherwise go to rival cloud providers. Driving the news: Under the agreement announced Wednesday, Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI's frontier models through Google's "Model Garden and Marketplace," including by using existing cloud spending commitments. The deal also brings OpenAI models to Google's Antigravity development environment and Gemini Agent. General availability is planned in the coming weeks. The big picture: The agreement follows OpenAI's expansion onto Amazon Web Services earlier this year, after changes to its Microsoft partnership opened the door to broader cloud distribution. AWS CEO Matt Garman said at the time that customers had long wanted to run OpenAI models where their existing applications and data already resided. Amazon has since expanded the OpenAI models and services available through its Bedrock platform, although neither company has publicly quantified the additional business generated by the arrangement. What they're saying: Mike Leone, VP and analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said the deal is significant for both companies, particularly because many Google Cloud customers want access to OpenAI models without moving their data. "For Google, I read the deal as confidence, because Gemini now has to win those customers with OpenAI sitting right next to it," Leone told Axios. But he doesn't see Google as necessarily hurting Gemini, since customers will still pay Google for its cloud platform, data services and security regardless of which AI models they choose. Yes, but: Distribution is only part of the equation. OpenAI still has to persuade enterprises to choose its models over those from Google, Anthropic and other competitors, many of which are available through the same cloud platforms. That could make the cloud providers' existing enterprise relationships and infrastructure as important as the models they offer. "Once every cloud has the top models, I think the competitive advantage goes to whoever does the best job with a company's data, governance, and costs," Leone said.

events.title: Aid groups told to account for $700M of Ebola funding
events.summary: The News Global aid groups, including the UN, are facing demands to inform the Congolese government of the whereabouts of more than $700 million that was donated to deal with the Ebola outbreak that has killed more than 4,600 people in the country. Last week, Jean Kaseya, who heads Africa CDC, the continental body coordinating the response to the spread of the virus, said that Kinshasa had only been told about what had happened to $220 million of the $962 million donated. In a pointed statement, Africa CDC said it “strongly deplores the lack of cooperation from organizations,” accusing them of not respecting Congolese sovereignty and threatening to withdraw their permission to work in the country if they fail to comply. Julien Harneis, the UN’s senior Ebola coordinator, told Semafor that Africa CDC itself has established a joint system with the World Health Organization (WHO) to track disbursements reported by donors. But, he said, the government’s request for recipients to report what they had received and spent was new and was taking time to implement, adding that 43 organizations had already submitted the information. WHO spokesperson Tarik Jasarevic said the UN body supported “clear and transparent processes for tracking financing … including the government establishing a mechanism to account for funds delivered by partners” — a message repeated by other UN bodies. Despite the demands for greater transparency, aid agencies say they still need more money. Jasarevic told Semafor that WHO’s $115 million budget for Ebola was 80% funded, while Fleur Vernat, UNICEF’s partnerships manager in DR Congo, said her agency’s response faced a 65% funding gap. Know More DR Congo is recording fewer daily Ebola cases and deaths than a month ago, but the outbreak is spreading to new provinces in the country, Harneis told Semafor. Nigeria has recorded a case of a woman who had travelled from Uganda, the authorities said and Kenya has now confirmed nine infections. The Ebola response has drawn funding from several countries, with the US as the largest donor. DR Congo’s health minister, Roger Kamba, had already accused aid organizations in August of withholding information about their spending. “You cannot tell people that $800 million has been given to Congo when we cannot find out how much you have spent,” he told reporters at a government briefing. “They demand traceability and compliance from us as local actors, but they do not do it themselves. It is a double standard,” De-Joseph Kakisingi, who heads a network of Congolese aid organizations, told Semafor. But he acknowledged that DR Congo lacked a law specifying what aid organizations must report to the government about the money they receive and spend. This latest Ebola outbreak is the second deadliest in history after the 2014-16 epidemic which killed more than 11,300 people, mostly in West Africa. There is no known vaccine for this species of the virus, known as Bundibugyo, but Ervebo, effective against another species, is being tested. So far 9,000 frontline workers have been vaccinated. Notable Ebola healthcare workers in DR Congo went on strike in August , citing unpaid wages since the outbreak had begun in mid-May.

events.title: Survey: Energy executives upbeat about Gulf opportunities despite war
events.summary: The News Middle East energy executives are more optimistic about their industry’s future than their peers elsewhere, a testament to their ability to keep oil flowing despite the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, according to research commissioned by the organizers of ADIPEC, the Abu Dhabi energy conference. Global demand for energy from all sources is forecast to rise over the next decade, driven by electrification and AI adoption. The International Energy Agency estimates energy investment at a record $3.4 trillion this year: $2.2 trillion in clean energy and grids, and $1.2 trillion in oil, gas, and coal. Almost two-thirds of the more than 1,800 decision-makers surveyed expect the pace of capital deployment to increase by more than a fifth over the next five years. The upbeat assessment isn’t surprising from producers who can get their product out of the Gulf amid higher prices from the US-Iran war. Most respondents said the energy system passed its biggest “stress test in 50 years” and proved more resilient than expected, thanks to quick adjustments to shocks, continued supply to customers, and the diversification of sources and routes before the conflict. But a third of executives from consuming countries in Asia — the most vulnerable to the disruptions — said the global energy system proved less resilient than expected. Know More ADIPEC, the world’s biggest energy exhibition , organized by dmg events, comes at a moment of unprecedented upheaval for a region that supplies a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas. The disruption has pushed dozens of countries to rethink their energy security priorities. While many governments may pursue domestic self-reliance to avert future shocks, those in the industry are betting on a connected system, ranking renewables, source diversification, and infrastructure protection as bigger priorities than self-sufficiency. The survey showed broad consensus on artificial intelligence, both as a driver of future demand and as a way to unlock efficiencies from the wellhead to distribution. Just 3% of respondents expect electricity demand from AI to be lower than forecast; a majority see the technology as becoming more influential than innovations in renewable energy over the next decade. AI applications in oil production have moved beyond the pilot phase: One executive said in the report that software “distributes the power on the drilling rig in the exact amount required and stores the unused energy for later use. It reduces the total power consumption of the rig by 25 to 30%.” Notable The Hormuz closure is the biggest energy security crisis the world has faced, according to IEA chief Fatih Birol, who expects it to reshape investment much as the 1970s oil shocks did . Asia is rethinking its reliance on Gulf energy. The region is shifting “from just-in-time supply chains to just-in-case supply chains,” one analyst told Fortune .

events.title: Washington won’t say what it wants on AGOA, says South Africa ambassador
events.summary: South Africa’s ambassador to the US says Washington has repeatedly rejected Pretoria’s trade offers without explaining what it wants instead. His complaint comes a day after President Cyril Ramaphosa told South Africans to brace for losing duty-free access under the African Growth and Opportunity Act. “It’s not helpful when we hear the answer is, ‘that’s not good enough,’” Roelf Meyer told Semafor. “It would have been more helpful if we could hear, ‘what is not good enough?’” The US Congress extended AGOA to 2028 last month, but the White House reviews country eligibility every year. Removing South Africa from Jan. 1 would require notice to Congress and Pretoria 60 days ahead, so a decision is expected by early November. That scenario has become a distinct possibility after nearly two years of a worsening relationship between Washington and Africa’s largest economy. Meyer, who took up the post this year after more than a year without a South African ambassador in Washington, describes relations with the Trump administration as a “stalemate.” “I’m not satisfied about where we find ourselves,” he said. The deeper rift, he suggested, is ideological. Meyer said he read the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025 early and saw a “deviation” from the Republican Party he knew in the 1980s. Asked why Pretoria’s rebuttals of white genocide claims aren’t landing, he said either Washington hasn’t heard him clearly, or there is “a fundamental ideological difference.” Meyer helped lead the apartheid government’s side opposite Ramaphosa in the talks that ended white minority rule. He says those negotiations worked because both sides were prepared to talk. “That is my experience, the difference here,” he said. “It’s hard to find a basis for real dialogue.” Yet he also signaled flexibility on the policy irritant most cited in Washington. Black EconomicEmpowerment rules in mining and telecoms “still leave room for further adjustments,” he said, adding that discussions are underway with companies looking to invest. Yinka: President Cyril Ramaphosa warned South Africans to prepare for the possibility that the country could lose its AGOA trade benefits. How confident are you that South Africa will remain eligible? Roelf Meyer: It is difficult to say because we have not had a clear response on AGOA and the eligibility question. There is a lot of speculation about the final result, and I don’t think it serves any purpose to add to that. From the South African side, we believe we have given clear enough answers. We would like an opportunity to hear where the shortcomings are in the US assessment. It is not helpful when the answer is simply, “That’s not good enough.” We need to know what is not good enough so we can address it from a negotiating perspective. I think the president is being realistic, so nobody is completely surprised if things go in the wrong direction. But he is also mindful that it would be better if we could stay in. What are the main sticking points in the negotiations? There are difficult issues on which South Africa cannot simply agree with everything the US is asking. We have local interests to consider, particularly in the poultry and pork industries. These are longstanding, technical issues involving imports and exports. Local producers react when imports affect their production or export potential, and experts from our respective departments have been negotiating with them for an extended period. But there are also political issues. The US government has raised a number of concerns about South Africa over the past 18 months, and those weigh on the discussions too. How much of your time is spent on those political disputes, as opposed to trade and investment? I think it is 50-50. The political relationship has been tense since the executive order on South Africa in February last year, which covered a number of issues and led to the five asks or demands. My responsibility is both political and commercial. It is about how we keep trade going and expand it. Do you think the tensions will ease, or have the problems become more entrenched? It is difficult to say. Some of the geopolitical issues concerning the US were already present under the previous administration, and some concerns coming from Capitol Hill are bipartisan. Part of the embassy’s job is to address misunderstandings and relay US concerns to our government. We may make assumptions in Pretoria that are wrong, too. It is my responsibility to give the president and government as clear a picture as possible. Could changes to Black Economic Empowerment policies help attract more investment, particularly in mining and telecommunications? The BEE framework has evolved from an initial focus on equity toward equity-equivalence measures. Many companies have adjusted to those measures and invested on that basis. There is still room for further adjustments, particularly in mining and telecommunications. Those sectors have a different character under the current framework, and we discuss possible changes internally and with companies that want to invest. You have been in Washington for about five months. How would you sum up the state of the relationship? South Africa had no representation in Washington for some period before I arrived, so there is a lot of catching up to do across the executive and legislative branches. I think we have started to make progress. But we are still in a stalemate with the executive. I am not satisfied with where we find ourselves. As long as this situation persists, further attention is required, and policy positions may need to change. My task is to establish exactly what the issues are and report back to Pretoria, while convincing decision-makers here that Pretoria’s intent is to establish a solid relationship. Does that mean engaging with conservative organizations such as the Heritage Foundation to understand the thinking behind the administration’s policies? It is important to understand the roots of this thinking and the American context. Some decisions are coming from a framework different from the one I knew in the past. I know the framework of the 1980s very well. It was relatively simple to understand: Republican and Democrat. Today, it is more splintered, with fundamental ideological issues at stake. events.title: Global private equity investor Advent opens ADGM office
events.summary: Advent, a global private equity investor with more than $109 billion in assets under management, has opened an office in Abu Dhabi’s ADGM , joining the growing list of financial institutions with a presence in the UAE capital. The opening of the new office follows a series of openings by the company globally, including in Tokyo and Hong Kong, the company said in a statement on Wednesday. “The new presence builds on Advent’s long-standing relationships across the Middle East, giving Advent a local base from which to deepen its engagement with investors and support the firm’s existing portfolio companies and explore potential investment opportunities,” the company said. Set up in 1984, the company has made 460 investments in 45 countries. It has 18 offices globally, including in Abu Dhabi. The announcement comes as a growing number of global financial institutions launch their operations at ADGM, despite uncertainty arising from the Iran war. Earlier this month, New Mountain Capital, an alternative investment firm based in New York, said it was opening an office in ADGM to strengthen its presence in the Middle East, while Capital Group, which manages $3.6 trillion in assets, has secured a licence from the Financial Services Regulatory Authority of Abu Dhabi's ADGM to operate as a regulated investment manager. The Paris-listed Eurazeo, a European asset manager with €40 billion ($45.2 billion) in assets under management, has also opened an office in the ADGM amid its expansion plans in the region. Other high-profile companies that the UAE capital has attracted in recent months include private credit lender Blue Owl Capital, the tech-focused US company Vista Equity Partners, the world’s largest listed hedge fund Man Group, Barings, Bain Capital, Cantor and the Swiss derivative investment company Adapt Investment Managers. “Advent’s decision to establish an office in ADGM reflects the strength of Abu Dhabi’s proposition as a leading destination for global investment firms,” Arvind Ramamurthy, chief market development officer at ADGM, said. Assets under management at ADGM grew 54 per cent annually in the first six months of 2026, with 49,027 professionals now based at Al Maryah Island and Al Reem Island, an increase of 34 per cent on the same period last year. Collectively, asset managers that established operations in ADGM in the first half of the year oversee more than $2.1 trillion in global assets under management.
