events.title: UN projections say world is losing ground in fight to curb climate change
events.summary: Humanity is losing more ground in its fight against climate change WASHINGTON -- Losing more ground in the fight against climate change, humanity is heading for a hotter world than experts projected last year — and the United States is a big reason for that, a new United Nations report says. If all the countries do what they promise to reduce heat-trapping emissions, Earth will likely still warm another 2.2 degrees Fahrenheit (1.2 degrees Celsius) above current temperatures, according to Wednesday's update of climate calculations by the United Nations Environment Programme. That's about two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit (0.1 degrees Celsius) more than last year's projections by the same science team. “This is a worse outcome than expected last year, as a result of the formal withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions,” the report said. The report also blames the United States for increased emissions last year, saying all the other top 20 major economies reduced their carbon pollution or at least slowed the growth in how much carbon dioxide was spewed from the burning of coal, oil and gas. “In terms of magnitude, the increase in the United States of America (133 megatons of CO2 equivalent) far exceeded that of all other countries and was driven by increased electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation,” the report said. The 124 countries that increased emissions — not counting the 63 that decreased like most European nations — added 189 million tons of carbon dioxide in 2025, and 70% of that increase came from the U.S., according to the report. The United States is going “hell-for-leather trying to block renewables while actively promoting and subsidizing dirty coal — and its diplomacy is trying to make other countries also pull back on action. It is looking at the fire, denying there is a fire, and then pouring more petrol on it,” said Australian climate scientist Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics that measures countries' climate fighting plans. He wasn't part of the U.N. report but like several other outside scientists said it was scientifically sound. The new calculations say that if countries do all they promise in the climate fighting plans they submitted to the United Nations, by 2100 the globe will be 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter than pre-industrial times. If the world continues on its current path — without national promises — it will be 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the last half of the 19th century, the same as last year's projection. Both of those temperatures blow far past the goal of less than 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) adopted by the 2015 Paris climate pact . The world is now at about 1.4 degrees Celsius (2.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times and earlier this year — and again in this report — United Nations officials conceded that there is no way of limiting warming to the 1.5-degree goal that they had embraced. Instead, officials are pinning their hopes of limiting warming to about 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) and then somehow pulling enough carbon dioxide out of the air to lower temperatures back down to 1.5 degrees. The world is falling “dangerously short” of even those goals, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said, “but we have the tools to change course and pull back from the brink.” Drastically cutting global carbon emissions — by 18% by 2030 and 69% by 2040 — “is the only way that we can get back to a semblance of a reality that is still largely manageable without major impacts and therefore that makes every sense,” said UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen. “The report's message is clear,” said climate scientist Adelle Thomas, vice chair of a United Nations scientific assessment on climate impacts. She wasn't part of this study. “We know what needs to be done. We have the tools to do it. And delay only makes the challenge more dangerous and more expensive for all.” Report lead author Anne Olhoff, director of UNEP Copenhagen Climate Centre, said the U.S. policy change will likely add one-tenth of a degree Celsius (nearly two-tenths of a degree Fahrenheit) to global temperatures by the end of the century. events.title: What a merger of SpaceX and Tesla would mean
events.summary: Elon Musk believes a merger between Tesla and SpaceX is a good idea, he said on Tuesday, publicly backing an idea that would create ​one ​of the most valuable companies in the ​world, worth about $3.5 trillion. While electric-vehicle maker Tesla and rocket company ⁠SpaceX were once seen as largely separate businesses, the lines between them have blurred as ⁠Mr Musk expands into artificial intelligence, robotics, advanced manufacturing , satellite communications and computing infrastructure, ​including data centres on Earth and potentially in orbit. Here's what a potential merger could mean: Why merge the companies? A merger would create a ⁠single company at the centre of Mr Musk's long-term vision: an integrated technology and manufacturing empire spanning AI, energy, robotics, communications, and transportation on Earth and beyond. “I do think there's a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, and there's a lot to be gained ⁠from co-operating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab obviously, robotics, mass-to-orbit with the Starmind constellation (of orbital data centres), connectivity,” Mr Musk said on Tuesday. Bringing ​the companies ⁠together could also simplify decision-making. Many of Mr Musk's projects ‌already cut across multiple companies, requiring approvals from separate boards and shareholders. A combined company would give management more freedom to deploy capital, engineering ​talent and infrastructure where it sees the greatest opportunity. Mr Musk has long argued that he needs greater influence over Tesla to pursue its AI and robotics strategy. He owns nearly a fifth of Tesla and holds voting control at SpaceX. A merger could consolidate his influence. What does it mean for investors? Tesla shareholders would gain access to SpaceX's rapidly growing Starlink broadband operation, launch services business and future space ventures. SpaceX investors would gain ownership of Tesla's vehicle, energy storage, autonomous driving and robotics businesses. A merged company could also become one of the world's most valuable corporations, with a market value of about $3.5 trillion, combining leadership positions in cars, robotics, satellite communications, launch services, energy storage and AI infrastructure. Supporters would likely argue that the combined company could allocate capital more efficiently across businesses that are increasingly interdependent. Critics, however, argue that investors would be assuming exposure to a much broader range of technical, regulatory and execution risks, some of which have little connection to one another. Where could SpaceX and Tesla work together? Starlink satellites could provide communications links for Tesla's robotaxis, autonomous systems and future generations of Optimus humanoid robots. Tesla's battery and energy-storage products could help support SpaceX's growing power needs, including future ​data-centre projects. Mr Musk has already announced one major Tesla-SpaceX collaboration, Terafab, a semiconductor and AI-computing project aimed at producing ‌the advanced chips needed for Tesla's autonomous vehicles and ⁠Optimus robots, as well as SpaceX's AI and data-centre ambitions. Mr Musk ​hopes it can start volume production by late 2028. Tesla's expertise in large-scale factory automation could complement SpaceX's efforts to industrialise Starship production, ​while SpaceX technologies ‌have already appeared in Tesla products, most notably the planned use of rocket-derived components in the next-generation Roadster. A merged company could also co-ordinate efforts to secure strategic ⁠supply chains, leveraging Tesla's scale in batteries, semiconductors and manufacturing equipment alongside SpaceX's demand for specialised metals, electronics, propulsion components and satellite ⁠hardware. What are the key risks? The biggest challenges may be geopolitics and regulation. SpaceX is a major contractor for the US military, intelligence agencies and Nasa. Tesla, meanwhile, remains deeply tied to China through its Shanghai factory, which plays a major role in vehicle production and sales. That combination could invite heightened scrutiny from US regulators and national-security officials as well as from Beijing. The merger would also face shareholder and governance hurdles. Investors ​would need to be persuaded that combining two already complex businesses creates more value than keeping them separate. Questions about conflicts of interest, voting control and capital allocation would inevitably follow. Then there is execution risk. Starship, robotaxis, humanoid robots, AI data centres, mobile communications and orbital infrastructure are all expensive, technically challenging bets. Combining Tesla and SpaceX would not reduce those risks. It would simply place them under one roof.

Protesters blocked the loading and unloading of fresh food and other goods at supermarket distribution warehouses near Naples on Monday, Sky TG24 reported. The truckers are adding their voices to demonstrations that have spread across Europe as the war disrupts economies. One supermarket in the city posted a note on empty shelves apologizing that “some products may be temporarily unavailable or available in a reduced range" due to the truckers' strike. Shortages of fresh pasta, packaged cheeses and meats as well as produce have been reported in Sicily, partly due to stockpiling by shoppers. events.title: An AI slowdown could be exactly what businesses need
events.summary: The artificial intelligence industry has spent years feathering the accelerator of frontier model development in a fierce contest to dominate the technology . Now, it is considering something that until recently seemed almost unthinkable: slamming on the brakes. The prospects of the frontier labs are closely linked to the fortunes of the US stock market, and they buttress vast spending on infrastructure. But for businesses still working out how to harness AI’s illusive productivity gains, a slowdown is not a bad thing. It will give them time to close the yawning gap between AI’s accelerating capabilities and their productive use of them. Still, calls to pace the frontier grow louder. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei made the case in an essay in which he said capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to understand, align and control them. His proposal was to deliberately slow the improvement enough to give safety research and independent evaluation time to catch up. Is it practical? There remains considerable disagreement over whether this is practical, desirable or possible. But that’s beside the point for businesses, since most of them are nowhere close to exhausting the AI capabilities they already possess. According to the Stanford 2026 AI Index, 88 per cent of organisations surveyed reported using AI in at least one business function last year. But breadth of adoption is not the same thing as depth. The research shows that the use of AI agents remained in the single digits across almost every business function. Relatively few have fundamentally redesigned how work gets done around it. Research from the Federal Reserve Bank of St Louis found that generative AI accounted for only 5.7 per cent of total working hours by August last year. This tells us that companies already have powerful AI, and are simply failing to make the most of it. They don’t need another massive leap in model capability to claim the productivity gains that are already on the table. A METR randomised study found that experienced open-source developers working on highly familiar repositories actually took 19 per cent longer when allowed to use early-2025 AI tools. The reason is that the bottleneck is increasingly organisational. Companies have to connect models to proprietary data. They have to integrate AI into existing systems. And they need to redesign workflows rather than simply insert a chatbot into them. They also need appropriate governance, security and human oversight, while employees have to learn how to delegate effectively to AI. Managers, meanwhile, need to rethink roles, performance measures and decision rights. Those changes happen at a comparatively glacial pace when compared with the speed at which AI labs have been pushing the frontier. More capabilities OpenAI's enterprise research finds that the heaviest AI adopters use substantially more capabilities across more tasks than the median employee. These intensive users report much larger productivity benefits. Seventy-five per cent of surveyed workers also reported being able to perform tasks using AI that they previously could not do. So the AI productivity frontier inside most companies sits far behind the technological one. This is not unusual. General-purpose technologies typically arrive before organisations learn how to exploit them. Electricity existed before factories were redesigned around distributed electric motors, and computers came along long before companies reorganised processes around digital information. AI is likely to follow the same pattern, which only strengthens the case for hitting the brakes. That will not stall the AI economy , which is so crucial to public equity markets, because it will give companies the badly needed time to extract value from the marvellous capabilities already at their fingertips. That means moving beyond experimentation towards workflow redesign. Moving from individual productivity tools towards end-to-end processes. Connecting AI to enterprise data and systems. Using agents where they genuinely add value. Building governance that allows experimentation without unacceptable risk. And, perhaps most importantly, developing the organisational capabilities required to use AI well. Executives should continue watching the frontier, of course. Better models will create new opportunities, and a substantial slowdown is far from guaranteed. But they should not confuse a slower technological frontier with a slower business opportunity. Even if frontier development paused dramatically tomorrow, companies would still have an enormous backlog of economically valuable opportunities across customer service, software development, finance , procurement, marketing and many other functions. So just because the frontier slows, it doesn’t mean the business opportunity does. The AI race, at least for enterprise users, needs to shift from simply building better AI to building better businesses around it.

events.title: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
events.summary: Voters in Alberta have overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with four-fifths of votes counted showing 75% support for staying EDMONTON, Alberta -- Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in the country, referendum results showed Tuesday, delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats rally Canadians around their country. With more than 1.9 million votes counted and results reported from 90% of voting areas and locations, 75% of voters supported remaining in Canada , while 25% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta. The referendum was not a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada . “It’s a great result for Canada that Albertans have chosen unity,” Carney told reporters Tuesday before a Cabinet meeting in Ottawa. Carney said the roughly one-quarter of voters who backed beginning the separation process did not necessarily want independence, suggesting only a smaller “hard core” favored leaving Canada. Some voters said they wanted to send Ottawa a message rather than separate. Alberta separatist organizer David Parker acknowledged the scale of the defeat. “Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat,” he wrote on social media. In a televised address Tuesday night, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the result and pledged not to hold another referendum on separation while she remains in office. “Yesterday, Albertans voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining a province of Canada,” Smith said. “The voter turnout was historic and a powerful testimony of the passion Albertans feel for our country and our province.” Smith said Alberta would continue pressing Ottawa for greater provincial autonomy, but disputes would be settled within Canada’s political and legal institutions rather than through separation. Carney said he spoke with Smith on Tuesday morning about the results and greater federal-provincial cooperation, including immigration. “Don’t mess with Canada. President Trump is watching this,” Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters. Alberta, home to the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves , is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada's federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn't traditionally translated into widespread support for independence. Despite the overwhelming rejection, separatist leaders vowed to continue pressing for independence. Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said. Trump’s trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular. Rep. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.” Rath said before the vote that he would be thrilled with 30% support. He also said he wanted Smith ousted as UCP leader and believed the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party. Ian Brodie, a University of Calgary political scientist and former chief of staff to Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper, dismissed Rath and fellow separatist organizer Mitch Sylvestre as “nobodies,” saying they failed to gain traction even in a district that elected a separatist to Alberta’s legislature in 1982. “Even on a very soft question — whether to hold a referendum on separation — they couldn’t gain real traction," Brodie said. Edmonton voter Shawn Campbell said he voted to begin the separation process even though he doesn’t want Alberta to leave Canada. “It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy,” he said. Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a “referendum on a referendum” rather than healthcare. events.title: The Secret Terms of Trump’s Venezuelan Oil Deal
events.summary: Alejandro Betancourt, a 46-year-old Venezuelan energy baron, is the key figure in a historic oil deal with the Trump administration. Venezuelan opposition leaders and U.S. congressional Democrats have criticized the agreement because Betancourt has been the target of investigations of alleged corruption. Antonio Heredia/El Mundo In late August, President Donald Trump announced what he called the “biggest oil deal in world history.” Since then, the full text of the accord — which grants the U.S. sweeping access to Venezuela’s oil reserves — has been one of the most sought-after secrets in Washington, D.C.  ProPublica has reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. The document reveals carefully constructed terms that favor U.S. interests at every turn and cements the power of a small group of people handpicked by the Trump administration to govern and profit from the deal. The role of the Venezuelan government and the potential benefits to its people are largely absent from the text. One of the most criticized aspects of Trump’s announcement has been his choice of a partner: Alejandro Betancourt, a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.  The Trump administration is taking a 35% stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners, by acquiring shares in a Barbados-registered parent company. The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement.  The agreement also safeguards Betancourt’s position as chief executive of NABEP and says the U.S. government will work with the parent company to appoint a powerful seven-member board to govern the venture for an initial 15-year term. Those aspects of the deal, according to people with knowledge of how it came together, were designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan leaders from dismantling the enterprise.  Orlando Alvarado, a name not disclosed by the Trump administration as a party to the accord, signed the agreement on behalf of the parent company, alongside Betancourt, Hegseth and Rubio. Alvarado has held senior roles in multiple Betancourt businesses, including as chief financial officer of an energy firm that became embroiled in scandals a decade ago. According to the Miami Herald , federal prosecutors identified Alvarado as an unindicted co-conspirator in a scheme to embezzle money from Venezuela’s national oil company. NABEP spokesperson Terry Wade said that “neither Mr. Betancourt nor Mr. Alvarado has ever been charged with any crime in any country, and any claims against them are baseless.”  Do You Know More About This Topic? We’re still reporting. If you know more about this topic, please contact our reporting team. Cate Brown I’m interested in talking to people who understand how members of the Trump administration, or their family members, are doing business, at home or abroad. Contact Me Key aspects of the plan differ from the Trump administration’s public pronouncements. Trump has said the deal will secure America’s energy dominance for the next century. But the text indicates that U.S. purchasing rights expire in half that time and that the underlying operating rights appear to run afoul of Venezuelan laws limiting oil concessions to 25 years. The agreement does ensure the United States a deep discount from fair-market value on 20% of NABEP’s oil, as Trump has said. It does not, however, explicitly guarantee that Betancourt’s company is obligated to pay the estimated $200 billion in royalties and tax payments to Venezuela that the White House has said would benefit the country .  There are also significant caveats related to Trump’s central selling point to Americans — that the deal will bring a gusher of low-cost oil imports.  The agreement gives the U.S. the right to purchase 20% of NABEP’s oil at a discounted rate of $30 a barrel, or less than a third of what oil has sold for in recent months, according to one of three supporting documents reviewed by ProPublica.  But this fee does not account for the cost of getting Venezuela’s oil out of the country. Much of Venezuela’s raw crude is so thick that it won’t flow through pipelines unless it is first blended with 20% or more of oil thinner products. Under the deal, the potentially significant cost of importing millions of barrels of those blending materials is not included in the price. The White House, the State Department, the Pentagon and the energy company NABEP all defended the agreement, saying in statements that their new public-private venture will provide meaningful and lasting economic benefits to both countries that cannot be captured in a legal document.  “This historic deal marks a major step toward stabilizing Venezuela’s economy after years of hyperinflation and almost no new investment, while more than doubling the United States’ oil reserves,” said White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers. Wade emphasized that NABEP was chosen because of its track record of expanding oil production in Venezuela in recent years and that the agreement was between the company and the U.S. government, not Venezuela. “Thanks in large part to the agreement,” Wade said, “there is a surge in confidence about the future of Venezuela’s oil industry and, as a direct result, substantial new investments are flowing into the country.” He added that much of NABEP’s oil comes from fields that require little or no blending materials and that blending costs would not meaningfully impact the price of production. “Our barrel economics are strong.” The newly revealed details of the agreement are nonetheless likely to raise more questions about whether the unorthodox marriage of the United States and a foreign energy baron can bring lasting benefits to either country — and which private parties might benefit along the way. Trump’s oil deal is likely to face scrutiny in both the United States and Venezuela, especially if Democrats win one or both chambers in the midterm elections, according to former U.S. diplomats and congressional staff. “Question number one in a new U.S. Congress will be: Why Betancourt?” said former Ambassador James Story, who served as the top U.S. diplomat in Caracas from 2018 to 2023, in an interview. “Why did he get this deal? events.title: When AI models refuse to fight hackers
events.summary: In the race to fend off AI-enabled cyber threats , security teams are confronting a new problem: The AI models they rely on to investigate attacks can suddenly refuse to help. Why it matters: While AI giants race to build AI tools that can respond quickly to hacking or other malicious online threats, strict guardrails on their most powerful models lock out defenders mid-investigation, leaving them scrambling for alternatives at critical moments. What's happening: OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, said it was compromised over the weekend, allowing attackers to obtain API keys belonging to some customers, including keys for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google services. OpenCode said the breach was "related to a large scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users." OpenCode co-creator Dax Raad said attackers had been targeting its systems continuously for 48 hours, forcing the company to keep its own AI agents running around the clock to respond. OpenAI , Google and Anthropic have said they worked with affected customers to revoke exposed API keys and address unauthorized usage charges. Zoom in: Raad said on X that frontier AI models initially helped investigate the breach but then "started refusing." The models' safety restrictions reportedly began blocking requests as the investigation turned to potentially malicious code, even though OpenCode was trying to defend its own systems. OpenCode then gained access to OpenAI's Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted cybersecurity defenders access to models with fewer restrictions. "We definitely need to be more proactive and we've made so many improvements over the last few days," Raad wrote on X Monday. The big picture: The incident underscored a dilemma facing cybersecurity teams trying to figure out when to use powerful proprietary AI models, which come with built-in restrictions, or open-weight alternatives that offer greater control over how they're deployed. When Hugging Face discovered suspicious activity on its systems that it later linked to OpenAI's own agents, its security team turned to a Chinese open-weight model to help investigate after encountering restrictions on frontier models. Yes, but: AI companies maintain that they need to gate access to their most powerful models to ensure that malicious actors can't abuse their cyber capabilities. Between the lines: Cybersecurity teams will have to figure out how to balance the need for faster AI-powered defenses with restrictions designed to keep those same capabilities out of attackers' hands, Chris Jones, chief technology officer at Nightwing, told Axios. "We're all going to have to figure out how that race gets modulated over time," Jones said. "That's a big piece here." Go deeper : Anthropic and OpenAI are now cybersecurity's kingmakers

events.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes following call with Rubio
events.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners following recent Russian attacks that he said occurred without enough notice to Ukraine KYIV, Ukraine -- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice , leaving civilians vulnerable. For at least a week , the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles. Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio . “We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I’m speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming,” Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. “So we are thankful to American side now that it works.” Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the U.S. and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue. In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help. Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff , who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war . Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway's capital. Gahr Støre said Witkoff planned to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders, exchange ideas from the Oslo meeting and share proposals from European and American colleagues. “Today was a good day for peace,” Stubb said. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but doesn’t expect any “miracle” from Washington. At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again . “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” If that doesn’t happen, “I think it’s going to be a very bad thing.” The conversation with Rubio came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes “some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us.” Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine. The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX’s satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations . Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia , a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow’s full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February. Zelenskyy said he had “a substantive conversation” with Rubio. “I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position,” Zelenskyy said on social media. Rep. The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said. “There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine,” he said. events.title: Netflix posts higher Q3 profit but revenue growth worries pull shares lower
events.summary: Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street’s expectations Netflix, which announced layoff plans last week, posted a third-quarter profit above Wall Street's expectations, but investors sent shares down after the streaming company lowered its ad sales guidance, prompting worries about slowing revenue growth. Netflix said Tuesday it earned $3.66 billion, or 87 cents per share, for the July-September period. That's up 44% from $2.55 billion, or 59 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 12% to $12.87 billion from $11.51 billion. Analysts surveyed by FactSet predicted earnings of 82 cents per share on revenue of $12.87 billion. “With Netflix under pressure to find alternative lines of revenue beyond subscriptions, it’s concerning that the company lowered its estimate for its ad business,” said Emarketer senior analyst Ross Benes. “Revamping content strategy is not enough to fix this challenge but it is a worthwhile start. Guidance is not as aggressive as investors have grown accustomed to.” Last week, the Los Gatos, California-based company announced that it plans to lay off about 6% of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions, as the company makes wider “organizational changes.” At the end of 2025, per regulatory filings, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees worldwide. The most recent layoff announcement marks the biggest round of cuts that the company has rolled out in years. Netflix also announced last week that Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria will be replaced by Peter Rice. Bajaria was with Netflix for nearly a decade. Rice will lead Netflix’s global content organization, overseeing scripted and unscripted series, film, live events and more across all regions. He takes over the post on Oct. 26. While Netflix has benefited from membership sign-ups and price increases, the company is dealing with intense competition in the streaming sector from companies such as Amazon’s Prime Video and Disney+. There's also Skydance , after Paramount’s $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery put HBO Max and Paramount+ under the same roof. Netflix walked away from its offer to buy Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming business in February. The company is also competing for people's attention with YouTube and TikTok, where short videos are extremely popular. Rep. Ilhan Omar says she will move from her Washington, DC, home after federal search Man hops onto moving school bus when he sees driver in distress Bend, Oregon, shooting: Suspect ID'd, had attended elementary school, police say For the current quarter, Netflix is forecasting revenue of $13.4 billion, slightly below analysts' expectations of $13.5 billion. New shows and movies coming this quarter include “East of Eden” and season four of “The Diplomat” as well as the sixth and final season of “Emily in Paris.” Netflix also released “La Bola Negra,” a Spanish film about the interconnected lives of three gay men across a history that spans the early 20th century, the Spanish Civil War and the modern day. “La Bola Negra” — which cost $15 million to make — is expected to challenge “The Odyssey” for best picture. Netflix disclosed box office numbers for the movie, for the first time in its history. It made $313,391 over the weekend through Monday with a release in just four theaters. As of Tuesday's close, Netflix's stock is down about 25% for the year to date. Analysts see several factors contributing to its difficulties. “Investors are concerned about soft engagement trends, decelerating revenue growth, a slower margin expansion outlook, and most recently content executive leadership changes,” said John Belton, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds. events.title: Exclusive: Ramaswamy doubles down on explosive ad featuring rival's mother, despite backlash
events.summary: Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor is pouring $4 million into a bombshell ad in which his opponent's estranged mother attacks her daughter — doubling down on the message despite fierce bipartisan backlash, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Ramaswamy is gambling that the deeply personal attack by Amy Acton's mother — who Acton has said sided with her stepfather after he sexually assaulted Acton when she was 12 — will resonate with voters. After the ad began appearing Tuesday on social media, many fellow Republicans urged Ramaswamy to distance his campaign from it. They warned it could backfire at a time when the controversy over the Epstein files has elevated the sexual abuse of children as a national campaign issue. Driving the news: Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed to Axios that it produced the ad, which began circulating on social media late Monday without language identifying its sponsor. Sources close to Ramaswamy's campaign said the ad tested well with "persuadable" voters, prompting the decision to launch a $4 million statewide campaign that began streaming Tuesday night. Catch up quick: The minute-long commercial features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and urging Ohioans not to vote for her. "She lies about her past," Arthur says. "She's lied her entire life." Arthur also disputes Acton's account of experiencing homelessness as a child. The other side: Acton, a physician, has said she was sexually abused at age 12 by her stepfather, who faced criminal charges, and that her mother sided with him. Acton and her brother were removed from their mother's custody. According to her brother, their mother remained married to Acton's alleged abuser until his death. Acton, 60, has said she hasn't seen her mother since childhood. In a statement posted to Facebook on Tuesday, Acton said that "between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me." "I've always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it's sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain." Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, called Ramaswamy's ad "disgusting." What they're saying: Despite bipartisan criticism, Ramaswamy's campaign continued to treat the mother's statements as campaign gold. "This is a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton. The people who know her best keep warning Ohioans about her," Ramaswamy campaign manager Jonathan Ewing told Axios. Several prominent Republicans and conservative commentators blasted the ad, arguing that it could generate sympathy for Acton. Republican strategist David Urban on CNN drew a parallel to the Epstein controversy, warning that voters are especially sympathetic to victims of sexual assault and that the ad could backfire. "It seems crazy to me one would assume this would work and not backfire," conservative commentator Mary Katharine Ham posted on X. Yes, but: Some conservatives defended the commercial, including Donald Trump Jr., who urged Ohio voters to "watch [it] and think about what it means." By the numbers: A mid-October Marist survey showed Acton leading Ramaswamy 50% to 43% among likely voters. What's next: Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted are set to campaign with Vice President Vance in Cincinnati on Wednesday.

events.title: House Democrats forced to make tough choices with limited midterm cash
events.summary: House Democrats' main super PAC is winding down its spending in several races where the party has struggled to make headway despite national trends working in their favor . Why it matters: Democrats' ambitions of winning heavily Republican districts are running into the reality of finite resources at the end of a long and expensive midterm campaign. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and its corresponding super PAC, House Majority PAC, have struggled to keep pace with their GOP counterparts' monster fundraising this cycle. Republicans also have the bonus advantage of a network of cash-rich outside groups, namely President Trump's MAGA Inc. and Elon Musk's America PAC . Driving the news: HMP pulled back its spending this week in three Republican-leaning districts, according to AdImpact and a source familiar with the matter. TN-05: Democrats were bullish about their star recruit, Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, until redistricting made the district redder and embattled Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) lost his primary to former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher . HMP has drawn down its ad reservations in the district from nearly $1.6 million this month to a little over $500,000 as of Monday. Trump carried the newly reconstituted 5th district by 21 percentage points in 2024. Cook Political Report rates the race as "solidly Republican." FL-07: Facing a situation similar to Tennessee, Democrats liked their odds of unseating scandal-tarred Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), who lost his primary to former local news anchor Ryan Elijah. Like Molder, Democratic candidate Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff, was a top DCCC recruit and is part of the committee's coveted "Red to Blue" program. HMP essentially halved its investment in the district on Monday, cutting ad reservations from $3.9 million to just $1.95 million. Cook rates the race as "likely Republican," though a poll released by the DCCC on Tuesday had the two candidates tied at 45% each. CO-03: A top target for Democrats when Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.) represented it, the seat has become a heavier lift for the party since she abandoned it and Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-Colo.) took office last year. Democrat Dwayne Romero, a real estate company CEO and Army veteran, is seen by party operatives as having failed to build the kind of momentum shown by Jessica Killin in the neighboring 5th District. HMP halved its investment in this district too, from more than $2.1 million last week to less than $1.1 million as of Monday. Between the lines: The group has also made partial cuts — what it calls "shaves" — in districts where Democrats have struggled to gain traction but still see a glimmer of hope. That includes Arizona's 2nd District, where Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.) is locked in a rematch with former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez in a race Cook rates as "likely Republican." HMP has also taken some money out of Texas' 23rd District, where Republican Brandon Herrera, a right-wing YouTuber, is facing Democratic lawyer Katy Padilla Stout in another race rated "likely Republican." Yes, but: Some HMP triages are in districts where they feel confident the Democratic candidate will prevail. That includes Reps. Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) and Kristen McDonald Rivet (D-Mich.), both of whose races are rated "likely Democratic" by Cook. The PAC has also pulled back in the districts of retiring Reps. Darrell Issa (R-Calif.) and Don Bacon (R-Neb.), which Democrats are increasingly bullish about flipping. The money from these cuts is funneled to districts the party views as more core battlegrounds — including some seats Trump carried by double digits in 2024 that Democrats nevertheless view as winnable. HMP has added at least $4.7 million to its existing investments in nearly two dozen districts over the last two days. What they're saying: Phil Gardner, a senior adviser for Blue Dog Action — a centrist group backing Dalton — told Axios of the cuts in Florida, "I'm not sure what HMP was thinking here." "The rest of the party is not triaging this seat," he said, citing the DCCC's poll and House Minority Whip Katherine Clark's (D-Mass.) plans to campaign there on Wednesday. Gardner said he agrees with "95% of the decisions HMP's made this cycle," but that it is "bonkers they're dumping so much money" into Maine's 2nd District "while leaving one of the party's best recruits high and dry in Florida." Blue Dog Action spent nearly $500,000 to help Dalton win the primary, but it hasn't yet invested any money in the general election. The bottom line: "We're focused on taking back the House," CJ Warnke, a spokesperson for HMP, told Axios in response to Gardner's criticism. Said Gardner: "I'm confident they'll rethink and make the right decision for the final week. Bale can win and hold that seat with everyone's help."

events.title: Witkoff to present Putin with peace proposal after talks with Zelensky
events.summary: White House envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Wednesday and present him with an updated proposal to end the war in Ukraine , a U.S. official said. President Trump's son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner will join the meeting virtually. Why it matters: The White House hopes Putin will show more willingness to compromise after Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales and took other steps welcomed by Moscow. Driving the news: Witkoff will arrive in Russia after a day of talks in Oslo , Norway, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, as well as the leaders of Norway and Finland and representatives from France, the UK, Germany, Poland, the EU and NATO. Zelensky said Tuesday that the next step should be a trilateral meeting between him, Putin and Trump — a format Russia has so far rejected. The U.S. hopes the new proposal will "create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations," a U.S. official said. Zoom in: The discussions in Oslo focused on developing a unified proposal for a "framework agreement" to end the war. The U.S. official said Ukraine "brought forward new ideas and proposals, which were discussed in detail." The official said the parties made "meaningful progress" and now have "strong alignment at the working level" on next steps. Behind the scenes: Kushner joined the meeting virtually and again pressed Trump's demand that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, according to a source with knowledge. "Jared was very direct," the person said. Zelensky said after the meeting that he's prepared to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow takes reciprocal steps. What he's saying: Trump said Tuesday that he thinks "Russia would like to get it done," but he expressed doubt that Zelensky wants to end the war. "If he does not, it's gonna be a very bad thing," Trump added. "We want Zelensky to make a deal … If they don't make a deal, it's just gonna get worse [for Ukraine]."

events.title: Instacart settles federal claims of discrimination against US-born job seekers
events.summary: The federal government has reached a $5 million settlement with Instacart for allegedly discriminating against U.S.-born workers in its hiring practices The federal government has reached a $5 million settlement with Instacart for allegedly discriminating against U.S.-born workers in its hiring practices. According to the U.S. Department of Justice Civil Rights Division and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, Instacart was advertising jobs through the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program. The program lets employers hire temporary visa holders and sponsor them for permanent resident status as long as they have also made a good-faith effort to hire U.S. workers. The agencies said Instacart created a burden for U.S. workers by requiring that applications be physically mailed to the company for jobs that were listed as part of its PERM recruitment program. Instacart allows electronic applications for its standard job recruitment process. San Francisco-based Instacart said Tuesday that its hiring practices complied with U.S. laws and regulations, but it agreed to the settlement in order to remain focused on its business. “We’re proud to be a U.S.-based grocery technology platform, employing thousands of American workers and serving millions of customers, retailers, shoppers and brands,” the company said. “Hiring and investing in American workers across our U.S. business is our priority, and we actively promote every role across many channels to ensure qualified U.S. candidates are always first in line for opportunities.” Instacart is the latest tech company to reach a settlement with the government over allegations that it favors foreign workers for certain jobs. What F1’s return to Africa means for a continent long overlooked by global sports Most Americans say AI is bad for society, oppose more data centers: Poll $1 million heist nets rare Pokémon cards In 2023, Apple agreed to a $25 million settlement after federal regulators said its hiring practices discriminated against U.S. candidates for jobs that went to immigrant workers seeking permanent resident status in the country. Facebook agreed to pay $14 million in 2021 to settle claims about its hiring practices. “Our record demonstrates that the Justice Department is holding companies who prefer workers with temporary employment visas accountable," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon said in a statement. "We will not stop fighting for U.S. workers until there is a fair playing field.” The settlement requires Instacart to establish a fund of up to $4 million to compensate job applicants and people who were allegedly deterred from applying to Instacart between December 2023 and February 2026. Instacart will pay $1 million in civil penalties to the federal government. The company is also required to post jobs that are part of its PERM recruitment program on its public career website and accept electronic applications. events.title: Mamdani takes on AI chatbot ‘doom loops’ in New York
events.summary: New York City could be the first place in the country where consumers are protected from a “doom loop” of AI-powered customer service chatbots, per a rule proposed today by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s administration. The rule would require businesses to connect people to a human customer service agent quickly if a chatbot cannot fulfill their requests. “When corporations force you to fight your way through an endless doom loop of AI-generated responses to speak to another human being, they’re stealing your time, money, and patience,” Mamdani said in a release. “This rule makes clear: Customer service cost-cutting can’t come at New Yorkers’ expense.” Businesses would have to disclose when customers are talking to AI and offer an “easy off-ramp” to a human representative, with violators subject to fines that would start at $525. At the helm of Mamdani’s consumer protection efforts are several Biden administration alumni: Samuel Levine, commissioner of the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, previously led the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection under the agency’s then-chair Lina Khan, and Deputy Mayor Julie Su was acting labor secretary during the Biden era. events.title: The Internet goes on high alert after discovery of 8 compromised TLS certs
events.summary: Security personnel around the world are on high alert Tuesday following the discovery of eight TLS certificates with private keys so weak they could allow anyone to mint trusted browser and app credentials for any site on the Internet. As of late morning Tuesday, browser makers and some major apps and programming languages had blocked all eight of the intermediate certificates. There are no reports of certificate transparency logs, which track the issuance of all browser-trusted certificates, showing the compromised keys being used maliciously. The threat remains far from over, however, because it will be hard and time-consuming to update other key parts of the Internet, such as Linux distributions and embedded and Internet of Things devices. One word: bonkers The eight intermediate certificates belong to India-based certificate authority eMudhra Limited. An informal advisory published to emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com over on Tuesday posted the message “We have a problem here - Wayne.” The words were digitally signed using the private key of one of the eMudhra certificates. With proof that the reporting party had control of the key, defenders scrambled because the same key could be used to sign unauthorized certificates that would be trusted by millions of servers worldwide. events.title: Trump goes full apocalypse in anti-Dems midterms message
events.summary: President Trump is escalating his doomsday warnings about a Democratic takeover of Congress, painting a nightmarish vision of an America consumed by burning cities, economic collapse, mutilated children and the destruction of Western civilization. Why it matters: Trump has long portrayed Democrats as an existential threat to the country. But in an effort to preserve Republicans' grip on Washington, he's taking that rhetoric to new extremes as he casts the election as a choice between Republican rule and national catastrophe. At the same time, Trump is offering voters a financial incentive to keep Republicans in power: $5,000 checks for every adult American citizen if the GOP retains control of Congress. The pledge would cost more than $1 trillion and has no clear path to becoming reality. What they're saying: "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Axios in a statement. "The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump's winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats' extreme liberal policies and obstruction." Reality check: Even if Democrats take control of Congress, Trump will remain president and retain veto power over legislation they pass. Here's what he's been telling voters. America will burn like France On Monday night, Trump told Kansas voters that under Democrats, America will burn like France, which is facing widespread student and union protests over public spending cuts and deficit concerns, per Reuters . "When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to do to America." Trump has blamed the riots in France on immigration , suggesting that border policies under Democratic Party leadership would unleash the same chaos in America. Yes, but: The unrest in France has been driven by disputes over living costs and public funding. There's no evidence that Democrats in the U.S. want to take up similar forms of violence. America will fall into another Great Depression Trump predicts Democrats will cause economic catastrophe and trigger a depression similar to the one that began in 1929. "If the Democrats win you will have a 1929-style economic depression," Trump told Tennessee voters on Saturday. "I hope I'm wrong on that." By the numbers: Unemployment peaked at roughly 25% during the Great Depression, compared with about 4% today. What's next: House Democrats, should they gain power, plan to repeal Trump's tariff policy, bring back Affordable Care Act tax breaks and undo Medicaid cuts as part of a general affordability push. Democrats will "mutilate your children" In Arizona, Trump warned last week that Democrats want to "mutilate, cut your children." "I mean, they can do whatever they want, and they do. Your son leaves as Jimmy and comes back home in three days as Janet, and they don't even ask you," Trump said . "They can take your child out of school and do whatever the hell they want." Reality check: Trump's claims about schools secretly performing gender-transition procedures misrepresent how such medical care works. Schools cannot perform gender-transition surgeries. Those operations take place in medical settings under relevant state laws. Democrats will "get rid of the border" Trump warned Democrats would dismantle the border and allow criminals from around the world to enter the U.S. He told voters in Kansas that "the Dumocrat agenda is a plan to extinguish Western civilization. They want to open the borders." Trump claimed prisons around the world will empty prisoners into the United States. The other side: A coalition of Democrats have proposed using advanced technology to protect the border, while rejecting mass deportation strategies. Trump: Democrats will take your guns — and wild animals will feast Trump also warned that Democrats will "take away your guns" if they control Congress. "You know who would love that to happen? Some of the wild animals you have up here that like eating you," he told voters in Montana. "... They would gain a lot of weight." Context: Mainstream Democrats have not called for repealing the Second Amendment. While some Democrats support banning certain types of guns, that's different from eliminating the constitutional right to own firearms. Democrats will destroy farms Trump also warned that Democrats would "decimate Kansas farms." On Monday, the Trump administration announced $8 billion in relief for farmers facing soaring fuel costs, driven in part by Trump's own policies and the Iran war. What's going on: Democrats have been making a push in farm country by appealing to rural voters in Kansas and Iowa . House Democrats have also proposed expanding support for rural development and family farms .

events.title: 'Dark fleet' under spotlight in latest US move to ease rising energy costs
events.summary: The US is turning to an unlikely saviour in its latest efforts to ease rising energy prices: the “ dark fleet ” that it has spent years sanctioning. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright revealed the administration's latest endeavour on Monday, telling those at a New York event that Washington wants to “move some of the ships from what I call the 'bad-guy fleet' to the 'good-guy fleet'". The dark fleet, sometimes referred to as the shadow fleet, refers to a group of ships that sail outside conventional shipping regulations. These vessels use deceptive shipping practices to transport cargo that is under sanctions or high risk, deliberately concealing it to avoid detection. Estimates on the size of the fleet vary. Mr Wright said he believes there are about 1,600 vessels. Data from TankerTrackers set the number at 1,480 active ships, while maritime company Windward said it has identified 1,100 dark fleet vessels. The dark fleet has grown in recent years after sanctions were imposed on Russian oil in response to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. Many of these vessels are past the 15-year threshold that marks the point at which technical failures begin to mount, adding to environmental safety risks. Mr Wright said the administration's plan would involve investors buying and refurbishing these idle sanctioned vessels before using them to transport legitimate oil. “They will not carry sanctioned oil any more,” he said. The US has delisted sanctioned vessels before. In March, the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control removed sanctions on the Panama-flagged crude oil supertanker Kiara M, which had been placed as part of the Trump administration's pressure campaign on Venezuela . Through #OpSouthernSpear , the @DeptofWar is unwavering in its mission to crush illicit activity in the Western Hemisphere in partnership with @USCG , @DHSgov and @TheJusticeDept . This morning, U.S. military forces, in support of the Department of Homeland Security, apprehended… pic.twitter.com/UPADtiw681 — U.S. Southern Command (@Southcom) January 20, 2026 Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University's Centre on Global Energy Policy, said the move does little to address the security issue facing seafarers today in the Strait of Hormuz. At least 15 container ships have been struck in the waterway in the past 10 days. “You can repurpose all the ships you want. If you can’t solve the security problem, then you’re not solving the security premium shippers are charging and thereby the consequence to energy markets,” Mr Nephew said. War risk insurance premiums have surged since the start of the conflict. Rates have climbed to as high as 10 per cent of hull value, compared to 0.25 per cent before the conflict, adding millions to the premiums ship and cargo owners pay. Mr Wright's comments also come less than two weeks after US President Donald Trump waived sanctions on Russian diesel in an agreement with President Vladimir Putin. Mr Trump said the agreement would include Moscow supplying millions of barrels of diesel to US and global markets. You can repurpose all the ships you want. If you can’t solve the security problem, then you’re not solving the security premium shippers are charging and thereby the consequence to energy markets Richard Nephew, senior research scholar at Columbia University With only two weeks until the US midterm elections on November 3, diesel prices at the pump have risen to more than $6 a gallon [$1.59 a litre] on average, compared to about $3 the same time last year. Wholesale diesel prices passed $200 a barrel in Singapore in mid-September and hit all-time highs of about $220 a barrel in Europe and the US, the International Energy Agency said in an October 14 report. The seven-day moving average for tanker traffic in the Strait of Hormuz was seven vessels for the week ending September 18, a small fraction of its pre-war levels, according to the International Monetary Fund's PortWatch monitor. Analysts at Kpler estimate only 24 of the about 160 vessels under sanctions from the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions. “If this is about getting ships out of sanctions, fine, no problem, proceed as you wish. If this is about solving the problem with whether we can get enough diesel and other products to market, this is not it," Mr Nephew said.

events.title: Mystery mailings put Congress and election offices on edge
events.summary: Over three dozen congressional lawmakers and election offices in at least 32 states have been targeted with suspicious letters, many containing a white powder. Why it matters: The letters have forced evacuations and disrupted election offices just weeks before the 2026 midterms , raising concerns about political intimidation . Driving the news: Rep. Adam Smith's (D-Wash.) district office received a letter Monday, prompting staff to evacuate. In an emailed statement, Smith's office confirmed it "received a suspicious letter containing a powdery substance, like others sent to Congressional offices across the country." Staff returned to the office Tuesday. What they're saying: "The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices, and Congressional offices," an FBI spokesperson said in an emailed statement. "Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident." Catch up quick: The U.S. Capitol Police, the House and Senate sergeants at arms and other officials sent notices to congressional offices last week warning about letters containing suspicious substances and urging staffers to be vigilant. Over 100 letters were estimated to be circulating around the country, law enforcement sources told ABC News. The USCP referred Axios to the FBI for comment. Here's what we know about the suspicious letters: Who was targeted At least three dozen lawmakers have been targeted with the letters, including both Democrats and Republicans. That includes prominent leaders such as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.). Election offices in at least 32 states were targeted with similarly suspicious letters, according to WIRED . Authorities intercepted many of the letters, including those addressed to election offices in Ohio , Minnesota and Connecticut . But in places like Oklahoma , Arizona and Delaware , the letters arrived and prompted evacuations. What's inside Many letters contained a white powder-like substance. So far, preliminary testing of the powder has found no hazardous materials. Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) also reported receiving suspicious letters but did not disclose their contents. Nebraska officials received a letter that they didn't open and instead turned over to the FBI for further analysis. Flashback: The Capitol Police's notice went out on the 25th anniversary of the anthrax attacks that terrified Capitol Hill in the wake of 9/11. On Oct. 15, 2001, a staffer opened an anthrax-laced letter in then-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle's office, forcing the Hart Senate Office Building to close for months. Anthrax attacks killed five people that year. Where are they coming from Law enforcement has not yet determined where the letters are coming from or if they're part of a coordinated attack. The FBI declined to say if the letters are linked, nor are they confirming "specific instances or letters." However, the bureau told Axios in an emailed statement it is working to identify whoever sent the letters. Worth noting: Some of the letters claimed to come from the Democratic Socialists of America, the left-wing insurgent organization that denies any involvement. Some letters bore a New York City return address that DSA previously used but has not occupied since 2013, a spokesperson said . DSA did not respond to Axios' request for comment. events.title: Exclusive: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio
events.summary: OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup building AI agents to help pharmaceutical companies manage drug development, the ChatGPT maker shared exclusively with Axios. Why it matters: Rival AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic are both pushing into science as they look to expand beyond their core competencies in coding and cybersecurity. State of play: OpenAI will integrate Orchestra's team and technology into Rosalind, its suite of AI models and tools designed for life sciences researchers, the company said. Orchestra's platform allows scientists to delegate tasks like monitoring studies, tracking drug development timelines and identifying potential delays to AI agents. Both companies aim to deploy agents that can connect scientific findings with the decisions and next steps required to advance potential treatments. Financial terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. Between the lines: AI companies don't just want to increase productivity, they want to say they are responsible for, say, curing cancer, solving math, and fundamentally changing every critical industry in the world. Those ambitions have fueled acquisitions from rival AI labs. Anthropic acquired AI biotech startup Coefficient Bio for roughly $400 million in April, according to The Information . Zoom in: OpenAI introduced its specialized GPT-Rosalind model in April to help researchers tackle complex problems in biology, chemistry and drug discovery. OpenAI has also partnered with pharmaceutical giants including Novo Nordisk and Moderna to bring AI into research and development workflows. OpenAI says developing a new medicine typically takes 10 to 15 years, a timeline it hopes AI can shorten. Zoom out Anthropic has been making its own aggressive push into life sciences. In June, Anthropic launched Claude Science , an AI-powered research platform that connects scientific databases, analysis tools and specialized agents. In September, the company announced a new biological research lab and said Claude had helped discover a previously unknown enzyme system with similarities to CRISPR, though some scientists said these finders were overblown, per Bloomberg . The bottom line: The AI race is shifting from building the best models to applying that intelligence across industries. Several AI investors told Axios a key question as AI companies go public is how far they can expand into new markets.

events.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
events.summary: TikTok and eBay were among six online platforms summoned by the French government this week, as authorities sought to contain widespread rioting and looting and prevent the resale of stolen goods. Anne Le Hananff, France’s minister of digital affairs, convened representatives from social media firms on Tuesday for an emergency meeting, after their platforms were blamed for fanning the flames of the worst civil unrest the country has seen in years. The goal of the meeting was to remind platforms that they need to moderate content on their sites, including livestream video, to avoid violent content or anything that could encourage people to break the imposed curfew, according to French TV station BFM . A review by WIRED of TikTok found that the search term “blocus”—meaning blockade in French— showed videos that were potentially altered or AI-generated, including viral images of a protester in a Pink Panther costume. The search term is also being used to promote “Act II” of the protests for October 24. The platform issued an “evolving situation” tag on the search term that said: “This situation is developing rapidly. Information available now may be unverified, incomplete, inaccurate, or subject to change. Take care when viewing this content, and report anything that may violate our Community Guidelines.” A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin. Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities. French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots. The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. events.title: Microsoft opens a hands-on STEM and AI hub for students at its Grange Castle data center campus
events.summary: Microsoft opens €1m Dream Space hub at its data centre campus in Grange Castle to bring STEM and AI skills to young people in surrounding communities Microsoft Vice Chair and President, Brad Smith, today joined students, teachers and community representatives from Dublin and Kildare at the company’s data centre campus in Grange Castle to officially open its new €1m Dream Space hub. Dream Space @ the Data Centre marks the next step in Microsoft’s mission to create lasting benefits for people living near its current and proposed data centre operations. More than 5,000 students from schools in Dublin and Kildare are expected to participate in learning sessions at the hub over the next 12 months. Providing a wide range of tailored STEM and AI experiences for primary and post-primary students, Dream Space @ the Data Centre will also help to build awareness of the wide-ranging career opportunities that exist in the digital infrastructure sector. Through the new hub, Microsoft is delivering on its Data Centre Community Pledge to be a responsible and supportive neighbour to communities that host its data centres. Since 2018, Microsoft has invested over €6.5 million in Irish communities close to its current and future data centre operations, supporting programmes that advance community prosperity, sustainability and wellbeing and directly benefiting more than 135,000 people. Dream Space was first introduced at Microsoft’s Leopardstown campus, One Microsoft Place, in 2018. Since then, more than 550,000 students have taken part in its STEM and AI education sessions, developing the skills and confidence to become the next generation of digital leaders. Building on Dream Space’s strong foundations in coding, robotics and AI, the new hub at the data centre features a new curriculum that introduces learners to the specific technology and skills needed to support the digital infrastructure sector. These will range from electrical engineering and physical computing to cloud operations. Supported by a mini data centre lab and many other hands-on learning experiences, the facility will bring to life the technology, skills and careers powering the digital world for learners. Microsoft has invested €1m in the development of the new hub. This comes from a €4m investment fund that was set aside by the company in March last year to help ‘Skill Up Ireland’ for the era of AI. An integrated approach to STEM skills development across Dream Space @ the Data Centre and Microsoft Ireland’s other skilling and education initiatives, such as the Collinstown Data Centre Academy, will help to build awareness of pathways into further education, apprenticeships and careers in the data centre and broader technology sector. Brad Smith, Vice Chair and President, Microsoft, said: “We have been part of Ireland for more than 40 years and see it as Microsoft’s home in Europe. As our presence continues to grow, so too has our commitment to creating lasting benefits for the Irish people. Since 2018, we’ve invested over €6.5 million in local data centre communities, benefitting more than 135,000 people. Microsoft ‘s Dream Space is the next step in that journey, giving thousands of young people the chance to experience and understand the technology behind the digital services they use every day, and envision a future career for themselves in Ireland’s digital economy.” Lavinia Morris, General Manager, Microsoft’s EMEA Data Centre Operations said: “Today is an exciting milestone for Microsoft as we officially open Dream Space @ the Data Centre. This new hub builds on Dream Space’s strong foundations in STEM, AI and digital skilling, while bringing students closer to the real-world skills, careers and opportunities shaping Ireland’s growing digital infrastructure sector. “Over the next year, more than 5,000 students and teachers from communities near our data centre will enjoy the hub. Through hands-on experiences in areas such as physical computing, electrical engineering and cloud operations, learners will gain practical skills and direct exposure to the technologies that power the digital world. The new hub will deepen our connection to the local community, helping young people develop vital STEM skills for the future and gain a better understanding of the exciting possibilities that exist in the sector.” To learn more, visit the Microsoft Dream Space website: https://DreamSpace.ie
